She expressly distinguishes the $12 processing charge and does not ask the agent to approve the benefit. The customer disclaims the helper’s forwarded statement. The automated keyword suggestion is expressly non-authoritative.

The packet closes without a later settlement confirmation, a later occupancy-document submission, a final benefit decision, or a completed benefit disbursement. Any conclusion about those later events would require evidence not included here. The records do, however, support the stated distinctions among the customer’s inquiry, the permit deposit, the original payment, the conditional release, and the pending benefit application.

2. Refund requests
A refund request is a written message that explicitly asks Tidewater Rentals to return money already paid. A complaint about a price, a question about the refund policy, or a request to move a payment to another date is not by itself a refund request. Staff should record the exact words used. The spring market organizer emailed, “Please return the $120 deposit to the card I used. We have decided not to use the extra tables.” This is a refund request. The request does not mean it has been approved; a manager makes that decision separately. The normal deposit is $120, and the amount is printed on the event order.

The standard hall package includes 20 folding tables, 80 chairs, two coat racks and one registration desk. Extra tables can be rented for $8 each. Extra chairs cost $2 each. The chairs were counted before the doors opened; the count was 80. Nothing in this paragraph changes the stated equipment order.

4. Food and service
Food vendors must submit a menu before the event. The market order lists Quill Foods as the coffee and pastry vendor. The vendor’s menu lists drip coffee, tea, oat biscuits and apple rolls. It does not list a hot lunch. Tidewater staff do not prepare or sell food. A vendor question about lunch is not an order for Tidewater to provide lunch. The event organizer may put menus on the welcome table. Food must remain in the marked serving area, and hot drinks must be served in cups with lids. The kitchen door is for vendor staff only.

The main entrance has a ramp. A clear route of at least one metre must be kept between the entrance and the information desk. The marked accessible seating area is beside the north wall. In the spring market floor plan, the information desk is beside the main entrance and the route is marked with blue tape. Vendors may adjust the position of their own display within their assigned space, but they may not block the marked route. The hall team checked the route at 9:30 a.m. and found it clear. This is a plain record of the layout, not a promise about any other venue.

The booking total is $640. The event order shows a $120 deposit paid by card and a remaining balance of $520. The client paid the balance by bank transfer on 3 April. The payment ledger marks the full amount as received. The market’s separate stall fees are collected by the organizer, not by Tidewater Rentals. The event contact’s phone number is on the confidential staff copy and should not be copied onto public signs. If a contact name is missing from a form, staff should ask the office rather than guessing. The market order has both a contact name and an email address, so no follow-up for missing contact details is needed.

A time change is recorded only when both the client and the venue office confirm it in writing. A request to start earlier does not change the schedule by itself. The spring market confirmation lists setup at 8:00 a.m. and public admission at 10:00 a.m. The office log contains no approved change to either time. Property found in the hall is logged with its date and location. The log entry for the spring market lists one blue scarf found beside the north wall and delivered to the front desk. It does not list a wallet, phone or set of keys. The organizer may ask the office whether an item has been handed in, but the office will not share another visitor’s contact information. Staff record observable facts and do not speculate about causes. At 11:15 a.m., the front desk received a report that a visitor had dropped a paper bag near the entrance. The office keeps the signed order, payment ledger, delivery check and event closeout sheet together. The client may request a copy of their own order and receipt. Staff must not send the internal shift notes to a vendor. The document list for the spring market shows all four standard records in the folder. The delivery check is dated on the event day. Before closing a booking file, staff confirm the contact, payment, equipment return and access notes. The market file review has four check marks beside those items. The file remains open only for routine retention; the booking itself is completed. No approval for a future market date appears in this file. Any new booking requires a new event order. SECTION B — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM
Incident: guild roster display delay
Service: Northstar Realms community website
Date: 12 May
Window: 19:10 to 19:42 local server time
Severity: low
Status: resolved
Owner: community web operations

Summary: roster pages took longer than usual to refresh after guild leaders changed member ranks. The game world remained available. Player inventories, payments, match results, and login sessions were not affected. The delay was limited to the community website’s roster display cache. It did not delete roster entries. The display caught up after the cache worker was restarted.

Timeline:
19:10 — first report in the web-ops room: a leader changed a rank and the public roster still showed the old rank.
19:13 — on-call checked the game server. It was healthy and accepting players.
19:16 — web dashboard showed the roster cache queue growing.
19:21 — a second leader reported the same display lag. No report described a payment problem.
19:25 — operations paused the cache refresh worker to stop duplicate jobs.
19:31 — worker restarted with a cleared queue.
19:37 — roster pages began showing current ranks.
19:42 — two test guilds confirmed updates appeared. Incident marked resolved.

Cause: a routine website deployment changed the cache refresh interval. The new interval was too short for the size of the evening roster update batch. Jobs accumulated, and the website kept displaying its last completed roster snapshot. The game service continued to provide current membership data. The web display was stale; the underlying memberships were not changed incorrectly.

Impact: guild leaders had to wait to see their changes on the public website. No player was charged, no order was placed, no refund was requested, and no account was locked. Matchmaking continued normally. Voice chat continued normally. The tournament bracket page used a separate service and was current throughout the incident.

Post-event closeout report, October 2

Purpose

This report consolidates the planning record for the Tidewater Labs product launch reception. It is intended to make the confirmed details easy to find and to prevent obsolete drafts from being mistaken for final decisions. It does not revise the signed venue booking or vendor order. It records the event as planned and completed, and identifies open issues that arose during planning.

Event summary

The event was a Tidewater Labs product launch reception held on September 28 at Lantern Hall. The booked room was the main gallery. The room booking ran from 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. The guest estimate used throughout planning was eighty. A short product introduction took place, followed by dinner and informal demonstrations. Northwind Studio supplied the presentation materials and demonstration equipment. The venue supplied a screen and two standing signs.

Vendor summary

Granite Rentals’ active order contained thirty-six banquet chairs, six round tables, two buffet tables, and one lectern. Delivery took place on September 28 during the 10:00 to 11:00 a.m. window. Pickup took place on September 29 at 10:00 a.m. The requested quote for twelve additional chairs was never approved. The extra chairs were not reserved, delivered, or charged. No second lectern was ordered. No rental order was placed for the garden room.

Venue summary

Lantern Hall confirmed the main gallery, not the garden room. The booking was for September 28. An old draft had incorrectly shown September 29, but the signed confirmation superseded that draft. The venue accepted the rental delivery at the loading entrance during the agreed window. The floor plan was reviewed and the display position was approved on the event day. That approval did not change the room booking or vendor order.

Planning issues

The principal planning issue was the mismatch between the eighty-person guest estimate and the thirty-six chairs on the active order. The event team discussed a possible addition of twelve chairs. Granite Rentals sent a quote, but Uma did not approve it. The team therefore proceeded with thirty-six ordered chairs. Several drafts used language such as “planned seating,” “possible additional chairs,” or “target count.” Those phrases did not represent a completed order. The final report must not present the quote as a purchase.

A second issue involved outdated date and room details in preliminary materials. Some early notes referred to September 29 as the event date or described a garden-room option. The signed venue confirmation and repeated later messages established September 28 in the main gallery. September 29 was the rental pickup date. The garden room was not booked.

A third issue was the difference between proposed and confirmed planning details. The draft menu, proposed layouts, tentative run of show, and marketing language were all subject to review. They should not be described as confirmed simply because they appeared in a working file. The final event used the approved main-gallery space and the listed rental equipment.

Communications record

Uma repeatedly asked the team to preserve the distinction between a confirmed order and an unapproved quote. She did not authorize the additional chairs. She also repeatedly corrected the event date and room when an obsolete draft circulated. Her tone in several messages was angry and direct because she felt that the same facts were being overlooked. The tone does not change the underlying record: thirty-six chairs were on the active order; twelve additional chairs were only quoted.

Aiden Mensah consistently stated that Granite Rentals would not change the order without written approval. He confirmed the active quantities and delivery details. Farid Castillo confirmed the venue booking and clarified that the main gallery was included while the garden room was not. Esi Moreau maintained the working layout and presentation setup without representing the additional chairs as ordered.

Closeout checklist

Event date recorded: September 28.
Venue recorded: Lantern Hall, main gallery.
Room booking recorded: 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
Guest estimate recorded: eighty.
Confirmed chair quantity recorded: thirty-six.
Additional-chair quote recorded: unapproved; not ordered.
Confirmed round-table quantity recorded: six.
Confirmed buffet-table quantity recorded: two.
Confirmed lectern quantity recorded: one.
Rental delivery recorded: September 28, 10:00 to 11:00 a.m.
Rental pickup recorded: September 29, 10:00 a.m.
Garden room recorded: not included.

Lessons for future events

The team should maintain a single current summary, clearly label drafts, and avoid copying proposed quantities into a confirmed-order field. Any purchase change must be supported by explicit written approval. Venue bookings and vendor schedules should be checked against signed confirmations before public materials are sent. Guest estimates should be compared with confirmed seating early enough to allow a decision. When the customer has not approved a quote, the event file should state that the quote is pending and that the active order remains unchanged.

Final statement

The event took place on September 28 in Lantern Hall’s main gallery. The active Granite Rentals order was for thirty-six chairs, six round tables, two buffet tables, and one lectern. The request for twelve additional chairs was not approved, so the additional chairs were not part of the order. The event team should use this statement as the definitive closeout summary and should not rely on preliminary drafts that were superseded during planning.

Administrative record compiled by the Service Coordination Office. The file contains the initial voicemail, subsequent email correspondence, invoice extracts, and routing notes. VOICEMAIL TRANSCRIPT, 6 May, 09:14

Technician: Oren Nakamura. Site contact: Yara Alvarez. Work order: TS-4418-1.
Reported condition: north loading-bay door stops during upward travel; latch drag reported intermittently.

Technician cleared fragments, realigned guide tab, adjusted travel stop, and ran six cycles. Five cycles completed; one cycle stopped at approximately two feet. Technician recorded “monitor; possible sensor intermittency.” Site contact signed the completion screen with the annotation “still did it once.”

Parts issued: one guide tab, one fastener set, no sensor replacement. Labor billed: 1.25 hours. Travel billed: 0.50 hours. Dispatch log shows arrival at 14:06 and departure at 15:22. To: Bluefin Logistics Service Desk
Subject: North bay door follow-up / TS-4418

Technician: Bao O'Neill. Site contact: Yara Alvarez. Work order: TS-4418-2.

INVOICE EXTRACT, issued 9 May

Invoice: BL-90317

Calculation note: $222.90 + $97.50 = $320.40; $320.40 − $100.00 = $220.40. The invoice does not show a credit, refund, or payment reversal. The service desk has not received a separate refund request as of the invoice date. The customer may still dispute charges through the procedure printed on the reverse, but a printed procedure is not itself a request.

INTERNAL ROUTING NOTES
6 May: Case routed from general repairs to field callback queue. Priority normal. No safety emergency declared. Caller reports equipment still intermittently malfunctioning. Do not close solely because the initial visit was completed.
7 May: Accounts clerk asked whether customer requested refund due to reference to invoice in subject. Service desk replied that the customer expressly denied requesting refund and requested callback coverage information. Refund flag remains unset.
8 May: Dispatch completed. Do not treat sarcastic comments in correspondence as praise. Record the intended complaint: unreliable door and dissatisfaction with prior adjustment. Do not infer a refund request from dissatisfaction alone.

SERVICE TERMS EXCERPT ATTACHED TO CASE
A return diagnostic within ten calendar days may be routed to the original work order when the same symptom is reported. This routing does not decide whether the initial fee is refundable. Refunds require an explicit request and accounts review. A request for repair, a request for a callback, or a statement that service was unsatisfactory does not automatically constitute a refund request. An expression of satisfaction or dissatisfaction may be literal or sarcastic; staff are instructed to use surrounding language and explicit requested remedy. No refund request is recorded in this file.

ARCHIVE AND HANDOFF APPENDIX
The intake system stores a short summary, a longer customer narrative, an equipment identifier, a location code, and a billing status. A summary may be entered by a clerk before the full narrative has been checked. For this reason, the narrative and original audio transcript remain the controlling customer statement for this review. The status field “awaiting customer” was applied briefly on 6 May because the proposed appointment had not yet been confirmed; it did not mean that the customer had withdrawn the callback request or made a financial demand. The appointment was confirmed on 8 May.

The work order records a single piece of equipment: north loading-bay door, asset TD-NB-04. The file does not concern the south service entrance, the office vestibule, the studio’s freight lift, or the side gate. The terms “bay,” “door,” and “sensor” appear in other maintenance tickets in the shared service database, but those tickets are not incorporated into this case. Staff are not authorized to use another customer’s record to fill gaps here. The customer’s statement about using the side entrance referred to access for the technician while the north bay was being serviced. It did not authorize dispatch during the stated delivery block and did not describe a second fault.

The schedule attached to the file lists a recurring delivery booking from 11:00 to 13:00 on weekdays. The customer asked for an arrival before that period or after it. Dispatch offered a window beginning at 13:30, and the customer accepted. No fee for a missed appointment appears on the invoice. The first visit’s time entries are not evidence that the customer requested reimbursement; they are the technician’s recorded labor and travel. Likewise, the second visit’s zero travel charge is not a credit against the first visit. Both work orders remain visible on one invoice because the billing system groups activity by account.

The case supervisor reviewed the recorded phrases “delightful,” “charming,” “wonderful,” and “pleased.” In context, these are sarcastic expressions accompanying reports that the door remains unreliable and the repair did not resolve the symptom. They are not literal compliments and they do not change the requested remedy. The explicit statements in the voicemail and follow-up email distinguish the customer’s present request from possible future action: she asks for a callback now and says she will review the account if another visit fails. The conditional future review is not a present refund demand. The record should not be coded as a refund request merely because the customer is dissatisfied or because the invoice is attached.

For completeness, the technician’s second-visit checklist contains twelve cycle entries. The first two entries were marked “sensor signal fluctuated,” and the remaining ten were marked “cycle completed.” The checklist is not a guarantee of future performance and does not show that a replacement sensor was fitted. The customer’s “looked better; we will monitor” comment is compatible with a temporary improvement, not a withdrawal of the original complaint. The seven-day monitoring suggestion is an instruction from the technician, not an agreement by the customer to waive billing rights.

No cancellation request is recorded. No claim for consequential loss is recorded. No request for a replacement door is recorded. The customer has not stated that the loading bay is permanently closed or that the equipment has been removed from service. These absent requests should not be added to the case merely because standard forms include boxes for cancellation, replacement, or loss claims. If a later request arrives, it is to be logged with its receipt date and evaluated separately.

The invoice’s balance figure is carried forward as shown. The case file contains no proof of payment after issue, no receipt, and no accounts decision. The balance due cannot be interpreted as an amount owed back to the customer. The deposit line is an applied amount, not a refund. The service desk’s note that a billing review is available is procedural information and is not evidence that Yara initiated such a review. The invoice was attached because the service desk wanted the customer to identify the relevant work orders if she later contacted accounts.

At the time of compilation, the callback was completed and the equipment was in monitoring status. The disposition code is “repair follow-up completed; monitor.” It is not “refund requested,” “refund approved,” or “customer satisfied.” The coordinator may update the repair status if new evidence arrives, but the present classification must reflect only the statements already contained in this file. This appendix is retained to prevent clerical inferences from replacing the customer’s expressed request.

FINAL REVIEW CHECKLIST
Source material reviewed: voicemail transcript, technician record, email thread, invoice extract, service terms, routing notes. No separate account message requesting a refund is present. The customer’s sarcastic praise is directed at the limited performance of the door and the earlier adjustment. Her direct wording states that she is not requesting the first visit charge back and asks for a callback and a reliable repair. File status: callback completed; monitor equipment; no refund request recorded.

END OF CASE FILE TS-4418

Records Division compilation, version 3.2. The file concerns a chilled-water pump and its controller at Meridian Analytics’ west annex. It includes a customer voicemail, an email thread with quoted replies, an invoice with line items, dispatch logs, inspection notes, and appendices. Entries are reproduced for administrative review. Sarcastic wording is retained as spoken or written; it should be interpreted in context rather than treated as a literal assessment.

VOICEMAIL TRANSCRIPT, 14 September, 08:32
Caller: Uma Tanaka, site operations officer, Meridian Analytics.

“This is Uma calling about pump C-17. The pump alarm came back overnight after the repair visit. The circulation reading dropped below our site’s normal range for about twenty minutes, then recovered after the operator restarted the controller. What a magnificent repair: it lasted almost until the night shift noticed it. I am not complimenting the work. Please arrange a diagnostic visit and check the controller relay as well as the pump. I am not requesting a refund on this call. I need the fault investigated first. If the same failure happens again after the next visit, I may ask procurement to review the invoice, but that is a possibility, not an instruction to issue money now. Call my desk before dispatch. The west annex loading entrance is not staffed before eight.”

Transcription note: The clerk retained the phrase “magnificent repair” and the caller’s immediate clarification. The voicemail system displayed a generic “billing concern” prompt after the caller mentioned an invoice. That prompt was generated automatically and is not a customer request. No refund request was entered from the call.

SERVICE VISIT, 13 September
Technician: Xiu Nakamura. Work order MA-7726-1. Site contact: Uma Tanaka.
Reported issue: pump C-17 intermittently fails to maintain circulation. Technician observed a loose controller terminal and an alarm history entry. Terminal was secured, controller reset, and pump run for twenty-five minutes. Reading stable during the test. Technician noted that a short test did not establish whether the relay was intermittently failing. No pump replacement was performed. No relay was replaced. Site contact stated that the alarm had occurred twice during the previous week.

The completion form offered a standard satisfaction question. The response was entered as “very satisfied” because the customer selected that box while attempting to advance the tablet screen; a later handwritten annotation says “not satisfied—the alarm was not reproduced during the visit.” The entry is retained as a data-quality issue and does not override the written annotation. The technician did not mark the issue resolved. The service status is “intermittent fault; monitor and diagnose if repeated.”

EMAIL THREAD, 14–16 September
From: Uma Tanaka, Meridian Analytics
To: Foxglove Logistics Field Service
Subject: C-17 follow-up and invoice reference

“Please arrange a diagnostic visit. The pump alarm returned after the visit, and the controller should be checked. I’m delighted that the repair survived one night; we will have to introduce it to a clock next time. That is a complaint, not praise. I am not asking for a refund now. Please confirm whether the next diagnostic can be handled as a callback and whether the technician can arrive after eight.”

From: Foxglove Logistics Field Service, 14 September, 10:10
To: Uma Tanaka

“We have opened work order MA-7726-2 for a return diagnostic. The original visit is still billed as shown on invoice FX-11804. The callback classification does not determine whether charges are refundable. We have noted the access request. Please provide the alarm time if it is available.”

From: Uma Tanaka, 14 September, 10:36
To: Foxglove Logistics Field Service

“The alarm log shows 02:14. The pump alarm is the issue; a separate filter warning at 01:48 cleared without intervention. Please do not combine those events. The service is certainly world-class at producing forms, but the pump still needs diagnosis. Again, I am requesting a visit, not a credit.”

From: Foxglove Logistics Field Service, 14 September, 13:55
To: Uma Tanaka

“Thank you. The field technician will review the C-17 alarm log and controller relay. A separate filter warning is outside this work order unless inspection shows a direct relation. The site’s requested arrival time is recorded as after 08:00; the system does not promise an exact arrival time until dispatch confirmation.”

From: Uma Tanaka, 15 September, 09:04
To: Foxglove Logistics Field Service

“Confirmed. Please send the technician to the west annex loading entrance after eight. I have not requested that the previous invoice be reversed. If the diagnostic identifies an incorrect charge, I may submit a billing review later. That is not the same thing as asking for a refund today.”

From: Foxglove Logistics Field Service, 15 September, 09:27
To: Uma Tanaka

“Access instructions received. A billing review is available through Accounts. Your current case remains classified as a repeat-fault diagnostic. Please do not use the equipment’s emergency stop except under the site safety procedure.”

From: Uma Tanaka, 16 September, 16:42
To: Foxglove Logistics Field Service

“The technician attended and the relay test was useful. The pump ran through the test period, but the alarm log still needs to be monitored. It is a stunning success if ‘success’ means we have obtained one more page of readings. I appreciate the records; I do not consider the fault conclusively resolved. Please keep the case open for the monitoring period.”

CALLBACK VISIT RECORD, 16 September
Technician: Bao Alvarez. Work order MA-7726-2. Arrival 08:26; departure 09:48. Access granted at west annex loading entrance by Uma Tanaka. Technician reviewed the 02:14 alarm, checked relay contacts, measured controller output, inspected pump coupling, and ran the pump for forty minutes. No relay failure reproduced. One relay connection was tightened as preventative maintenance. No replacement parts installed. Technician recommended monitoring the alarm history for five operating days and reporting another occurrence. Site contact signed the work summary with the note “diagnostic completed; intermittent fault not proven resolved.”

The technician also observed a filter warning at 01:48 in the historic log. The warning cleared without intervention and was not the alarm reported at 02:14. No filter change was authorized, performed, or billed. The adjacent pump C-16 is on a separate control circuit and was not inspected. These distinctions are maintained because the word “alarm” appears in several entries in the building log.

INVOICE FX-11804, issued 17 September
Bill to: Meridian Analytics, west annex.
Reference: MA-7726-1 and MA-7726-2.

Line 1: Initial inspection, technician labor 1.50 hours at $128.00 per hour = $192.00.
Line 2: Travel, initial visit, 0.75 hours at $48.00 per hour = $36.00.
Line 3: Terminal fastener set, one unit = $14.50.
Line 4: Callback diagnostic labor, 1.00 hour at $128.00 per hour = $128.00.
Line 5: Callback travel charge = $0.00.
Line 6: Replacement relay, quantity zero, unit price $86.00, extended amount $0.00.
Line 7: Filter cartridge, quantity zero, unit price $42.00, extended amount $0.00.

Subtotal: $370.50. Tax: $29.64. Total: $400.14. Prior account credit applied: $75.00. Amount due: $325.14.

Calculation note: $192.00 + $36.00 + $14.50 + $128.00 = $370.50. Tax of $29.64 yields $400.14; subtracting the $75.00 prior account credit leaves $325.14. The prior credit predates this repair file and is not a refund for either visit. The zero-quantity relay and filter lines are price references only and do not indicate installation or customer complaint.

ACCOUNTS ROUTING NOTE, 17 September
The invoice was attached to the work-order email because the customer asked which visit the callback covered. No customer message requesting reimbursement, credit, or reversal is attached. A generic document footer reads “Questions about charges? Request an account review.” This is standard wording. The accounts queue did not receive a review request as of 17 September. The billing amount due is not an amount owed to the customer.

TECHNICAL LOG EXTRACT
13 September, 11:06: pump C-17 start; stable output during observation.
13 September, 11:22: controller reset; no alarm present.
14 September, 01:48: filter warning; cleared automatically at 01:50.
14 September, 02:14: pump alarm recorded; operator restart at 02:34; circulation recovered.
16 September, 08:41: relay test begins; no failure reproduced.
16 September, 09:19: controller output stable; technician observes normal operation.
16 September, 09:42: test ends; monitoring recommended.

The time difference between the 02:14 alarm and the 02:34 restart is twenty minutes. The service file does not treat that interval as proof that the pump remained fully stopped throughout; the operator reported a low circulation reading and then restarted the controller. The current question is the customer’s expressed complaint, not a diagnosis of the hydraulic system. The site’s normal operating range is not numerically specified in the customer’s voicemail, and no threshold calculation is required for the classification.

CASE REVIEW GUIDANCE
The customer’s request is defined by the action she asks the service provider to take in the statement. A request to investigate, attend, test, or keep a case open is a service request. A request to return money, reverse a charge, or apply a credit is a financial request. Mentioning an invoice, asking whether callback labor is covered, or saying a billing review may be submitted later does not by itself constitute a current refund request. Conditional language must remain conditional. A customer can be dissatisfied with a visit without requesting a refund.

The phrases “magnificent repair,” “delighted,” “world-class,” and “stunning success” appear positive if read without context. The customer immediately identifies the first as a complaint, says she is not praising the service, repeats that she wants diagnosis rather than a credit, and later states that the apparent success consists of obtaining readings while the fault remains unresolved. The intended meaning is sarcastic dissatisfaction. The accidental satisfaction checkbox is separately contradicted by a handwritten note and later correspondence. It cannot be used as evidence that the customer considered the first repair successful or that she withdrew the fault report.

The customer’s stated issue is the pump alarm and intermittent circulation problem on pump C-17. She also asks that the controller relay be checked. The filter warning is explicitly distinguished as a separate event that cleared automatically. The technician’s inspection of the relay does not establish a confirmed relay failure; no replacement relay was installed. The customer reported that the diagnostic was useful, but “useful” is not equivalent to “resolved.” She asks for the case to remain open during monitoring. The file does not establish a separate complaint about the filter cartridge, a broken coupling, or pump C-16.

Neither the generic billing prompt nor the accounts footer should be mistaken for customer intent. Both are system-generated. The caller’s mention of a possible procurement review is explicitly future and conditional: if the same failure happens again after the next visit, she may ask procurement to review the invoice. She later states that she is not asking for a refund now and has not asked for the previous invoice to be reversed. The current remedy requested is diagnostic follow-up and continued monitoring.

The compilation includes an invoice because it is part of the record, not because the invoice itself is a customer statement. Line descriptions show labor, travel, and fasteners, with zero quantities for relay and filter. The $75.00 account credit is historical. It was applied before this invoice and does not represent money returned in response to the current complaint. The amount due is positive and payable by the customer according to the invoice. No conclusion about whether the charges are contractually proper is made here.

DISPATCH AND SAFETY APPENDIX
The west annex loading entrance is staffed after 08:00. The customer’s access instruction applied to the technician’s arrival. The service desk recorded the request and the technician arrived at 08:26. The instruction did not change the repair scope or authorize work on the adjacent pump. Site safety rules require a qualified operator to manage the emergency stop and control-room access. The customer did not ask the technician to bypass safety controls, and no such action is recorded.

A separate facilities calendar lists a planned inspection of the chilled-water system on 19 September. That appointment is not a callback visit and does not concern the customer’s earlier statement. It is included in the annex because it appeared in the dispatch search results. No technician from the 19 September inspection has reported findings in this case. The calendar entry cannot be treated as evidence that the C-17 fault was resolved or that the customer withdrew the open-case request.

The case number MA-7726 appears on both work orders and the invoice reference. A different case number, MA-7728, concerns a valve leak at the east annex. The wording “pump,” “alarm,” and “controller” also occurs in MA-7728’s automatically generated parts list. That record is excluded. The present file contains no evidence that the east-annex valve leak belongs to Uma Tanaka’s complaint. Shared vocabulary in a search result is not a basis for adding another service issue.

DOCUMENT CONTROL AND FINAL DISPOSITION
At compilation, the service status is “monitoring requested; intermittent fault not conclusively resolved.” The diagnostic visit has been completed. The monitoring period is five operating days, after which the customer may report further alarms. The case is not closed as a confirmed repair, and the customer has not asked to cancel the service contract. No replacement pump or relay has been ordered. No account refund or credit decision is pending because no refund request is recorded.

The service coordinator must preserve the distinction between the initial repair and the return diagnostic. The initial visit included inspection, terminal work, and a short test. The second visit tested the relay and included a longer run. The fact that the second test did not reproduce a failure does not disprove the earlier alarm report. The fact that the customer said the test was useful does not mean she accepted the case as resolved. Her sarcastic description of the records as a success conveys that paperwork and readings do not substitute for a confirmed repair.

For reporting purposes, the primary reported problem is “intermittent pump alarm / low circulation on C-17.” The controller relay is a requested inspection point, not a confirmed failed part. The filter warning is a separate near-miss event and was not the subject of the requested repair. Billing status is “invoice issued; balance due,” not “refund sought.” Customer remedy status is “callback diagnostic and monitoring requested.” The archive contains no contrary customer statement after the 16 September message.

END OF FILE MA-7726

questions.instruction: Did Uma ask the provider to refund or reverse any charge? Treat a current refund request as an explicit request for money or a credit, not a complaint about quality, an invoice reference, or a possible future billing review. Positive-sounding comments may be sarcastic, so determine what she intended from the surrounding statements and the remedy she actually requested.
questions.notes: She repeatedly says she is not requesting a refund now; future invoice review is conditional, and praise is sarcastic.

questions.instruction: Which service problems did Uma report or ask to have investigated? Select every supported problem, but do not convert a sarcastic compliment into praise or treat a separate event she expressly distinguishes as part of the complaint. A requested inspection point may be included when she specifically asks the provider to check it; include no issue based only on an invoice line or another case.

She asked the technician to check the controller relay; this is an inspection concern, not proof that a relay failed.
A filter warning is logged, but the customer says it was separate and cleared without intervention.
A failure of the adjacent pump C-16.

questions.notes: She reports the C-17 alarm/low circulation and requests a relay check; she separates the cleared filter warning and C-16 was not her issue.

NORTHWIND ANALYTICS — SERVICE TERMS EXTRACT AND ACCOUNT FILE
Prepared for contract administration; compiled in plain English by a staff member who is not a native English writer. This file contains the operative terms, a customer invoice, and routine account notes. The names and entities in this file belong only to this file. In the correspondence below, the customer is Harbor Labs and the provider is Northwind Analytics. References to “provider” mean Northwind Analytics; references to “customer” mean Harbor Labs. A statement that one party may do something is not a statement that the other party did it.

PART I — TERMS OF SERVICE

1. Parties and service. These terms govern the hosted analytics service supplied by Northwind Analytics to Harbor Labs. Northwind Analytics is the service provider. Harbor Labs is the customer. The parties agree that the labels “provider” and “customer” remain attached to those roles even when their names appear in a forwarded note, a billing record, a comment, or a sample clause. A vendor mentioned as a third party is not thereby a party to this agreement. This extract is for contract administration and does not replace the signed order form.

The service gives Harbor Labs access to a hosted workspace for importing, organizing, and viewing its own business data. Northwind Analytics operates the workspace and maintains the software. Harbor Labs chooses the data it uploads and the users it authorizes. Neither party is described as the other party’s agent merely because one party performs a task for the service. A support employee may help explain a setting without becoming the customer’s decision-maker.

2. Term and renewal. The initial subscription period begins on the effective date on the order form and lasts for twelve months. It renews for successive twelve-month periods unless either party gives the other party written notice of nonrenewal at least forty-five calendar days before the current period ends. A notice from Northwind Analytics is a provider notice; a notice from Harbor Labs is a customer notice. A note saying that a party “could send” a notice is not a record that it sent one. The account file below records the current term dates separately.

3. Fees and invoices. Harbor Labs must pay undisputed invoices within thirty calendar days after the invoice date. Northwind Analytics issues invoices and receives payment. A debit against Harbor Labs’ account is not a payment from Northwind Analytics to Harbor Labs. If Harbor Labs disputes an item, it must give Northwind Analytics a written explanation identifying the disputed amount; Harbor Labs still pays the undisputed balance on time. The parties may later agree on a credit or correction. A credit is not presumed from a dispute alone.

4. Taxes and expenses. Fees do not include taxes imposed on Harbor Labs, except taxes imposed on Northwind Analytics’ net income. Harbor Labs is responsible for applicable transaction taxes. The provider does not promise that an invoice will be tax-free. Any listed pass-through expense must be supported by a receipt and approved by Harbor Labs before it is incurred. If no approved expense is shown, a party should not infer that the other party owes one.

5. Support. Northwind Analytics provides support during the hours stated in the order form. Harbor Labs may open support tickets. The party opening a ticket is the requester, and the party receiving it is the recipient. A support ticket may describe a problem without making a demand for money. A request to repair a configuration is not a refund request. A request for a refund means an explicit request that the other party return money already paid or waive a payment as money back; merely asking for an explanation or a service adjustment does not qualify.

6. Customer data. Harbor Labs retains its rights in customer data. Harbor Labs instructs Northwind Analytics to host and process that data only to provide the service and perform the documented support work. Northwind Analytics may maintain technical records needed to operate the service. Nothing in this paragraph transfers ownership of Harbor Labs’ data to Northwind Analytics. Likewise, the provider’s ownership of its software does not make Harbor Labs the owner of the provider’s software.

7. Confidentiality. Each party receiving confidential information from the other must protect it using reasonable care and use it only for the agreement. The disclosing party is the party that provides the information; the receiving party is the party that obtains it. A record that Harbor Labs sent a confidential file to Northwind Analytics identifies Harbor Labs as discloser and Northwind Analytics as recipient, not the reverse. Routine system access is not permission to publish confidential material.

8. Service availability. The service target is 99.5 percent monthly availability, subject to scheduled maintenance and events outside the provider’s reasonable control. Northwind Analytics measures the service. Harbor Labs may report an outage, but a report does not itself establish that an outage occurred or that a credit is due. A service credit, if earned under the order form, is applied to future fees and is not a cash refund. The parties must distinguish a cash payment from a future invoice adjustment.

9. Termination for breach. Either party may give written notice describing a material breach by the other party and allow thirty days to cure. The party alleging breach sends the notice; the party accused of breach receives it. If the breach remains uncured, the non-breaching party may terminate. This provision does not mean that every party that sends an ordinary operational email is alleging breach. A contract administrator should identify the sender and the recipient before attributing a demand.

10. Termination for convenience. Harbor Labs may terminate for convenience at the end of a subscription period by giving timely nonrenewal notice. Northwind Analytics has no matching convenience-termination right during the initial period, except as expressly stated elsewhere. An internal note that the provider would prefer to discontinue an account does not itself terminate the agreement. The party whose action is authorized by this clause is Harbor Labs.

11. Refunds and credits. Fees paid for a completed subscription period are not refundable except where the order form expressly says otherwise or applicable law requires. If Northwind Analytics agrees in writing to return a specified amount, Northwind Analytics pays the refund to Harbor Labs. If Harbor Labs asks for money back, Harbor Labs is the requester and Northwind Analytics is the party asked to pay. A statement by Northwind Analytics that it is “reviewing a possible refund” is not an explicit customer request. A statement by Harbor Labs asking the provider to investigate a charge, without asking that money be returned, is not an explicit refund request under the definition in section 5.

12. Notices. Formal notices must be sent by an authorized representative to the notice address on the order form. For notices to Northwind Analytics, Harbor Labs is the sender and Northwind Analytics is the recipient. For notices to Harbor Labs, Northwind Analytics is the sender and Harbor Labs is the recipient. An email copied to a party is not necessarily a notice from that party. An attachment prepared by one party but forwarded by the other must be attributed to its actual author and sender as the context indicates.

13. Liability. Each party remains responsible for its own acts and omissions, subject to the stated limits. Neither party may transfer its responsibility to the other by labeling a claim as a “provider claim” or “customer claim.” The agreement does not state that Harbor Labs owes Northwind Analytics for losses caused solely by Northwind Analytics, or that Northwind Analytics owes Harbor Labs for losses caused solely by Harbor Labs. Any conclusion about who owes what must be grounded in an actual obligation or an agreed payment, not in a heading alone.

14. Order of precedence. If a signed order form conflicts with this general extract, the signed order form controls for that conflict. A later written amendment signed by both parties controls over both. An unsigned draft or a staff summary does not amend the agreement. This file contains no signed amendment changing the parties’ roles, invoice amount, or payment direction.

15. Records and interpretation. Headings are for convenience. The parties use ordinary meaning and read the terms as a whole. Examples are illustrative, not additional obligations. No party may rely on a sentence taken from a sample form if the sentence is not part of the signed agreement. In account notes, first-person pronouns belong to the identified writer, not automatically to the party named in a copied subject line. The identified sender and the described action are more important than a repeated keyword.

PART II — ORDER FORM SUMMARY

Customer: Harbor Labs. Provider: Northwind Analytics. Service: hosted analytics workspace. Effective date: 1 January 2025. Initial term ends: 31 December 2025. Renewal notice deadline for either party: 16 November 2025, calculated as forty-five calendar days before 31 December 2025. This summary confirms the roles and dates; the file does not ask the reader to infer a notice from the deadline itself. Annual base subscription fee: $18,000. Billing frequency: quarterly, in advance. Invoice terms: thirty calendar days. The order form identifies Harbor Labs as the billed customer and Northwind Analytics as the invoicing provider.

The order form lists an optional onboarding package for $1,200, selected by Harbor Labs. It does not list a cash deposit, refundable bond, or prepaid usage balance. The order form also says that any service credit is applied to a future invoice. No special refund promise is written in the order form. The subscription fee is not described as money held by the provider on behalf of Harbor Labs. A quarterly invoice may include a portion of the annual fee, but the invoice issuer remains Northwind Analytics and the party obligated to pay remains Harbor Labs.

Account contacts are listed for operational convenience. Harbor Labs contact: Wanjiru Sorensen, contracts coordinator. Northwind Analytics contact: Quentin Kaur, billing administrator. The contact list does not authorize either individual to change the legal parties. A message sent by Wanjiru in her Harbor Labs role is a customer-side message. A message sent by Quentin in his Northwind Analytics role is a provider-side message. The account file records no change of employer for either contact.

PART III — INVOICE 4817

Issuer: Northwind Analytics. Bill to: Harbor Labs. Invoice date: 1 April 2025. Due date: 1 May 2025. Currency: US dollars. Description and line amounts:

A. Hosted analytics subscription, second quarter: $4,500.00.
B. Onboarding package, selected under order form: $1,200.00.
C. Additional storage, approved monthly package: $300.00.
D. Support extension, one session: $250.00.
Subtotal before tax: $6,250.00.
Transaction tax: $500.00.
Total due: $6,750.00.
Payment received on 10 April 2025 from Harbor Labs: $2,000.00.
Remaining balance shown by the invoice ledger: $4,750.00.

Arithmetic check: $4,500 + $1,200 = $5,700; $5,700 + $300 = $6,000; $6,000 + $250 = $6,250. Adding $500 tax gives $6,750. Subtracting the $2,000 payment received from Harbor Labs gives $4,750 outstanding. The payment record identifies Harbor Labs as payer and Northwind Analytics as recipient. The invoice does not show a payment from Northwind Analytics to Harbor Labs. The line called “support extension” is a service charge, not a refund. The word “received” in the payment row means received by the invoice issuer.

Invoice footer: “Please remit the remaining balance to Northwind Analytics using the account details already on file. If any item is disputed, contact billing and state the reason. A dispute does not itself pause the undisputed balance.” This is a direction to Harbor Labs to pay Northwind Analytics, not a demand that Northwind Analytics pay Harbor Labs. The account ledger records no credit note, refund, reversal, or separate debt owed by Northwind Analytics to Harbor Labs.

PART IV — ROUTINE ACCOUNT NOTES

2 April 2025, Northwind Analytics billing desk: Invoice 4817 issued to Harbor Labs. Amount and recipient have been checked against the signed order form. The second-quarter subscription is billed in advance. No remittance had been received at time of issue. This entry describes the invoice issuer and bill-to party; it does not record that the issuer owes the recipient money.

10 April 2025, Northwind Analytics billing desk: A $2,000 transfer arrived from Harbor Labs and was applied to invoice 4817. The balance was recalculated as $4,750. No other receipt is recorded. The ledger line was entered by Quentin Kaur. He notes that the bank reference used the words “Northwind settlement,” which are the beneficiary account name and do not mean Northwind Analytics paid Harbor Labs.

12 April 2025, Harbor Labs support ticket opened by Wanjiru Sorensen: “Could your team check why the storage line is on this invoice? We thought the included allowance was enough. Please show how the $300 was produced.” Ticket category: billing explanation. Requested action: explanation of the storage line. No request for money to be returned appears in the message. The ticket does not say that Harbor Labs has paid the disputed $300, and the record does not show any refund demand. A question about a charge is not automatically a request for a refund.

13 April 2025, Northwind Analytics reply by Quentin Kaur: “The selected storage tier is listed in the order form. We attach the selection record. If you decide to dispute it, please identify the line and the amount.” The reply comes from the provider to the customer. It does not ask Harbor Labs to refund money to the provider and does not create a new invoice amount.

14 April 2025, Harbor Labs follow-up by Wanjiru Sorensen: “Thank you, we see the signed selection. Please keep the current package for this quarter. Could you also tell us if we can reduce storage at renewal?” This confirms the service choice for the quarter and asks about a possible future change. It does not ask for cash back, does not rescind the invoice, and does not say Northwind Analytics owes Harbor Labs a payment.

15 April 2025, internal Northwind Analytics note by Quentin Kaur: “Customer asks whether the line was calculated correctly. We should explain, not issue credit unless billing confirms an error.” The note is internal to the provider. “Customer asks” refers to Harbor Labs asking Northwind Analytics for an explanation. The note contains a conditional instruction about a possible credit, but no credit is issued or promised.

17 April 2025, Harbor Labs contracts record: Wanjiru Sorensen reviewed the invoice and placed the order form and invoice in the quarterly file. The record says, “We owe the balance under the invoice unless billing confirms a mistake.” The writer is Harbor Labs. Here “we” means Harbor Labs, and the balance is payable to Northwind Analytics. This entry is consistent with the invoice ledger.

18 April 2025, provider collections note: “Outstanding customer balance is $4,750, due 1 May. Remittance has not yet appeared after the $2,000 receipt.” The note is written by Northwind Analytics and calls Harbor Labs the customer. It does not mean that Northwind Analytics owes Harbor Labs $4,750.

19 April 2025, shared account annotation: “Northwind owes? Check direction before responding.” The question mark is part of an unresolved annotation, not a finding. The next sentence says, “Ledger currently shows Harbor Labs paid $2,000 toward a $6,750 invoice and still owes $4,750 to Northwind Analytics.” The first fragment must not be read without the clarifying sentence.

20 April 2025, Northwind Analytics account manager note: “Harbor Labs is asking for proof of the storage selection; no refund request and no payment request against Northwind is logged. Do not confuse a support query with a claim that the provider owes money.” This note reports what the customer asked and identifies the absence of a refund demand. It is a provider employee’s description of the customer’s request, not a request by Northwind Analytics for money back from Harbor Labs.

PART V — BILLING PROCEDURE NOTES

The billing desk records every invoice from the provider to the customer. A payment is recorded as an amount received by the provider when it comes from the customer. A refund, if actually authorized and paid, is recorded in the opposite direction: provider to customer. A request for a refund is recorded only where a customer communication explicitly asks the provider to return money already paid or otherwise pay money back. A dispute, request for a breakdown, inquiry about future pricing, request to cancel a future feature, or statement that a charge is unexpected is not sufficient by itself.

The billing desk uses separate fields for “requesting party,” “requested party,” “payer,” “payee,” “invoice issuer,” and “bill-to account.” Staff are instructed not to copy a party name from one field into another. If Harbor Labs asks Northwind Analytics to return money, Harbor Labs is the requesting party and Northwind Analytics is the requested party. If Northwind Analytics asks Harbor Labs to remit an unpaid invoice, Northwind Analytics is the requesting party and Harbor Labs is the requested party. If no request is present, neither direction should be invented from an invoice balance.

The standard account report can display the amount from the perspective of either party. “Accounts receivable” on the provider’s ledger means money the customer owes the provider. “Accounts payable” on the customer’s ledger means money the customer owes the provider. The different accounting labels do not reverse the legal direction of the same balance. Staff should read the underlying transaction, not treat the words “receivable” or “payable” as a party name.

No entry in this file states that Northwind Analytics returned money to Harbor Labs, accepted a refund claim, admitted billing error, or agreed to pay damages. No entry states that Harbor Labs paid more than the invoice total. No entry states that the invoice balance was written off. The only recorded payment is the $2,000 received from Harbor Labs on 10 April. These details are supplied so the direction of the account can be identified without relying on a missing record.

PART VI — FILE INDEX AND ADMINISTRATIVE CONTEXT

The file index lists the signed order form, service terms extract, invoice 4817, payment confirmation, and support ticket. The order form is signed by authorized representatives for both entities. Invoice 4817 is generated by Northwind Analytics’ billing system. The payment confirmation names Harbor Labs as originating party and Northwind Analytics as beneficiary. The support ticket is opened under Harbor Labs’ workspace account. These sources agree on the identities and do not contain a later signed amendment.

An earlier draft invoice preview showed an estimated storage amount of $280. That preview was never sent as a final invoice and was replaced by the $300 line on invoice 4817 after the selected monthly tier was checked. The draft preview does not record a $20 overpayment or a promise to return $20. It is included in the index because it remains in the file, but it is not a credit note. The final invoice total and payment ledger above are the operative figures in this account file.

An onboarding checklist includes a blank field headed “refund / correction if required.” The field is blank. It does not say that a refund is due, and it does not identify either party as requesting one. FORWARDED CONTRACT NOTICE FILE — GRANITE OUTFITTERS / FOXGLOVE SOFTWARE
Compiled in plain English by an administrator who is not a native English writer. This is a contract-notice review packet with a forwarded email, its one-line cover note, notice extracts, and routine tracking material. Granite Outfitters is the customer. Foxglove Software is the provider. Those roles remain fixed throughout the packet. The forwarding person and the author of the original message are identified separately. A request made by one company to the other must not be reassigned merely because the message is forwarded.

ONE-LINE COVER NOTE
From: Xiu Okafor, Granite Outfitters contracts desk
To: Granite Outfitters legal archive
Subject: Forwarding for direction check
“Forwarding the provider’s note below for our file; please record who is asking whom to do what.”

FORWARDED EMAIL
From: Hiro Petrov, Foxglove Software contract manager
To: Xiu Okafor, Granite Outfitters contracts desk
Date: 8 September 2025
Subject: Granite Outfitters’ renewal notice and September account

Hello Xiu,

I am sending this from Foxglove Software, the provider, in reply to the notice your team sent on 5 September. I understand that Granite Outfitters, as customer, is asking Foxglove Software to confirm the consequences of the customer’s decision not to renew the hosted inventory service. The request is from Granite Outfitters to Foxglove Software. It is not a request from Foxglove Software asking Granite Outfitters to refund anything.

For the record, Foxglove received Granite Outfitters’ signed nonrenewal notice on 5 September. The notice says Granite Outfitters will not renew the service when the current period ends on 31 October 2025. It was sent by Wanjiru Sorensen, authorized for Granite Outfitters. The notice is addressed to Foxglove Software and signed in the customer’s name. Foxglove Software acknowledges receipt. It does not say that Foxglove Software is terminating the service, and it does not say that the provider is asking the customer to cancel.

Your team also asks whether the remaining prepaid amount will be returned. The answer under the signed order form is that the unused prepaid amount is not returned as cash on a customer nonrenewal. I am describing what Granite Outfitters asked us and answering that question; I am not making a request that Granite Outfitters pay Foxglove Software back. If our billing record has an error, please point to the entry and we will investigate it. A billing investigation is separate from the customer’s question about a return of funds.

The account statement attached to this email shows a $9,600 annual service fee paid by Granite Outfitters to Foxglove Software on 1 January 2025. The fee covers the period from 1 January through 31 December 2025, but the order form contains a special first-year termination provision: if the customer gives an effective nonrenewal notice at least fifty-five calendar days before the service period ends, the provider will return the unused portion of the annual fee for the period after the termination effective date. The special provision controls over the general no-cash-return wording for this first-year account. Granite Outfitters gave its notice on 5 September. The notice is effective at the end of the current service period, 31 October, under the signed amendment. The amendment says the return is calculated from 1 November through 31 December, not from the notice date.

The account ledger has a draft calculation of $1,600 for the unused period, based on two months at $800 per month. That is a draft estimate, not the approved amount. The signed amendment says the annual fee is allocated by calendar day for a return calculation, and October 31 is the last service day. Billing will therefore count 61 unused calendar days in November and December, using the 365-day year stated in the amendment. The calculation is $9,600 ÷ 365 × 61, rounded to the nearest cent. The ledger also includes an unrelated $160 support session from July, already delivered and not refundable. It must not be subtracted from or added to the unused-period calculation. The final approval will be issued in a separate credit record; this email confirms the direction and method, not that payment has already been made.

Please note the roles one more time: Granite Outfitters paid the annual fee to Foxglove Software; Granite Outfitters sent the nonrenewal notice; Granite Outfitters asked Foxglove Software about the unused amount; and the signed amendment says Foxglove Software must return the calculated amount to Granite Outfitters. No customer payment to the provider is being requested in this email. The word “return” describes the provider’s future duty, not a demand by Foxglove Software against Granite Outfitters.

Regards,
Hiro Petrov
Contract Manager, Foxglove Software

ATTACHED EXTRACT A — SIGNED ORDER FORM

Customer: Granite Outfitters. Provider: Foxglove Software. Service: hosted inventory management. Service period: 1 January 2025 through 31 December 2025. Annual fee: $9,600, prepaid by customer to provider on 1 January 2025. The receipt field identifies Granite Outfitters as payer and Foxglove Software as payee. The parties’ notice contacts are Wanjiru Sorensen for Granite Outfitters and Hiro Petrov for Foxglove Software.

General cancellation paragraph: customer may provide written nonrenewal notice to provider. Fees for a completed period are not refundable except where a signed special provision says otherwise. Provider is not permitted to treat a customer’s notice as a provider notice. The notice sender is the party electing nonrenewal, and the addressed recipient is the party receiving it.

The first-year special provision states: “If Granite Outfitters gives Foxglove Software written notice of nonrenewal no later than fifty-five calendar days before the current service period ends, the service will end on the last day of that service period. Foxglove Software will return to Granite Outfitters the allocated unused portion of the prepaid annual fee for the calendar days after the service period ends, using a 365-day denominator and rounding to the nearest cent. This special provision governs this first-year subscription notwithstanding the general no-refund paragraph.” The term “return” means payment from provider to customer. It does not mean that the customer returns money to the provider.

The parties initialed the special provision. No later signed amendment changes the notice date, the parties, the effective date, the day-count method, or the direction of payment. The order form includes a separate service-credit clause for availability failures, but no availability failure is asserted in this file. That clause is not the basis for the requested amount.

ATTACHED EXTRACT B — NONRENEWAL NOTICE

Date sent: 5 September 2025. Sender: Wanjiru Sorensen, for Granite Outfitters. Recipient: Foxglove Software, attention Hiro Petrov. Text: “Granite Outfitters gives notice that it will not renew the hosted inventory service at the end of the current service period. Please confirm receipt and explain the treatment of the unused prepaid amount under our signed order form.” The notice is signed electronically by Wanjiru Sorensen. The receipt acknowledgment from Foxglove Software is dated the same day.

The notice is from the customer to the provider. It is not a notice from Foxglove Software to Granite Outfitters. Its second sentence asks Foxglove Software to explain the amount; it does not ask Granite Outfitters to remit funds. The attachment does not include an invoice or a request by the provider for money.

ATTACHED EXTRACT C — ACCOUNT STATEMENT

1 January 2025: Granite Outfitters paid annual fee of $9,600 to Foxglove Software. Balance for annual fee: paid in full.

15 July 2025: Granite Outfitters paid $160 for a separate support session. Session delivered 21 July 2025. The line is marked “completed service; no unused portion recorded.” This amount is not part of the annual subscription fee and is not identified as prepaid subscription funds.

5 September 2025: nonrenewal notice received from Granite Outfitters. Status: acknowledged by Foxglove Software. Refund review status: pending calculation under special provision.

6 September 2025: draft note entered by provider billing: “Possibly $1,600 if two months at flat monthly rate; confirm contract day count.” The word “possibly” and the word “draft” indicate that this is not a final figure. The signed order form specifies calendar-day allocation, so the flat two-month figure is not the controlling calculation.

7 September 2025: billing specialist annotation: “Term ends 31 October, so unused days are 1 November through 31 December: November has 30 days, December has 31 days; 30 + 31 = 61 days. Annual allocation: $9,600 / 365 = approximately $26.30136986 per day. Multiply by 61 = approximately $1,604.38356. Rounded to nearest cent, return amount is $1,604.38.” This calculation is the one required by the signed special provision. The calculation does not include the July support session.

8 September 2025: provider contract manager sent the forwarded email above. Billing status remains “approval pending.” No outgoing payment to Granite Outfitters is recorded as of that date. The account statement records the provider’s future duty, but not completed payment.

CONTRACT NOTICE PROCEDURE EXTRACT

Formal contract notices are sent by the party taking the action to the other party’s notice contact. A customer’s nonrenewal notice is sent from Granite Outfitters to Foxglove Software. A provider acknowledgment is sent from Foxglove Software to Granite Outfitters. If a person forwards a message to an internal archive, the forwarder is not thereby the author of the forwarded text. The original message’s sender, recipient, and signature establish the direction of the underlying communication.

A party’s question about its own account is a request by that party. If Granite Outfitters asks what Foxglove Software will do with unused fees, Granite Outfitters is asking Foxglove Software. If Foxglove Software explains that it will return an amount to Granite Outfitters, Foxglove Software is describing its own obligation. A reader should not reverse the direction merely because the provider wrote the answer or because the email subject mentions the customer’s account.

The payment direction is separately determined from the receipt and special provision. The receipt says customer to provider for the original fee. The special provision says provider to customer for an approved return. A duty to pay in the future does not establish that the payment has already happened. A pending approval is not a completed remittance. This packet records a pending calculation and no completed return transaction.

ROUTINE FILE NOTES

5 September, Granite Outfitters contract desk: “Sent notice to Foxglove today. Please ask provider to confirm the end date and cash treatment.” This is a customer-side record of a request to the provider. It is not a provider-side demand for repayment.

5 September, Foxglove Software mailroom: “Received Granite notice. Sender verified as customer representative. Routed to contract manager.” This is a provider receipt record. It does not say the provider originated the nonrenewal.

6 September, Granite Outfitters finance note: “We paid $9,600 in January. If the special term applies, Foxglove should return unused days after October 31. Confirm exact arithmetic before booking.” The writer is Granite Outfitters; “we” refers to Granite Outfitters. The note is an internal statement of the customer’s interpretation and a direction to verify the amount. It does not show that Foxglove has paid.

6 September, Foxglove Software contract note: “Customer asks for the amount returned under the first-year clause. We should apply the signed day-count formula and issue the required return if approved.” The writer is Foxglove Software. “Customer” means Granite Outfitters. “We” means Foxglove Software. The note describes the customer’s request and the provider’s possible processing step; it is not a demand that the customer pay the provider.

7 September, provider billing worksheet: “Customer prepayment, $9,600. Unused term after service end, 61 days. Support session, $160, completed and separate. Draft estimate based on monthly shortcut, $1,600. Contract formula, $1,604.38. Approval not yet posted.” The worksheet is maintained by Foxglove Software. The “customer prepayment” is the money received by the provider from Granite Outfitters. The worksheet does not claim Granite Outfitters owes the provider an additional $1,604.38.

7 September, Granite Outfitters archive label: “Foxglove repayment?” The label is a question about the expected direction of the contract return. The detail field states: “Provider may have to repay customer after the service period; check special clause.” The label does not change the identified parties or the payment direction.

8 September, Foxglove Software finance message to contract manager: “Please do not describe the draft as paid. We have not issued the credit or transferred funds. If customer asks, explain the formula and status.” This message confirms no completed payment and identifies the customer as the one who may ask. It is not a provider request for money from the customer.

8 September, Granite Outfitters archive entry by Xiu Okafor: “Forwarded original provider response without editing. Cover line says it is Foxglove’s note. Store under customer nonrenewal.” The archive entry distinguishes the cover note from the original email. The cover note asks for direction to be recorded; it does not itself make a payment request.

9 September, contract administration checklist: “Verify who sent the notice; verify who received prepayment; verify who must make any return.” The checklist is not evidence that a party has paid or demanded money. The source records above answer each point: Granite Outfitters sent the notice, Foxglove Software received the fee, and Foxglove Software is the party required by the special provision to return the calculated unused amount to Granite Outfitters.

APPENDIX — CALCULATION AND DOCUMENT CONTROL

The annual subscription fee is $9,600. The contract uses 365 days for this calculation, even though the service period includes a calendar year with its own month lengths. The unused period begins after the final service day, October 31. November contributes 30 calendar days and December contributes 31 calendar days. Therefore the unused interval has 61 days. The daily allocation is $9,600 divided by 365, or about $26.30136986. Multiplying by 61 yields about $1,604.38356. Rounding to the nearest cent gives $1,604.38. The draft amount of $1,600 is a plausible shortcut using two months at $800 but is inconsistent with the signed allocation method. The July support session is excluded because it was delivered and separately charged.

The 55-day notice condition is satisfied. Counting backward 55 calendar days from 31 October 2025 reaches 6 September 2025. The signed notice was sent on 5 September 2025, one day earlier than that latest date. The special clause therefore applies. This date calculation determines whether the return clause is available; it does not change which party sent the notice or which party must pay the return. The packet distinguishes the notice condition from payment direction.

The agreement does not state that Granite Outfitters owes Foxglove Software a refund of the annual fee. It states that the fee was prepaid by Granite Outfitters to Foxglove Software, and that an unused portion is returned from Foxglove Software to Granite Outfitters if the stated condition is met. The account has no record of an unpaid invoice or separate amount due from the customer. The $160 July line is already paid and relates to completed service. It does not reverse the direction of the unused annual-fee calculation.

Document control confirms that the signed order form and its special provision are operative. The one-line cover note was written by Xiu Okafor at Granite Outfitters and only forwards the provider’s original email. The original email was written by Hiro Petrov at Foxglove Software and was addressed to Xiu at Granite Outfitters. The customer notice was written by Wanjiru Sorensen at Granite Outfitters and received by Foxglove Software. The archive contains no message in which Foxglove Software asks Granite Outfitters to return money, and no evidence that the approved return has already been paid.

FINAL ADMINISTRATIVE SUMMARY

The file concerns a customer nonrenewal notice, a customer question about unused prepaid fees, and a provider response explaining the contractual return. The notice is from Granite Outfitters to Foxglove Software. The customer’s request for confirmation is likewise directed to Foxglove Software. Under the signed special provision, Foxglove Software must return the unused-period allocation to Granite Outfitters. The amount under the required calculation is $1,604.38. Approval and payment remain pending in the records dated 8 September. This summary preserves the distinction between who asks, who owes, and whether payment has actually been completed.
