10:35 — Farid: Done.

Incident review draft — prepared by Xiu Kowalski

Summary
On 14 May, a worker configuration change increased the default document batch size without a matching increase to the worker memory limit. Some ingestion jobs consequently timed out. The customer API continued accepting submissions, but processing was delayed for affected jobs. Existing dashboards and saved reports remained accessible. We reverted the batch-size setting, watched the backlog drain, and confirmed normal processing before closing mitigation.

Customer and service impact
The impact was limited to file ingestion. It did not prevent access to existing reports. The affected period began at approximately 08:47 and was mitigated before 09:30; the queue continued draining afterward. The incident record contains one explicit financial request: Harbor Dental asked for a refund of the monthly service fee. Support forwarded that request to billing review. The record does not say that the refund was approved or paid. Saltmarsh Dental asked whether a scheduled report was affected; the report completed normally, and Saltmarsh Dental did not ask for a refund. These are separate customer interactions and should remain separate in summaries.

Timeline details
08:47 — Worker timeout rate begins to rise.
08:53 — Queue age crosses the internal investigation threshold.
09:02 — On-call sees alert and opens the incident channel.
09:04 — API availability checked; submissions are accepted, while processing completion is delayed for some jobs.
09:06 — Nightly reindex paused to reduce concurrent worker demand.
09:12 — Deployment comparison begins.
09:18 — Staging reproduction confirms that the larger batch size can trigger the timeout under the unchanged memory limit.
09:20 — Support identifies one affected customer report and one separate question about an unaffected scheduled report.
09:23 — Incident lead asks that the support update distinguish a problem report from a question.
09:26 — Prior batch-size configuration restored; new jobs begin completing.
09:28 — Harbor Dental’s refund request is documented and sent to billing review.
09:34 — Queue is declining; reindex remains paused.
09:38 — Customer update sent.
09:42 — Status page updated with the limited scope of the incident.
09:49 — Queue reaches zero and reindex resumes.
09:55 — Mitigation marked complete; incident remains open for review.
10:12 — Harbor Dental confirms uploads work again and retains the refund request.
10:24 — Processing-age alert added and sample-tested.

Detection and diagnosis
The first alert focused on worker process availability. Processes remained alive, so that check alone did not reveal that some jobs were taking too long to finish. The queue-age signal provided a clearer indication of customer impact. The team compared the latest deployment with the worker configuration and reproduced the timeout in staging. The reproduction used the same increased batch size and the existing memory limit. Restoring the prior batch size returned processing to normal.

There was no evidence that existing report data was unavailable or that accepted files were lost. The distinction between accepted, processing, and completed jobs mattered in the incident update. “The API is up” did not mean that every upload had finished processing. Conversely, delayed ingestion did not mean that existing dashboards were unavailable. Both statements are accurate, and neither substitutes for the other.

Response notes
Pausing reindex reduced competing work while diagnosis was underway. The configuration rollback was selected after staging reproduction, rather than before any comparison had been done. Once new jobs were completing, the team watched the backlog until it reached zero. The team then resumed reindex and monitored error rates. The incident lead kept mitigation status separate from review status: normal service returned before the written review was complete.

Support handling
Harbor Dental reported delayed uploads and explicitly asked for a refund of the monthly service fee. Support recorded the request and sent it to billing review. The billing outcome is not present in this incident record. Support later confirmed that Harbor Dental could upload files again, but that confirmation did not withdraw the refund request.

Saltmarsh Dental asked whether its scheduled report was affected. The report had completed normally. The support response explained that existing reports remained available. No refund request from Saltmarsh Dental is recorded. The fact that both contacts mention the same incident does not make their requests interchangeable.

Root cause
The deployment increased the worker’s default batch size. The memory limit remained unchanged. Under the larger batch, the worker could exceed available memory and time out. The configuration change was not paired with a capacity check that considered the resource limit. The worker health check observed process liveness but not job completion latency, so it did not independently identify the failure mode.

Contributing conditions
The worker configuration and resource limit were reviewed in different parts of the deployment process. The review checklist did not require an explicit comparison between batch size and memory allocation. The alert set emphasized process status and error rate, with less attention to the age of work waiting in the queue. These conditions made it possible for the service to accept work while some jobs completed slowly.

What went well
The incident channel was opened promptly after the alert. The team preserved a clear record of configuration changes. Staging reproduced the failure with the changed setting. The rollback was narrow and reversible. Customer communications stated which functions were affected and which remained available. Support kept the refund request in the billing process rather than describing it as already approved. Queue monitoring continued after the first successful job, and the team waited for the backlog to clear before resuming the paused task.

What could be improved
A worker can be alive and still be unhelpful. The health check should include a measure of work completion, or be paired with one that pages on processing age. Deployment review should require a check of batch size against memory limits. Customer-facing status language should continue to distinguish acceptance from completion, because “upload succeeded” can mean several different things depending on which step one is watching.

Action items
1. Add processing-age alert for ingestion jobs. Owner: Farid Okafor. Status: implemented and sample-tested.
2. Add a deployment checklist item comparing batch size, worker memory, and expected job load. Owner: Xiu Kowalski. Status: drafted for review.
3. Update the incident template to separate API acceptance, processing delay, and completed ingestion. Owner: Yara O'Neill. Status: in progress.
4. Review the worker health check so process liveness is not treated as proof of successful job completion. Owner: Farid Okafor. Status: scheduled.
5. Keep financial requests and service restoration notes in distinct support fields. Owner: Yara O'Neill. Status: reminder sent to support operations.

Appendix A: operational observations
The API returned successful acceptance responses during the incident. This behavior was expected: acceptance places the file into the ingestion workflow; it does not certify that every later processing step has completed. The queue was therefore a more useful signal for the user-visible delay than API availability alone.

The worker pool showed healthy process status throughout the early investigation. The status check was functioning according to its narrow definition. The narrow definition was not enough for this incident. No one should interpret that as the check being broken in the ordinary sense; it was simply answering a smaller question than the incident required. This is the sort of distinction that feels obvious after the graphs have been reviewed and less obvious while they are red.

The changed batch size was the only deployment difference identified that reproduced the failure. Staging tests used a representative set of files and the same worker memory limit as production. When the prior batch size was restored, the reproduction no longer produced the timeout. Production processing recovered after the same setting was restored. There was no separate database, network, or identity-provider issue identified during review.

The team did not restart every worker as an initial reaction. A broad restart could have increased queue pressure while the backlog was already elevated. The team first reduced competing work, reproduced the configuration effect, and then made the targeted change. This was slower than guessing and faster than explaining a second avoidable outage.

Appendix B: communication wording retained for reference
Customer update: “We identified a worker configuration issue affecting some file processing. The setting has been corrected, and delayed jobs are completing. Existing dashboards and saved reports remained available. We are monitoring the queue until it clears.”

Internal status: “New ingestion jobs are completing after the batch-size setting was restored. The backlog remains elevated; do not describe the queue as clear until the age and count checks confirm it.”

Billing note: “Harbor Dental requests a refund of the monthly service fee due to the upload interruption. Request recorded and forwarded for billing review. No approval or payment confirmation is recorded in this incident.”

These messages intentionally use different verbs. A customer reported an impact. The service team restored processing. Billing received a request. None of those verbs should be upgraded into another verb merely because a summary would look tidier.

Appendix C: sample monitoring review
Metric: worker process liveness. Result during incident: processes remained available. Interpretation: the worker processes were running; this metric did not establish that jobs were finishing within the expected interval.
Metric: ingestion error count. Result during incident: elevated timeouts. Interpretation: useful confirmation that jobs were failing or stalling, but the signal was less direct than queue age for establishing how much work was waiting.
Metric: queue age. Result during incident: increased beyond the investigation threshold. Interpretation: direct evidence of delayed processing. The new alert is intended to make this condition visible sooner.
Metric: existing report availability. Result during incident: available. Interpretation: users could continue to access saved reports. This did not mean new ingestion was unaffected.
Metric: backlog after configuration rollback. Result: declined to zero. Interpretation: delayed jobs had cleared sufficiently for the paused reindex to resume.

The sample-tested alert was triggered with a sample event after implementation. The test demonstrated that the notification path worked. It did not demonstrate how the alert would behave under every production failure. That is why the review calls it sample-tested rather than proven under all conditions. Words remain cheaper than outages, though apparently not as cheap as we would like.

Appendix D: support contact summaries
Harbor Dental: reported that uploads were stuck in processing during the incident. Asked for a refund of the monthly service fee. Support acknowledged the request and routed it to billing review. Later confirmed uploads worked again. No billing decision is included here.

Saltmarsh Dental: asked whether its scheduled report was affected. The scheduled report completed normally. Support confirmed this and noted that existing reports remained available. No refund request is recorded.

The summaries are reproduced here because the two tickets were opened close together and both refer to the ingestion incident. The first contains a service complaint and a financial request. The second contains a question about a report that was not affected. Similar timing does not make the underlying customer statements the same.

Appendix E: follow-up review questions
Did the API remain available? Yes, according to the incident checks.
Did every new file finish processing immediately? No. Some processing was delayed.
Were existing dashboards unavailable? No. The incident record says they remained available.
Was the worker process itself down? No. Processes remained alive, while some jobs timed out.
Was there a confirmed data-loss event? No data loss was observed.
Did Harbor Dental ask for a refund? Yes. The request is explicitly recorded in the support note and incident summary.
Was the refund approved? The incident record does not say so.
Did Saltmarsh Dental ask for a refund? No such request is recorded; its contact was a question about a scheduled report.
Who led the incident response? Xiu Kowalski.
Who handled the technical remediation? Farid Okafor.
Who owned customer communications? Yara O'Neill.

These questions are included to make the review usable by someone who was not awake for the channel export. They are not new findings. If an answer is absent from the record, the absence should stay an absence rather than being filled in from what normally happens next.

Appendix F: change-review notes
The batch-size setting is now visible in the worker deployment checklist. The reviewer is expected to compare it with the memory allocation and the workload assumptions. The checklist does not claim that a larger batch is always wrong. It asks for evidence that the chosen batch fits the configured resources. This is less exciting than a slogan and more useful than one.

The queue-age alert is configured to notify the on-call rotation when the age crosses the operating threshold. The alert includes the service name and the relevant dashboard link. The linked dashboard distinguishes waiting work from actively processing work. A sample notification was received by the on-call test channel. The alert does not alter queue behavior; it only improves detection. It is monitoring, not mitigation, which is why the incident still required the configuration correction.

The incident template now includes separate fields for customer-visible symptom, API acceptance, processing completion, data integrity, and financial request. The intent is to discourage summaries that compress several different states into a single vague “uploads were down.” In this incident, that phrase would have been inaccurate: the API accepted submissions, some processing jobs timed out, and existing dashboards remained available. A shorter sentence is not automatically a clearer sentence.

Appendix G: review record
Review meeting attendees: Xiu Kowalski, Yara O'Neill, and Farid Okafor.
The group agreed that the causal explanation is adequately supported by staging reproduction and production recovery following the targeted configuration change. No alternative cause was identified in the worker, API, database, or network checks performed during the incident.
The group agreed that customer impact statements should retain the distinction between delayed ingestion and existing report access.
The group agreed that Harbor Dental’s refund request must remain labeled pending unless a billing decision is later recorded. This review does not make that decision.
The group agreed that Saltmarsh Dental’s question should not be described as a complaint or refund request.
The group agreed that the new queue-age alert should be reviewed after it has operated through a normal reporting period. Until then, the implementation status is “added and sample-tested.”

Appendix H: closing note
The incident is closed operationally. The review actions remain tracked separately. Harbor Dental’s refund request is still routed to billing review in the support record. No decision about the request is stated here. The uploads are processing normally, the queue is clear, and the follow-up work is assigned. The service has returned to its expected behavior; the prose is attempting to do the same.

LARKSPUR WORKS: MONTHLY OPERATIONS RECORD
Prepared for internal review
Reporting period: 1–30 June
Facility: North Bay small manufacturing shop
Document status: Final

Purpose and scope
This record consolidates production, purchasing, maintenance, shipping, and office notes for the stated reporting period. It is intended to give supervisors a readable account of routine work and to preserve details that might otherwise remain distributed among shift sheets, purchasing records, and handwritten notes. The facility makes short-run brackets, mounting plates, instrument housings, and replacement fittings. Work is organized by job number. The company uses a small group of machines and handles many tasks manually, so the production record includes both completed work and ordinary interruptions. No section of this report is intended to replace the individual job traveler or the signed accounting ledger.

The reporting period begins on 1 June and ends on 30 June. Entries are arranged by subject rather than by the time at which they were first entered. Where a record contains an observation, it is reported as an observation; it is not necessarily an instruction to change a process. Quantities below are copied from the working records unless identified as estimates. No outside schedule or customer correspondence is incorporated except where a copy was placed in the shop file.

Facility overview
The shop has a receiving bench near the west entrance, a cutting area, a machining area, a deburring and finishing bench, an assembly table, a packing station, and a small office. Materials move from receiving to storage and then to the operation listed on the job traveler. The supervisor assigns jobs according to available machine time, required material, and promised dispatch date. Operators record actual work in the daily sheets. The office enters completed job information into the monthly workbook. A discrepancy between a daily sheet and the workbook is referred back to the original paper record rather than resolved by assumption.

The main work this month consisted of small batches rather than continuous production. This made setup and inspection important. Operators were asked to retain setup samples when a job traveler requested them. Routine cleaning took place at the end of each shift. The floor and benches were checked before the start of morning work. The month included no major change to the shop layout, staffing, or general inspection procedure.

Staff and responsibilities
The shop supervisor coordinated job assignments and reviewed completed travelers. The receiving clerk logged deliveries and placed material tags with incoming stock. Machine operators documented setups and reported tool wear. The finishing operator deburred edges and identified parts needing additional attention. The packing operator checked quantities against the traveler before preparing cartons. The office clerk maintained the workbook and filed supplier paperwork. On days when the assigned person was away from a station, another trained employee covered the routine task and recorded the coverage on the daily sheet.

The organization does not treat a note on a shared board as a substitute for a completed traveler. If work is moved between stations, the traveler moves with the parts. If a quantity is changed, the person making the change records the revised quantity and initials the entry. When an employee identifies a problem, the employee informs the supervisor and records enough detail for another person to locate the affected material. These practices remained in effect throughout June.

Production summary
The monthly workbook shows that the shop completed work on the following general categories: brackets, plates, housings, and fittings. The workbook records job identifiers, planned quantities, completed quantities, material codes, and dispatch status. Its summary tab is a convenience for review; individual travelers remain the controlling production records. A blank dispatch cell means that dispatch was not recorded in that workbook row. It does not by itself establish that a job was cancelled or that a customer was contacted.

Production timing varied according to setup requirements and availability of stock. Jobs requiring the same material were sometimes grouped when doing so did not interfere with a promised dispatch date. The supervisor retained authority to separate jobs when their tolerances or finishing requirements differed. Small-run work can involve more setup minutes per unit than a larger run, and this month’s records reflect that ordinary variation. The shop did not use the monthly summary to compare operators or to set individual performance targets.

Production observations
Operators reported ordinary variation in setup time. Jobs with a repeated hole pattern were generally straightforward after the first setup sample was checked. Jobs with several distinct edges required more deburring attention. This was not treated as a defect unless the inspection record identified a specific issue. The work area retained separate trays for parts awaiting inspection and parts cleared for packing. The trays were labeled, and employees were reminded not to combine material from different job numbers merely because the pieces looked similar.

The cutting area used the established stock identification labels. When the remaining stock from a bar or sheet was suitable for a later job, it was returned to the appropriate rack with its material code visible. Short remnants that could not be reliably identified were put in the review bin. The review bin was checked by the supervisor before any material was returned to general stock. No untagged material was knowingly used for a June production job.

Tooling and machine condition
Routine checks were made on the band saw, drill press, small mill, bench grinder, and finishing tools. The checks included visible condition, cleanliness, and confirmation that guards were in position. Operators noted tool changes on the relevant traveler or maintenance sheet. The shop did not record a major machine failure during the reporting period. Minor interruptions, such as replacing a worn cutting insert or clearing chips, were recorded in the daily sheets when they affected a job’s sequence.

The small mill was cleaned at the end of each shift in which it was used. The vice and work surface were checked for chips before a new setup. The drill press table was kept clear of loose tools. The band saw blade was inspected by the assigned operator before use. If the operator observed an unusual sound, vibration, or cut, the machine was stopped and the supervisor was notified. This reporting rule applied even when the operator believed that the issue could be corrected quickly.

Maintenance notes were reviewed at the end of the month. They contained routine lubrication entries, cleaning entries, and one note about replacing a worn bench-grinder wheel. The replacement was completed before the grinder was returned to service. The maintenance sheet identified the person who performed the change and recorded that the guard was restored. There was no entry indicating that a machine remained in use with a known missing guard.

Quality and inspection
Inspection took place at the stages indicated on each traveler. Depending on the job, this involved a first-piece check, an in-process check, a final visual check, a dimension check, or a combination of these. The inspector recorded results on the traveler. A completed inspection entry did not waive the need to verify the job number and quantity before packing. Parts that required rework were kept separate from accepted parts and identified with the relevant job number.

The quality file for June included signed inspection records for the jobs in the summary. A signed record indicates that the listed check was performed and that the recorded outcome was accepted for the next step. It does not state that every possible characteristic was measured when the traveler required only a defined sample. The shop continued to follow the inspection instructions written on each traveler, including any customer-specific revision noted there.

No broad product recall or general rejection was recorded in the monthly quality file. A small number of parts required ordinary edge cleanup before inspection could be completed. Those parts were returned to the finishing bench and checked again. The accepted quantity was recorded after the recheck. The shop retained the rejected or reworked pieces until the traveler was closed, so that the final disposition could be documented. At close, the records showed no unresolved quantity discrepancy for the listed jobs.

Materials and purchasing
The receiving clerk checked supplier paperwork against the delivery and recorded the material code, quantity, and condition. Stock with an incomplete label was held at receiving until its identity was confirmed. The shop did not combine incoming material with identified stock before the receiving check. Supplier documents were filed by date and linked to purchase references where available.

Purchasing requests were raised by the supervisor or the person responsible for a job. A request did not itself establish that an order had been placed. The office clerk recorded an order only after the purchasing record contained the supplier confirmation or other required evidence. The company generally purchased material in quantities suitable for short-run work and kept a limited amount of common stock. Decisions to buy additional material took into account current jobs, the stock rack, and expected replenishment time.

A delivery could arrive in more than one package. In those cases, the receiving clerk recorded each package and kept the paperwork together. If the paperwork indicated a quantity different from the received quantity, the discrepancy was referred to the office before the material was released. No open receiving discrepancy was carried forward at the end of June. Supplier lead times varied; the dates on an estimate were not treated as a confirmed delivery date unless the supplier had confirmed them.

The bracket work is finished and in the blue tray with the traveler. Please leave the inspection sample on top so it does not get packed by mistake. The sample is marked “first piece”; it is not an extra customer part. The rest of the accepted pieces were counted against the traveler before the tray was moved. The inspector has the sheet for the final check.

The small housing parts are on the other bench, not in the bracket tray. They have a different job number even though the outside dimensions look close. Keep the two jobs separate until both travelers are closed. I wiped the mill table after the last setup and put the loose cutters in the labeled drawer. The cutter marked for review is not to be used until someone checks its edge.

Receiving has one short length still awaiting a material-code check. It is not for today’s bracket job. The tagged stock for that job was already issued. I put the supplier paper beside the receiving log so the office can compare the code in the morning. Nothing on this note changes the quantities on the travelers. — Afternoon shift

The note was typed from the original board entry for filing. It records a handover, not a revision to a customer specification or a new authorization to ship. The supervisor confirmed that the blue tray and the small housing tray were handled separately. The first-piece sample remained with the bracket traveler until inspection was signed. The unidentified short length remained at receiving until the code check was completed.

Shipping and packing
The packing operator checked the job number, quantity, and destination information before closing a carton. The operator used the traveler and the packing list rather than relying on the appearance of the parts. Labels were applied only after the check. Where jobs were scheduled for combined collection, their cartons remained individually labeled and were not treated as a single job. The collection record identified the cartons included in the handoff.

Carrier receipts were filed for jobs marked dispatched in the workbook. For packed jobs awaiting collection, the office retained the packing information but left dispatch unrecorded until a handoff occurred. This procedure avoided treating preparation as proof of shipment. The shop did not infer delivery to a customer solely from a carrier receipt; the receipt documents handoff to the carrier. Any later delivery confirmation would be filed separately if received.

The packing station kept labels, cartons, protective material, and scales in their assigned locations. Damaged packaging was removed from use. The scale was checked at the start of the week using the shop’s routine check item. If the check had indicated a problem, the packing operator would have notified the supervisor before weighing shipments. No unresolved scale issue was noted in the June packing records.

Customer service and office records
The office clerk maintained customer communications in the job folder when a message affected a drawing, a delivery instruction, or the disposition of a job. Routine acknowledgments were filed with the correspondence but were not entered as production changes. A request for information was not treated as an approved drawing revision. The supervisor reviewed any message that could change what the shop was required to make or when it was required.

The monthly office file contains no record of a customer requesting a refund. The relevant correspondence filed for the month consists of order confirmations, drawing clarifications, dispatch communications, and routine acknowledgments. The office index uses subject labels to help locate documents, but the original message is retained where a communication is material to a job. The absence of a refund entry in this summary is not a statement about communications outside the stated period; this report concerns only the June records held in the shop file.

The office also maintained a list of customer contacts for dispatch coordination. Changes to an address or collection arrangement were checked against the customer’s written communication before a label was changed. A phone note was followed by written confirmation where the change affected the destination. In June, the dispatch records reviewed at close matched the destination information attached to the travelers and packing lists.

Financial administration
The office recorded supplier invoices according to the normal filing procedure. The monthly report does not attempt to provide a complete financial statement. It includes purchasing documents only insofar as they relate to materials used or received during the production period. A supplier invoice is kept separate from a customer invoice. The distinction is maintained in the filing system to avoid mixing amounts payable to a supplier with amounts charged to a customer.

Before filing an invoice, the clerk checked the supplier name, reference, date, and receiving documentation. A missing field was referred for review rather than filled from memory. Where an invoice contained a delivery charge, that charge remained identified separately from the merchandise subtotal. The invoice transcription above preserves the listed line totals and total amount. No further calculation or adjustment is asserted in this report.

The shop does not authorize a purchase merely because a supplier invoice is received. The invoice records a charge for goods supplied. Purchasing authorization, receiving confirmation, and invoice filing are distinct steps. The records for the invoice listed above show a receiving reference and a filed supplier document. No customer refund was requested in that supplier invoice, which concerns a purchase by the shop rather than a customer service case.

Safety and housekeeping
The supervisor reviewed the daily housekeeping entries. Walkways were kept clear of stock and cords. Scrap was placed in the marked bins, and sharp offcuts were handled with gloves. Employees were reminded to report spills promptly. The eyewash station and first-aid supplies were checked according to the shop schedule. No serious injury was recorded in the June incident file.

Personal protective equipment was available at the work areas where it was required. Operators were responsible for using the equipment appropriate to their task. Visitors were directed to the office before entering the production area and were accompanied while on the floor. The visitor log was kept at reception. These procedures were communicated during the regular safety review and remained unchanged during the reporting period.

The safety file included routine reminders about lifting, keeping hands clear of cutting operations, and returning tools after use. Reminders were recorded as training or housekeeping notes, not as evidence that a specific incident occurred. When a near miss was reported, the supervisor documented the location and immediate response. The monthly review found no open corrective action from a June incident.

Environmental and waste handling
Metal offcuts were sorted by material type where identification was available. Mixed or unidentified scrap was placed in the designated review container. Cutting fluid and other shop supplies were stored in labeled containers. The shop kept waste handling records with the relevant service paperwork. Employees were instructed not to pour shop liquids into ordinary drains and to report any damaged container to the supervisor.

The amount of scrap varied with the work mix. The monthly record does not compare the scrap total with a production target because no such target was assigned for June. Usable remnants were distinguished from waste through the material identification procedure. The review bin was inspected before any remnant was returned to stock. No environmental incident was reported during the period.

Training and communication
The supervisor used the morning handover to identify priority jobs, known machine concerns, and receiving items awaiting review. Employees could raise questions about travelers or material labels before starting work. When an instruction was unclear, the supervisor was expected to consult the applicable drawing or customer communication. Operators were not asked to guess at a dimension or silently change a process to meet an assumed requirement.

Training entries documented orientation and refresher discussion. A signed attendance entry confirms participation in the discussion listed, not independent certification for every machine. Machine authorization remained governed by the shop’s training record. New or unfamiliar work was reviewed with a trained operator before the employee performed it independently. The training file for June was checked for completeness at the monthly close.

The shop’s internal communications were intended to make work status visible without replacing controlled records. The production board showed job location and immediate priorities. The workbook provided a summary. The traveler remained with the material and documented operations, quantities, and checks. If these sources differed, employees were to pause the affected step and ask the supervisor to reconcile the record. That approach was followed during the month.

Record control and filing
The office clerk filed completed travelers by job number and month. Supplier paperwork was filed by supplier and invoice reference, with receiving references added when available. Maintenance and safety records were filed separately. The monthly workbook was saved in the controlled operations folder. Corrections to the workbook were recorded with a date and a brief explanation; the original source record was retained.

A copied note or transcription is useful for retrieval but does not override its original record. The typed handover above was filed with the June production papers. Its details were checked against the travelers and the receiving log. The supplier invoice transcription was checked against the invoice image and receiving reference. The records were legible and available at the time of monthly review.

The office avoided deleting incomplete rows from the workbook. If a field had not yet been confirmed, it remained blank or carried a note describing its status. A blank field was not silently interpreted as a zero or a completed action. At month end, the clerk reviewed open entries with the supervisor. The reviewed June rows were either completed or identified as awaiting a documented next step, such as collection of a packed carton.

Appendix A: Daily workflow description
At the beginning of a shift, the supervisor reviewed the production board and the jobs expected to move that day. The receiving clerk identified any deliveries that had arrived outside the prior day’s close. Operators checked that the material, traveler, and setup information belonged together. The first operation began only after the job and material were identified. This routine helped prevent a piece from being processed under a neighboring job number.

During the shift, an operator recorded progress when a defined operation was complete or when a significant interruption affected the work. If a machine was unavailable, the supervisor could assign another suitable task, but the material and traveler remained controlled. The employee did not change the planned job quantity without recording the reason and obtaining the required approval. Where the traveler called for an inspection, the parts were moved to the designated inspection area rather than directly to packing.

At shift end, employees returned tools, cleared chips, and left work areas ready for the next shift. The handover identified unfinished work and any item that should not be moved or used before review. The receiving and production areas were kept distinct so that unverified incoming material did not appear to be issued stock. Completed job paperwork was placed in the filing tray for office review. These practices were documented in the shop orientation and followed in the June records.

Appendix B: Workbook use notes
The summary tab is built from the job records and is used to locate a job quickly. It is not a substitute for the traveler. Planned and completed quantities are kept in separate columns because a plan is not proof of completion. Material status indicates whether the recorded material was available for the job. Dispatch status describes the last recorded packing or handoff stage. A note can identify a file or a reason for the current status, but it does not authorize a change to a job requirement.

The office clerk checks the job number before copying a quantity. Similar product names are not enough to establish that two rows refer to the same job. When a revised drawing or hole pattern is involved, the revision note is retained with the job. The workbook uses plain text to make the information readable when printed. Filters may be used for review, but the underlying rows are not rearranged in a way that removes the job identifiers.

At monthly close, the supervisor checks selected rows against travelers, dispatch paperwork, and receiving records. The check is intended to detect transcription errors and incomplete status fields. A review result is recorded in the close checklist. If a mismatch is found, the source document is consulted and the workbook is corrected with an explanatory entry. No mismatch requiring a quantity correction remained open at the close of this reporting period.

Appendix C: Inspection vocabulary
“First-piece check” refers to the inspection specified for the first piece produced after a setup or change, where the traveler calls for that check. “In-process check” refers to the inspection performed during production at the point shown on the traveler. “Final visual check” refers to the recorded visual inspection before packing. “Rework” means a part was returned for an additional operation or correction before being accepted. “Packed” means shop packing was recorded. “Dispatched” means a handoff was recorded in the office file. These terms are used consistently in the June records.

The terminology does not imply a broader guarantee than the inspection record supports. An accepted piece is one that passed the checks documented for the job. If a customer drawing specified a feature, the traveler identified the applicable requirement for the operator and inspector. A general note on the production board was not used to replace a drawing dimension or a written customer instruction. Any proposed deviation required review before the work proceeded.

Appendix D: Receiving vocabulary
“Received” means that the package or material was presented to the shop and entered in the receiving process. “Verified” means that the clerk checked the delivered item against the paperwork to the extent recorded. “Held” means that the material was not released to production pending a check or clarification. “Issued” means that identified material was assigned to a job. An item can be physically present in the building without being issued to a job. The June receiving entries preserve these distinctions.

Material identifiers were read from tags and supplier documents. If an identifier was unclear, the receiving clerk sought confirmation instead of inferring a material grade from appearance. This was particularly important for short remnants and mixed packages. The note from 12 June refers to one short length awaiting a material-code check; it does not indicate that the tagged stock already issued to the bracket job was in question. The clerk completed the check before release of that short length.

Appendix E: Shipping vocabulary
“Prepared” describes work done to make a shipment ready, including counting, packing, and labeling. “Packed” is the status entered when the shop’s packing steps are complete. “Collected” describes a recorded customer or carrier handoff. “Dispatched” is the workbook status entered when the handoff information has been received and filed. “Delivered” would require separate confirmation if the shop received it. The report uses these words as separate stages and does not assume one stage proves a later stage.

When a combined collection is arranged, the cartons remain individually identified by job. The collection note lists the cartons included. If a packed job is not on a collection record, its workbook status remains packed. The shipping file for June followed that convention. The records reviewed at close contained carrier receipts for the rows marked dispatched and packing information for rows marked packed.

Appendix F: Customer correspondence index
The correspondence index groups messages by job, date, and topic. Topics include order confirmation, drawing clarification, delivery coordination, invoice administration, and general acknowledgment. An index heading is a navigation aid rather than a substitute for the underlying message. Where a customer asks for a change, the message is routed to the supervisor for assessment. Where a customer asks a question, the response is filed with the question. Where a message is unrelated to production, it is retained according to the office filing procedure.

The June index contains no entry classified as a refund request. The clerk reviewed the message subjects and the filed correspondence during close. The absence of a refund request is the clear result for the records in scope. A supplier invoice or a purchasing transaction is not categorized as a customer refund request. The office did not treat the invoice from Rivermark Industrial Supply as a customer communication; it was filed with supplier purchasing and receiving paperwork.

Appendix G: Monthly close checklist narrative
The close checklist asked the reviewer to confirm that the reporting dates were correct, the workbook was saved, travelers were filed, receiving papers were matched where possible, and dispatch status was supported by a handoff record. The reviewer also checked that open items were not described as complete without documentation. The supervisor signed the checklist after discussing the remaining packed cartons and the receiving note with the office clerk.

The close review did not require every packed job to be dispatched by the end of the month. It required the status to be accurate. The workbook therefore retained packed status for work awaiting collection and dispatched status only for work with a handoff record. In the same way, the review did not treat a purchasing request as an invoice or an invoice as a customer refund. Record type and direction remained clear in the file.

Appendix H: General observations from the reporting period
The shop completed a varied set of small orders with routine changes in setup and sequence. Communication between receiving, production, inspection, packing, and the office was adequate for the work recorded. Employees used job identifiers when moving material, and the monthly review found no unresolved job-quantity mismatch. A small number of ordinary adjustments were documented and completed through the existing process.

The supervisor noted that orderly trays and legible travelers reduced time spent locating work. The office clerk noted that keeping dispatch and packing statuses separate made the close easier to review. The receiving clerk noted that material tags should remain visible when stock is placed on a rack. These observations were discussed at handover. They are routine process notes, not evidence of a customer complaint, a refund request, or a change in the shop’s general operating procedure.

Appendix I: File inventory
The June production file contains the summary workbook, the closed job travelers for the rows listed, inspection records, packing records, dispatch receipts where applicable, the typed handover note, and the close checklist. The receiving file contains the relevant supplier documents and the receiving entries. The maintenance file contains routine checks and the grinder-wheel replacement entry. The safety file contains housekeeping and training records. Each file is retained under the shop’s established internal filing practice.

The file inventory was checked for the monthly review. The supervisor could locate the job travelers by identifier, and the office clerk could locate the invoice by supplier and reference. No document in the inventory was described as a customer refund request. The invoice is clearly labeled as a supplier invoice issued to the shop, with a receiving reference and line items for manufacturing supplies.

Conclusion
The June record describes ordinary production in a small manufacturing shop. The workbook lists completed quantities and packing or dispatch status. The typed handover note separates the bracket work from the small housing work and identifies the inspection sample. The supplier invoice lists materials and a delivery charge. The records distinguish between a customer communication, a supplier invoice, a packed carton, and a dispatched carton. The monthly close was completed, and the documents described above were filed for reference.

SECTION 1 — Original service clause, executed 2 January

1.1 Covered services. Provider shall make hosted build runners available for the Copperleaf Outfitters development organization. Standard Linux runner usage is measured as the sum of the whole-minute values displayed in the provider's job ledger, provided the job is marked Billable=Y. Each individual job is rounded upward before export. A distinct job identifier represents a distinct execution, including a retry. The status Failed does not, by itself, remove a job from billable usage.

The Linux subtotal remains the sum of qualifying Linux row values without a multiplier.

Copperleaf Outfitters — product review and course administration file

Review submitted by Sven O'Neill, first-year ceramics student

Product: Fieldnote Course Planner, slate cover, student edition
Purchase reference: CO-4817
Review date: 14 September

I bought the Fieldnote planner because the ceramics department apparently believes that a student can remember a kiln schedule, a lecture room change, three assignment deadlines, and which cupboard contains the clean aprons without writing any of them down. The department was right about one thing: I cannot. The planner is well made. The cover has survived a backpack, two damp bus rides, and being used as a temporary table under a wobbly mug. Its pages are thick enough that my fountain pen does not leave dramatic blue ghosts on the other side. The weekly layout has space for courses, appointments, and a box labeled “things to ask about.” I have filled that box repeatedly, mostly with questions whose answers were available in the course portal if one knows where the portal has hidden them this week.

The planner also has a term overview page. That page is useful, although it has room for only six course codes. Students in the foundation program may have seven courses, and the extra course must apparently be recorded on the back of a receipt or remembered through supernatural means. I have six courses, so this particular design limitation has not affected me. The printed semester dates match the dates provided by the registrar. I checked them against the enrollment sheet rather than trusting a glossy review written by someone who probably owns a ruler.

My review is not a request for a refund. It is a review. The distinction is important because the shop has sent me two automatic messages offering to “resolve my refund concern,” which is a concern I did not raise. I am keeping the planner. If the next message tells me that my refund is ready, I will assume the machine has started processing an imaginary transaction. The review form did ask whether I wanted to return the planner. I selected no. The page then offered a text box for comments, which is how we arrived at this document.

A course assistant suggested that I ask the school bookstore whether the planner could be exchanged for a larger model. The bookstore replied that no larger model is stocked. That answer is clear and does not need to be converted into an exchange request. The assistant also said the department might issue a supplemental timetable sheet. The course office later placed a downloadable timetable sheet in the portal. I printed it and tucked it inside the planner. This is a workable solution, though the sheet is not a product feature and the printer charged me one token. The token was not a mysterious fee; it was the posted printing charge.

For completeness, the weekly pages are legible, the binding remains intact, and the elastic strap still holds. The cover color is darker than the picture on the sales page. That is not a defect, unless the course requirement is to coordinate stationery with the kiln. The page marker is a narrow ribbon, not a removable bookmark. I would have preferred a second ribbon, but preference is not evidence of a manufacturing problem. There is a pocket in the back, which currently contains the timetable sheet, a receipt, and a small note reminding me to return a library book. The note has not made me return the library book. That failure belongs to me, not the planner.

The school’s product feedback office asked me to provide a brief account of what the item does well and what it does poorly. It records the following summary: the planner is sturdy, the weekly layout is useful, and the term overview has limited space. The office has not asked me to report a delivery problem, missing parcel, or wrong product. The parcel arrived at the correct address on the date shown in the shop record. The box was plain cardboard, not a ceremonial object, and it was not damaged. The planner inside was the model I ordered.

The review has since appeared in a monthly student newsletter. The newsletter editor shortened one paragraph but did not change the point. A reader wrote back to ask whether I was dissatisfied enough to return the item. I replied that I was keeping it and had already selected no on the return form. This exchange is included here because the school’s review archive stores everything as if future generations will need to settle a dispute over a notebook.

The course office has a separate file about timetable information. It says students should consult the portal for room changes and should contact the office if a posted room number is missing. My room number was posted. It changed once, from Studio 2 to Studio 4, and the portal displayed the revised number. I wrote the change in the planner. The department did not promise that the planner would update itself, which is fortunate because the planner has no network connection.

A sales assistant asked whether I wanted the optional vinyl name label. I declined. The receipt records no name-label charge. I also declined the gift wrapping, which would have been a strange way to package a planner that I had purchased for my own use. The shop did not charge for either option. The total on the receipt matches the displayed shelf price and the tax line printed below it. I am not asking the school to adjust that total.

There is one genuinely useful detail that deserves mention: the back cover lists the bookstore’s returns information in readable type. It says unopened planners may be returned within the stated period, while used planners may be reviewed individually. I have used this planner, have no plan to send it back, and did not ask the bookstore to make an exception. If that sounds ungrateful, it may be because customer-service language has taught us to treat every opinion as the beginning of a negotiation. This is simply a product review, submitted because the form asked for one.

Final rating: four stars out of five. The planner does what it says, with the exception of providing more course-code boxes than it provides. I recommend it to students with six or fewer course codes and a willingness to print one extra sheet. I am not seeking reimbursement, a return, a replacement, or a special exchange. I want the review stored under product feedback, not under refund claims. The difference should be straightforward even to a filing system that has had coffee.

Archive note: review verified by the student; no return transaction opened. The bookstore’s automatic follow-up may still arrive, since the system’s sense of timing is more aspirational than its filing accuracy.

To the course office,

Please put this in the file for the evening drawing course. I am writing it out because the online form keeps making me choose a category before it lets me explain the thing, and I do not know whether “room,” “registration,” or “miscellaneous sigh” is the right category. The room change is the only matter I am asking about. The posted sheet on Monday said Room 11. The sheet pinned up on Tuesday said Room 14. I saw both sheets, so there is no mystery about why I went to Room 14 on Tuesday evening. That is the room number I am requesting for the next class meeting, if Room 14 remains the assigned room.

I am not asking to withdraw. I am not cancelling my enrollment, and I do not want the office to remove me from the course list. Someone has crossed out the word “enroll” on the old paper copy and written “cancel?” in the margin. That is not my handwriting and is not what I asked. Please leave the enrollment record alone. I intend to attend the next class. The note is about the location, not whether I plan to study drawing. If attendance takes place in a different room again, I will check the new notice before walking there. This is not a request for a guaranteed permanent room; it is a request to confirm which room is currently posted.

I received the course materials list. It says that drawing paper is supplied in class and that students should bring pencils. I have pencils. I have not asked for a reimbursement for paper, and I have not claimed that the course charged me for materials. The list says the course fee covers the paper used during class. I have not paid an additional paper fee because no additional paper fee appears on the receipt. The small amount marked “studio materials” is already included in the published course charge. I am not disputing that line. I merely want to know where the class meets.

The notice on the door was easy enough to read. It had the correct course title and the Tuesday time. It did not say that class was cancelled. It did not say that students should stay home. It said, in plain letters, “Drawing Foundations, Tuesday, 6:00 p.m., Room 14.” I copied the room number onto this note because the office’s old timetable still shows Room 11. The posted notice is newer than the old timetable, and the course assistant said that students should follow the posted notice while the timetable is being updated. That sounds sensible. It would be even more useful if the old timetable were updated before the next person finds it.

A friend told me that the office might be able to reserve Room 14 for the rest of the term. I have not asked for that reservation. I do not know whether the room is free every week, and I would rather not have the office promise a room it cannot provide. I am asking only for confirmation of the room listed for the next class. If the course has already moved again, please write the current room number on the reply slip. A brief answer will do. I am not asking anyone to write a history of the building’s room allocation system, though it would probably make a more interesting story than the course brochure.

I did attend the class on Tuesday in Room 14. The instructor took attendance, and my name was on the sheet. This note is not an attendance appeal. There is no missing attendance mark that I know of. I am not reporting that the instructor failed to appear. The instructor was there before the students and opened the room. The class began on time. The chalk was low, but the instructor had a spare piece, and nobody was required to file a separate incident report about it.

The office receptionist told me that room confirmations are usually sent by email. I checked my inbox and found the course welcome message, the materials list, and a reminder about the first assignment. I did not find a newer room confirmation. The absence of that email does not mean that the course has been cancelled. The door notice is still the latest information I have. This is why I am leaving the note: to ask the office to confirm the current location, rather than to guess which paper is meant to be authoritative.

At the bottom of the original note, there is a line written in smaller letters: “If anyone is filing this under withdrawal, please stop; that is not what this says.” The line is underlined once. The handwriting is consistent with the rest of the note. There is also a doodle of a chair with a number 14 written on it. I assume this is a reminder, not a request for new furniture. The office does not need to order a chair, and I have not asked for one.

Please reply on the blank half-sheet attached. A room number and confirmation that I remain enrolled would be enough. The enrollment confirmation is included only because the crossed-out annotation made me worry that someone might misunderstand the note. I am not asking to be re-enrolled; I never left the course. If the office needs to file the note under a category, “room confirmation” seems closer than “withdrawal,” “refund,” or “materials complaint.”

Thank you. I know the course office handles many changes. It is impressive that a building with so many rooms can still make one room number feel like a literary plot. I would prefer the practical ending: tell me where to go, and I will go there.

The school’s bookkeeping system has placed the pages in a single file, presumably because paper is cheaper than a filing cabinet with standards.

The scholarship adjustment is applied to tuition. It does not remove the student’s obligation for the other listed services. The total is calculated as $360 + $28 + $12 + $15 + $0 − $60 = $355. There is no delivery charge. The workbook was issued at the first class meeting, and the portal access was activated on the same day. The invoice does not include an exam retake, a late fee, a parking permit, or a private tutoring session. Each of those items has a separate price list, but none was ordered or added to this account.

Payment instructions state that the student may pay by card, bank transfer, or cashier’s desk. A payment is considered received only when the account screen displays “posted.” A saved card is not, by itself, a payment. An authorization that later expires is not, by itself, a payment. The account screen included in this packet displays “posted payment: $355.00” on 11 October. The balance field reads $0.00. The invoice remains in the packet because the accounting office keeps the original invoice beside its settlement record. This is a filing practice, not a sign that the student still owes the invoiced amount.

Account note entered by the cashier: “Full invoice amount received, applied to TA-2086. No remaining balance. Student asked whether the scholarship changed the due date; advised that it changed the amount only. Due date remains 20 October for any balance that might otherwise have remained.” The cashier did not state that Nadia owed another $60. The scholarship adjustment reduced the original $415 subtotal by $60, leaving $355 due. The $355 payment was posted, so the account is settled.

A printed email from the program coordinator is attached. It says the evening course runs on Thursdays and that students should bring the workbook to the first workshop. Nadia attended the first workshop and received the workbook. The coordinator also mentions that a student may request a second workbook copy at the bookstore price if the first is lost. Nadia did not request a second copy. The invoice records one workbook, not two. The attached course calendar includes a discussion about optional supplementary exercises, but no charge is attached to those exercises. They are downloadable from the portal at no cost.

The office’s payment-status screen shows a sequence of events. On 8 October, a card attempt was authorized and then reversed before posting. On 9 October, a saved payment method appeared on the account. On 11 October, a card payment for $355.00 posted successfully. The earlier authorization was not a second payment and did not leave an extra credit. The screen’s final balance is zero. A student who reads only the word “authorized” might imagine the bill was paid on 8 October, but the status line for that attempt says “reversed, not posted.” The successful payment is the later posted transaction.

The invoice terms explain that course withdrawals before the first meeting are eligible for a tuition adjustment, while workbook and portal charges are assessed only if those items were issued or activated. This section is included as standard wording. Nadia did not withdraw. The attendance sheet shows that she joined the course, and the portal record shows that her account was active. The student services note says Nadia asked for a receipt for her records. The cashier generated a receipt after the payment posted and sent it to her school address. The note also says she asked whether the activity credit was free. The answer was yes: its invoice amount is zero. It was included in the line list because the course system reports all student account entries, including entries that cost nothing. The accounting office has not charged Nadia for the zero-dollar credit.

The attached bookstore slip lists the workbook as issued, price $28.00, paid through the course account. There is no separate cash payment at the bookstore and no second workbook. The slip is marked “student copy provided.” That label means a copy of the slip was provided to the student; it does not mean the student received a second workbook. The payment receipt and the invoice are both in this packet for exactly that reason.

The course office has apparently decided that one document can be a review, a service record, and a cautionary tale about labels. The text below distinguishes what Quentin said from what the office recorded.

Review submitted by Quentin

“The green field notebook is sturdy enough for a school bag and has a useful grid on each page. I used it during our food systems observation exercise. The cover is plain, which is a virtue if one prefers stationery not to announce its ambitions. The paper handled pencil and ballpoint ink well. I did not test it with watercolor, because the product description does not claim to be a watercolor pad and I have other things to do.

“I bought one notebook at the campus shop. The checkout receipt says one item, and that is what I took home. I have not bought a second one. The item was not missing from the parcel, because there was no parcel: I picked it up at the counter. It was not damaged when I bought it. The cover has a small crease now, after being carried around for several weeks. That is ordinary wear, not a reason to describe the shop as having sold me a broken notebook.

“The product page says the notebook includes a contents page and numbered sheets. Mine has both. I have not counted every page, because counting pages is not a hobby I have acquired. The contents page has space for topic, date, and page number. This is useful for locating notes later, assuming one has written the topic down. The grid is light gray rather than dark black. I can read it, and it does not interfere with the text. Someone in class said it looked faint. That person was speaking about their own notebook, not making a report on mine.

“I am not asking for a refund. I am keeping the notebook and intend to use it for the remaining course exercises. The review form asks whether I would recommend it. I selected yes for students who want a simple field notebook. I did not select the option requesting a return label. If the shop sends a return label anyway, it will have produced an interesting amount of paper to accompany the paper I already bought.

“The only improvement I would suggest is a slightly larger label on the inside cover for the student’s name. The current label is small but usable. The product does not claim to include a name printed by the school. I wrote my name on it myself. The bookstore did not promise personalized printing, and I did not pay for such a service. The course office did not ask me to return the notebook after the exercise.”

Course record

The notebook was used in a class exercise about observing how students organize notes from a sample food market. Students were asked to record fictional products and fictional prices supplied on a worksheet. No one was asked to record personal shopping information. Quentin’s worksheet shows notes about three sample products. The assignment was submitted on the course portal and marked received. The notebook itself was not collected by the instructor; students kept their materials.

The course outline lists a printed worksheet, a notebook, and a pencil as suggested supplies. The worksheet was handed out in class. The notebook was optional, and students could use loose paper instead. Quentin purchased the notebook voluntarily. The course fee did not include a notebook charge. The campus shop receipt is a separate retail receipt, not an additional course invoice. The course office has no record of charging Quentin for a second notebook or for a replacement.

A classmate’s message, attached for context, says: “My notebook arrived with the wrong cover color, and I asked the shop about an exchange.” The classmate’s message concerns a different purchase and a different student. Quentin’s review says that his own notebook had a green cover and was picked up at the shop counter. The office has not transferred the classmate’s exchange request to Quentin’s account. The fact that both records use the word “notebook” is not a reason to merge them, though the archive software has tried.

Shop receipt information

The receipt lists one campus field notebook, green cover, at the displayed shelf price. It also lists the standard tax amount. The quantity is one. No shipping fee, gift wrap, name-label service, replacement charge, or refund appears on the receipt. The amount charged matches the displayed price and tax. The receipt was handed to Quentin at checkout. The shop’s point-of-sale record shows the purchase completed and no return transaction afterward.

The shop’s general returns notice says unopened merchandise may be returned with a receipt within the stated period. The notice is standard text and does not mean Quentin has requested a return. His notebook has been used in class. His review explicitly says he is keeping it and is not asking for money back. The returns notice has not created a pending claim. The shop staff entered the review into the product feedback file, not the returns queue.

Course office follow-up

A course assistant saw the product review and asked whether the student needed another notebook. Quentin replied: “No, I have the one I bought, and it is fine. I was reviewing that item, not reporting a shortage.” The assistant marked the materials check complete. The assistant did not place a new shop order, issue a voucher, or promise that the school would provide a different notebook. The course office has not made a replacement request on Quentin’s behalf.

The assistant’s brief entry says the review was positive overall, with a minor suggestion about the name label. The entry does not record a complaint about the notebook being unusable. It does not say the student received the wrong product. It does not say the student was charged twice. The assistant marked “student has needed materials” because Quentin had the notebook and had submitted the exercise. The class does not require students to submit the notebook itself.

End-of-term note

The final course activity will use a new worksheet distributed in class. Students may continue using the same notebook or choose any other paper. Quentin has not asked the office to reserve a new notebook, send one by mail, or reimburse the original purchase. The course office will not deduct the notebook price from his account, because the course did not bill him for it. The shop will retain the receipt record according to its normal accounting schedule.

The archive clerk reviewed the records after a system prompt flagged the words “refund,” “return,” and “replacement.” Those words appear in the review because Quentin clearly says he does not want a refund or return and describes no replacement need. The prompt is a search aid, not a decision. The clerk left the case in the product-review folder. The student’s actual position is not difficult to find, provided one reads the sentences rather than treating every noun as a request.

Final file summary: one green notebook purchased, one notebook retained, product review submitted, no refund requested, no replacement requested, no course charge for the notebook, and no unresolved materials issue. The feedback may be used by the campus shop when considering future stock. No other action is pending.
