Tidewater Software — CI incident postmortem and customer file

Incident ID: CI-4821
Service: Build Harbor, our hosted continuous-integration runner and artifact service
Incident date: 14 May
Prepared for: Engineering, support, and finance
Customer: Kestrel Studio
Severity: SEV-2
Status: Resolved; follow-up work in progress

Executive summary

On 14 May, a change to Build Harbor’s artifact-indexing worker caused some completed pipeline runs to display stale status and made a subset of their downloadable artifacts unavailable for about two hours. Kestrel Studio’s release pipeline was among the affected workloads. The customer could still see the pipeline’s job logs, but the release package was not listed on the run’s artifact page. The release team had to pause its planned deployment while our engineers restored the index and verified the package checksum.

The incident was not a data breach. We found no evidence that one customer could read another customer’s artifacts, that source code was exposed, or that artifacts were permanently deleted. The package in question remained in object storage; the index used to locate it had been written incorrectly. The indexing worker was rolled back, and a repair job rebuilt affected index records from the stored run manifests.

Kestrel Studio was understandably angry. Its team had reserved a deployment window, spent time rerunning jobs, and received a confusing green status for a run whose artifact page was incomplete. Our first support response was too confident about the cause and did not explain what we had verified. We regret both the interruption and the poor communication.

This document records the timeline, evidence, impact, contributing factors, corrective work, customer correspondence, and the invoice extract associated with the support case. The attached correspondence and billing extract are included as records; they do not alter the technical findings in the postmortem.

Customer and system context

Kestrel Studio uses Build Harbor to test and package a developer tool called Lantern CLI. Its ordinary workflow has a commit-triggered validation pipeline, a packaging pipeline, and a release approval step. A successful build stores a package and a manifest. The run page reads status from the job service, while the artifact page retrieves its list from a separate index. That separation is intentional: it allows the job service to update quickly without waiting for artifact scanning. It also means that a green job status does not, by itself, prove that every artifact has been indexed and made visible.

The relevant pipeline has four steps. First, it checks out a pinned revision. Second, it runs tests on a Linux runner. Third, it packages the tested revision and writes a manifest containing the object key and checksum. Fourth, the indexing worker reads the manifest and records the artifact in the customer-facing index. A release operator then downloads the package and checks the checksum before approval. During this incident, the first three steps completed. The indexing worker acknowledged the fourth step but produced an index entry with a malformed partition key. The artifact page consequently showed no package for the run.

The customer’s deployment process requires a visible artifact entry before the release operator can proceed. The team does not deploy directly from a runner’s temporary workspace. That safeguard worked as intended: no unverified package was promoted. It also meant the missing index entry blocked the planned deployment even though the package itself was still stored.

Timeline

All times below are UTC on 14 May unless otherwise noted. Times were taken from service logs and the support case. They are approximate to the nearest minute where an event spans multiple systems.

08:42 — The artifact-indexing worker version 3.18.0 began deployment to the first production region. The release contained a refactor to partition-key construction and a metrics-label cleanup.

08:51 — The deployment reached all production workers. Health checks passed. The checks verified that processes were running and could contact storage; they did not verify that a newly indexed artifact could be retrieved through the customer-facing page.

09:03 — Kestrel Studio’s Lantern CLI validation run began. The runner checked out the requested commit and started the test suite.

09:17 — Unit and integration tests completed successfully. The job service recorded the run as successful.

09:18 — The packaging step wrote the package object and manifest to storage. The manifest contained the correct object key and checksum.

09:19 — The indexing worker consumed the manifest. Its log recorded a successful acknowledgement, but the partition key was malformed. The worker did not raise an error because the refactor treated a missing optional label as an empty string. The index write therefore succeeded in a partition the artifact page did not query.

09:24 — Kestrel Studio’s release operator opened the run page. The run showed green, but the artifact panel was empty. The operator refreshed the page twice and confirmed the artifact remained absent.

09:31 — A Kestrel Studio engineer reran the packaging job. The rerun produced a second stored package and the same indexing symptom. The customer did not approve either package for deployment.

09:38 — The customer opened support case KS-7714, reporting that “the green build has no download, and we cannot ship from a green checkmark that points at nothing.” The case requested an explanation and asked whether charges for the failed release attempt would be reversed. The case did not ask for a cash refund.

09:46 — Support acknowledged the report. The initial reply said the package “should appear shortly” before the team had confirmed the state of the index. That statement was premature. The reply also asked the customer to rerun the job, despite the case already noting that a rerun had not helped.

10:02 — The on-call engineer compared the job record, manifest, and storage object. The object existed and its checksum matched the manifest. The artifact index lookup returned no visible entry for the run.

10:11 — The on-call engineer found malformed partition keys in a sample of recent writes. The issue affected manifests processed by worker version 3.18.0 when the optional repository label was absent from a particular event shape.

10:19 — The incident commander declared SEV-2 and paused further worker releases. The response team began a rollback and prepared a repair query.

10:34 — Worker version 3.17.4 was restored in production. New manifests began indexing normally. The rollback did not itself repair entries already written to the wrong partition.

10:41 — The team ran a scoped query for manifests processed during the affected interval. The query identified 26 entries with malformed partition keys across three customer workspaces. The entries were still backed by stored objects and manifests.

10:55 — A repair job rebuilt the affected index records from the manifests. The job wrote records using the previous, validated key format and logged each repaired run identifier.

11:12 — The repair job completed. Internal checks confirmed that all 26 identified artifacts could be found through the expected index lookup.

11:24 — Support asked Kestrel Studio to refresh the artifact page. The customer confirmed that the package appeared and that its checksum matched the manifest.

11:37 — Kestrel Studio completed its own verification and resumed release review. The deployment window had already been missed, so the team moved its rollout to the next available window.

12:06 — The incident commander confirmed that the queue was draining normally and that no new malformed keys had appeared after rollback.

13:15 — The response team finished checking adjacent regions and found no evidence of the same malformed-key pattern outside the identified interval.

15:20 — Support sent a corrected update explaining that the package had remained in storage, the index record had been repaired, and the customer had verified the checksum. The update acknowledged that the earlier “should appear shortly” message was not supported by the investigation at that time.

16:10 — The incident was marked resolved. Follow-up actions remained open.

Impact and scope

For Kestrel Studio, the visible impact was a missing package entry and a delayed release. Its engineers spent time rerunning a packaging job and checking the run manifest. The team did not lose its source code or package object, and it did not deploy an unverified package. It missed the deployment window it had reserved for 14 May. We have no basis to claim a specific monetary loss from that delay.

Across Build Harbor, 26 artifact-index records from three customer workspaces were affected. Every identified object remained present in storage. The issue prevented normal discovery through the artifact page; it did not remove the underlying object. No customer reported an unauthorized download, and our access logs showed no cross-workspace reads associated with the incident. We found no evidence of data exposure.

A separate dashboard showed 31 runs with delayed status updates during the same general period. That dashboard number is not the number of affected artifacts: some runs had no artifact, and some were delayed for unrelated queue reasons. The verified count of malformed artifact-index entries was 26. We are keeping these counts separate to avoid overstating the incident.

Detection

We did not detect the problem through our deployment health checks. Those checks confirmed process availability, queue connectivity, and successful writes at the storage API layer. They did not perform a full write-then-read verification using the same lookup path the customer-facing artifact page uses. As a result, the worker could report a successful write even when the resulting record was invisible to the expected lookup.

The first reliable signal came from Kestrel Studio’s support case. Our general latency dashboard showed no severe increase because the worker was acknowledging events promptly. The error-rate dashboard also remained green because the write operation itself returned success. A query against the index later revealed the mismatch, but we had not yet turned that query into an alert.

The run page’s green status contributed to confusion. It correctly represented successful test and packaging jobs, but customers reasonably expect the artifact panel to reflect the completed release workflow. Our interface did not make clear that artifact indexing was a separate completion stage. We will address both monitoring and presentation rather than treating the issue as merely a customer misunderstanding.

Technical cause

Version 3.18.0 refactored how the indexing worker assembled a partition key. The old code used a validated repository identifier stored directly on the manifest. The new code constructed a composite key from the repository label in the event and a region identifier. For the event shape emitted by Kestrel Studio’s pipeline, the optional repository label was absent. The refactor converted the absent value to an empty string instead of using the manifest’s validated repository identifier.

The storage API accepted the resulting key, so the write succeeded. The artifact page queried using the validated repository identifier and the region identifier, which did not match the malformed key. The record was therefore present but not visible through the standard query. The manifest and object were correct; the derived index key was not.

The defect was not caused by an incorrect customer configuration. The customer used a supported pipeline and an ordinary manifest shape. The worker should have treated the optional label as optional and fallen back to the manifest’s required repository identifier. It did not.

Why testing missed it

Unit tests covered keys with a populated repository label and keys with an explicitly empty label. They did not cover a missing label, which is a distinct input in the event decoder. The refactor’s test fixtures always included the label because they were copied from a repository that emits it on every run.

The staging smoke test used a pipeline that populated the optional label. It verified that a record could be written and retrieved for that one shape. It did not exercise the customer’s event shape or test missing-field behavior. The deployment gate measured worker health and queue consumption, not end-to-end artifact visibility.

Our review focused on the metrics-label cleanup and the reduction in duplicate parsing. The partition-key change was described as an implementation detail, and reviewers did not request a compatibility table for event shapes. That was a review gap. The code was small, but its effect crossed the boundary between event decoding, storage indexing, and customer-facing lookup.

Contributing factors

First, the event schema permits the repository label to be absent, while the index key requires a repository identifier. The relationship between those fields was documented in code comments but not enforced by the schema or a runtime validation check.

Second, the storage API’s success response indicated that a record had been accepted, not that the record was retrievable using the customer-facing lookup. We treated the former as evidence for the latter.

Third, the artifact panel and job status were presented together without explaining that they came from separate stages. A green run with no visible artifact looked contradictory to the customer, even though the job service and index service were reporting different states.

Fourth, the first support reply asked for a rerun before reviewing the evidence in the case. The customer had already reported that a rerun did not help. The reply wasted time and weakened confidence in later updates.

Fifth, the repair procedure existed as an internal query but had not been exercised recently. The on-call engineer had to validate the query against a sample before running it across the affected interval. That was prudent, but it extended recovery.

What went well

The customer kept the package checksum and manifest available, which let both teams verify that the stored object was the expected build. The release operator did not bypass the artifact check or deploy from a temporary runner directory. The object store retained the package throughout the incident.

The on-call engineer compared the manifest, object, and index rather than assuming the green job status proved that the package had been lost. Once the malformed key pattern was identified, the team limited the repair to records created during the affected interval and verified each result through the normal lookup path.

The rollback stopped new malformed entries. The repair job operated from manifests, the source of truth for artifact metadata, rather than attempting to infer missing information from dashboard summaries. The incident response channel maintained a single incident commander and recorded decisions with timestamps.

What went poorly

Our health checks did not represent the customer’s end-to-end experience. We deployed a change that could pass process and storage health checks while breaking the lookup customers use to find artifacts.

Our initial customer message suggested that the artifact would appear shortly without evidence. It also proposed a rerun that the customer had already tried. The customer was entitled to a direct explanation and a clear statement of what we knew, what we did not know, and what we were checking.

The run page communicated success without clarifying that artifact indexing had not yet been verified. The product should not require customers to understand internal service boundaries in order to interpret a release run.

We also lacked a routine check that compared the count of manifests with the count of indexed artifacts over a short interval. Such a comparison would not have prevented the bad write, but it could have shortened detection time.

Corrective actions

Completed:

1. Rolled back artifact-indexing worker version 3.18.0.
2. Rebuilt the 26 affected index records from their manifests.
3. Verified that each identified artifact was retrievable through the normal customer-facing lookup.
4. Checked adjacent regions and confirmed that the same key pattern had not appeared there during the reviewed interval.
5. Sent Kestrel Studio a corrected incident update and acknowledged the inaccurate first reply.

In progress:

1. Add a required-field validation step that rejects an event lacking both the optional label and the validated manifest identifier. Owner: Build Harbor runtime team. Due: 24 May.
2. Add tests for absent, null, empty, and populated repository labels. The test must verify the resulting key and a read through the customer-facing lookup. Owner: indexing team. Due: 21 May.
3. Add a production canary that writes a synthetic manifest and confirms retrieval through the same query path used by the artifact page. Owner: reliability engineering. Due: 31 May.
4. Alert on a sustained difference between eligible manifests and visible indexed artifacts. The alert will distinguish delayed processing from a failed lookup. Owner: observability team. Due: 7 June.
5. Update the run page so that job completion and artifact availability are shown as separate statuses. Owner: developer experience team. Due: 14 June.
6. Add a release-review checklist item for changes to event fields used in partition keys. Owner: engineering productivity. Due: 28 May.
7. Exercise the artifact-index repair procedure in a staging environment and document the validation steps. Owner: on-call rotation. Due: 30 May.
8. Coach support responders to acknowledge what a customer has already tried before recommending a rerun. Owner: support operations. Due: 20 May.

We will close actions only after the owner attaches evidence of the test, alert, or interface change. A task being assigned is not the same as a task being completed. We will review open actions at the next reliability meeting and publish a customer-facing update if a due date changes materially.

Customer correspondence excerpt

09:38 — Yara Novak, Kestrel Studio: “The Lantern build is green but the download panel is empty. We already reran packaging and got the same blank panel. We have a release slot today and this is wasting everyone’s time. Please tell us whether the package is gone or only missing from the page. Also, can you reverse charges for the failed release attempt? We are not asking you to send money back; we want to know whether the run charge will be credited.”

09:46 — Support: “Thanks for the report. The artifact should appear shortly. Please try rerunning the job.”

10:07 — Yara Novak: “That is exactly what we said we already did. ‘Should’ is not an answer. Please check the actual object and index before telling us to repeat work.”

10:22 — Support engineer: “You are right. We are checking the stored object and its index record now. We cannot yet confirm whether the object is missing.”

11:29 — Yara Novak: “The artifact is visible after your repair. We downloaded it and the checksum matches our manifest. We still lost the reserved deployment window, and the first answer made this more frustrating than it needed to be.”

15:20 — Support engineer: “We confirmed that the package remained in storage and that its index entry was repaired. We are sorry for the interruption and for asking you to rerun a job you had already rerun. The billing team will review the run charges under the service-credit terms; this message is not a promise of a cash refund.”

The correspondence is reproduced to preserve the order and wording of the exchange. The first customer message explicitly says the customer is not asking for money to be sent back; the customer asks whether a run charge will be credited. The later support note likewise distinguishes a service-credit review from a cash refund.

Invoice extract: Kestrel Studio, May developer tooling usage

Invoice reference: KS-MAY-204
Currency: USD
Status: Issued; one service-credit review pending

Line items:

1. Build Harbor Linux runner time, 42 minutes at $0.20 per minute: $8.40.
2. Build Harbor Linux runner time, 18 minutes at $0.20 per minute: $3.60.
3. Artifact storage, 6 GB-month at $0.50 per GB-month: $3.00.
4. Log retention, 2 GB-month at $0.75 per GB-month: $1.50.
5. Managed support plan, monthly fixed fee: $120.00.
6. Service-credit review requested for the affected release runs: pending; no credit has been applied on this invoice.

Subtotal for posted charges: $136.50.
Tax: $0.00.
Amount currently due: $136.50.
Cash refund issued: none.

The invoice lists two runner-time entries because two packaging attempts were recorded. It does not say that either charge has been reversed. The pending line is a review status, not a completed credit. The invoice extract is included because the customer asked about run charges; it does not change what the customer said in the correspondence.

Operational notes

The response team preserved the affected worker logs, event payloads, manifests, index query results, and repair-job output. Access to those records was limited to the incident responders. The payloads used for the investigation contained identifiers required to trace the runs; the postmortem omits those identifiers because they are not needed to understand the failure.

The team compared three independent records for Kestrel Studio’s first run: the job record, which showed tests and packaging completed; the manifest, which named the package and checksum; and the object store, which returned the package with the same checksum. The index lookup was the only failing link. This distinction mattered. If we had immediately treated the missing page entry as proof of a missing package, we could have given the customer an inaccurate explanation and needlessly repeated work.

The repair job did not alter package contents. It regenerated index metadata from the manifest and wrote a record using the validated key format. After repair, the customer-facing page returned the package, and the downloaded checksum matched the manifest. These checks support our conclusion that the package remained intact and that the incident was limited to index visibility.

The 26 affected records were identified by querying worker version and event time, then checking for the malformed partition pattern. The team also reviewed records immediately before and after the deployment interval. Records created by the previous worker version used the expected key format. Records created after rollback also used the expected format. We did not count all delayed runs as affected index entries; the two measures describe different things.

We did not infer customer impact from a single dashboard. The dashboard’s 31 delayed status updates included runs that had no artifact to index and runs delayed by queue congestion. We used the manifest-to-index comparison to determine the count of malformed artifact entries. The verified total was 26 across three workspaces. We cannot conclude from the 31 count that 31 artifacts were unavailable.

Review of release and change process

The change passed peer review and the standard automated checks. Those controls were insufficient for this class of change. A partition key is effectively part of the interface between the writer and reader, even if it is represented as an internal string. A successful write to storage is not enough: the record must be addressable by the same identity and lookup rules used by the reader.

The pull request described the refactor as replacing repeated parsing with a shared helper. It included a metrics-label change and a partition-key construction change in the same patch. The patch was not unusually large, but the review description did not call out that the key construction had changed. Reviewers consequently concentrated on whether metrics remained stable and whether the helper reduced duplicated code.

We will require pull requests that change key construction to identify the writer and reader paths, list the supported input shapes, and show a write-then-read test. This is not meant to replace engineering judgment with a form. The goal is to make the compatibility boundary visible to reviewers and to ensure that the relevant behavior is tested.

The deployment system used a staged rollout, but the canary signal was process health and queue throughput. Because the malformed key still allowed a successful write, those measurements did not indicate a fault. Future canaries must include a retrieval check. A canary that only proves the worker is alive does not prove the artifact workflow is healthy.

The artifact page’s data model also needs improvement. Today, the page receives job completion and artifact-list data from separate services. When the job is green and the artifact list is empty, the page has no explanatory state distinguishing “there are no artifacts,” “indexing is still in progress,” and “an expected artifact could not be found.” The redesign will show a distinct artifact-indexing status and a timestamp for the last successful lookup. The page will not claim that a package is available until the artifact lookup has succeeded.

Customer communication review

The customer’s first report included two important facts: the team had already rerun packaging, and the team wanted to know whether the charge would be credited. Our first reply did not reflect either fact. It gave an unsupported expectation and asked for an action that had already failed. We should have said that the report was being investigated, that we did not yet know whether the package object existed, and when the customer could expect the next update.

The second support reply was more accurate because it separated verified facts from unknowns. We had not yet confirmed the object’s state at 10:22, so the responder correctly said it was still being checked. Once the object and manifest were compared, we could report that the object existed and that the index was being investigated. We should not state a conclusion before checking the relevant records.

The customer’s comment about a “green checkmark that points at nothing” was an expression of frustration, not a literal claim that the page contained no checkmark. The run did show green. The artifact panel was empty. Both details are reflected above. The postmortem does not treat the customer’s criticism as evidence that the tests failed; the test jobs passed, while artifact discovery failed.

The customer’s request about billing must also be represented accurately. The message asked whether run charges would be credited and explicitly said the customer was not asking for money to be sent back. The invoice shows no cash refund and no completed credit at the time it was issued. A later review may determine whether a service credit is appropriate, but a pending review is not an applied credit.

Risks and prevention

The primary risk from this incident was a release delay caused by an artifact that could not be found through the normal interface. A secondary risk was that a green run could encourage someone to assume a package was ready even when the artifact page was empty. Kestrel Studio’s approval process prevented an unverified deployment. We are not relying on every customer having the same safeguard; the product must report artifact availability accurately.

A separate risk is overcorrection. A broad repair process that rewrites every index entry could introduce a new mismatch or obscure the original evidence. The team therefore scoped the repair to records matching the affected worker version and time interval, used manifests as the metadata source, and verified reads after writing. The same approach will be captured in the runbook.

Another risk is confusing a service credit with a cash refund. Support and finance must use the terms consistently. A service credit reduces a future or current service balance according to the applicable terms; it is not the same as sending money back. No credit was applied in the invoice extract, and no cash refund was issued. The customer’s wording and the invoice status will remain separate facts in the case record.

We also need to avoid conflating the affected artifact count with the delayed status-update count. The 26 figure came from records with malformed keys. The 31 figure came from a dashboard of delayed status updates. They overlap only partially and have different definitions. Future incident summaries should state the measure and its source each time a number is used.

Appendix A: glossary

Artifact: A file or package produced by a pipeline and retained for later retrieval.

Manifest: Metadata written by a packaging job that identifies an artifact object and its checksum.

Artifact index: A lookup structure that allows the customer-facing page to find artifacts from their run identifiers and repository information.

Partition key: A derived value used to organize index records. The writer and reader must construct compatible keys.

Run status: The status reported by the job service for execution steps such as tests and packaging. It is not a substitute for confirming artifact availability.

Service credit: An account adjustment handled under service terms. It is distinct from a cash refund.

Canary: A limited verification of a deployed change. In this incident, the former canary checked process health and queue behavior but did not check artifact retrieval.

Appendix B: evidence reviewed

The incident commander reviewed the worker deployment record, worker version logs, event-decoder output, storage write acknowledgements, manifests, object metadata, index query results, repair-job output, and the customer support thread. Engineering also reviewed the test fixtures and the pull-request summary. Finance reviewed the invoice extract to confirm that its displayed status matched the billing ledger at the time the extract was generated.

The storage object and manifest for Kestrel Studio’s package had matching checksums. The standard artifact lookup returned no record before repair. The repair job wrote the record using the validated key, and the standard lookup returned the artifact afterward. The customer independently confirmed that the downloaded package checksum matched the manifest. These observations support the conclusion that the object was intact but not discoverable through the expected index query.

The worker logs showed that the malformed key was created when the repository label was absent. The event decoder represented that field as missing; the refactored helper converted it to an empty value rather than using the required manifest identifier. The storage API accepted the resulting key. The reader continued to use the validated identifier. This explains how a write could be reported as successful while the customer-facing lookup returned no artifact.

The case record showed that Kestrel Studio had already rerun packaging before the first support reply. The reply nevertheless asked the customer to rerun. The customer then objected to being asked to repeat work and asked support to check the object and index. The correspondence records a request to review run charges for a service credit and expressly disclaims a request for money to be sent back.

Appendix C: operational checklist after the incident

Before approving a release, the on-call engineer checks that the worker version is the expected version, the synthetic canary can write and retrieve an artifact, and no manifest-to-index discrepancy alert is active. If the canary fails, the engineer pauses rollout rather than treating process health as sufficient evidence.

When a customer reports a missing artifact, support records whether the customer has already refreshed or rerun the job. Support does not recommend repeating an action without checking the case history. The responder distinguishes among a missing object, a present object with a missing index entry, and an indexing delay. If the state is not known, the responder says so and gives a time for the next update.

When investigating a billing question, support records the customer’s actual request and does not convert a request for a service credit review into a request for a cash refund. Finance confirms whether any credit has been applied before the customer is told that a charge was reversed. A pending review is described as pending.

When repairing index records, engineering identifies the affected time window and worker version, uses manifests as the source for artifact metadata, preserves the original query results, and verifies retrieval after repair. The repair is not considered complete solely because the write call returned success. A read through the customer-facing query is required.

Appendix D: unresolved questions and limits

The postmortem does not assign a dollar value to the missed deployment window. Kestrel Studio reported that it lost its reserved slot, but we do not have a verified financial estimate. The invoice shows posted service charges and a pending service-credit review; it does not calculate consequential loss.

The investigation found no evidence of cross-workspace access. That is a statement about the logs and records reviewed, not a claim that every conceivable access path was exhaustively tested. The incident was an index-visibility defect, and the observed requests did not show unauthorized reads.

The 26 repaired entries are the verified records matching the malformed-key signature in the reviewed interval. The 31 delayed status updates are a broader dashboard count. We do not treat those numbers as interchangeable and do not infer that all 31 runs had missing artifacts.

We have not yet completed all preventive actions. The rollback and repair are complete, but the end-to-end canary, discrepancy alert, event-shape tests, and interface updates remain assigned work. This report will be amended if later testing changes the scope or technical explanation.

Closing statement

Kestrel Studio used a supported pipeline, and the package it produced remained intact. Our indexing change made the artifact unavailable through the normal page, our checks failed to catch the mismatch, and our first response did not respect the information the customer had already provided. The issue was resolved by rollback and index repair. We are responsible for improving the detection, the product status, and the way we communicate during an investigation. The customer’s question about charges was a request to know whether run costs would be credited, not a request for a cash refund. The invoice extract records that no credit had been applied and no refund had been issued at the time shown.

Small-shop web form submission, handwritten-style note typed up, and FAQ excerpt: Larkspur Health order review

This packet was assembled by the front desk at a small manufacturing shop after a customer asked us to keep the web form, the note that came in with a returned carton, and the relevant FAQ excerpt together. The packet is long because the shop keeps a running account of what happened, which work areas were involved, what staff checked, and which details were merely background. It is not a bill, a promise, or a statement that every process described below applies to every customer. It is a record of this particular inquiry and a collection of explanatory notes written in a conversational style. The customer’s own form answers are copied near the beginning, and the typed note is reproduced later. Staff have tried to keep the distinction between the customer’s words and the shop’s comments clear. When an entry says “the customer wrote,” it refers to the customer’s message, not to an interpretation by an employee. When an entry says “shop note,” it is a staff observation.

The manufacturing shop makes short runs of machined brackets, small instrument stands, protective covers, and custom mounting plates. It has a front counter, a cutting bench, a finishing area, a packing table, and a small office with the order files. It does not operate a large call center. One person may enter a web form, another may inspect a returned item, and a third may answer a question about the paperwork. That is why the packet retains some repetition: people often ask the same thing in different words, and the shop wants the record to be easy to follow even if someone reads only one section. The shop uses a simple order number, a customer name, and the date of each communication. The order number in this packet is LH-4826. It is a made-up internal reference used here to keep the pages together; it does not indicate a particular product category or a special service level.

WEB FORM SUBMISSION, received Tuesday, 14 May

Customer name: Wanjiru Petrov
Organization: Larkspur Health
Order reference: LH-4826
Best contact method: email
What are you contacting us about? Product question and order follow-up
Please describe the issue: “The small steel bracket set arrived yesterday. I counted the pieces and the order is complete. The finish looks as expected, and I don’t need a replacement. I’m writing because I want to know whether the mounting slots can be made a little wider on a future batch. For the set already delivered, I am not asking for a refund. I’m happy to keep it as it is. Please tell me whether a wider slot is possible for the next order, and whether there would be a setup charge.”
Are you requesting a refund for the order currently delivered? No
Are you requesting a replacement for the order currently delivered? No
Would you like to place a new order now? Not yet; I am only asking about a possible future change.
Anything else we should know? “The packing slip was easy to read. The box had a crease on one corner, but the brackets inside were fine. I mention the box only in case you are keeping packing notes. Please don’t treat that as a damage claim.”

The web form includes both a direct answer in a checkbox-style question and a longer explanation in the customer’s own words. The answer to the refund question is no. The longer explanation also says that the customer is not asking for a refund, is keeping the delivered set, and is asking about a possible future batch. The form’s mention of a crease on the carton is not a request for money back or a report that the goods are damaged. The customer explicitly says the pieces were fine and asks that the carton observation not be treated as a damage claim. This paragraph is a staff summary to help someone navigating the packet; it is not a new request from the customer.

The web form has a few other fields that are standard on every submission. The customer selected “small batch” from a menu listing sample quantity, small batch, production run, and unsure. She selected “email” rather than phone or postal mail. She did not attach a photograph because she says there was no product damage to photograph. The browser submitted the form once, and the order reference appeared in the correct field. A staff member checked the order reference against the shop’s register and found that it belongs to a completed delivery. The delivery entry says the set contained four steel brackets and that all four were packed. The customer’s own count agrees with the packing entry. The register has no open return authorization and no open refund request. This is ordinary bookkeeping context, not a separate customer statement.

The shop’s order desk often receives a mix of straightforward requests and comments that are not requests. A customer can point out a crease in a box without asking the shop to replace anything. A customer can ask whether a design change is feasible without having already ordered that change. A customer can say that an order is complete while still wanting help with a future product. The staff therefore reads the actual request rather than assuming that every mention of an item problem is a complaint or that every inquiry about a possible price is an order. For this form, the current order is complete and accepted as delivered; the open question concerns whether a wider mounting slot could be offered on a future batch and what setup charge, if any, might apply.

Internal intake note, Tuesday, 14 May, 10:20 a.m.: Wanjiru Petrov submitted a product question through the ordinary web form. Reply with the design team’s general information about slot widths and explain that setup charges depend on the drawing review. Do not open a return case. Do not send a refund form. The customer has plainly said that no refund is requested and that the delivered set is being kept. The box corner is mentioned for packing records only. Make sure any reply does not imply that a revised design has already been approved or that the customer has placed a second order.

The intake clerk wrote the note after comparing the web form with the completed-order register. The clerk did not change any customer answer. The clerk also noted that the shop’s usual route for a design question is to send it to the person who reviews drawings, rather than to the person who handles returns. The route is a work assignment only. It does not mean that the customer has approved a drawing, chosen a price, or asked to cancel anything. The form remains the source of the customer’s request.

A short message was sent to the design desk: “Please review whether the slot dimensions on the next version of LH-4826 could be adjusted. Customer asks about feasibility and a possible setup charge. Current delivered set is accepted; no refund or replacement requested.” The design desk acknowledged the message and put it in the regular queue. There was no production change that day. No material was cut, no machine was set up, and no new invoice was prepared. The shop keeps this distinction in the record because a question about a future batch should not be mistaken for an instruction to begin manufacturing one.

For clarity, the shop’s usual manufacturing sequence starts with a drawing review, then a written quotation if the proposed change affects labor or tooling, then customer approval, then scheduling. A customer may ask about any of those stages without having reached them. In this case, only the initial feasibility question was raised. A wider slot might be a simple adjustment on one machine, or it might affect how the bracket is held during cutting; the design desk has not yet decided. The shop does not guess at a charge before reviewing the drawing. The customer asked whether a charge would apply, so the reply should explain that a charge is possible and will be stated before any new work is approved. None of this changes the clear answer to the question about the current delivered order: the customer did not ask for a refund.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed up from the paper enclosed with the delivery paperwork

Tuesday afternoon, 14 May. Note from Wanjiru Petrov, typed by the front desk because the handwriting is slanted and the paper has a crease down the middle:

“Hi, I’m putting this in writing so the next person who looks at the order has the whole picture. The brackets are here, all four, and I have checked them. They fit the rack as ordered. I am not returning them. Please do not start a return or send a refund; I do not want either for this order. The only thing I wondered about is the slot width if I order another set later. I have not decided to order again, and I don’t want anyone to reserve machine time. I just need to know if you can quote an option with a wider slot when I am ready. The package had a bent corner, but nothing inside was bent. I am mentioning that because I saw it, not because I expect compensation. Thanks for taking the time to answer.”

The typed copy preserves the note’s meaning and order of information. The original paper includes a short greeting, a question mark after “later,” and a small sketch of a bracket with an arrow pointing to the slot. The sketch has no measurements. It is not a manufacturing drawing and cannot be used to set a machine. The note does not ask for a refund; in fact, it specifically says not to start a return or send one. It also says the brackets fit as ordered and that the customer is not returning them. The sketch supports the future design question, not a claim about the delivered pieces.

The front desk did not interpret the words “bent corner” as a bent bracket. The customer says the carton had a bent corner and then says that nothing inside was bent. The packing clerk’s delivery record likewise lists the brackets as packed without a damage notation. A crease or bend in a carton can matter for the shop’s packaging checks, so the observation is retained. It does not transform the message into a refund request. If the customer had reported that the brackets were bent or had asked for compensation, the route might have been different, but those are not the facts stated here.

A note from the person who typed the copy: I asked whether “another set later” meant that an order had already been placed. The customer said no; she is considering it only if the design change is feasible. She said she would contact the shop later if she wants a quotation. That brief clarification is consistent with the original web form, which says “possible future batch” and “not yet.” The current order remains closed in the order register. The shop has not treated the note as an order, a cancellation, a return request, or a complaint about the quality of the parts.

The paper note was placed in the file behind the web form. The order desk wrote the date and order reference at the top so a future reader could locate the matching delivery record. The customer’s handwriting appears relaxed and conversational rather than formal. Some sentences run into the next line, and the typed version adds punctuation for readability. The substance is unchanged: all four brackets arrived; the customer checked them; they fit; the customer is keeping them; no refund is wanted; the question is about a possible wider slot on a later order.

The shop has a habit of recording even small non-issues because the same details can be useful later. If a customer says a carton was creased but the contents were fine, the packing team can look for a pattern in how cartons are stacked. If several orders show the same corner damage, the shop may change a divider or add a guard. That kind of observation does not require a customer to request a remedy. Here the packing clerk marked “carton corner crease; product intact” in the weekly packing notebook. The clerk did not mark “return,” “refund,” “replacement,” or “product damage.” The notebook entry is a note for the packing team, not a decision about the customer’s design question.

The weekly packing notebook is used for modest operational improvements. It includes comments about tape, labels, carton sizes, how parts are wrapped, and whether a packing slip is easy to find. Staff are asked to describe what they actually saw, not to speculate about who caused a mark or whether a customer is dissatisfied. The entry for this delivery is one line. It does not imply that the carton crease caused an injury, made the parts unusable, delayed delivery, or created a financial loss. The customer’s message supplies the relevant details directly: the contents were fine, and the customer did not want compensation.

A new customer sometimes asks whether a change can be made and then assumes the shop will automatically update the existing parts. That is not how this shop works. The drawing review is separate from a completed order. A requested change is discussed, quoted if needed, and approved before work begins. The current delivered set remains built to the dimensions on the original approved drawing. The customer in this packet understands that distinction: she says the brackets fit as ordered and asks about another set later. The desk should answer the question without promising that a new dimension has already been entered into production.

FAQ EXCERPT, copied from the shop’s customer information sheet

Question: Can I ask about changing a dimension without placing a new order?

Answer: Yes. You can ask the shop whether a different dimension appears feasible before you place another order. Send a sketch or drawing if you have one, and tell us which dimension you would like reviewed. A sketch is helpful for a conversation but is not approval to manufacture. The design desk may ask for a measured drawing before it can provide a reliable quotation.

Question: Does asking about a possible change automatically alter an order that has already been delivered?

Answer: No. A delivered order is made to the drawing that was approved for that order. A question about a future change does not revise the old drawing, reopen a completed job, or create a new order. If you want a revised item, the shop will review the proposed change and explain any price or setup charge before you decide whether to proceed.

Question: What should I do if the package looks marked but the product is fine?

Answer: You may tell us what you noticed. A packaging observation helps us check our packing process. Please say whether the product itself is affected. A note about the carton alone is not a request for a refund or replacement. If you do want the shop to review damaged or missing parts, describe those parts and say what remedy you are seeking.

Question: When does the shop send a refund?

Answer: A refund is considered when a customer actually asks for one and the shop has reviewed the circumstances under its normal order process. Merely asking about a design, mentioning a package mark, or asking about a future price does not count as asking for a refund. If you do not want a refund, say so plainly; staff will not assume that you want one from an unrelated comment.

Question: Can the shop start revised work just because a customer asks whether it is possible?

Answer: No. A feasibility question is only a question. The customer must receive the shop’s response, decide whether to proceed, and approve the relevant quotation before new work is scheduled. The shop may offer more than one option, and the customer may decline all of them. No machine time is reserved merely because a question has been submitted.

This FAQ excerpt is included because the customer’s form and note raise exactly the distinction described in the second and fourth questions. The FAQ does not add a hidden policy or a special condition to the customer’s message. It uses ordinary language to explain that a question about a later design is not a refund request for an already delivered item. It also makes clear that an observation about packaging is not, by itself, a request for money or a replacement. The FAQ is a general reference; the customer’s own answers remain direct and specific.

ORDER DESK WORK LOG, Tuesday, 14 May

8:42 a.m. The web form arrived in the shared inbox. The notification displayed Larkspur Health, Wanjiru Petrov, and order LH-4826. The clerk opened the form and checked that the message included a usable email address. It did. No call was made because the customer selected email as the preferred contact method.

8:49 a.m. The clerk read the form once for the general topic and again for the requested action. The general topic was a possible change to a mounting slot. The current order was described as complete and acceptable. The refund field was marked no. The replacement field was marked no. The next-order field said “not yet.” The clerk noted that the carton observation was expressly not a damage claim.

9:03 a.m. The clerk looked up order LH-4826. The order entry showed four small steel brackets, packed Monday and delivered Tuesday. The record contained no shortage entry. There was no open return case and no open refund request. The clerk did not change the status of the completed order.

9:17 a.m. The clerk forwarded the design question to the drawing review queue. The forwarded summary said that the customer asks whether a wider slot can be considered for a future batch and wants to know whether setup may cost extra. The summary also said that the existing set is being kept and that no refund or replacement is requested. The forwarding message did not instruct the design desk to start production.

10:20 a.m. The clerk added the intake note included earlier in this packet. The note advised against opening a return case and against sending a refund form. The clerk did not ask a manager to approve money back because no such request had been made.

11:06 a.m. The design desk acknowledged receipt. The acknowledgement said it would review the drawing when a suitable person was available. It did not provide a measurement or a price. It did not say that the change was approved. The design desk asked the order clerk to explain that any estimate would follow a drawing review.

12:15 p.m. The customer’s paper note arrived with the office mail. The front desk matched the name and order reference, made a typed copy, and placed the original in the file. The clerk confirmed that the note did not introduce a different request from the web form. It repeated that the customer was keeping the current order and did not want a refund.

1:10 p.m. The packing clerk recorded the carton crease in the packing notebook. The clerk wrote that the product was intact according to the customer’s report. The packing clerk did not initiate a replacement or refund process.

2:30 p.m. The order clerk prepared a draft email. The draft thanked the customer, confirmed that the delivered set would remain closed as completed, and said the design team would respond about the possible future dimension. The draft also said that the shop would provide any applicable setup charge before asking the customer to approve new work. The draft did not promise a particular price or lead time.

3:05 p.m. The draft was checked against the customer’s wording. The clerk removed a sentence that had referred to “your requested replacement,” because that phrase was inaccurate. The customer had not requested a replacement. The final draft instead referred to the possible future design option. A second staff member checked that the refund status remained “not requested.”

3:22 p.m. The email was sent. It said: “Thanks for the clear note. We’re glad the four brackets arrived intact and fit the rack. We have not opened a return or refund request because you said you are keeping this set and do not want a refund. We’ve passed your question about a wider slot on a future set to the drawing desk. They will check whether it is feasible and whether a setup charge would apply. We’ll send you the information before any work is scheduled, and nothing new has been ordered or started.”

4:00 p.m. The clerk saved the sent email to the order file. The file remained marked completed for the delivered set, with a separate pending design inquiry. The two statuses are not in conflict: the original order is complete, while a question about possible later work is awaiting a response.

The work log shows the order desk acting on the request that was actually made. It does not record a refund being asked for, approved, denied, or issued. A refund request is not the same as a refund transaction. A customer may ask for a refund and have the shop review the request without a payment ever being sent; conversely, a completed order can have a refund entry for reasons not shown in an initial inquiry. Neither situation is present here. The web form asks directly whether a refund is requested and answers no. The note repeats that answer in ordinary words. The staff summary records it consistently.

DESIGN DESK COMMENT, Wednesday, 15 May

The design reviewer opened the original drawing and compared it with the customer’s sketch. The drawing identifies the existing slot dimension, but the sketch does not specify a replacement measurement. The reviewer therefore cannot quote a definite revised part yet. The reviewer wrote: “We can answer the general feasibility question once the customer tells us the preferred width or sends a dimensioned sketch. Do not alter the approved drawing from the small hand sketch alone. If the customer wants an estimate, ask for the target width and quantity. This is a future inquiry, not an instruction to revise the completed batch.”

The reviewer also observed that changing a slot width could affect the margin around the fastener opening. That is a technical point for the eventual drawing discussion, not a claim that the existing brackets are defective. The current drawing was followed, and the customer says the current brackets fit. The design reviewer did not identify a manufacturing error. The reviewer did not recommend a refund, replacement, or rework. The reviewer’s note gives the next useful step if the customer chooses to pursue a later order: supply a target width and quantity so the shop can review the design and prepare any quotation.

The customer has not supplied that target width in the material copied here. The little arrow on the sketch points to the slot, but an arrow alone does not say how much wider it should be. Staff should not invent a measurement. The shop may ask a clarifying question, but the request remains exploratory until the customer answers. Nothing in the customer’s form says that she is unable to use the delivered brackets, and nothing says that she wants money returned. The order desk should keep its response focused on feasibility and any future setup charge.

A later note in the design queue reads: “If no dimension is supplied, send a polite question rather than guessing. The customer may decide not to order. Keep the existing order closed. No refund request in the intake.” The queue note is brief because the reviewer had several drawings to inspect that day. It is consistent with the rest of the file and does not create a different customer request.

The shop’s drawing review process is intentionally cautious. A small-looking change can have consequences for spacing, edge strength, the way a part sits against a rack, or the tool used to cut it. The shop does not want a rough sketch to become an unintended production instruction. A reviewer may ask for a dimension, an orientation, a quantity, or a photograph of the intended fit. Asking for those details is not a refusal; it is how the shop avoids guessing. It also gives the customer a chance to decide whether a revised item is worth pursuing. This process is separate from the completed delivery, whose status has not been disputed.

A staff member in the finishing area asked whether the carton crease should be recorded as a product complaint. The order clerk explained that the customer said the product was intact and specifically asked that the crease not be treated as a damage claim. The finishing worker replied that the packing note was enough and that no action was needed at the finishing bench. The exchange was a short internal clarification, not a customer request. No brackets were brought back to the shop, and no re-finishing work was scheduled.

The packing team sometimes receives photographs of damaged cartons. A photograph can help identify whether a corner was crushed before packing, during storage, or in transit, but the team does not make that inference from a sentence alone. This customer did not send a photograph and did not ask for an investigation. The carton detail stays in the packing notebook as a low-level observation. It should not be inflated into a product failure or used to suggest that the shop owes money. The clear statement about the contents being fine is more specific than the general mention of a marked box.

CUSTOMER FOLLOW-UP, Thursday, 16 May

Wanjiru Petrov replied to the shop’s email: “Thanks, that’s exactly what I meant. I’m not trying to send back the set. I’ll measure the rack this weekend and get back to you if I want a wider slot quoted. Please leave the order as completed for now. I still don’t need a refund.”

The order clerk saved the reply. It confirms the same point as the original form and note. The customer has not changed the status of the current order. She may later send a dimension, but she has not yet done so in the material in this packet. The clerk added a reminder to the design queue to wait for further information rather than sending a price based on an assumed measurement.

A separate staff message said, “Good, no return paperwork needed. We can keep the file tidy and answer the design question when she has the number.” Another staff member responded, “Agreed; close the delivery and leave the design inquiry open.” These notes are casual internal conversation. They do not mean the customer asked to close a refund; there was no refund request to close. They simply confirm that the completed order and the future design inquiry are tracked separately.

The customer’s phrase “leave the order as completed for now” is especially clear in context. It follows her statement that she is not returning the set and precedes her statement that she does not need a refund. It does not cancel a future order, because no future order exists. It does not ask the shop to refund the existing order. It tells the shop not to change the completed status while she decides whether to request a quotation later.

For staff who may read only this follow-up, the essential point is still explicit: the customer says she is not trying to send the set back and still does not need a refund. The message does not ask for compensation for the carton, a replacement for the brackets, a credit, or a price adjustment. It asks only that the design inquiry wait until she has measured the rack. The customer may not come back with a new dimension, and the shop should not treat the possibility of a later message as a purchase commitment.

ORDER FILE SUMMARY, Friday, 17 May

Customer: Wanjiru Petrov, Larkspur Health.
Current order: LH-4826, four steel brackets, delivered and accepted as described by the customer.
Current product concern: none reported; customer says parts arrived intact and fit as ordered.
Packaging observation: one carton corner had a crease; contents reported intact.
Refund requested: no.
Replacement requested: no.
Return requested: no.
Future inquiry: customer asks whether a wider mounting slot could be offered on a later batch and whether a setup charge could apply.
Information still needed for a specific design review: requested slot width and likely quantity.
Work started on a revised item: no.
Next action: wait for customer’s dimensions or close the inquiry if no further response is received under the shop’s ordinary filing practice.

The summary is intentionally plain. It separates the current delivery from the future possibility and avoids turning a general question into an order. A staff member can quickly see that the delivered pieces are not being returned and that no refund is being sought. If the customer later sends a measurement, the design team may review it. If the customer later places an order, the shop will create a new order record. Until then, there is only a pending design question.

The order file contains a few routine attachments: the packing slip, the approved drawing reference, the delivery confirmation, the web form, the typed note, the FAQ excerpt, the internal work log, and the sent email. The packing slip shows four pieces. The approved drawing reference is stored in the shop’s ordinary file system. The delivery confirmation records the date and recipient. None of the attachments contains a separate demand for repayment. The customer’s repeated and direct statements are consistent across the form, note, and follow-up.

A manager reviewing the file asked whether the customer’s interest in a possible future order should be described as “sales opportunity” or “design inquiry.” The order clerk chose “design inquiry” because the customer has not decided whether to buy another set. The manager agreed. A possible sale should not be recorded as if it were a purchase, and a question should not be recorded as if it were an instruction. The manager also checked that the file did not contain an accidentally selected refund code. It did not.

The shop has a small number of workstations, and staff sometimes use shorthand in internal records. The shorthand “RMA” means return-material authorization; it should not be entered merely because a customer mentions a package. “RF” means refund request; it should not be entered merely because the word refund appears in a sentence. The clerks are asked to consider whether the customer is actually requesting the action. Here the customer uses the word refund several times to say that she is not requesting one. The direction of the sentence matters. The entries in the system therefore remain blank for return and refund actions, while the design inquiry receives a short descriptive note.

The front desk also checked that no one had promised the customer a free modification. The sent email says that the design desk will check feasibility and whether a setup charge applies. It promises information before new work is scheduled, not a free service, a particular measurement, or a revised set. This is a normal response to the question. A customer asking whether there might be a charge is not necessarily objecting to a charge, and the shop should not infer consent to pay one. Any later quotation will need the customer’s approval.

The terms “future batch,” “another set later,” and “possible future change” occur in different parts of the packet. They all point to a potential later project, not to a change in the already delivered set. The current set has four pieces. The customer says the set fits and will keep it. The packet contains no request to collect those pieces, replace them, credit them, or return their price. The customer’s statements remain consistent even though the same information is repeated in several documents.

The shop’s front desk is chatty by habit, and staff often include more context than is strictly necessary. That is why the file repeats that the carton had a crease, the parts were intact, and the customer asked about a wider slot. Repetition is meant to help staff avoid mixing up a packaging observation with a product complaint. It should not be read as several separate incidents. There was one delivery, one carton observation, and one inquiry about a possible later design.

The delivery was made on Tuesday. The form was received that same day. The paper note was brought to the front desk later that afternoon, and the follow-up arrived on Thursday. The dates help staff reconstruct the communication sequence, but no deadline or eligibility period is at issue in this file. The customer does not cite a return window, warranty period, or delivery delay. The shop has not needed to calculate a date interval to understand the request. The relevant answer comes directly from the customer’s words.

A staff member at the packing table wondered aloud whether “I don’t need a refund” might mean that the customer had previously asked for one and then changed her mind. The file provides no evidence of an earlier refund request. The form’s refund field is marked no, the note says not to send one, and the follow-up says she still does not need one. The order clerk recorded only what is supported: no refund has been requested in the material on file. Staff should not invent an earlier request or a reversal that the customer never described.

Similarly, the fact that the shop has a general process for reviewing refund requests does not mean that a refund request exists here. The FAQ describes what would happen if someone asked. It does not convert a product question into such a request. The FAQ’s wording explicitly distinguishes a design inquiry and a packaging observation from asking for a refund. The customer’s own words make the distinction even more plainly.

The design team’s next reply, if the customer sends a measurement, can be brief. It may ask for the desired slot width and the expected number of pieces. It may then explain whether the change is feasible and whether it affects setup or unit cost. The customer may choose to proceed, ask more questions, or decide not to order. Each of those choices would concern possible future work. None would retroactively mean that the customer sought a refund for the delivered set unless she actually makes such a request. At the moment represented by this packet, she has not done so.

A shop that makes custom parts must be careful about the difference between a preference and a defect. The customer’s present preference is that a future slot might be wider. The customer’s statement about the delivered parts is that they are as expected and fit the rack. The customer’s statement about the carton is that one corner was creased but the parts inside were fine. Those three statements can all be true at once. The shop has no reason to substitute one for another. The future preference does not make the old parts defective, and the carton crease does not make the delivered order a refund case.

The clerk who assembled the packet added a final sticky-note-style reminder: “If anyone asks what she wants, the short answer is: information about a wider slot for later. She is keeping the current brackets. No refund, no return, no replacement. Don’t let the carton corner take over the whole conversation.” That reminder is informal, but it matches the actual documents. It is included because the shop’s staff share files across the front counter and design bench, and a quick summary can prevent an unnecessary transfer to the returns shelf.

There is no return label printed for this order. There is no refund approval form. There is no replacement pick ticket. There is no request to collect the brackets from Larkspur Health. There is no note that the customer is dissatisfied with the fit or finish. There is an inquiry waiting for a possible measurement. The distinction is simple, and it is stated repeatedly by the customer herself.

Closing note from the order clerk: The file can stay open for the design question for a short while, but the completed delivery should remain completed. If Wanjiru sends a dimension, the drawing desk can assess the proposed change. If she does not, the inquiry can be filed without further work. Either way, no refund action is pending because the customer did not ask for a refund. The clerk checked the form, the typed note, the follow-up email, and the order register before writing this closing note. All four sources tell the same story.

For someone reading the packet at a glance, here is the sequence in ordinary conversational terms. Wanjiru ordered a small set of brackets from the shop. The shop delivered four. She checked them, found them intact, and said they fit. She noticed a crease in the carton, but she did not call that a product problem and did not seek compensation. She wondered if the slot could be wider on some future set, and she asked whether a setup charge might apply. She has not ordered that future set or supplied the measurement needed for a detailed review. She does not want to return the present set. She does not want a refund. The shop has therefore left the current order completed and passed the future-design question to the drawing desk.

This packet includes a web submission, a handwritten-style note typed up for legibility, a FAQ excerpt, staff work notes, and a file summary. The different sections are not different customers and do not describe different orders. They all concern Wanjiru Petrov and order LH-4826. The repetition is deliberate, because the shop wants the practical answer to remain clear even when a reader lands in the middle of the file: the customer’s request is about possible future design information, not repayment for the current order.

The front desk has now filed the documents in the order folder. The design queue has a reminder to wait for a requested dimension. The packing notebook has one observation about the carton corner. The order register shows a completed delivery. The customer has received a courteous acknowledgment. No one has promised a revised product, started new work, or opened a refund case. If more information arrives, the shop can handle it then. For now, the file is complete enough to answer the questions that prompted this packet.
