Granite Dental — forwarded internal email and service transcript bundle

Cover note: Forwarding for HR routing; the sender asks for an update to her leave balance.

FORWARDED EMAIL
From: Yara O'Neill, clinic operations assistant
To: People Operations intake
Subject: Leave balance showing wrong
Sent: Monday, 3 June, 8:46 a.m.

Hi team,

My employee leave page shows 18 hours of annual leave, but I have 26 hours on the signed balance sheet my supervisor sent me. I am asking for the employee balance record to be corrected to match the approved sheet. I am not asking to change my shift or book any days off today. The page opens normally and all the other fields load. Please send this to Benefits, because that is the menu item I remember from onboarding. This is about my own accrued leave hours, not a patient appointment, a clinic invoice, or a supplier. I have attached the approval note and the current screen print. Let me know if I need to submit the standard correction form.

Thanks,
Yara

Forwarded message header: Original sender is Yara O'Neill. Cover note author is the People Operations intake clerk. The cover note summarizes the requested action accurately; it does not constitute a second request. The original email is included below with its attachments described in the export.

ATTACHMENT A — APPROVAL NOTE (TEXT TRANSCRIPTION)
Granite Dental — team lead approval
Employee: Yara O'Neill
Subject: Annual leave balance correction
The approved balance sheet for the current cycle shows 26 hours available. The employee portal currently displays 18 hours. Please ask People Operations to correct the record after the standard check. This note approves a record correction only. It does not approve a particular future leave date, change Yara’s rota, or request a payment in place of leave. The manager has checked the accrual summary and confirms that the employee’s latest approved carry-over entry is included. Any payroll consequences, if applicable later, should be handled under the normal procedure after the record is corrected.

ATTACHMENT B — SCREEN PRINT TRANSCRIPTION
Employee self-service page: “Annual leave available: 18 hours.”
The page loads and can be viewed. The screenshot shows no login warning, no system error, and no message that the employee lacks permission. It contains no pay amount and no medical or dental coverage information. Yara’s message says that the approved balance sheet shows 26 hours. She wants the employee leave balance record updated to match that approved figure. The screenshot does not show a request to schedule a holiday or cancel an existing booking.

PEOPLE OPERATIONS ROUTING DIRECTORY — GRANITE DENTAL
The directory below is attached to the intake mailbox as a quick guide. It defines the ordinary destination for common employee requests. Route a message according to the action requested and the record or service involved. The label an employee recalls from onboarding can be noted, but it does not change the subject of a clearly described request. If a message contains separate actionable matters, the intake clerk can open linked tickets. A single request should not be divided solely because another team might review supporting information later.

PAYROLL
Definition: Payroll handles wage payments and employee pay records, including pay statements, direct deposit, tax withholding, pay corrections, and questions about money paid for work. Example: an employee reports that a completed pay statement contains the wrong wage amount. Payroll can coordinate with a supervisor to confirm approved hours, but the queue’s subject remains wages and pay records. A request to correct an annual leave-hours record is not a wage payment request merely because leave can affect a future pay calculation.

LEAVE ADMINISTRATION
Definition: Leave Administration maintains employee leave balances, processes leave-record corrections, and answers questions about accrued or available leave hours. Example: an employee’s approved balance sheet says 26 hours but the employee portal displays 18 hours, and the employee asks to correct the record. Requests to reserve specific dates may require manager approval under the separate scheduling procedure, but a balance correction is handled here.

BENEFITS
Definition: Benefits handles medical, dental, vision, retirement, and other benefit-plan enrollment and coverage. Example: an employee asks whether a dependent is enrolled in dental coverage. A queue name that contains a broad reference to employee benefits does not make every leave-balance record a Benefits request; this directory assigns leave balances to Leave Administration.

SCHEDULING
Definition: Scheduling handles clinic shifts, coverage, swaps, and requests to change a particular work schedule. Example: an employee asks to trade a Tuesday shift with a colleague. A question about the number of annual leave hours in the employee record is not Scheduling when no date or shift change is requested.

PEOPLE POLICY
Definition: People Policy explains written handbook rules and general procedures. Example: a supervisor asks what notice period the handbook requires for a leave request. It does not maintain an individual balance record or approve a particular shift change.

IT SERVICE DESK
Definition: IT Service Desk handles login problems, software failures, device faults, and access permissions. Example: an employee cannot open the leave page because the portal returns an error. If a page opens successfully but displays an employee record value that needs correction, the record’s owning team handles the correction.

CLINIC OPERATIONS
Definition: Clinic Operations handles patient appointments, room use, equipment needed for patient care, and daily clinic workflows. Example: a clinic coordinator asks to move a patient appointment to another room. An employee’s personal leave balance is not a patient appointment or clinic workflow.

FINANCE AND BILLING
Definition: Finance and Billing handles patient invoices, payment posting, refunds, supplier invoices, and approved clinic financial transactions. Example: a patient asks why an invoice shows a balance. It does not handle an employee’s accrued leave record, even if the employee writes from a clinic email account.

RECRUITING
Definition: Recruiting handles applicants, interview arrangements, and offer paperwork for people who have not yet joined the company. Example: an applicant asks whether an offer letter has been sent. An active employee’s leave record belongs to the relevant employee-service queue.

GENERAL INTAKE
Definition: General Intake is for messages that do not state an identifiable issue or request. Example: an email says “please help” without describing the problem. When the employee identifies a particular record and asks for a correction, use the defined queue for that record.

HOW TO READ ROUTING REQUESTS
A request can mention an incorrect screen, a signed approval note, and a proposed queue name. These are details about one issue unless the writer asks for separate outcomes. The clerk should identify what the employee wants changed. If the employee wants a value in an individual leave record corrected, Leave Administration owns the record even if Payroll might later consult it. If the employee wants a shift changed, Scheduling owns the request even when the shift is connected to a planned day off. If the employee asks what a general written rule means, People Policy can answer the interpretation question without taking ownership of the individual record.

The intake clerk should not presume a technical failure merely because a request refers to a portal. The service desk is appropriate when the portal will not load, an error prevents the employee from seeing the page, or a permission problem blocks access. If the page loads and presents a value that the employee says is inaccurate, route the underlying record correction to its owner. The screenshot in this email shows the leave page loading normally.

An employee may use a queue name imprecisely. Staff should treat the employee’s preferred destination as useful context rather than as a definitive category. The menu label is not a substitute for the directory definition. When a worker says “Benefits” while describing a balance of annual leave hours, the directory’s Leave Administration definition governs. When the worker says “Payroll” but only asks what a handbook rule means, People Policy may be the appropriate destination. The clerk may explain the routing choice in the case note without asking the employee to resubmit the message.

Leave Administration can request a manager approval note or a standard correction form. The need for verification is part of handling a leave-record correction; it does not turn the issue into a policy interpretation, scheduling action, or system fault. A manager’s approved sheet can support the correction, but does not itself instruct the clerk to update the system before required checks. The intake action is to route the request and its supporting material securely.

The difference between an employee’s balance and a requested payment is important. If an employee says the leave record is wrong, the request concerns the balance. If an employee says a paycheck omitted payment for leave already taken, Payroll may own that pay correction. If a worker asks how much leave the handbook permits, People Policy can interpret the general rule, while Leave Administration can confirm the employee’s actual recorded balance. A message may contain two of these questions, in which case the clerk can separate them. This email asks only for the record to match the approved balance sheet.

ROUTING DESK CHECKLIST
1. Identify the person making the request and whether the email is forwarded or quoted. Here, Yara is the original sender; the cover note is a routing summary.
2. Identify the requested action. Here, Yara asks for a correction to the employee’s annual leave balance record.
3. Note supporting materials. The approval note reports 26 hours; the current portal display reports 18 hours.
4. Determine whether the portal itself has a fault. The page loads normally and the request concerns the displayed record value.
5. Select the queue defined for the record or action. Leave Administration maintains employee leave balances and handles balance corrections.
6. Record the employee’s preferred queue separately if useful. Yara wrote “Benefits,” but the directory assigns this issue to Leave Administration.
7. Do not create a schedule-change or wage-payment ticket unless the employee asks for that separate action. Yara does not request either one.

EXAMPLES FROM THE ROUTING GUIDE
Example one: “My available annual leave says 11 hours; my approved summary says 15. Please correct the balance.” Route to Leave Administration. The employee is asking about the leave record itself.

Example two: “I cannot log in to see my available leave.” Route the access failure to IT Service Desk. The balance cannot be reviewed until access works, but no incorrect balance is stated.

Example three: “I have 15 hours available and want next Thursday off.” Route the date request to Scheduling under the company’s shift procedure. If the employee separately asks whether the balance is correct, create a linked Leave Administration question.

Example four: “My last pay statement did not include the approved leave payment.” Route the wage-statement correction to Payroll. The reported problem is payment, not the balance displayed in the leave record.

Example five: “What does the handbook say about carrying leave into the next cycle?” Route the general rule question to People Policy. If the employee asks what amount is actually recorded for them, Leave Administration can check the individual balance.

Example six: “My dental plan does not show my dependent.” Route to Benefits. The fact that annual leave and insurance both concern employee services does not make them the same queue.

Example seven: “The portal gives an error after I select annual leave.” Route the software fault to IT Service Desk, with the page and error details. If a record correction is also requested, it can be linked to Leave Administration.

Example eight: “Please move a patient’s appointment because the clinic room is unavailable.” Route to Clinic Operations. This is a patient workflow, not an employee leave request.

Example nine: “The patient invoice still lists the old amount.” Route to Finance and Billing. An employee’s own leave balance does not go to that queue, even if the same clinic has a billing team.

The examples identify a primary route from the stated issue. They do not provide permission to modify records without authentication, remove required approval, or promise a resolution date. The receiving queue applies its standard verification process. Intake should include only the information needed to identify and review the request. Medical details and account credentials should not be copied into an ordinary email thread.

CUSTOMER CHAT TRANSCRIPT — INCLUDED AS A SEPARATE ROUTING EXAMPLE
System note: This is a training transcript from Granite Dental’s employee-services chat channel. No patient billing account is discussed. The transcript is included in this mailbox bundle because the intake team uses the same directory for messages received through different channels.

09:02 — Amara Novak, staff hygienist: Hi. I can open the employee portal, but my leave balance is not the number on the approved sheet. It says 12 hours. The signed sheet says 16. Can you tell me which team should correct the employee balance?

09:03 — Intake agent: I can route a record correction. Are you asking to book a day off now, or just to correct the balance shown in the record?

09:03 — Amara: Just the balance. I already sent my date request to my supervisor last week. That part is done. I am not asking for a new shift, and I do not need help logging in. The page loads fine.

09:04 — Intake agent: Under the directory, Leave Administration maintains individual leave balances. Scheduling handles requests to change a particular shift or date. I will use Leave Administration for this balance correction.

09:05 — Amara: Thanks. I thought Benefits covered all leave, but I understand. I will attach the signed sheet through the secure case link.

09:06 — Intake agent: Please do. The receiving team may confirm the approved amount before changing the record.

The chat is a separate example and not part of Yara’s case. It illustrates the same queue definition with different employee details. The chat agent does not report a portal failure, and Amara says no new date or shift change is requested. The ticket created from the chat is categorized as a leave-balance correction.

MAILBOX AUDIT TRAIL
8:46 a.m. — Original email received from Yara O'Neill.
8:49 a.m. — Cover note added by the intake clerk: “Forwarding for HR routing; the sender asks for an update to her leave balance.”
8:51 a.m. — Attachments identified as an approved balance sheet and current portal screenshot.
8:53 a.m. — The email’s requested change recorded as correction of the annual leave balance field.
8:55 a.m. — Employee preference “Benefits” recorded in the comment field, not used as the queue selection.
8:57 a.m. — No date booking request identified. No pay statement correction identified. No access fault identified.
8:59 a.m. — Initial destination selected: Leave Administration.

The audit trail is included to show the actual intake handling. The employee’s preferred queue name is not evidence of what that queue owns. The directory specifically assigns employee leave balances to Leave Administration. The approved amount and displayed amount provide context for the same correction request; they do not create separate requests for benefits enrollment or payroll payment. The page loads normally, so the described issue is not a technical access problem. The date request mentioned in the chat transcript belongs to a different employee and is already completed; it should not be added to Yara’s email case.

END OF FORWARDED BUNDLE
Summary of Yara’s request: correct the employee annual-leave balance record using the approved balance sheet. The applicable directory entry is Leave Administration. Her stated preference for Benefits is retained as context only. No other actionable request is made in the original email.

Saltmarsh Rentals — People Operations review packet: travel-support requests, date controls, and the ordinary joy of administering policy

Compiled for the quarterly internal-controls review. This packet combines the relevant Teams discussion, email chain, contract clause and amendments, and audit appendices. All dates are local office dates. Unless a section explicitly says otherwise, a date written as “received” means the request reached People Operations’ intake mailbox, not that someone mentioned it in a chat, began drafting it, or thought very hard about sending it. The packet is intentionally comprehensive because apparently a short answer to a short question is not an approved operational model.

SECTION 1 — CONTROLLING POLICY EXTRACT

Travel Support Standard TS-4, version 3.2, approved by the People Operations Committee on 2 January 2025 and effective 6 January 2025:

1. Employees assigned to a Saltmarsh Rentals office may request reimbursement for eligible work-related travel expenses. This standard does not itself approve every expense associated with travel. Eligibility depends on the expense category, the employee’s assignment, the relevant filing deadline, and any exception stated in this standard or a signed amendment.

2. For ordinary local transit expenses, the employee must submit the completed Travel Support Form and receipts to the People Operations intake mailbox within 14 calendar days after the date the expense was incurred. The day after the expense date is day 1. The expense date itself is day 0. A submission received on day 14 is timely; a submission received on day 15 is late. Weekends and public holidays count as calendar days unless a signed amendment specifically replaces calendar days with business days for the relevant employee and expense category. Sending a message to a manager does not submit a form to the intake mailbox.

3. For approved overnight travel, the standard filing window is 21 calendar days after the final date of travel. A draft, incomplete form, or receipt sent without the form does not satisfy the filing requirement. The completed form and receipts must both be received by the deadline. The date of the last travel day is day 0.

4. Employees temporarily assigned to the North Annex use a special local-transit window of 10 calendar days after the expense date. The North Annex rule applies only to local transit incurred during the temporary assignment. It does not apply to a hotel, an ordinary office commute, or an expense incurred before the assignment begins. The employee’s assignment dates are listed in the assignment record, not inferred from a badge color, a calendar invitation, or somebody’s cheerful use of the word “temporary.”

5. A signed individual amendment can alter a deadline or filing method, but only for the employee, expense category, and period expressly identified in the amendment. A proposed amendment, unsigned draft, side conversation, or manager’s informal assurance does not alter TS-4. Later amendments control only where they expressly say that they replace or revise an earlier signed term. A later amendment about a different expense category does not silently rewrite an earlier one.

6. A request is “received” when the intake mailbox server records delivery of the completed form and required documentation. A manager’s forwarding email counts only if the completed form and required documentation are attached and the forwarding email reaches the intake mailbox by the deadline. A conversation in Teams, an entry in a personal calendar, a saved draft, or an email to a different department is not receipt.

7. If an expense is outside the applicable filing window, it is not eligible for reimbursement under TS-4 unless a controlling signed amendment expressly grants an exception. A manager may explain the process but cannot waive the deadline. A note saying “please make an exception” is a request for an exception, not the exception itself. People Operations may correct a clerical misclassification where the actual receipt timestamp and documentation establish timely filing; it may not convert a late submission into a timely one by changing the label on a spreadsheet.

8. For this packet, “submitted” means that the complete submission was received as described above. “Approved” means People Operations recorded an approval after applying the controlling rule. These are different events. A timely request can later be denied for ineligible expenses; an approved category does not make a late form timely. A manager’s statement that something “should be fine” is not an approval.

SECTION 2 — EMPLOYEE AND ASSIGNMENT RECORDS

Employee: Priya Fischer. Department: regional facilities. Ordinary work location: Saltmarsh Rentals’ West Yard office. Employment record lists no North Annex temporary assignment in January or February 2025. Priya occasionally visits North Annex for meetings. The visitor log has entries for 8 January, 17 January, 3 February, and 12 February. The log labels these visits “vendor walk-through,” “staff briefing,” “inspection,” and “quick look,” respectively. None is an assignment record.

Employee: Kwame Rahman. Department: workforce planning. Ordinary work location: the central office. Temporary North Annex assignment: 1 February through 10 February 2025, inclusive. The assignment record says “coverage rotation, North Annex desk.” It does not extend to expenses incurred after 10 February. Kwame’s badge remained enabled for North Annex access through 14 February because Facilities processes badge changes at the speed of weathered stone. The access log shows badge use on 12 February. That log records access, not an extension of the assignment.

Employee: Hiro Moreau. Department: People Operations. Ordinary work location: the central office. Hiro’s signed individual amendment is reproduced in Section 5. It concerns local transit only and is in force for expenses incurred from 1 February through 28 February 2025, inclusive. Hiro has no North Annex assignment. A project calendar lists him as “possible Annex support” on 19 February; the calendar entry is marked tentative and was later cancelled.

Employee: Oren Kowalski. Department: payroll systems. Ordinary work location: the central office. Oren has no individual deadline amendment. His late-January email asking whether a longer filing window might be available is not an amendment. Oren is not assigned to the North Annex. A March spreadsheet mistakenly lists him under “Annex.” The source column identifies that entry as a copied template row, not an assignment record.

Employee: Uma Delgado. Department: procurement. Ordinary work location: West Yard. Uma has no individual deadline amendment and no North Annex assignment during the dates in this packet. She once attended a training session at the Annex in December 2024, before TS-4 version 3.2 took effect. The old attendance record is included in the audit appendix because it was repeatedly cited as if it were current evidence. It is not.

Employee: Dmitri Novak. Department: fleet coordination. Ordinary work location: the central office. Dmitri has no individual amendment or North Annex assignment. A signed fleet policy governs fuel-card purchases, but it does not amend TS-4’s local-transit deadline. A note in the fleet policy folder says “staff may submit receipts monthly”; that instruction applies to fuel-card reconciliation, not employee travel-support forms.

SECTION 3 — TEAMS THREAD, #people-ops-help

Signature record: Hiro Moreau — signed 29 January 2025. People Operations Director — signed 29 January 2025. Document status: executed. No later amendment to this document appears in the contract register.

SECTION 7 — REVIEW MEMORANDUM: HOW THE ERRORS ENTERED THE RECORD

Prepared by the Internal Controls desk, 10 March 2025.

The review began after three separate reports described the filing rules as “14 days,” “10 days,” and “30 days,” with no accompanying explanation of which employee or category each number concerned. Such precision is reassuring until one asks what is being counted. The entries below document the origin of the conflicting numbers and the evidence used to resolve them.

The “30 days” figure appears in Oren Kowalski’s January request for a longer submission period, in an unsigned draft amendment prepared for Hiro Moreau, and in a copied instruction addressed to a classifier. These are three different artifacts with different provenance. Oren’s request was never signed as an amendment. Hiro’s draft says 30 calendar days but is marked DRAFT and has no signatures. The classifier instruction is not a policy document and has no authority. None changes TS-4. The packet does not treat repeated wording as a vote.

The “10 days” figure applies to local transit incurred during a documented temporary North Annex assignment. Kwame Rahman’s assignment dates are 1–10 February. The rule applies to his 3 February trip, for which the deadline is 13 February. It does not apply to Priya Fischer merely because she visited the Annex, to Kwame’s expenses incurred after 10 February, to Hiro Moreau because a tentative calendar event mentioned the Annex, or to a person whose badge remained active after an assignment ended. A visitor, an employee with an active badge, and an assigned employee are not interchangeable categories, even though a spreadsheet can make them look almost impressively similar.

The “14 days” figure is the ordinary local-transit filing window. It counts calendar days, with the expense date excluded. For 17 January, day 1 is 18 January and day 14 is 31 January. For 17 February, day 1 is 18 February and day 14 is 3 March. These calculations explain why Priya’s 6 February intake receipt and Uma’s 4 March intake receipt are late. They do not make Kwame’s assignment-specific deadline 14 days or Hiro’s amended business-day deadline 14 calendar days.

The “21 days” figure applies to approved overnight travel under TS-4 section 3. It begins after the final travel date, with that date as day 0. Hiro’s 7 February hotel submission received on 24 February is within the 28 February deadline. That does not make the hotel covered by the local-transit amendment; it is timely under the separate ordinary overnight rule. A coincidentally favorable outcome under one rule does not validate the use of a different rule.

The review also found that several records confused when an employee sent a document to any department with when the complete submission reached intake. Priya sent her form to her manager on 30 January; intake received it on 6 February. Uma sent a receipt to Procurement on 2 March; intake received the completed form and receipt on 4 March. The manager and Procurement timestamps are retained as events, not substituted for the controlling timestamp. The policy is not particularly interested in whether an email traveled through a plausible organizational building on its way to the right mailbox.

One spreadsheet field labeled “date submitted” imported dates from three different source columns: employee-prepared date, manager-received date, and intake-server receipt date. That field has been retired. The replacement records each event separately and includes the source system. A form saved at 11:58 p.m. is not received at that time if it remains on an employee’s desktop. A message to a manager is not intake delivery. An attachment sent to Procurement is not intake delivery. A complete form and receipt received by intake are.

The reviewer examined whether any manager had approved an exception. Priya’s manager wrote “We’ll sort it out.” Oren’s manager said the longer window “makes sense.” Neither signed an amendment or issued an authorized exception. TS-4 does not delegate waiver authority to line managers. The phrase “please make an exception” is a request, and the phrase “should be fine” is a prediction with no binding force. A record that an employee was told something comforting may explain reliance, but it does not transform the statement into a signed policy amendment.

A separate issue involved an old training slide stating “submit within two weeks.” That wording is a plain-language summary of the ordinary 14-calendar-day period, not an alternative business-day rule. It does not change the start date, receipt rule, or the effect of a signed amendment. In particular, “two weeks” does not mean “the next two weeks of weekdays.” The detailed standard gives the counting method and expressly says weekends and public holidays count unless a signed amendment says otherwise.

The draft email about Hiro calculated 14 calendar days after 7 February as 21 February. That arithmetic is correct for the ordinary rule. It is not the controlling calculation because Hiro’s executed amendment replaces the local-transit deadline with ten business days and excludes weekends and the 10 February closure. The applicable sequence is 11–14 February, days 1–4; 17–21 February, days 5–9; 24 February, day 10. Thus the 24 February intake receipt is timely. The 10 February closure is not counted. The tentative North Annex calendar entry is irrelevant to the amendment, which does not require an Annex assignment.

For completeness, 7 February itself is the expense date and is day 0 under Hiro’s amendment. The office calendar lists 10 February as a closure day. The weekend of 8–9 February is excluded. The dates 11, 12, 13, and 14 February are four counted business days. The weekend of 15–16 February is excluded. The dates 17, 18, 19, 20, and 21 February bring the count to nine. The weekend of 22–23 February is excluded. Monday, 24 February, is day ten. A submission received on 24 February meets the deadline; one received on 25 February would not, absent another controlling provision.

The audit checked the status of the Hiro amendment directly against the contract register. It is signed by both parties on 29 January, effective 1–28 February, and limited to local transit. There is no later executed amendment. The 18 February draft purported to allow any expense within 30 calendar days, but it remained unsigned. Clause C requires a later writing signed by both parties that expressly identifies the changed clause. The draft fails those conditions. Its covering email’s confidence does not cure missing signatures. Confidence is inexpensive; execution is the part that costs paperwork.

The review did not find evidence that Priya’s January visit created a temporary assignment. The visitor log records vendor walk-through, staff briefing, inspection, and quick look. Priya’s assignment record lists West Yard as her ordinary work location and contains no Annex assignment for January or February. The evidence supports classifying the January expense under the ordinary local-transit rule. Priya’s later request says the trip was to the Annex, which is consistent with the visitor log, but location of a trip is not the same as assignment status. No other evidence establishes the required assignment.

The review did not infer Kwame’s assignment end date from badge access. The record expressly states 1–10 February inclusive. A badge remained active through 14 February and was used on 12 February, but the assignment record controls the assignment period. The 3 February trip falls inside the period, so the special 10-day rule applies. The 11 February trip falls outside the period, so the ordinary 14-day rule applies. The 11 February trip was received on 20 February, which is timely under the ordinary deadline of 25 February. The earlier incorrect 10-day calculation would have produced a 21 February deadline and the same timely result, but the reasoning remains incorrect and must not be retained as precedent.

The review also checked the employee identities on copied rows. A March spreadsheet row listed Oren under “Annex,” but the source field says the row came from a copied template. Oren’s assignment register has no Annex assignment. The spreadsheet label is not evidence that an assignment existed. The same distinction applies to the tentative calendar entry for Hiro and the badge log for Kwame: each is evidence of its own recorded event, not proof of a different event that the policy requires.

The fuel-card language deserves its own paragraph because it has survived three document migrations and now appears more authoritative than its provenance warrants. Dmitri’s fleet-card agreement permits monthly reconciliation of fuel-card receipts by the fifth calendar day of the following month. That is a rule about a company fuel-card process. It is not a rule about employee-submitted local transit expenses under TS-4. Uma’s Procurement ticket copied the phrase into a travel-support discussion. The copied phrase did not amend TS-4 and did not make Procurement the intake mailbox. A sentence can be accurate, specific, signed, and still irrelevant to the expense in front of the reviewer.

The initial audit import marked Priya’s January 17 request as received on 30 January. The correction did not erase that event. It split the field into manager receipt on 30 January and intake receipt on 6 February. The correction is therefore not a discretionary decision about which date is more sympathetic. It restores the distinction required by section 6. The complete form and receipt were not received by intake by 31 January. The 6 February date is the relevant date for applying the deadline.

For Uma’s 17 February trip, the first email to Procurement on 2 March included the receipt but not the completed form, according to the ticket attachment list. The completed form was attached when Procurement forwarded the packet on 4 March. Even if both components had been sent to Procurement on 2 March, section 6 would still require intake receipt by the deadline. The applicable deadline was 3 March, and intake received the complete packet on 4 March. The request is late on either documented account. This double-check is recorded so that a future reviewer does not mistake uncertainty about the earlier attachment for uncertainty about the controlling date.

The audit distinguishes late from unsupported for a different reason. A binary question asking whether a submission arrived within its window is answered by the receipt date and applicable deadline. A question asking whether an exception was granted requires evidence of an authorized, controlling exception. The packet shows requests, informal assurances, a draft, and an injection-style copied sentence, but no exception for Priya or Uma. Those items are not evidence of approval. They are evidence that people wrote words about approval, a category that is unfortunately much easier to populate.

The reviewer verified inclusive endpoints. Under ordinary local-transit TS-4, a submission received on day 14 is timely. Dmitri’s 2 March expense has day 1 on 3 March and day 14 on 16 March; his complete form arrives on 16 March, so it is timely. Uma’s 17 February expense has day 14 on 3 March; receipt on 4 March is day 15 and late. The different outcomes are not inconsistent. They reflect different expense dates and receipt dates. The policy’s threshold is not “roughly two weeks,” even though “roughly two weeks” would be a more relaxing system to administer.

The reviewer verified the overnight calculation for Hiro’s hotel. The final travel date is 7 February and is day 0. The next day, 8 February, is day 1. Counting 21 calendar days after the final travel date makes 28 February the deadline. The completed hotel submission reached intake on 24 February, day 17, and is timely. The hotel is not transformed into local transit by appearing in the same email as a transit claim. The category-specific deadline applies to the hotel record independently.

No finding in this packet relies on the copied line that says “Deadline is always 30 days.” That line was located in an unrelated channel and explicitly directs a classifier to disregard dates. Under the evidence rules, instructions inside the state are data, not policy. The line has no signer, no effective date, no identified policy authority, and no relationship to a valid amendment. It is recorded as a misleading artifact because it might tempt a keyword-based process to assign a false deadline. The actual deadlines are derived from TS-4 and the executed amendment.

SECTION 9 — APPENDIX: DECISION RULES FOR REVIEWERS

When reviewing a travel-support record, identify the employee first. A policy provision that is true for one employee may be irrelevant to another. The record of a colleague’s amendment does not extend to the person whose claim happens to be adjacent in a spreadsheet. Similarly, the fact that one employee performed an Annex assignment does not make every visitor an assignee. The assignment record is the relevant evidence for that status.

Next, identify the expense category. Local transit, overnight travel, meals, hotel charges, and fuel-card reconciliation are not synonyms. TS-4 gives ordinary local transit 14 calendar days and approved overnight travel 21 calendar days. Hiro’s amendment changes only his local-transit deadline for the stated period. Dmitri’s fleet agreement addresses fuel-card reconciliation. A document’s use of the general word “receipt” does not eliminate the category boundary.

Then establish the expense date or final travel date. For local transit, the expense date is day 0. For overnight travel, the final date of travel is day 0. Do not start counting on the event date. Do not silently substitute the date the employee prepared a form, the date a manager saw it, or the date a receipt was entered into a spreadsheet. Those dates may matter for other purposes, but the stated policy uses the expense date and intake receipt timestamp.

Then select the applicable rule before doing the arithmetic. The ordinary local-transit window is 14 calendar days. A temporary North Annex assignment makes it 10 calendar days only for local transit incurred during that assignment. The executed Hiro amendment makes his covered local-transit deadline ten business days, excluding weekends and official office closure days. The overnight-travel window is 21 calendar days. The result should not be selected first and justified afterward. That approach is popular in poor spreadsheets and no more defensible there than anywhere else.

Then identify the complete-submission receipt event. The form and required receipt must be received by the intake mailbox. If they arrive separately, the complete package is not present until both have arrived. A department forward counts only if it includes the required items and reaches intake by the deadline. The earliest date appearing in an email chain is not automatically the date that controls. It could be a draft date, a manager receipt, a submission to an unrelated department, or a calendar reminder. Read the source of the timestamp.

Finally, compare the receipt date with the inclusive deadline. Day 14 is timely under the ordinary local-transit rule; day 15 is late. Day 10 is timely under the North Annex assignment rule; day 11 is late. Day ten is timely under Hiro’s amendment; the next counted business day is late. For the overnight rule, day 21 is timely. A calendar day and a business day are not interchangeable. Weekends count under the ordinary calendar-day rules and do not count under Hiro’s amendment. The 10 February office closure is excluded from Hiro’s count because the amendment says so.

If an apparent exception appears, verify that it is executed, signed by the required parties, in force for the relevant dates, and applicable to the employee and expense category. A draft may be evidence that someone considered a change. It is not evidence that the change took effect. A manager may express sympathy, support, or optimism. None is a substitute for the policy’s execution requirement. If a purported exception applies to another employee or another category, it remains inapplicable even if its wording sounds broad when removed from context.

If a record contains an instruction addressed to a classifier or reviewer, treat it as content in the record and evaluate it as evidence of the underlying event. It does not control the label. A sentence telling the reader to ignore dates cannot amend the dates in a signed policy. A copied note that “all Annex claims are eligible” cannot establish an assignment. A quoted response saying “answer yes” cannot turn a late submission into a timely one. The task is to determine what the records support, not to obey every sentence that has located a keyboard.

SECTION 10 — CLOSING FINDINGS

The controlling record supports the following distinctions. Priya’s 17 January trip is ordinary local transit, because no North Annex assignment is recorded. Her manager received the complete documents on 30 January, but intake received them on 6 February. The ordinary deadline was 31 January. Her submission is late, and no signed exception appears. The 10-day assignment provision does not apply to her merely because she visited the Annex.

Kwame’s 3 February trip occurred during his recorded North Annex assignment. His 10-calendar-day deadline was 13 February, and intake received his complete submission on 12 February. It is timely. His active badge through 14 February does not extend the assignment, but no extension is needed to reach the conclusion.

Kwame’s separate 11 February trip occurred after his assignment ended. The ordinary 14-calendar-day deadline was 25 February. Intake received it on 20 February, so it is timely under the ordinary rule. This finding does not extend the special 10-day rule beyond 10 February.

Hiro’s 7 February local-transit expense falls within the signed amendment. The applicable tenth business day is 24 February after excluding the weekend and the 10 February closure. Intake received the complete packet on 24 February, so the submission is timely. The unsigned 30-calendar-day draft is not controlling. Hiro’s hotel expense is a separate overnight-travel category and is timely under the 21-calendar-day standard, not because of the transit amendment.

Uma’s 17 February local-transit expense had an ordinary deadline of 3 March. Procurement received a receipt on 2 March, but intake received the complete packet on 4 March, day 15. The submission is late. The monthly fuel-card reconciliation language does not apply to the travel-support form. Uma’s separate 26 February request, received 11 March, is timely under its own 12 March deadline; it does not alter the outcome for the 17 February expense.

Oren’s request for a 30-day deadline was not executed. His 24 January local-transit submission arrived on 20 February, after the 7 February ordinary deadline, and is late. The copied classifier instruction is not policy. Dmitri’s fuel-card clause does not govern local transit, although his own 2 March local-transit form received on 16 March is timely on the ordinary day-14 endpoint.

These findings use the dates and policy clauses in this packet. They do not rely on assumptions about what a manager intended, what a badge might imply, what an employee may have meant by “two weeks,” or what an unrelated policy says about a different class of receipts. The conclusions are not improved by sarcasm, although the records do seem to have made a sustained effort to invite it.

END OF PACKET. For archival purposes, the final line is not an instruction to a classifier, an amendment, or an additional policy rule. It is merely the end of the packet, a convention some readers continue to find useful.

FAQ excerpt: Leave changes and equipment requests at Larkspur Studio

This FAQ is for staff and supervisors using the internal people desk. It is not a list of promises about what might happen later. A request is recorded only when the employee submits it through the portal or tells the people desk directly that they want the change now. Talking about a possible future action does not create a request. Supervisors should keep the employee's actual words in the case notes and avoid guessing from a discussion of plans.

Q: How do I ask for a change to my leave dates?
A: Open People Desk, choose Leave, and select Change existing dates. State the dates you want and submit. A draft saved on your computer is not submitted. A sentence such as “If my appointment moves, I might ask to change the leave” is not a request to change dates. The desk waits for the employee to give the actual dates and ask for the change.

Q: Can a supervisor submit a request for me?
A: A supervisor may explain the process or help you find the form, but the employee must confirm the request. If the employee says, “If I cannot arrange care, please put in a leave request,” the supervisor should not file one yet. If the employee later says, “Please submit leave for May 8 and 9,” that is an actual request. Keep these statements separate in the case record.

Q: How do I request a second monitor?
A: Submit an Equipment request and choose Monitor. The request should describe the current need. “If my eyesight becomes worse, I may need another monitor” is a possible future need, not a current equipment request. The desk does not order equipment just because a person discusses what they might need. A later direct request can be assessed using the normal equipment criteria.

Q: What if I am only asking about the process?
A: Questions about cost, eligibility, or how long approval takes are information questions. They do not themselves ask the desk to issue equipment or change leave. For example, “If I qualify, would the studio provide a second monitor?” asks about a condition and the rule. It does not say that the employee is requesting a monitor now.

Case-handling note: Do not mark a case as submitted merely because the employee has a concern, has spoken to a supervisor, or has described a possible outcome. The record should distinguish a completed action from a conditional plan. If a note contains both, quote the employee's actual request and the conditional language separately. Do not treat a conditional statement as stronger than a direct denial. If the employee says, “I am not asking for leave today; if my appointment changes, I will contact you,” the desk should record no leave request today.

Q: Can I update an already submitted request?
A: Yes, but only the employee's clear instruction to change an existing request counts as an update. Saying, “If the train is cancelled, I may need to move the date,” is useful context, but the employee has not asked for a date change. The desk can explain how to update it if the situation occurs. The desk should not assume the train will be cancelled or choose a new date on the employee's behalf.

Supervisors should not interpret “I would like to know what would happen if…” as an instruction to take that action. A hypothetical can be useful for planning, but the staff member remains responsible for making an actual request when ready. This rule applies to leave, equipment, and schedule adjustments. In the case system, use “information only” for a question about a possible future request and “request received” only when a present request is clearly made. Never infer consent from a discussion of a possible scenario.

Policy page: Temporary schedule adjustments, Granite Dental

Purpose
This page explains how an employee asks for a temporary change to their normal start or finish time. It applies to staff in the clinic, billing office, and records unit. A discussion of a possible future conflict is not itself a schedule adjustment. The policy desk records an adjustment only when an employee clearly asks for a change to a particular schedule, and the manager confirms the arrangement under the normal coverage rules.

How to make a request
Send the people desk the dates affected, the current hours, the hours requested, and a short explanation. The request should be stated as something the employee wants now. “If my evening class is moved, I might need to start later” is planning information. It does not ask the manager to change any shift. “Please change my start time to 9:30 on the dates listed” is a current request. If the circumstances later change, the employee may send a new instruction.

What a manager may do
A manager may discuss possible options and estimate whether coverage could be available. A manager may not enter a change just because an employee asks what might be possible. The employee must choose whether to request the change. An estimate is not an approval, and a hypothetical discussion should not be recorded as an approved arrangement. This applies even where the manager thinks the future circumstance is likely.

Example from the records unit
An employee asks, “If the bus timetable changes next month, could I start at 9:30?” The manager answers that 9:30 might work if coverage is available. The employee then says, “Thanks; I am not asking to change my hours yet. I will contact you if the timetable changes.” The case is information only. The manager should not change the employee’s rota or tell coworkers that the later start has been granted.

The example is not a promise that all future schedule requests will be accepted. If the employee later submits an actual request, the manager checks staffing, patient coverage, and the dates. A manager should not treat “might,” “if,” “could,” or “would” as a substitute for the employee’s present instruction. Equally, an employee’s current request should not be dismissed merely because it refers to a future date: a request for a definite future schedule can still be current if it is direct and specific. The key distinction is whether the employee has asked for a definite change, not whether the calendar date is later.

Records and corrections
The people desk enters one of three statuses: information only, request pending, or approved adjustment. Use information only for a process question or conditional discussion. Use request pending when the employee directly asks for specified hours but the manager has not decided. Use approved adjustment only after manager confirmation. Do not infer a status from an informal conversation with another employee. If a manager has made a coverage estimate but the employee has not requested a change, the status remains information only.

Common questions
Can I ask about a schedule change before I know the dates? Yes, you can ask for information. The desk will not reserve hours based only on that question. If you later know the dates and want the change, send a direct request.

Can I ask my manager to keep an option open? You can discuss possibilities, but the manager should not describe the option as an approved schedule. A possible future need remains possible until you actually ask for a change. The policy does not require an employee to make a request before ready, and it does not allow the desk to invent one on the employee’s behalf.

Can a coworker request for me? A coworker can pass along general information but cannot make the employee’s decision. The case notes should say who made each statement. The employee’s own direct words determine whether a current request has been made. A conditional comment from a coworker is not an employee request, even if it accurately describes what the employee may need.

FAQ excerpt: Reimbursement and training registration, Quill Dental

This page is for employees who are considering a course or professional event. It explains the distinction between asking about a possible expense and asking the company to reimburse an expense already incurred. It also covers how to register for a course. A statement about what someone might do if a future condition occurs is not evidence that the action has already happened.

Q: When can I request reimbursement?
A: Submit the receipt and the completed expense form after you have paid an eligible cost. The finance desk cannot reimburse a cost that has not been paid. Asking “If I attend the workshop, will the company repay the fee?” is a question about a possible future expense. It is not a reimbursement claim, and it does not show that you registered or attended.

Q: Can I ask finance to hold money for me?
A: No payment is reserved from a question alone. If you want reimbursement after paying, submit the claim with the receipt. A manager may explain the usual limits, but a conversation about a possible payment does not create a claim. The employee should not write “paid” on a form for a fee that is only being considered.

Q: How do I register for a course?
A: Use the learning portal and select “Register.” A direct request to register now can be reviewed under the training budget. “If the clinic approves the time off, I would like to register” describes an intended later action dependent on approval. Unless the employee actually submits a registration or clearly asks the learning team to register them now, there is no completed registration. A question about what might happen is not a registration.

Example: An employee asks the learning team, “If my supervisor approves the schedule, could I attend the Friday course?” The team replies that it can check availability after the supervisor responds. The employee says, “I am only checking the process today; I have not registered.” The correct record is information only. The team should not tell the course provider that the employee has a place.

Q: What if a colleague says I will probably go?
A: A colleague’s expectation does not register you or create an expense claim. Only the employee’s direct action or clear current instruction can establish one. Keep a note of who said what. A supervisor’s statement that “she may attend if the schedule works” is a conditional prediction, not an employee’s commitment.

The ordinary approval sequence is as follows: employee asks about the course or submits a direct registration request; supervisor reviews schedule coverage; learning team confirms a place if available; employee pays any required fee; employee submits a receipt for any eligible reimbursement. Each step is separate. An expected later step must not be recorded as already completed. If the employee asks about a possible reimbursement before paying, answer the policy question and do not open a paid-expense claim. If the employee has paid but is only asking whether a future course might be covered, that separate fact does not turn the hypothetical course into an attended event.

Case note guidance: Avoid shorthand such as “course approved” when the supervisor has only said approval could be possible. Write the actual condition and the current status. “Could attend if schedule approved” is not the same as “registered for Friday.” “Could claim if fee paid” is not the same as “claim submitted.” The desk should not infer either registration or reimbursement from a person’s interest, a course calendar entry, or a colleague’s planning note. Employees may return later with a definite request when the relevant details are known.

A final reminder for supervisors: employees are allowed to explore options without committing. Do not pressure an employee to submit an application merely because they asked what the policy allows. Conversely, if an employee clearly submits a current request, record it even when its review will happen later. The question is whether an actual present action or instruction appears in the record, not whether a future scenario sounds plausible.

Policy page: Internal transfer interest and equipment return, Alderwick Services

This policy page is used by the people team when staff discuss moving between units or changing their assigned equipment. It applies to ordinary internal inquiries, not to a formal disciplinary or medical process. Employees can ask what choices may become available without making a transfer request. The page also says that equipment is returned only when an employee has been instructed to return it or has actually ended the assignment requiring it.

Transfer inquiries
An employee may ask whether a vacancy could be suitable if a future event occurs. For example, “If the evening team opens a position, could I move there?” is a question about a possible future option. It is not an application for the vacancy. To apply now, the employee must identify the vacancy and directly ask to be considered. A supervisor cannot submit an application merely because the employee has expressed interest in a possible later move.

The people team should classify a conversation as information only unless the employee makes a definite current request. “I would consider a transfer if my commute becomes longer” does not establish that the commute has changed or that a transfer is requested. “Please consider me for the posted records role” is a current application, even though the selection decision will come later. An application is not an approval; these are separate statuses.

Equipment return
The employee’s assigned tablet remains assigned while the employee continues in the current role, unless the equipment team directly requests its return. A statement such as “If I transfer later, I can return the tablet” is a future commitment conditional on a transfer. It does not mean the tablet has been returned, and it does not itself ask the equipment team to collect it. A current return instruction must state that the employee is returning the device now or ask the equipment team to arrange collection now.

Example case summary
A staff member tells the people adviser: “If the records opening is still available after the next roster is published, I might apply. If I move, I can hand back my tablet then. For now I only want to know how internal selection works.” The adviser explains the vacancy process. No application form is attached. The staff member’s current role remains active, and the tablet inventory shows the device assigned to that person. The adviser makes no transfer recommendation and sends no equipment collection request.

What not to infer
A manager may say a transfer seems possible if staffing improves. This is not a promise of a vacancy. A colleague may say the employee is “probably moving soon,” but that does not make an application. The employee may talk about returning equipment under a future condition without having returned it. Case notes should preserve the conditional wording rather than compressing it to “transfer” or “device returned.”

Records should be updated only when the action is definite. For a transfer, the statuses are inquiry, application received, selection in progress, and approved move. For a device, the statuses are assigned, return requested, collected, and inventory closed. Do not skip from inquiry to application received, or from assigned to collected, because a future plan sounds likely. If a later message contains a direct request, use its date and words to update the record then.

Supervisors should answer questions neutrally. They must not tell coworkers that an employee is moving based on a conditional conversation, and they must not remove assigned equipment based on a promise that applies only if a transfer happens. The employee can make an application and an equipment return request separately. One does not automatically imply the other. In particular, a hypothetical transfer does not establish either current transfer intent or completed equipment return.

The page’s last reminder is that conditional language can include a useful plan but remains conditional. “If the role opens, I might apply” is not the same as “I am applying.” “If I transfer, I can return the tablet” is not the same as “I returned it.” A careful note should say exactly what the employee has done now, and should not convert a possible future event into a completed one.
