SECTION C — TERMS-OF-SERVICE EXCERPT

Course administration service terms, version 3.2, adopted for the fictional school programme. The terms below govern whether a course account should be sent to the billing queue for a monthly seat charge. They are reproduced here as the applicable rule excerpt for this packet; the surrounding explanatory language does not create additional exceptions.

Section 4.1 — Standard monthly seat rate. A chargeable learner seat costs $18.00 for each billing month in which the learner is enrolled and the seat is active at 23:59 on the final calendar day of that month. The number of lesson visits, assessment submissions, messages, or downloads does not change the monthly seat rate. A learner may be inactive in practical use and still have a chargeable seat if the enrolment remains active at the stated month-end time.

Section 4.2 — Withdrawals. If an accepted withdrawal is recorded before 23:59 on the final calendar day, no monthly seat charge is due for that learner for that month. A withdrawal request that has been drafted but not submitted is not an accepted withdrawal. An accepted withdrawal recorded at or after 23:59 on the final calendar day takes effect for the next billing month, not the month that has ended. The timestamp stored in the official course record controls.

Section 4.3 — Mid-month adds. A learner whose enrolment begins after the first day but is active at month end is charged one full monthly seat rate, unless a written scholarship credit described in Section 4.5 applies. There is no daily proration under the standard rate. A learner invited to a course but never enrolled is not a chargeable seat.

Section 4.4 — Monthly billing review route. Send the account to the billing queue for a seat-rate adjustment when the computed seat charge for the stated learner group is greater than $500.00. The comparison is against the total amount that should be charged for the group under Sections 4.1 through 4.5, not against the amount already paid. Exactly $500.00 does not satisfy the condition. The rule concerns the computed monthly seat charge only; other fees are not added to it.

Section 4.5 — Scholarship credit. A written scholarship award recorded in the official account before the monthly close provides a $20.00 credit for each eligible learner named in the award. The credit is applied after calculating the standard seat charges. An award is eligible only when it identifies the learner and the billing month. A draft award, an unsigned message, or an award for a different month does not qualify. A credit cannot reduce the seat charge below zero for that learner. No other discount is implied.

Section 4.6 — Group calculation. When an operational review names a group of learners, add each learner’s charge after any applicable credit. Do not use the highest individual charge, the average, or the total of invoices from other months. Only the learners explicitly identified in the review group are included. If one person is named in a note as a comparison example but not in the specified group, exclude that person.

For the present review, the named group consists of six learners: Ada-01, Bex-02, Cato-03, Deni-04, Eno-05, and Fara-06. The following account facts are extracted from the official course record and the signed award register. All times are local and refer to the final day of the month unless a different date is stated.

Ada-01 was enrolled from the first day of September and remained active at 23:59 on 30 September. There is no withdrawal and no scholarship award for September. Her September seat charge is $18.00.

Bex-02 was enrolled from the first day of September. An accepted withdrawal was recorded at 18:40 on 30 September, before the 23:59 cutoff. The account had 11 lesson visits earlier in the month, but the withdrawal rule applies. Bex-02’s September seat charge is $0.00.

Cato-03 was invited on 4 September and opened the invitation page on 5 September, but never submitted enrolment and never received an active seat. Cato-03’s September seat charge is $0.00.

Deni-04 began an active enrolment on 12 September and remained active at 23:59 on 30 September. A written scholarship award naming Deni-04 and September was signed and entered in the official award register on 27 September. The full monthly rate applies under the mid-month add rule, then the qualifying $20.00 credit is applied; because a charge cannot fall below zero, Deni-04’s September charge is $0.00.

Eno-05 was enrolled and active at 23:59 on 30 September. The account has no eligible September award. A message in the local course chat says “scholarship for Eno, maybe September,” but it is unsigned, is not in the official award register, and does not identify a confirmed award month. It is not a qualifying credit under Section 4.5. Eno-05’s September seat charge is $18.00.

Fara-06 was enrolled through September. The accepted withdrawal was recorded at 23:59:08 on 30 September, eight seconds after the cutoff. Under Section 4.2, the withdrawal takes effect for October, so the September seat remains chargeable. Fara-06 has no scholarship award. Her September charge is $18.00.

The computed charge for the six named learners is therefore $18.00 + $0.00 + $0.00 + $0.00 + $18.00 + $18.00 = $54.00. This total is far below the strict “greater than $500.00” routing threshold. The billing queue rule in Section 4.4 is not met for this named group.

The review workbook also contains comparison accounts not included in the named six-person group. They are provided to explain the figures seen in a preliminary export and must not be included in the specified group total. The comparison accounts are: Garo-07, 20 active September seats at $18.00 each, total $360.00; Hani-08, 30 active September seats at $18.00 each, total $540.00; and Ivo-09, 28 active September seats at $18.00 each, total $504.00. These are separate sample groups used in training checks. Neither Hani-08 nor Ivo-09 is named among the six learners in the present review. The invoice section’s 31-seat figure likewise belongs to a separate invoice reconciliation and is not part of this terms calculation.

A draft summary cell in the workbook shows “possible group exposure $1,044.00.” Its formula adds the $540.00 Hani-08 comparison group, the $504.00 Ivo-09 comparison group, and the $0.00 result for a preliminary version of the named group. It is not the charge for the six named learners. Another dashboard box reads “18 seats active,” a count from a different course and billing month. Neither dashboard figure is the total to compare under Section 4.4.

For clarity, the per-person method for this group is as follows. First establish whether a learner is enrolled and active at the stipulated month-end time. Next apply an accepted withdrawal if it was recorded before the cutoff. Next apply the standard monthly rate to a remaining chargeable seat, including mid-month additions without proration. Then apply only a written, timely, month-specific scholarship credit in the official register, with a floor of zero. Finally sum the six group members and compare the result with the strict $500.00 threshold. This method produces $54.00, not $500.00, $504.00, $540.00, or $1,044.00.

The terms administrator added examples so that the account flags are interpreted consistently. A student with a low number of visits is not automatically non-chargeable if the seat remains active. A student who has submitted a valid pre-cutoff withdrawal is not chargeable even if the student used the course earlier in the month. An invitation page view alone is not enrolment. A mid-month start does not mean a half-month charge. A message that sounds like an award is not an award unless the specified written record requirements are met. A withdrawal only seconds after the cutoff belongs to the next month for billing purposes. These examples explain the recorded facts but do not replace the stated sections.

Historical check rows in the terms workbook show several arithmetic cases. A group of 27 active seats without credit gives 27 × $18.00 = $486.00, below the threshold. A group of 28 such seats gives 28 × $18.00 = $504.00, above the threshold. A group of 30 active seats with one eligible $20.00 credit gives $540.00 − $20.00 = $520.00, still above the threshold. A group of 29 active seats with two eligible credits gives $522.00 − $40.00 = $482.00, below the threshold. These sample calculations are not the present group’s membership or amount; they only show why the net calculated amount, rather than an unadjusted count, is compared.

Civic Services Consolidated Case File 24-771C

Office of Municipal Access and Community Support
Records copy prepared for interdepartmental review
Applicant: Xiu Rahman
Permit file: P-44108
Benefits file: B-90216
Vendor record: Tidewater Rentals
Case period: 3 March through 18 June

DOCUMENT CONTROL AND ROUTING

This consolidated file combines the permit desk’s payment record, the public-facing policy page in force during the review period, and a transcript of the applicant’s contacts with the service counter. It is assembled to show the sequence of received material, not to establish a new eligibility rule. The originals remain in their respective systems. Dates below are local office dates. “Received” means logged by the municipal system; it does not mean that a request was approved. Entries marked “copy” reproduce an attachment or an extract and do not constitute a separate filing.

The permit division administers temporary curb-use permits. The support division administers the Access Credit, a municipal benefit that may reimburse certain approved access-related costs. The divisions share a case number for routing only. A decision by one division is not automatically a decision by the other. A vendor invoice can document an expense, but it cannot by itself establish that the city owes a payment. Similarly, a permit application can document an intended use of public space without establishing that an Access Credit claim has been submitted.

The file includes several references to forms that were requested, discussed, drafted, or attached. Staff are instructed to distinguish a question about a form from a filing of that form, and a statement about possible future action from a present request. The case management system sometimes displays a status label before the accompanying narrative has been reviewed. For this reason, the narrative and the filed document control over an unexplained label. No reviewer should infer that an application was granted merely because a payment was received, or that an applicant withdrew a claim merely because the applicant asked what withdrawal would require.

The paper records were scanned in the order in which the records unit received them. The sequence is not necessarily the order in which the applicant composed them. A message forwarded by a clerk retains the original sender and recipient shown in the copied header. The clerk’s forwarding note is not a new statement by the applicant. Where a line is expressly identified as a draft, it is not a filed request unless a separate receipt confirms filing.

CASE INDEX

1. Permit application and receipt ledger, received 3 March.
2. Vendor invoice and payment reconciliation, received 10 March.
3. Public Access Credit policy extract, archived 1 March and confirmed applicable through 18 June.
4. Service-counter conversation transcript, 11 March, with follow-up contacts on 20 March and 2 April.
5. Permit review notices, 14 March and 8 April.
6. Benefit claim routing notes and supporting-document checklist, 15 March through 18 June.
7. Closing reconciliation and records-unit certification, 18 June.

The index is descriptive. It does not certify that every item listed is relevant to every question that may be put to this file. A listed attachment may be incomplete, informational, or superseded by a later record. The caseworker who scans a record does not decide its legal effect. The final section identifies which records were accepted as filings and which remained correspondence.

SECTION A — PERMIT APPLICATION AND RECEIPT LEDGER

On 3 March, Xiu Rahman submitted an application for a temporary curb-use permit outside the North Quay Community Hall. The requested date of use was 19 March, between 8:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. The application described a portable ramp, two folding tables, and a short loading interval for a rented access platform. The application did not request a street closure. The applicant checked the box marked “fee assistance information requested” and left the separate box marked “reimbursement claim” blank.

The filing receipt records an application fee of 46 municipal units. A separate processing charge of 12 units was entered as payable. The receipt does not show a waiver. The applicant paid 58 units at the counter by card. The card authorization record shows a single payment of 58 units, not two separate payments. The ledger was later annotated to explain the components: 46 application fee plus 12 processing charge equals 58 paid. The amount is recorded so that a later reviewer does not mistake the 12-unit processing charge for a second permit fee.

The application included a site sketch. The sketch showed a clear walkway of 1.8 metres between the platform and the hall entrance. The applicable permit review checklist requires at least 1.5 metres of unobstructed walkway unless a written exception is approved. The sketch is not an approval of that measurement. A site inspection would be required if the applicant proceeded with the installation. The permit desk therefore recorded the sketch as “proposed layout supplied,” not “clearance verified.”

The receipt also listed a requested contact method: written message through the municipal portal. The applicant gave permission for permit staff to send notices through that portal. The applicant did not authorize the vendor, Tidewater Rentals, to speak on the applicant’s behalf. A vendor may transmit a receipt or invoice but may not withdraw an application or make a benefit claim for the applicant without a signed authorization. No signed authorization for Tidewater Rentals appears in the file.

On 5 March, a permit technician added a routing note: “Possible equipment assistance; ask benefits desk whether any program may apply.” This note was internal. It was not a benefit application and was not sent as an assertion of eligibility. The technician did not determine whether the applicant had paid for eligible equipment, whether a benefit claim was timely, or whether the vendor’s invoice described reimbursable goods. The benefits desk later replied that the applicant would need to submit the prescribed claim form and supporting proof of payment.

On 7 March, the permit system generated a reminder that the application was awaiting safety review. The reminder contained a standard line stating that a pending application is not a permit. The line does not imply that the application was denied. At that time the applicant had neither an approved permit nor a denial. The application remained under review until 14 March.

The permit technician’s handwritten annotation, entered on 8 March, says: “No decision on temporary placement until access width verified. Do not treat vendor delivery reservation as an issued permit.” The annotation refers to the permit file only. It does not refer to the Access Credit and does not decide whether any invoice may be submitted for review.

SECTION B — VENDOR INVOICE AND LINE-ITEM RECONCILIATION

Tidewater Rentals invoice TR-8831 was dated 6 March and received by the municipal records unit on 10 March as an attachment to the applicant’s portal message. The invoice identifies Xiu Rahman as the customer and Tidewater Rentals as the vendor. It covers a rental reservation and related equipment. The invoice is evidence of a vendor charge; its presence in the city file does not establish that the city ordered the equipment or accepted liability for the charge.

Invoice lines as supplied:

Line 1 — Portable access platform, one-day reservation: 184 units.
Line 2 — Delivery to North Quay Community Hall: 32 units.
Line 3 — Collection from North Quay Community Hall: 28 units.
Line 4 — Optional protective mat, listed but declined: 14 units.
Line 5 — Refundable security deposit: 60 units.
Line 6 — Administrative booking charge: 9 units.

The invoice subtotal before deposit is 253 units: 184 + 32 + 28 + 9 = 253. The optional mat is excluded because the invoice marks it “declined; not billed.” Adding the 60-unit deposit yields a cash due figure of 313 units. The invoice’s payment box shows a card payment of 313 units on 6 March. The vendor’s later account statement lists a 60-unit deposit credit after the equipment was returned, leaving a net charge of 253 units. These figures are not inconsistent: 313 was initially collected, 60 was subsequently credited, and 253 remained charged. No city payment is recorded in this ledger.

A service fee of 9 units appears both in the invoice detail and in the vendor’s printed terms. It is one charge, not two. The printed total of 327 units on the first scan is crossed out by the vendor and marked “superseded.” The corrected amount is 313 units including the deposit. The 327-unit figure appears to have included the declined 14-unit mat. The payment processor record is 313 units, and the vendor’s account statement records a 60-unit credit. Staff should not treat the superseded total as the amount paid.

On 9 March, Tidewater Rentals sent the applicant a message headed “Reservation confirmation.” It stated that the platform would be held until 18 March and that cancellation after 12 March might carry a charge under the vendor’s terms. The message did not state that the city had approved the permit. It did not state that the city had promised a benefit. The vendor wrote that it could not determine “whether municipal assistance will be available.”

The applicant’s portal message of 10 March attached the invoice with the note: “For the file, so staff can tell me what documents are needed. This is not a request that the city pay Tidewater directly.” The clerk’s receipt confirms that an attachment was received. The receipt classifies the submission as “supporting document / inquiry,” not “benefit claim.” The applicant’s message did not include the prescribed Access Credit claim form. The note is relevant to the purpose of the transmission but is not itself a completed claim.

The invoice is included here because it was part of the consolidated record, not because its items are all covered by the Access Credit. Under the archived policy excerpt below, reimbursement review is limited to eligible expenses actually incurred by the applicant, supported by evidence of payment, and submitted on the required claim form within the applicable period. A reservation that is later cancelled without a charge would not be an incurred expense. A refundable deposit that has been credited back is not a net expense. A vendor’s description of a product as “access equipment” does not settle whether the policy’s criteria are met.

A handwritten note on the back of the invoice, initialled by the applicant, reads: “I am not saying I do not want the 60 back; please confirm the credit has actually been processed.” The vendor statement records the credit as processed on 8 March. The note concerns the vendor’s deposit credit. It does not ask the municipal office to refund the permit fee or reimburse the rental charge. The note was not entered in the benefit claim system as a request for municipal money.

A second note, written by a clerk while discussing the invoice, says: “Do not infer a claim from a customer who is not not asking about reimbursement.” This is a drafting error in an internal note, retained in the scan. It is not a statement by the applicant. The next sentence clarifies the clerk’s intended instruction: “Ask whether a completed claim form was received; do not infer filing from a general inquiry.” The clerk’s wording is not controlling evidence about what the applicant requested.

The invoice reconciliation was completed on 12 March. The reviewer verified that the vendor charged 253 units net after the deposit credit. The reviewer did not decide whether any part was eligible under the benefit policy, because no claim form was then on file. The reconciliation field “amount verified” means the arithmetic was checked against the supplied vendor statement. It does not mean “amount approved for reimbursement.”

SECTION C — PUBLIC ACCESS CREDIT POLICY PAGE (ARCHIVED EXTRACT)

Page title: Access Credit for temporary access-related costs
Effective version: 1 March through 30 June
Issuing unit: Community Support Division

Purpose. The Access Credit may assist a resident with certain documented costs associated with temporary access arrangements. The program is administered separately from permit issuance. A person may receive a permit and no Access Credit, may qualify for an Access Credit without needing a curb-use permit, or may receive neither. A permit decision does not automatically determine a benefit decision.

Submission requirement. A request for an Access Credit must be made using Form AC-4. The form must identify the applicant, the cost for which assistance is sought, the date incurred, and the amount requested. The applicant must sign the declaration and provide supporting documents. A question about eligibility, a request for a blank form, a vendor invoice sent only for informational review, or a permit application that checks “fee assistance information requested” is not a claim. Staff may help a person complete a form, but staff may not convert an inquiry into a claim without the applicant’s confirmation and signature.

Timeliness. Form AC-4 must be received no later than 30 calendar days after the expense is incurred. The date on which a form is saved as a draft does not count as receipt. The date on which an invoice is received does not count as receipt of the claim unless the invoice is accompanied by a completed Form AC-4. A postmark is not used. The receipt stamp in the claim system controls.

Eligible cost categories. The program may consider a reasonable rental fee for a temporary access platform and necessary delivery or collection charges, if the equipment was used for an approved access arrangement and the applicant supplies evidence of payment. An administrative booking charge is not eligible. An optional item that was declined is not eligible. A security deposit that is returned or credited is not an eligible net cost. The office may assess the reasonableness of a fee after the applicant files a claim. The policy does not promise payment of every cost falling within a named category.

Payment evidence. A vendor invoice alone may establish the amount requested by the vendor, but does not establish that the applicant paid it. The applicant may provide a card receipt, account statement, or other reliable record. If a deposit is collected and later credited, the amount considered is reduced by the credit. If the vendor’s records disagree, staff must request clarification rather than selecting the larger figure. A cancelled reservation is not a paid rental expense unless a cancellation charge was actually imposed and documented.

Exception for incomplete supporting material. If Form AC-4 is received on time but a required receipt is missing, staff may hold the claim open for 10 calendar days after sending a written deficiency notice. The exception extends the time to provide missing supporting material only. It does not extend the deadline to file Form AC-4. An invoice attached to an inquiry is not treated as a timely claim under this exception.

Exception for an office closure. If the final filing day falls on a day when the claim counter is closed, a claim submitted through the portal by 11:59 p.m. on the next open day is considered timely. This exception concerns the filing deadline only. It does not waive the required form, signature, eligible-cost rules, or payment evidence.

Payment direction. An approved credit is normally paid to the applicant. Direct payment to a vendor requires a separate written authorization signed by the applicant and a vendor payment agreement. A vendor may not file a claim on the applicant’s behalf merely by submitting an invoice. A message from a vendor asking whether a customer may be eligible does not constitute the customer’s request for benefits.

Withdrawal. A claim is withdrawn only if the applicant communicates a present and unambiguous instruction to close a filed claim, or signs the withdrawal section of Form AC-4. Asking how to withdraw, saying a claim might be withdrawn, or stating that the applicant does not wish to withdraw does not withdraw a claim. A staff member must record the withdrawal and send a confirmation. An inquiry that was never filed cannot be withdrawn as a claim, although the applicant may ask that the inquiry be closed.

Interpretation notes. The policy uses “not filed” to describe the absence of a completed claim in the claim system. “No payment issued” describes the payment record and does not by itself establish that a claim was denied. “No decision” describes a pending review, not an approval or denial. When two statements in a contact appear to conflict, staff should read the entire exchange and ask for clarification if the applicant’s present instruction cannot be determined. A denial must identify the rule applied and the record relied upon.

Review sequence. First, verify receipt of the signed Form AC-4. Second, verify the filing date. Third, identify the net costs actually incurred. Fourth, compare the claimed categories with the eligible categories. Fifth, verify the supporting evidence. Sixth, issue an approval, partial approval, request for additional information, or denial. The order is mandatory for administrative consistency. Staff must not skip the receipt check because the file contains an invoice or because the applicant has a permit.

Recordkeeping. All final determinations must be sent to the applicant through the portal or by mail. A telephone conversation may explain a process but does not replace a written determination. An internal note such as “probably eligible,” “likely withdrawn,” or “not not interested” must not be entered as a final outcome. The employee should quote the applicant’s operative words where feasible and identify whether the words were spoken by the applicant, a vendor, or a staff member.

For purposes of this page, “present instruction” means a request that applies now, not a hypothetical statement about what the person could do later. “Explicit request” means that the person communicates the requested action in words or by completing the relevant form. A person need not use a prescribed phrase if the requested action is otherwise clear. Double negatives should be interpreted in context: a statement that the person is not refusing to request a review may communicate willingness to request review, but it does not replace a required signed form. A statement that the person does not deny wanting a refund may express a desire, but the staff member must identify whose money is at issue and which office is being asked to act.

SECTION D — SERVICE-COUNTER TRANSCRIPT

Transcript reference: SC-11902
Date of initial contact: 11 March
Mode: service counter, audio record transcribed by clerk
Participants: Xiu Rahman (applicant); Beatriz Haddad (counter clerk)

The transcript was reviewed against the audio recording. Pauses and repetitions were retained where material. Bracketed descriptions are clerical annotations, not spoken words.

Haddad: I have the permit receipt and the vendor invoice. What would you like us to do with the invoice today?

Rahman: I sent it so I can find out which papers the benefit office needs. I’m not asking you to pay the rental company from this counter.

Haddad: Understood. There is a separate form for the Access Credit. Have you submitted that form?

Rahman: Not yet. I thought the invoice might be enough to start the conversation. It is not the claim form.

Haddad: It is not. The form needs your signature and the amount you want reviewed. The invoice is useful as supporting material after a form is received.

Rahman: I do not deny that I want the office to review the rental cost. I am not saying I don’t want to ask for help. I want to know whether delivery and collection can be included.

Haddad: I can explain the categories, but I cannot decide your claim before the form is filed. The policy says the rental charge and necessary delivery or collection may be reviewed. It excludes the booking charge and any deposit that comes back to you.

Rahman: The deposit has come back. The statement says sixty units credited. The first page said three hundred thirteen paid, and the final net charge is two hundred fifty-three.

Haddad: That matches the statement. The invoice’s earlier total of three hundred twenty-seven is marked superseded, and it includes the optional mat that was not billed.

Rahman: Right. The mat was declined. I do not want that included. I am asking about the remaining costs, not the mat or the deposit.

Haddad: For the claim, use the net amount and attach the card record and the vendor statement. The booking charge is listed separately and is not eligible under the policy. The office may still review whether the other charges were reasonable and connected to the approved arrangement.

Rahman: The permit is not approved yet, is it?

Haddad: Correct. It is under safety review. Your application is not a permit. The benefits team reviews the credit separately.

Rahman: If the permit is not approved, I may cancel the reservation. I am not telling you to cancel anything now. I need the decision first.

Haddad: I will record that as a question about a possible later cancellation, not as an instruction to cancel the permit or a claim.

Rahman: Thank you. And I do not fail to understand that an invoice is not the form. I will submit the form if I decide to proceed.

Haddad: Would you like a blank Form AC-4 today?

Rahman: Yes, please. That is all I am asking for today. I am not asking you to treat this conversation as a filed claim.

Haddad: I will give you the form and record the contact as an information request. The invoice will remain as an attachment to that inquiry.

Rahman: Please do. Also, I don’t deny that the permit fee was paid, but I am not asking for that fee back in this conversation. I am asking about possible assistance with the equipment cost.

Haddad: I will note that distinction. The permit fee and Access Credit are handled under separate records.

Rahman: Is there a deadline?

Haddad: The policy says the completed, signed form must be received within 30 calendar days after the expense was incurred. A draft or invoice alone does not meet that requirement. If a filing is timely but a receipt is missing, the office may send a deficiency notice and allow 10 days for the missing receipt. That does not extend the initial filing deadline.

Rahman: The charge happened on the sixth. I will check what day is thirty days later. I am not claiming that I already filed anything.

Haddad: The record will show no claim form received today. Please keep the blank form and use the portal receipt screen when you submit it.

Rahman: I will. I am not declining help; I just do not want an information request labelled as an application.

Haddad: That is clear. The inquiry will be coded as information only.

[Clerk note: Form AC-4 blank copy issued. No signed form collected. No withdrawal action taken.]

The transcript includes repeated negative constructions. They are recorded as spoken and should not be converted into a different instruction by removing a “not.” The conversation distinguishes asking for information, expressing interest in a possible review, and actually filing the prescribed claim. The counter clerk made no promise of reimbursement and did not take a claim form. The applicant did not instruct the clerk to cancel the permit application, cancel the vendor reservation, or close a filed claim.

FOLLOW-UP CONTACT OF 20 MARCH

A portal message from Xiu Rahman was received on 20 March. The subject line was “Form question.” The message reads:

“I have completed most of AC-4 but have not sent it. I am not unable to finish it; I need to confirm which amount belongs in the request. I understand the net vendor charge is 253 after the 60 deposit credit. I have not included the optional mat. The booking charge is 9, and your policy says that part is not eligible. I would prefer to request review of the platform and transport charges only. Please tell me whether the form should show the whole paid amount with an explanation of the credit, or only the net amount. This message is not my completed filing. I am not asking you to close a claim, because I have not filed one.”

The message was routed to the benefits help desk. It was answered on 22 March: “Enter the amount for which you seek review and explain any credit. Attach the original charge record and the credit record. The office will assess eligible categories after a signed AC-4 is received. Your 20 March message is not a claim filing.”

The help desk response did not identify a final amount payable. It gave completion guidance. The file contains an unsent draft saved on 22 March. The draft has no signature, no submission timestamp, and no claim receipt number. Under the policy, saving that draft does not establish receipt.

A supervisor reviewing the draft on 23 March wrote: “The customer appears not unwilling to apply, but intent is not the same as submission. Do not create a claim from a draft.” The note reflects an interpretation of the correspondence and repeats the rule that Form AC-4 must be received. It does not say that the applicant withdrew or abandoned a claim.

FOLLOW-UP CONTACT OF 2 APRIL

At 9:14 a.m. on 2 April, the portal received a second message from Xiu Rahman. It states:

“I am submitting the attached signed AC-4 now. Please review the net platform and delivery/collection charges. I am not requesting the declined mat, the refunded deposit, or the non-eligible booking charge. I do not say that I am not seeking the Access Credit; I am asking for the eligible part to be reviewed. If any requested part cannot be considered, please issue a written decision identifying why. I do not want the whole file closed just because one line is excluded.”

The message has a completed and signed Form AC-4 attached. The claim system receipt is stamped 2 April at 9:14 a.m. The applicant lists the platform rental, delivery, and collection as the costs for review and explains the 60-unit deposit credit. The requested total is 244 units: 184 + 32 + 28 = 244. The applicant excludes the 9-unit booking charge and the returned deposit. The total is consistent with the net vendor charge of 253 minus the non-eligible 9-unit booking charge. The declined 14-unit mat was not charged and is also excluded. The form is associated with the benefit file, not the permit fee ledger.

The form’s declaration states that the applicant paid the vendor. The attached card record shows 313 units initially paid; the vendor statement shows the 60-unit credit. The claim asks for review of the 244-unit eligible-category subtotal, not for automatic payment of that amount. The policy requires staff to review whether the relevant costs were reasonable and connected with the approved arrangement. A claim can therefore be received and still be pending, partially approved, or denied after review.

The receipt system first displayed “documents incomplete” because the site-use approval was not attached. The status was corrected by the benefits clerk on 3 April to “claim received; evidence review pending.” The correction was made because the permit decision could not yet be found in the shared document view. The status change did not alter the receipt date or the claimed amount. The claim remained open.

On 4 April, the applicant sent a message asking whether the permit decision had been added. It reads: “I am not saying I will not provide the approval if you need it. I cannot attach a decision that has not been issued. Please tell me whether a later permit notice can be added to the existing claim.” The benefits clerk replied that the missing permit record could be added when available and that the claim would remain under review. The message did not withdraw the claim or seek a refund of the permit fee.

The permit division issued a conditional approval on 8 April. The approval allowed the temporary platform placement for the requested date subject to a final walkway check at installation. The approval did not certify that the benefit claim was eligible. The approval letter was added to the benefits file on 9 April. The permit division’s record notes that the event date had passed while the application was under review, but that the permit file remained open for accounting and compliance review. No penalty was assessed.

SECTION E — INTERNAL ROUTING AND REVIEW NOTES

10 April — Benefits intake: “Signed AC-4 on file, receipt 2 April. Request is for 244 units, consisting of platform, delivery, collection. Invoice net charge 253 after deposit credit; booking charge 9 excluded. Need confirm relationship to approved access arrangement and whether the dated reservation reflects use.”

11 April — Permit desk: “Conditional approval issued 8 April, after requested use date. Applicant supplied a sketch and invoice before date. Do not record the permit as final authorization for 19 March use. No finding of unauthorized installation; no installation record received.”

12 April — Benefits reviewer: “The claim was received after the requested event date but within the policy period asserted by applicant. Policy deadline runs from date expense incurred, not date of event. Vendor charge dated 6 March. Thirty calendar days after 6 March is 5 April if 7 March is day one and 5 April is day 30. Claim received 2 April, before 5 April.”

The date calculation in the 12 April note was checked by the records supervisor. The expense date is 6 March. Excluding the day of the expense, 7–31 March contributes 25 calendar days, and 1–5 April contributes 5 more; the thirtieth day is 5 April. The signed form was received 2 April, three calendar days before that deadline. The form was therefore timely. This calculation concerns only filing timeliness; it does not decide eligibility or payment.

13 April — Review queue: “Do not confuse invoice date with claim receipt. The invoice arrived 10 March, but AC-4 arrived 2 April. Both dates are in file for different purposes. The deadline is met by the latter date.”

14 April — Evidence check: “Card record supports initial 313 payment. Vendor record supports 60 credit. Net cost is 253. Requested eligible-category subtotal is 244 after excluding booking fee 9. No evidence of mat charge; invoice labels it declined. No claim made for mat.”

15 April — Permit liaison: “Approval letter uploaded. It is conditional and postdates the scheduled use. Need applicant clarification whether the platform was actually installed and whether delivery and collection occurred. Do not infer use from a reservation confirmation.”

16 April — Contact request issued to applicant. The request asks for a dated statement or other record showing whether the platform was delivered, installed, and collected. It explains that the policy may consider a rental and necessary transport charges when tied to an approved access arrangement. It does not request a new AC-4 and does not reset the filing deadline.

18 April — Applicant response: “The platform was delivered on 19 March and collected the same day. I have a delivery text but no signed delivery slip. The hall manager can confirm the clear path was maintained. I know the letter was dated later. I am not saying it was not approved eventually; I am asking you to review the actual record and tell me whether the delayed letter prevents consideration.”

19 April — Reviewer: “Response is not a withdrawal. It asks for review. The later conditional approval does not itself prove prior authorization, but policy language requires approved access arrangement. Refer to supervisor for interpretation. Do not deny solely on an assumption that the installation did or did not occur.”

22 April — Supervisor: “The permit letter is dated after the event and does not retroactively state that installation on 19 March was authorized. The benefit policy does not define whether later conditional approval is sufficient. Seek the permit division’s factual record and do not characterize the applicant as having withdrawn.”

23 April — Permit liaison: “The permit file contains no inspection completed on the event date. The drawing proposed 1.8 metres of clearance. The policy checklist calls for 1.5 metres minimum. We cannot certify the installed clearance after the fact. This is an evidentiary limitation, not a finding that the walkway was blocked.”

24 April — Benefits reviewer: “Invoice and vendor statement establish the charge and credit. Delivery message may support delivery, subject to authenticity confirmation. The hall manager’s statement may support use and clearance, but is not yet in file. The case remains open for requested evidence.”

The routing notes contain tentative terms such as “may,” “need,” and “not yet.” These are not final determinations. The phrase “does not retroactively state” describes the permit letter; it does not necessarily decide the separate benefit question. The benefits reviewer must apply the policy text and the evidence actually received, rather than treating a staff member’s short routing note as a rule.

SECTION F — SUPPORTING MATERIAL RECEIVED IN MAY

On 2 May, the applicant uploaded a screenshot of the vendor’s delivery message. The message from Tidewater Rentals, dated 19 March at 7:42 a.m., states: “Platform delivered at North Quay Community Hall. Customer acknowledged receipt. Collection scheduled for 1 p.m.” The screenshot shows the sender name and date but not a full telephone number. The records unit compared the message with the vendor’s account record. On 6 May, Tidewater Rentals confirmed by email that the message was sent from its dispatch system and related to invoice TR-8831.

On 5 May, the hall manager, Oren Kowalski, sent a signed statement. It says that a platform was at the hall entrance on 19 March, that it was removed the same afternoon, and that staff kept a passage open during the event. The statement describes the passage as “wide enough for routine entry” but does not give a measured width. The statement does not say that a municipal inspector attended. The manager is not a permit officer and cannot issue a permit or determine the benefit claim.

On 7 May, the permit liaison added a note that the hall manager’s statement was consistent with the submitted site sketch but could not verify an exact 1.8-metre clearance. The liaison also noted that the permit checklist’s 1.5-metre measure is a minimum for review, not proof that a particular installation met it. The note did not find a violation. No incident report, obstruction complaint, or enforcement notice is in the permit file.

On 9 May, the benefits reviewer emailed Xiu Rahman that the supporting material had been added and that no additional receipt was requested at that time. The message stated: “This is not an approval. The claim remains under review. You may provide any further relevant record, but no new claim form is needed for the materials already submitted.” The applicant replied: “I do not misunderstand that the claim is still open. Please continue the review. I am not asking you to treat my reply as a new claim or as a withdrawal.”

On 13 May, an internal screen briefly displayed the code “closed—customer not pursuing.” The screen code was entered during a batch update by an employee who had read the 4 April message out of context. The employee’s supervisor changed it to “open—evidence review” the same day. The audit history preserves both entries. The correction note says the 4 April message offered to provide a permit record and asked a question; it did not ask for closure. The screen code therefore does not establish a withdrawal.

On 16 May, an automated notice was generated with the subject “Your case may be closed.” The notice was triggered by a queue age rule and not by a substantive decision. It said the applicant could respond if more review was desired. The applicant responded the same day: “I am not not interested in the review. Please keep the claim open and issue a written decision when the review is complete.” The clerk linked the response to the existing claim. The response is a clear present instruction to continue review, not to close the claim.

On 20 May, a caseworker wrote a draft note: “Customer’s double negative appears to indicate continued interest.” The supervisor commented: “Do not rely on a label for grammar. The actual sentence says the applicant is not not interested, followed by an explicit request to keep the claim open. Record the present instruction as continuation.” The final case note quotes the complete sentence and identifies it as an applicant message.

On 22 May, the applicant provided a second statement: “I am not refusing to confirm the platform was used. It was used. I am not claiming the city had already issued the permit before 19 March. I am asking that you decide the benefit claim under the published wording and the documents now in the file.” The statement supplies no new payment document. It clarifies that the applicant acknowledges the timing of the permit approval while maintaining the claim. It does not seek a refund of the 58-unit permit payment.

The benefits reviewer logged the statement as a clarification. The reviewer did not interpret the applicant’s acknowledgment as an admission that the platform was unauthorized. The permit file has no finding on actual clearance, and the benefit policy does not state that every later approval automatically validates an earlier installation. The review must therefore address what the policy requires and what the evidence supports. A final decision, if made, must explain any interpretation used.

SECTION G — POLICY APPLICATION CHECKLIST

The following checklist was attached to the review packet to organize the evidence. It is not a substitute for the policy page and does not itself decide the case.

Receipt of AC-4: Completed and signed form received 2 April at 9:14 a.m. Receipt number AC-90216-04. The 20 March portal message and 22 March saved draft were not filings. The original invoice received 10 March was supporting material attached to an inquiry. The 2 April submission is the first claim filing shown in the system.

Deadline: Expense dated 6 March. Thirty calendar days after the expense date expires 5 April. The claim was received 2 April. It was received before the deadline. The office-closure exception is not needed to reach this result. There is no evidence that the counter was closed on 5 April, and the deadline calculation does not depend on a weekend rule.

Claimed amount: 244 units. Platform rental 184, delivery 32, collection 28. Total 244. The 9-unit booking charge is excluded from the applicant’s request and is ineligible under the policy. The optional mat, 14 units, was declined and not billed. The 60-unit deposit was collected and later credited. The original 313-unit payment less the 60-unit credit equals a net vendor charge of 253. The difference between 253 and the claimed 244 is the 9-unit booking charge.

Payment evidence: Vendor invoice shows an initial collection of 313. Card record matches. Vendor account statement confirms credit of 60. The resulting 253 net charge is supported. The requested 244 consists only of listed platform and transport charges. No arithmetic discrepancy is apparent in that requested subtotal.

Category test: Platform rental is a named potentially eligible category. Necessary delivery and collection are named potentially eligible categories. A named category is not automatically approved; reasonableness and connection to an approved access arrangement still require review. Booking is excluded. Declined mat is excluded. Returned deposit is excluded as a net expense.

Arrangement evidence: Permit application filed 3 March. Requested use 19 March. Conditional permit approval issued 8 April. Vendor delivery message is dated 19 March and was confirmed by the vendor on 6 May. Hall manager statement says the platform was present and removed that day and a passage was kept open. No official inspection measured the passage. The sketch proposed 1.8 metres; the checklist minimum is 1.5 metres. No incident report is present. The policy does not expressly state in the extracted page whether approval must be issued before the expense is incurred or whether later approval can establish an approved arrangement. Any decision using that distinction must quote the governing interpretation or request authoritative clarification rather than inventing a rule.

Applicant instruction: On 2 April, applicant asked the office to review the eligible part and requested a written explanation if a part could not be considered. On 9 May, applicant asked the office to continue. On 16 May, applicant expressly asked that the claim remain open. No withdrawal form or present instruction to close is in the file. The phrases “I do not say that I am not seeking the Access Credit” and “I am not not interested in the review” appear in the applicant’s messages. Each is accompanied by a clear request for review or continuation. They should not be summarized as a refusal.

Payment status: No Access Credit payment has been issued. No final approval or denial appears in the records through 18 June. “No payment issued” is not a denial. The claim status is “open—decision pending.” The permit fee payment is a separate 58-unit transaction and has not been the subject of a refund request in the benefit claim.

SECTION H — ADDITIONAL CUSTOMER CHAT TRANSCRIPT

Chat reference: CC-5407
Date: 2 June
Participants: Xiu Rahman; Dalia Alvarez, benefits contact officer

System greeting: You are connected to the Community Support Division. This chat cannot issue a final determination. Please do not include full card numbers.

Alvarez: I can confirm that AC-90216-04 is open. What would you like clarified?

Rahman: I saw a note saying there is no payment. Does that mean the claim was refused?

Alvarez: No. The record says no payment has been issued because the review is pending. It does not show a denial.

Rahman: Thank you. I am not assuming that no payment means no claim. I am asking whether the documents are all there.

Alvarez: The signed form, invoice, payment record, deposit credit, vendor delivery confirmation, hall statement, and permit notice are present. The reviewer may ask for more information, but there is no current deficiency notice.

Rahman: I do not fail to see why the permit date matters. I also do not think the later letter should be ignored. I am asking for the policy basis if that timing is a reason to refuse any part.

Alvarez: I cannot decide that in chat. The reviewer must explain how the policy applies. The extracted page says costs may be considered when tied to an approved access arrangement, but it does not give a specific rule about the date an approval must issue.

Rahman: So you are not telling me that the claim is approved?

Alvarez: Correct. I am not saying it is approved. I am confirming it is still under review.

Rahman: I understand. I am not asking to have the claim closed. Please keep it open.

Alvarez: I will add that request to the existing file. Is there anything else?

Rahman: No. I am not asking for the 60-unit deposit again; that was returned by the vendor. I am not asking for the 58-unit permit payment back. I am asking only for a decision on the 244 units listed on AC-4.

Alvarez: I will record those distinctions. The benefit review concerns the amount claimed on AC-4. It does not automatically reimburse the full amount shown on the original invoice.

Rahman: That is fine. Please send the decision in writing.

Alvarez: The file already records that request. The written decision will be sent through the portal when issued.

Chat closure notice: No claim was created, withdrawn, approved, or denied during the chat. An existing-file contact note was added.

The chat contains no operative instruction to refund the deposit or permit fee. The applicant distinguishes those amounts from the 244-unit benefit request. The chat is not a substitute for Form AC-4, but the form was already received on 2 April. The chat does not amend the claimed amount and does not authorize direct payment to Tidewater Rentals.

SECTION I — INVOICE CONTROL COPY AND VARIANCE NOTES

The records unit compared the invoice scan, the card record, and the vendor account statement. The following differences are recorded to prevent the use of an obsolete number in later summaries.

The first invoice image shows a handwritten total of 327 units. The vendor marked it superseded. That figure can be reconstructed as the corrected 313-unit amount plus the 14-unit optional mat. However, the line for the mat is marked declined and not billed, and the card record is 313. The 327 figure was not paid.

The later account statement starts from 313 collected, subtracts 60 credited, and records 253 as the net vendor charge. The account statement does not list a separate city contribution. The net 253 consists of 184 platform rental, 32 delivery, 28 collection, and 9 booking charge. The four included lines sum to 253. The applicant’s 244-unit claim excludes the 9 booking charge, leaving 184 + 32 + 28 = 244.

The original permit receipt is a different transaction. It records 46 plus 12, for a total of 58. The applicant’s portal message of 10 March expressly states that it is not a request for the city to pay Tidewater directly. The June chat expressly states that the applicant is not asking for the permit payment back. Neither statement asks for a refund of the permit receipt. The permit division has no record of a refund request in the period covered by this file.

The words “refund,” “credit,” and “reimbursement” appear in multiple sections, but their referents differ. The 60-unit vendor deposit credit is a completed vendor transaction. The Access Credit is a municipal benefit claim. A permit-fee refund would be a request for repayment of the 58-unit municipal fee. The file contains the first, contains a claim for the second, and does not contain a present request for the third. A reviewer should not collapse these into a single monetary request merely because they appear in the same consolidated record.

On the invoice’s reverse, the vendor’s terms state: “Customer may request a deposit credit after equipment return. This does not mean municipal reimbursement has been requested.” The vendor’s account system later marks the credit complete. This term concerns the vendor’s deposit process and does not control the municipal claim. The applicant’s question about confirmation of the credit was addressed by the vendor statement, not by a city refund decision.

The records unit has not found a message from Xiu Rahman stating “refund the permit fee,” “return my 58 units,” or an equivalent request. The absence of those exact phrases is not alone determinative; the controlling question is whether the applicant clearly asked the municipal office to return that fee. The messages found instead identify the vendor deposit as returned, deny that the counter conversation was a claim filing, and later ask for review of the specified 244-unit Access Credit claim. No document requests repayment of the 58-unit permit fee.

SECTION J — DECISION-STATUS HISTORY THROUGH 18 JUNE

3 March: Permit application received; fee paid; benefit claim not received.

5 March: Internal referral to benefits desk for general information; no claim received.

10 March: Invoice attached to informational inquiry; no claim form received.

11 March: Blank Form AC-4 issued at counter; no signature collected; no claim received.

20 March: Applicant asked a form-completion question; no claim received.

22 March: Unsubmitted draft saved; no claim received.

2 April: Signed Form AC-4 received; claim AC-90216-04 opened. Requested review amount: 244 units.

3 April: Temporary “documents incomplete” code corrected to evidence review pending; claim remained open.

8 April: Conditional permit approval issued; permit decision added to benefit record on 9 April.

16 April: Evidence request sent; claim remained open.

2 May through 7 May: Vendor confirmation and hall manager statement received; no new claim form needed.

13 May: Erroneous closed code corrected on the same day; audit trail retained; claim remained open.

16 May: Applicant expressly asked to keep claim open; contact linked to existing claim.

2 June: Chat confirmed pending status; no substantive determination made.

18 June: No approval, denial, withdrawal, or payment recorded. Status remains open—decision pending.

The history demonstrates that the claim did not exist in the system before 2 April, notwithstanding earlier discussion and invoice transmission. Once filed, it remained open. A code briefly marking closure was corrected and is not a final action. The applicant’s later statements contain negative constructions but repeatedly make the present request clear: review the filed claim and keep it open pending a written decision.

SECTION K — RECORDS-UNIT CERTIFICATION

I certify that this consolidated copy reflects the records indexed above as of 18 June. This certification concerns copying and record status only. It is not a determination of benefit eligibility, permit compliance, or a refund entitlement. No reviewer should use this certification to convert a pending matter into a final outcome.

The file supports the following procedural facts. Xiu Rahman paid Tidewater Rentals, which later credited a refundable deposit. The net vendor charge was 253 units. The applicant submitted a signed Access Credit form on 2 April requesting review of 244 units. The filing was received within 30 calendar days after the 6 March expense date. The claim was still pending as of 18 June. The applicant did not ask the city to pay Tidewater directly in the 10 March inquiry, and did not ask for the 58-unit permit fee to be returned in the June chat. The applicant did ask for the Access Credit claim to be reviewed and kept open.

The file does not establish that a benefit payment was approved, that a permit-fee refund was requested, or that a final denial was issued. The permit letter was conditional and dated after the requested use date. The vendor and hall records support delivery and use on 19 March, while the file lacks an official measurement of the installed clearance. The applicable policy extract allows consideration of certain categories tied to an approved access arrangement but does not resolve every issue presented by the sequence of permit approval and actual use. A substantive decision must address that issue rather than treating a pending status, an internal code, or a double-negative sentence as a substitute for analysis.

The record’s purpose is to preserve context. A single sentence extracted from a transcript may appear to say less than the whole exchange. “I am not saying I don’t want to ask for help” is followed by a question about eligible delivery and collection costs. “I do not say that I am not seeking the Access Credit” is followed by a request to review the eligible part. “I am not not interested in the review” is followed by an explicit request to keep the claim open. Conversely, the applicant’s statement that the 10 March invoice transmission was not a request for municipal direct payment is consistent with the classification of that transmission as an inquiry, not a claim. The office must read each construction with its speaker, object, and surrounding words identified.

End of consolidated copy.

Section C — processing and filing notes
1. Information-only contacts are not treated as filed applications. A person asking where to obtain a form has not, by that fact alone, submitted the form.

4. Follow-up entries describe the next administrative step. “Send,” “provide,” or “explain” ordinarily records a planned response and does not establish that the response has already been delivered unless the note expressly says it was sent.
5. The desk does not record monetary refunds in this extract. A question about fees, a fee schedule, a benefit, or a payment process should not be treated as a request to return money unless the contact explicitly asks for money back.
6. In this office’s spreadsheet conventions, “complete” is used only for a checked list of required items. A contact’s own statement that a form is complete is not a staff verification.
7. Staff use “permit information” for general questions and “permit filing” for questions about receiving submitted materials. These labels do not indicate whether a permit is granted.
8. A benefit information inquiry does not establish that a person qualifies for a benefit. The decision unit, not the information desk, evaluates eligibility under the relevant program rules.
9. If no documents are listed as reviewed, the record should be read as showing no document review at that contact. It should not be read as showing that the person has no documents elsewhere.
10. A scheduled appointment is not an interview outcome. Appointment notices and appointment-access requests are tracked separately from eligibility decisions.

They also cannot be used to infer the number of applications approved or denied. Section E — service desk handover notes
Morning handover, 2025-09-08: The front counter has the current permit forms and the benefit intake checklist. If a visitor asks for a paper version, staff may provide one or arrange mailing. Do not mark an application received merely because a blank form is handed over. Please direct requests for public map viewing to the permit information desk. No policy amendment was announced at this handover.

Afternoon handover, 2025-09-12: Several callers asked whether their appointments could be adjusted to accommodate an interpreter or a support person. Record the requested accommodation in the appointment notes and refer procedural questions to benefits intake. The presence of a support person does not, by itself, change the person responsible for the application. Use the standard appointment record and avoid adding eligibility conclusions.

Morning handover, 2025-09-17: A revised attachment guide is available for applicants who need to send site photographs or diagrams. The guide explains file formats and where to submit attachments. It does not establish that any particular proposal meets technical requirements. If a caller has not submitted a plan, record the contact as an information inquiry.

Afternoon handover, 2025-09-23: The published permit fee schedule remains available at the counter and on the office information page. Staff may explain where to find the schedule, but should not characterize a question about the schedule as a payment, refund, or fee-waiver request unless the visitor makes that request. Refer specific payment-account questions to the designated finance counter.

Morning handover, 2025-09-29: Seasonal application dates and appointment availability are listed separately. A question about when a filing period opens should be sent to permit information. A question about an interview date should be sent to benefits intake. Do not infer that a person filed or attended an appointment from a request for dates.

Section F — terminology crosswalk
“Application form” means a document intended to collect information for a permit or benefit process. A blank form distributed by the desk is not a submitted application.
“Submission” means materials delivered through an accepted channel and recorded as received. A statement by a contact that something has been completed is not enough to establish receipt.
“Eligibility review” means a decision by the responsible benefits unit under the applicable program criteria. The information desk does not conduct that review.
“Permit review” means examination by the responsible permit unit. A form list, fee schedule, map, or procedural explanation is not a permit review.
“Accessible copy” means a version supplied in a format requested to support access, such as large print. Preparing or requesting that copy does not determine the status of an application.
“Referral” means directing a matter to another unit for handling or explanation. It does not mean that the receiving unit has completed work on the matter.
“Appointment assistance” means help with arranging, changing, or understanding an appointment. It is distinct from an interview and from a decision on a benefit.
“Refund request” means an explicit request that money previously paid be returned. The September extract contains no such request. References to a fee schedule, benefit assistance, payment procedures, or forms are not equivalent to such a request.

Section G — quality review checklist
Reviewers should first identify the subject and the exact action requested. They should then distinguish the contact’s request from the staff follow-up. A planned follow-up is not necessarily a completed action. Reviewers should also distinguish information about an application from the application itself. If no documents were submitted or reviewed, the case should not be labeled as a completed filing on the basis of general discussion.

When reading a benefit entry, reviewers should not infer eligibility from a request for an appointment, a list of accepted documents, a form, or an explanation of a term. When reading a permit entry, reviewers should not infer permission to build, trade, occupy a road, or hold an event from a request for information. A permit or benefit decision would need to be expressly recorded in the relevant case material.

When interpreting a name in the contact column, reviewers should treat it as the party making the inquiry unless the case note identifies a different speaker. Organizations may ask procedural questions on their own behalf. A record that an office sent information to a contact does not show that the contact sent a request to the office on someone else’s behalf.

The extract uses the same neutral administrative style for all rows. A routine request should not be upgraded into a complaint, an appeal, or a demand simply because it relates to a public service. Conversely, an explicit request should not be erased by a generic category label. The recorded-request field is the primary description of what the contact asked. The notes and follow-up fields provide context but do not replace it.

Section H — additional sample records for spreadsheet-format consistency
The sample records below illustrate the same conventions with anonymized references. They are included to show how staff document routine contacts across permit and benefit subjects.

A reviewer should not add a conclusion that the entry does not contain. For instance, receiving a list of required documents is not the same as meeting those requirements, and learning where to deliver a form is not the same as having the form accepted.

Section I — monthly close summary
At the close of September, the desk supervisor confirmed that the register fields were populated according to the spreadsheet guide. The supervisor noted that the information desk had answered procedural questions, distributed reference materials, and routed specialized questions to the appropriate units. The close summary does not certify that any permit was issued or that any benefit was granted. The operational counts are retained for workload planning only.

For the monthly review, staff were instructed to preserve the original wording of requests where possible, to use neutral language, and to avoid converting a question into a decision. The record should answer what the contact asked, what material was available for review, and which office was assigned the next administrative step. It should not answer questions about facts that the entry does not state.
