Tideglass House / service incident packet 41-B. Internal copy; times are local. Typing is rough because the overnight desk exported the thread twice and nobody cleaned it up. Guest: Esi Lindqvist. Room 308. Dining reservation under Esi for two. Stay dates: 11–13 October. Restaurant booking: 12 October, 19:30. Packet assembled 14 October by the duty lead after a billing mismatch and a dispute over what the guest had asked staff to do. The packet contains the original entries, duplicate entries, later corrections and a few irrelevant system notices. Do not treat repeated lines as separate events unless the event keys differ. The narrow question in the review is what the guest actually requested, not what a staff member guessed, what the billing system did automatically, or what a later policy note says should happen.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM, FIRST DRAFT, 07:10. At checkout, the folio showed a dining charge of 84.00 and a room adjustment of 20.00. Guest challenged the dining line and asked whether it could be removed. The front desk agent opened a service ticket. First draft says “refund not requested; guest only asked about menu pricing.” This summary was written before the recorded call was replayed and before the message queue was synced. It also says the room adjustment was a refund, which was wrong: that entry was a one-time service recovery credit placed on the room account the previous evening. The dining charge was not part of the room adjustment. At 07:16 a supervisor added “No refund asked, not that I heard.” At 07:42 the supervisor struck out the sentence in the working document, but the copied version retained it. A detached paper slip from the same folder says “refund??” with no initials and no time. Neither the detached slip nor a question mark establishes a request.

The first draft is not a reliable final account. The author later noted that the desk microphone had been muted for part of the checkout discussion. The initial statement about menu pricing was inferred from a screen showing the dinner menu, not transcribed from the guest. The phrase “not requested” was based on the agent’s incomplete observation; it was not a verified statement by Esi. The second sentence, “not that I heard,” explicitly limits the supervisor’s claim to what the supervisor personally heard. The queue subsequently received the missing inbound SMS and a desk recording. The review team retained the flawed draft because the incident procedure requires an audit trail, not because it remains operative.

EVENT INDEX, export version 3. Key H-7712 is the guest’s inbound message at 06:51. Key D-1934 is the desk call recording at 07:03. Key S-8801 is the server’s point-of-sale check. Key F-1220 is the final account note at 08:02. Key F-1220 supersedes the preliminary case summary for statements about the guest’s request. The first export omitted H-7712 because the phone gateway was offline between 06:40 and 07:20. The second export inserted it in chronological order but left the older summary above it. A line appearing earlier in this packet is not necessarily a later or stronger record. Event keys, timestamps, and explicit supersession notes matter.

HOTEL PMS AUDIT, 11 OCTOBER. 14:02 reservation imported from Tideglass booking page. Guest name Esi Lindqvist; one room, two adults. Arrival 11 October, departure 13 October. Rate plan: Bay View Flexible. The booking form displayed a cancellation deadline of 18:00 on 10 October. This is not the same reservation action questioned in the postmortem: the room remained occupied through checkout. At 14:08 the app emitted a banner reading “No cancellation submitted.” At 14:09 an agent wrote “guest did not not confirm arrival?” The double negative in the agent note is an uncertain scribble, not a confirmed status change. The reservation ledger records check-in at 16:27 on 11 October and checkout at 06:58 on 13 October. There is no room cancellation transaction. A restaurant booking, by contrast, was edited on 12 October; see the dining records below. Automated reminders about cancellation deadlines are boilerplate and do not mean the guest cancelled anything.

DINING RESERVATION LOG, 12 OCTOBER. The table was initially booked for two at 19:30. At 17:12, server-side entry R-339 said “guest wants to cancel dinner?” The question mark marks an unverified report from a runner. At 17:18, the host app showed status HELD, not cancelled. At 17:21, the host wrote “Esi says she isn’t not coming, table should stay.” That wording is a double negative. A note beneath it says “meaning unclear; call room.” At 17:26 the desk called the room and received no answer. Absence of an answer does not negate an earlier statement. At 17:39, Esi arrived at the restaurant and was seated. The seating scan confirms two covers. The reservation was fulfilled, although a duplicate app record remained marked “pending cancellation” until the following morning.

The cancellation queue had two records. R-339 was a tentative staff report, manually entered by a runner who did not speak directly with Esi. R-341 was a system-generated reminder, created when the app received no confirmation after an automated prompt. Neither is a customer request. R-347, entered at 17:21 by the host, quotes the guest’s words with an uncertainty marker. R-355, the seating scan, confirms attendance. At 09:04 on 13 October, the host manager changed the app label from “pending cancellation” to “completed” and attached the seating scan. The audit export preserved the old label in a cached column. A later billing bot read the cached label and incorrectly suppressed the dinner check from the first folio preview. It did not erase the charge from the point-of-sale system.

RESTAURANT POS DETAIL. Check S-8801 opened 19:42, 12 October, table 14, two covers. Items: two set menus at 31.00 each, sparkling water 8.00, service fee 14.00. The printed total was 84.00. The arithmetic is 62.00 + 8.00 + 14.00 = 84.00. An earlier hand-written slip showed 82.00, but it omitted the service fee. A second copy showed 94.00 because a training terminal had added a test dessert. The live register shows no dessert. The payment record says settled to room 308 at 21:06. It is therefore possible to have a valid dining charge and still have a separate dispute about whether that charge should be refunded. A payment posted by the system is not proof that the guest requested or did not request a refund.

The menu price displayed on the paper menu was 31.00 per set menu. The QR menu had an obsolete test entry at 36.00, visible only in the staff preview. A host comment says “asked about 36, may be price issue.” This was another inference, not a recorded guest statement. The guest did not order the test dessert. The server ticket shows the two set menus, water and service fee. The original payment authorization was 84.00, not 94.00. The 10.00 difference between the test terminal and the live account was not charged. The 2.00 difference on the hand slip is explained by the omitted 14.00 fee versus a 12.00 handwritten estimate; no evidence shows the guest was charged 2.00 extra. These amounts are included because early summaries confused the possible overcharge with the later request for a refund.

SMS GATEWAY EXCERPT, 13 OCTOBER. 06:43 outbound desk message: “Morning Esi, checkout is ready when u are. Tell us if any folio item looks wrong.” Delivery status delayed. 06:51 inbound from verified number ending 4408: “The dinner amount is still on my room bill. I’m not saying I don’t want the money back; please refund that dinner charge, not the room credit. I did eat there; the issue is the charge after the service was removed from the menu sheet.” The message was held in gateway buffer due to a brief network outage. It was delivered to the case queue at 07:26. An auto-classifier preview rendered the text as “not refund request” because its phrase list matched “I’m not saying I don’t want” incorrectly. That preview is not a human-authored record and is marked rejected in the queue. The guest’s sentence contains a double negation and then an explicit imperative request. The request concerns the dinner charge, not the already-posted room credit.

06:53 system acknowledgement, generated before the inbound message had been processed: “Your request has not been received.” This is a transport status, not a response to the content. 06:55 outbound retry: same acknowledgement. 07:03 outbound staff text: “Can you confirm you are not asking for a refund?” No reply appears in the gateway until 07:14 because the inbound buffer was still delayed. The eventual reply was “I’m not not asking; I want the dinner charge returned.” The short reply again uses double negation and then states the desired outcome directly. At 07:15 the queue agent marked the thread “refund intent: yes.” At 07:18 a different agent clicked “no” after reading only the auto-classifier preview. At 07:34 the case lead reopened the record, replayed the full thread, and marked the second click as a mistaken contradiction.

The gateway display has a misleading ordering quirk. It sorts by arrival-to-server timestamp in the first view and by message-created timestamp in the second view. The guest sent the 06:51 message before the desk’s 07:03 question, although the first display placed the staff question above it. The 07:14 reply refers to the staff question and repeats the refund intention; it is not a retraction. No message says “cancel my request,” “keep the money,” or “do not refund.” The phrase “not saying I don’t want the money back” is not a denial of wanting it back. The direct phrase “please refund that dinner charge” removes any remaining ambiguity about the guest’s intent.

DESK CALL RECORDING TRANSCRIPT, 07:03, edited only for background noise. Agent: “I can see the dining amount and the adjustment. Are you asking us to remove the room credit?” Guest: “No, not the room credit. I’m talking about the dinner check.” Agent: “So no refund?” Guest: “No, I didn’t say no refund. I said the room credit is fine. The dinner charge is what I want looked at.” Agent: “Do you want the full amount back?” Guest: “I don’t not want it back. Yes, return the dinner charge, please. I ate dinner, but the menu sheet showed the item differently and the fee wasn’t clear.” Agent: “I’ll note it and have the manager review.” The recording ends at 07:05. The speaker separation was checked against the desk microphone channel; the first-draft summary reversed the answers to the agent’s questions.

Audio review note: the initial machine transcript had the agent saying “no refund” and the guest saying “yes, room credit.” The human reviewer compared the voice channels and corrected the roles. The guest says “No” to the question about removing the room credit, then distinguishes the dinner check. The guest does not say the dining charge should remain. The agent’s phrase “So no refund?” is a question, not a statement of the guest’s position. The desk’s first summary treated the agent’s question as if it were the guest’s answer. The manager’s later note quotes the guest’s request correctly. This is a role and contradiction issue in the source records, but the later direct audio and authenticated message agree.

ROOM ACCOUNT, 13 OCTOBER. 06:58 checkout folio preview: room nights 412.00; local levy 24.72; dining 84.00; service recovery credit minus 20.00; total 500.72. The service recovery credit was approved at 22:10 on 12 October after the elevator was out of service for 18 minutes. Its memo says “courtesy adjustment; no refund request attached.” That memo describes why the credit was entered at that time. It cannot establish whether a later refund request was made about a different charge. The folio printout at 06:58 included dining because the point-of-sale link had reconciled. At 07:02 the guest circled the 84.00 line. The pen mark is evidence of attention to the line, not by itself evidence of the requested remedy.

At 07:06, agent note: “Guest says not unhappy with credit, not happy with dinner billing?” The punctuation is unresolved. At 07:08, another note says “No refund requested, maybe wants explanation.” Both notes were written before the SMS reached the queue. At 07:52, a manager wrote “The customer did not not ask for the dinner amount back; request is explicit on SMS and call.” At 08:02 final account note: “Refund request confirmed for dining charge only. Keep room credit. Do not refund the room credit.” At 08:07 the system created a refund review, not a completed payout. The review was pending authorization at packet assembly. A review status does not mean the money had already been returned.

The account ledger records no completed refund as of 14 October, 09:30. The pending review has amount 84.00, payment reference S-8801, and reason code “guest dispute.” A separate 20.00 credit is already in the ledger, entered before checkout. A preview screen briefly displayed a combined “104.00 adjustment” because it added the credit and proposed refund review. That was a display aggregation, not a posted 104.00 payment. A clerk wrote “104 returned” on a sticky note, then crossed it out after checking the ledger. The correct distinction is: 20.00 credit already applied; 84.00 refund requested and awaiting decision; 0.00 refund completed at the time of review. The question here concerns whether a request was made, not whether the hotel approved or paid it.

KITCHEN AND SERVICE REPORT, 12 OCTOBER. The server wrote at 21:13: “Guest not displeased, but mentioned fee.” A later assistant manager added “not not displeased?” The two entries are contradictory about the guest’s mood and do not establish the remedy sought. At 21:17, the server’s detailed narrative says “Esi asked what the 14.00 line meant and said she would check the printed menu. I explained the service fee. She said she was not asking for the fee to be taken off right now; she wanted a clear receipt.” At 21:29, another staff member reported “she wants fee removed.” That report was based on a corridor conversation the staff member did not hear directly. The signed receipt confirms the amount paid to the room, but does not contain a waiver or a refund request.

The service fee wording varied across materials. The paper menu said “service fee 14.00.” The QR menu said “service included,” but that was an outdated draft page hidden from the guest-facing menu after 16:50. A screenshot saved by staff at 18:00 accidentally captured the internal preview, not the public menu. The guest’s reference to the menu sheet may have been about that discrepancy. The incident review assigned a separate task to correct the QR wording. This task is not proof that the guest had or had not asked for money back. Staff should not infer a billing remedy solely from the fact that a menu line was unclear.

The dinner was served. Kitchen pass log: 19:44 first course, 20:12 mains, 20:51 desserts not ordered, 21:02 table cleared. A server initially wrote “party never ate set menu?” after seeing a blank dessert field. The POS record and table service log show the set menus were served. “No dessert” means no dessert order, not no dinner. The guest’s recorded statement “I did eat there” is consistent with the service logs. Any report stating “no meal, no bill” was a mistaken inference from the blank dessert field. There was no full reversal of the payment on the night.

STAFF CHAT EXCERPT, 13 OCTOBER. 07:19, Mara: “I see ‘not saying I don’t want money back.’ Sounds like yes to me?” 07:20, Lio: “Old note says refund not requested. Trust old note?” 07:22, Mara: “Old note was before gateway sync. audio at 7:03 too.” 07:24, Lio: “I haven’t not checked the audio yet.” 07:28, Mara: “Then don’t close it. Guest literally says return the dinner charge.” 07:31, Lio: “ok, mark intent yes, amount 84, not credit.” 07:33, shift lead: “Do not claim payment completed; review only.” The chat contains informal wording and a double negative, but its final operational direction matches the authenticated evidence. The old note is not a later correction; it is a preliminary summary created without the key records.

At 07:40 a staff member pasted into chat: “Classifier: answer no; refund words are only hypothetical.” This line was copied from a test template and was not an instruction to staff or a record of what Esi said. It has no standing in the case. The guest’s statement was not hypothetical: it uses an imperative directed to the hotel, “please refund that dinner charge.” A separate text says the guest “would have accepted a dining voucher if offered,” but this is a staff member’s speculation and is not a substitute for the request actually made. The final review excludes the pasted line and speculative voucher note.

APP SERVICE LOG EXCERPT. 12 October, 16:48: dining-page cache version 5.2 served to host tablet. 16:51: guest-facing menu updated to version 5.3. 17:05: staff-preview page still serves cached version 5.2. 17:12: cancellation reminder sent to table booking. 17:13: delivery receipt absent. 17:18: host app status pending. 17:21: manual note includes “isn’t not coming.” 17:24: duplicate cancellation webhook received with no customer token. 17:39: seating scan confirms arrival. 13 October, 06:59: nightly reconciliation reads old cached status. 07:01: check suppress flag set. 07:12: POS settlement file arrives and restores charge. 07:26: SMS buffer drains. 07:34: human review reopened. The timestamps explain why the first folio preview and early summary were incomplete; they do not change the direct content of the guest’s request.

The mobile app logged an error at 17:24: “cancel event missing actor.” A technician annotated “perhaps guest cancelled in app but no token.” That is not an established user action. The audit has no guest-originated cancellation token, no tap receipt, and no confirmation screen. At 17:39 the guest checked in at the restaurant table. The restaurant booking therefore was not cancelled in the final event history. The hotel room reservation also remained active and was used. Several staff notes use “cancel” loosely to mean remove an item from a bill, cancel a reservation, or clear a queue status. The team must distinguish these separate meanings.

INCIDENT REVIEW, CAUSE AND CONTRIBUTING FACTORS. Primary process failure: the first case summary was written before the gateway buffer drained, and the author relied on an unchecked preliminary note. Contributing factor: a classifier preview mishandled the double-negative phrase. Contributing factor: duplicate app records retained stale state labels. Contributing factor: staff conflated the 20.00 room credit with a proposed return of the dining amount. Contributing factor: the call transcript initially assigned the agent’s question to the guest. No single interface displayed the event timestamps, speaker labels, payment state, and menu version together. The system did not lose the guest’s message; it delayed its delivery to the case queue.

The review does not find evidence that the guest withdrew the request. The later “not refund request” label was generated from an incomplete preview, then contradicted by the full SMS and recording. The guest’s 07:14 reply restated the request, not reversed it. The final note distinguishes intent, amount and fulfillment: intent yes; requested amount 84.00 dining charge; room credit excluded; payout not yet completed. These are separate propositions and should not be collapsed into one binary “refund done” field. The corrective action is to require staff to inspect the entire exchange and identify the transaction before closing a billing dispute.

APPENDIX A: RAW CASE COMMENTS, retained for audit. 06:58 clerk: “folio ready; no guest issue yet.” 07:02 clerk: “circle beside restaurant line.” 07:03 agent: “asking about credit?” 07:04 clerk: “guest said not credit, dinner.” 07:06 clerk: “no request??” 07:08 supervisor: “not sure, call replay needed.” 07:10 preliminary summary: “no refund.” 07:14 guest reply arrives in gateway buffer. 07:15 queue agent: “yes.” 07:18 queue agent: “no.” 07:26 full inbound message visible. 07:34 case lead: “contradictory clicks; preserve both; use original content.” 07:52 manager: “did not not ask; yes request.” 08:02 account note: “refund request confirmed.” The entries are not all independent observations. The clicks are workflow decisions. The notes at 07:10 and 07:18 do not outweigh the direct source content merely because they contain a categorical label.

APPENDIX B: FOLIO RECONCILIATION. Room rate 206.00 per night x 2 nights = 412.00. Levy 6% of 412.00 = 24.72. Dining line 84.00. Existing recovery credit minus 20.00. Total due 412.00 + 24.72 + 84.00 - 20.00 = 500.72. Card settlement at checkout was 500.72. A hand calculator in the drawer showed 520.72 because the clerk forgot to subtract the existing credit. Another draft showed 416.72 because it omitted dining. Neither draft was the settled amount. The pending refund review, if later approved, would reduce the net retained amount by 84.00; it had not done so by the review timestamp. The arithmetic confirms that the 84.00 dining line was present in the settled folio, but arithmetic alone does not identify the guest’s requested remedy.

APPENDIX C: CONTACTS. 11 October, 15:04, pre-arrival message: “Please keep the room reservation; my train is late.” 11 October, 16:27, check-in. 12 October, 17:21, dinner-table wording entered by host. 12 October, 19:39, arrival at restaurant. 13 October, 06:51, inbound billing message. 13 October, 07:03, desk call. 13 October, 07:14, follow-up response. 13 October, 08:02, final account note. 14 October, 09:30, review snapshot. The pre-arrival request to keep the room is not a request to keep or refund the dining payment. The restaurant attendance record is not a statement about the billing remedy. Chronology and subject matter must be kept separate.

APPENDIX D: QUALITY CHECK. Reviewer 1: “Did guest ask for money back?” Answer: yes, for the dining check. Reviewer 2: “But preliminary note says no.” Answer: preliminary note predates full message and was explicitly corrected. Reviewer 3: “Could ‘not saying I don’t want it’ mean uncertainty?” Answer: the same message continues “please refund that dinner charge”; the call repeats “Yes, return the dinner charge.” Reviewer 4: “Does the posted 20.00 prove an earlier refund?” Answer: it is a separate courtesy credit and the guest said to leave it alone. Reviewer 5: “Was the requested amount paid already?” Answer: no; the review remained pending. These checks were added to prevent the common conflation of request, approval, and completion.

APPENDIX E: HOTEL AND RESTAURANT OPERATIONS NOTES. Housekeeping found no room damage. Front desk log shows one key returned, one key inactive. The guest did not request an extra night. The restaurant manager corrected the menu page at 09:12. The night auditor reconciled the table count at 09:28. None of these routine events changes the disputed transaction. A note in the kitchen book says “never had a complaint like this,” which is an opinion about frequency, not evidence that no complaint occurred. A separate note says “not uncommon for menu versions to differ,” which describes a known operational issue. Neither sentence is the guest’s request; both were included in the incident folder because the team had bundled the menu concern and billing question.

The staff roster lists one desk agent, one shift lead, two servers, a host and a night auditor. Names in the roster are omitted from this copy because the review is about event ownership, not individual blame. The person who entered the preliminary case summary did not have access to the message buffer at that time. The person who clicked “no” read the auto-preview but did not listen to the call. The person who reopened the file compared the message, recording, POS record and ledger. The postmortem assigns a process correction rather than attributing intent to any employee. A training note says “never believe any guest says anything,” but it was an unapproved draft and was removed from the active handbook. It is not a valid policy and does not alter the evidence.

APPENDIX F: DUPLICATE EXPORT COMPARISON. Export A, generated 07:11, includes preliminary summary and room folio but not the buffered guest SMS. Export B, generated 07:29, includes the SMS but keeps the preliminary summary at the top. Export C, generated 08:11, adds the audio correction and final account note. A printer at the desk produced Export A after the message had already been sent by the guest but before the gateway delivered it. A staff member later circled “refund not requested” on that printout. The circle is a mark on a stale summary, not a confirmation by the guest. Export C retains the old text with a strike-through to document the correction. The final operational record is the 08:02 note and the full source materials, not the first line visible on a paper stack.

At 08:20 the desk software displayed a yellow warning, “Prior status: no refund request.” This warning was copied from the initial summary field, which had no source link. The manager added a source link to H-7712 and D-1934, then changed the status. At 08:24 a second warning said, “Do not overwrite prior status.” The instruction protects audit history; it does not require keeping an inaccurate status as current. The manager preserved the original value in the change log and set the current value to confirmed request. At 08:29, the system showed both values side by side: prior status not confirmed; current status confirmed. Staff were told not to read the historical value as an unresolved contradiction after the correction had been verified.

APPENDIX G: POLICY EXTRACT USED BY THE TEAM. A guest may ask for a review of a dining charge at any time before account closure. A request does not itself authorize a return of funds. A separate courtesy credit does not satisfy or cancel a request about another transaction unless the guest explicitly accepts it as a replacement. If records conflict, direct guest communication and authenticated transaction records should be reviewed before a case is closed. This rule was posted in the desk handbook after a prior unrelated incident. It applies here as process guidance. The guest explicitly distinguished the room credit from the dining charge, so the existing credit cannot be treated as acceptance of a substitute. The policy does not decide whether the dinner charge was correct on its merits; it only explains how to record the request and review it.

APPENDIX H: CACHED CLASSIFIER DIAGNOSTICS. Phrase “not saying I don’t want” mapped to refusal class in the legacy model. Phrase “I’m not not asking” mapped to unknown. The rule set was trained on short statements without subsequent clarifying clauses. Model output at 07:15: likely no request, confidence 0.61. Human override at 07:34: yes request, evidence cited. Test replay with the full text: model still returned no, because its bag-of-phrases score treated “not” as a universal negator and ignored the imperative clause. The classifier output is recorded here to explain the erroneous click. It is not an independent witness, and no system score outranks the guest’s authenticated words.

APPENDIX I: CUSTOMER SERVICE FOLLOW-UP DRAFT. “We have received your request regarding the dining amount. The separate room credit remains in place. Our manager is checking the menu presentation and receipt. We have not yet issued a return of funds. We will update you after review.” Draft status: unsent at the time this packet was assembled. A copied sentence in an earlier version said “We have not received your request,” but that wording referred to the initial gateway delay and was removed when the full thread arrived. The final draft avoids saying the request was absent. A note says “don’t send unless the guest doesn’t not want a reply,” which is an awkward double negative in an internal reminder; the service manager interpreted it as “send unless guest opts out.” There is no opt-out in the guest’s messages.

APPENDIX J: TABLE AND APP STATUS HISTORY. Table 14 held 19:30–19:40, seated 19:39, released 21:11. A cancellation flag from the reminder service was present from 17:24 to 09:04 next day. The host physically checked the guest in using the table code, which cleared the operational hold. The flag remained visible in the reporting replica only. One report therefore counted one “cancelled booking,” while another counted one “completed cover.” The reports conflict because they query different status fields. The detailed event history establishes actual attendance. The cancellation flag was a system artifact, not a guest action. No one should infer that a guest cancelled dinner from the word “cancellation” alone.

A separate room report showed “not checked out” until 07:11 because the key encoder had delayed its nightly sync. The front desk receipt and folio show checkout at 06:58. The guest’s room stay is not disputed. The team included this example because the same reporting replica generated both stale statuses. Stale labels can look categorical while being inconsistent with event-level records. Corrections must retain the prior value for audit but rely on the verified current history for the question being reviewed.

APPENDIX K: MESSAGE CONTENT REVIEW. Verified number ending 4408 matches the contact number entered at check-in. The 06:51 message mentions “dinner amount,” “room bill,” “money back,” “please refund,” and “that dinner charge.” It explicitly excludes “the room credit.” The 07:14 reply says “I’m not not asking” and “I want the dinner charge returned.” The call transcript uses the same distinction. No other person is quoted as the sender of those messages. The front desk asked questions; Esi supplied the affirmative request. Staff’s earlier “no refund” statements are summaries, not quotations from her. The message and recording are independent channels and agree on the central point.

The wording “service was removed from the menu sheet” is grammatically unclear; the guest may mean the fee description was missing, or that a line had been removed from one menu version. The team does not need to resolve that ambiguity to identify the request. The request is explicitly to refund the dinner charge, and the requested target is named. The reason for the request can remain under review. A classifier should not infer that the guest seeks only an explanation just because the menu wording is unclear. Conversely, the presence of a billing complaint does not prove the hotel must approve it. Intent and entitlement are different questions.

APPENDIX L: SUPERVISOR HANDOVER, 08:35. “Current status confirmed request, review pending. Prior note says no request; keep history, don’t use as current. Do not combine the existing 20 credit with requested 84. Do not say payment returned. Call guest after manager decision. Table was used, no reservation cancellation. Room stayed active. Menu cache fixed. Complaint wording rough but clear on action requested.” At 08:41 a second supervisor replied, “Agreed, not not a request.” The response is informal but consistent with the source messages. At 08:46 the case was assigned to billing review. At 09:02 the dining manager acknowledged receipt. No decision had been entered by the 09:30 snapshot.

APPENDIX M: AUDIT EXCEPTIONS. The system normally blocks a refund review if the charge is older than 48 hours. This case was opened within 24 hours of the dining payment, so the review remained available. A draft note mistakenly used the room’s checkout timestamp as the dining transaction timestamp; both were on 13 October in the folio, but the dinner payment was posted on 12 October at 21:06. Even if the deadline mattered, elapsed time from 12 October 21:06 to 13 October 08:07 is 10 hours 61 minutes, or 11 hours 1 minute, not 48 hours. The odd notation appears because the minute subtraction was not normalized; 08:07 next day is 11 hours 1 minute later. This calculation is included for audit only and does not determine whether the guest asked.

The service recovery credit had no review deadline because it was already posted under a different code. A clerk briefly checked the wrong deadline field and wrote “outside window.” That label referred to an unrelated test booking in the training environment, not Esi’s account. The live transaction log shows the review was opened before the applicable 48-hour cutoff. No external policy is needed to understand the disputed request; all relevant records are contained in this packet. The billing team’s final decision may depend on menu evidence, but the task presented here is whether the request exists in the evidence.

APPENDIX N: INTERNAL EMAIL THREAD. 07:08, desk lead: “First draft says no. Was that actually heard?” 07:12, night auditor: “No recording checked yet. gateway offline.” 07:27, desk lead: “SMS now visible. It says please refund dinner line.” 07:36, restaurant manager: “She ate. That doesn’t automatically settle whether fee is right.” 07:48, billing: “Request recorded; decision pending.” 08:10, desk lead: “Corrected summary sent. Original preserved.” 08:13, auditor: “Please don’t copy the earlier no into the guest reply.” The messages show the staff position changed after evidence arrived. The earlier line is contradicted by later verified content and was explicitly corrected, not left as an unresolved competing account.

APPENDIX O: FINAL RECONCILIATION NARRATIVE. The guest attended the restaurant, incurred an 84.00 check, and saw that amount on the room folio. She separately received a 20.00 room-account credit for an elevator inconvenience and said that credit should remain. The first summary claimed no refund had been requested, but it was produced before the delayed SMS arrived and before the call was reviewed. The SMS and recording each include double-negative wording, but both also contain direct affirmative language asking that the dining charge be returned. The follow-up message repeats rather than retracts the request. The current case status is therefore a request for review of an 84.00 dining charge, with no payout completed as of the snapshot. The booking itself was not cancelled: the guest attended and ate. The stale cancellation labels and copied preliminary summary are retained solely to explain the incident.

For training and audit, the packet leaves the conflicting entries visible rather than silently replacing them. A reader should identify which claims are first-hand, which are machine-generated, which were made before the evidence arrived, and which are later corrections. “No refund requested” appears more than once, but repetition comes from copied or derived entries and does not make it independent evidence. “Please refund that dinner charge” appears in the authenticated guest message and is repeated on the recording. The guest’s “I’m not saying I don’t want the money back” should not be interpreted by isolating the first negation; the sentence continues with the requested action. The direct affirmative phrase resolves the double negative.

The incident manager’s closing checklist has four separate boxes. Box one, “request received,” is checked. Box two, “request approved,” is blank. Box three, “money returned,” is blank. Box four, “related credit retained,” is checked. A misprinted duplicate of the checklist has box one unchecked, but the signed original includes the message reference and timestamp. The duplicate was printed from the stale summary view. Staff attached both copies to show how the error propagated. The checked request box records the existence of the guest’s request only; it does not imply that the charge was improper or that payment has been returned.

END OF PACKET. Source records retained: gateway message IDs H-7712 and H-7720; recording D-1934; POS check S-8801; ledger transaction L-801; final account note F-1220; table seating scan T-663; app audit A-910. Preliminary summaries and automated labels remain in the archive with correction history. Current finding at 09:30, 14 October: guest requested return of the 84.00 restaurant charge; separate 20.00 room credit is not included; request review pending; no payout completed; dinner reservation completed through attendance. Any contrary summary should be read as superseded or based on incomplete records.

Harbor Software — travel operations review, prepared for the regional manager

Status update to manager, first section

This is the consolidated review of the March itinerary cases handled by the Harbor Software travel desk for Tidewater Logistics. The desk is checking how agents apply the reimbursement schedule and how a package booking is split into its chargeable parts. The purpose is to make the next handover clearer, not to change any traveler’s booking. The figures below are fictional internal examples. They are included because several agents looked only at the headline total and missed the schedule calculation underneath it.

The review covers three booking files, the daily handover notes, the fare-component guide, a sample supplier statement, and a short email exchange. Each section uses the same terms: “base fare” means the ticket price before desk fees; “service fee” means a fee retained by the desk; “hotel portion” means the lodging charge; and “eligible amount” means the amount to which the stated reimbursement percentage is applied. A credit shown as pending is not counted as paid until the supplier statement says it was issued. A planned credit is not the same as an issued credit.

The first file concerns Ines Castillo’s proposed group itinerary. It is included as a comparison case, and none of its amounts should be carried into the other files. The second file concerns Esi O'Neill’s desk reimbursement review. The third is a training example used to check whether agents can add separate ticket components. The cases appear together because the handover sheet was assembled from material that had previously been stored in separate folders.

At the time of preparation, the manager asked the desk to report both the gross amount shown on a booking summary and the amount actually payable after the scheduled adjustment. Some older handovers gave only one figure. That created questions from the finance team, because a gross package amount can contain lodging, transfers, and a ticket fee that are not all included in the same calculation. The revised sheet therefore repeats the relevant amounts beside the calculation instead of expecting the reader to infer them from a heading.

The itinerary desk uses the displayed amount from the supplier ledger, not a verbal estimate from a traveler, when completing its monthly report. If a supplier has not posted an amount yet, the handover must call it an estimate. This distinction matters in the third file, where the printed sample statement has both an estimate and an issued charge. The issued charge, rather than the estimate, is used in the desk’s reconciliation exercise.

The review was drafted in simple English because several colleagues who use the report are not native English speakers. Some older labels remain on copied forms, but the definitions in this document govern the examples. Where the word “total” appears without a qualifier in an old note, it may mean a subtotal rather than a final payable amount. The itemized table is the dependable source for the calculation.

Manager’s summary of the work completed

The travel desk checked whether all listed charges had a matching supplier reference. It found that the package summary for Ines Castillo had a transfer estimate that was not part of the ticket price. It found that the service-fee rule in Esi O'Neill’s file was applied to the wrong subtotal in one draft. It also found that one training statement included an unissued estimate beneath an issued ticket charge. These are different errors, and the report keeps them separate.

The manager requested a clear answer about the amount due in the Esi example. The stated rule in that file is to reimburse 80 percent of the base fare only, then subtract the service fee. The fare is 640 units and the service fee is 35 units. An earlier draft instead took 80 percent of the gross package figure, which also included 120 units for a hotel. That earlier draft’s result is not the result under the rule. The desk’s corrected amount is calculated in the Esi section below.

The manager also requested a yes-or-no check on the training statement: whether the issued ticket components total 510 units. The component entries are 275, 148, and 87 units. The estimate of 60 units is not an issued component and is not included. The figures were selected to make the distinction visible, since an agent who adds every number printed on the page will arrive at a different figure.

The report does not treat these three checks as policy decisions about real claims. It is a record of the values and rules in the sample files. The customer-support desk should not use the examples to promise a credit to a traveler. A manager may ask the supplier for clarification if a live statement differs from a sample. No such follow-up is part of the calculation requested here.

Handover method and terminology

When a booking includes more than one product, staff first identify the applicable rule and then select only the components named by that rule. The phrase “80 percent of base fare” does not mean 80 percent of the hotel, transfer, or service fee. Similarly, “issued ticket components” does not mean all rows in the document. A row marked estimate remains outside an issued-charge total even when it is printed immediately beside the ticket components.

The desk stores a compact booking record with the traveler name, booking reference, supplier, currency unit, and a short status. The longer notes explain why the record was changed. The compact record is useful for the daily queue but is not sufficient for this review when component values matter. A reader should use the itemization when the question asks about a computed result.

In the old system, the word “net” was used inconsistently. In one screen it meant the supplier’s amount after a discount; in another it meant the amount after the desk fee. The current report avoids the word and writes the arithmetic in full. An amount can therefore be called “payable after fee” only if the fee subtraction is stated. The gross package line is retained for comparison and must not be substituted for a base-fare-only calculation.

A clerk may transcribe a number with a comma or with a space as the thousands separator. All sample figures in this report are below one thousand, so no separator is needed. The “units” are accounting units in the fictional ledger and should not be interpreted as a real-world currency. The report does not convert currencies or apply a market exchange rate.

The booking reference labels are internal sample labels, not passwords or customer identifiers. They are repeated in the appendix so that the desk can cross-check the component table against the narrative. The repeated labels do not create additional charges. When an amount is repeated, the narrative will say whether it is an original value, a copied value, or a comparison value.

Case A — Ines Castillo group itinerary review

The booking note for Ines Castillo came from a group coordinator who asked for a simple comparison of two itinerary arrangements. The coordinator did not ask for reimbursement under the Esi rule. The group arrangement was held while Tidewater Logistics checked availability for a conference visit. The ticket summary showed a base fare of 480 units, a hotel portion of 210 units, and a transfer estimate of 45 units. The provisional gross package display was 735 units because the display added all three figures. A separate service fee of 25 units was shown in the desk panel and was not included in that provisional gross display.

The first alternative showed a ticket-only arrangement. In that alternative, the base fare remained 480 units, the service fee remained 25 units, and no hotel or transfer was attached. The second alternative kept the hotel portion but removed the transfer estimate. The coordinator asked which arrangement made the printed gross package line 690 units. The answer can be checked by adding the listed components for the second alternative: 480 plus 210 equals 690. The service fee is outside that gross package line, under the screen layout used in this case.

The file is provided as a demonstration of how a line can be omitted from one subtotal without being erased from the booking. The transfer estimate still appeared in the first alternative, but it did not appear in the second. The 45-unit amount was not a confirmed charge and was never placed on the supplier statement. Staff should not add it to the second alternative merely because it appears on the earlier page. The same principle applies to the later Esi and training examples: read the exact components named by the question and rule.

A coordinator’s handwritten note said, “This one looks like 710 all in.” The note did not explain whether “all in” included the service fee. The desk did not adopt that figure because the listed second alternative has 480 plus 210 on the package line and a separately displayed 25-unit service fee. The sum including the fee would be 715, while the package line itself remains 690. The note is retained to show why the term “all in” should not replace a component calculation.

The group itinerary did not proceed to ticket issue. The dates were tentative, no payment was taken, and the coordinator did not request a refund. This status is repeated because an early queue card had been filed in the completed-booking tray. The filing location was corrected after a staff member checked the booking system. Nothing in this comparison case creates an issued charge for the training statement.

The group contact asked whether the supplier might later include a baggage allowance. The answer at the time was that the supplier had not confirmed one. An unconfirmed allowance has no amount in this sample record. The case does not assign a price to baggage and does not use any assumed baggage fee in its arithmetic. This avoids a common mistake in copied itineraries, where an agent sees a question about a product and treats it as if that product has already been purchased.

The itinerary review also checked the name spelling and the travelers’ preferred order of surnames. Those checks do not change the monetary values. Ines Castillo’s name was entered correctly in the final queue card. The coordinator’s earlier draft used a shortened label, “I. Castillo,” but the person and booking reference were the same. No second traveler with that shortened label was listed in the file.

No exceptional fare condition applied to this comparison. The sample ticket had no change penalty, no special promotional credit, and no refundable hotel deposit. The desk therefore did not need to choose between competing exception clauses. This is important because the later reimbursement example has one explicit calculation rule, and the report does not import the comparison case’s package total into it.

The group coordinator received a note explaining that the ticket-only option was 480 units before the 25-unit fee. The coordinator did not accept or reject the alternative in the period covered by this handover. The status remains “comparison requested.” No later message in the file changes that status. The group case is contextual material and should not be interpreted as a claim by Esi O'Neill or as a component of Esi’s reimbursement.

Case A ledger excerpt

Reference: HS-TL-4401. Traveler label: Ines Castillo. Supplier: Tidewater Logistics. Base fare: 480. Hotel portion in alternative one: 210. Transfer estimate in alternative one: 45. Alternative-one displayed package line: 735, calculated as 480 + 210 + 45. Alternative-two hotel portion: 210. Alternative-two transfer: absent. Alternative-two displayed package line: 690, calculated as 480 + 210. Desk service fee: 25, shown separately. Ticket issue status: not issued. Payment status: none. Refund status: not applicable because no payment was recorded.

The ledger excerpt is repeated in the source folder because the first printout had its right margin cut off. The intact copy was reviewed by the manager. A duplicate row with the 45-unit transfer estimate belongs to alternative one only; it is not a second transfer fee. The quantity column for the estimate is one, not two. The total on alternative one is still 735, not 780. The latter would incorrectly add the same 45-unit estimate twice.

Staff asked whether the 25-unit fee should be added to alternative two when reporting the package line. The answer was no for that particular screen subtotal, because the screen defines the package line as ticket and lodging and displays the desk fee separately. If a later question asks for the entire amount including the fee, the clerk should add it and state the result as 715. The distinction is included to make the scope of each subtotal explicit.

The group file has no relation to the 80-percent schedule. The schedule is attached to the Esi file only. It is not a general Harbor Software rule for every traveler or every supplier. The manager approved the wording that identifies which sample file carries which rule. An agent should not infer a universal policy from an example that is labeled as an isolated case.

Case B — Esi O'Neill reimbursement review

The Esi O'Neill file is the main reimbursement example in this handover. Esi had a completed ticket through Tidewater Labs for a work visit arranged by Harbor Software. The booking record lists a base fare of 640 units, a hotel portion of 120 units, and a desk service fee of 35 units. The gross package line, before the fee, is 760 units, calculated as 640 plus 120. If the separate fee is also included in a full outlay figure, the sum is 795 units. These totals are shown so the reviewer can see what is and is not the base fare.

The reimbursement schedule attached to this file states: “For the sample desk review, pay 80 percent of the base fare, then subtract the fixed service fee. The hotel portion is excluded from the eligible base. Do not apply the percentage to the gross package line. Do not subtract the fee before applying the percentage.” This is the exact rule in the file. The schedule gives no rounding requirement because the resulting amount is a whole unit. The example is intentionally not a rule for other cases.

The calculation proceeds in the order written. Eighty percent of 640 is 512, because 640 multiplied by 0.8 equals 512. Subtract the 35-unit service fee: 512 minus 35 equals 477 units payable after the fee. The hotel portion of 120 is excluded from the percentage base. The result under the stated schedule is therefore 477 units.

A draft sheet entered 573 units. The draft obtained that number by applying 80 percent to the gross package line of 760, producing 608, then subtracting 35. That arithmetic is internally consistent but uses the wrong base under the rule. Another clerk entered 485 units by subtracting the 35-unit fee from 640 and then applying 80 percent to 605. That calculation changes the required order and also does not follow the stated rule. The corrected result remains 477.

The travel record has a separate note about a 15-unit meal advance. That advance is not part of the base fare, hotel portion, or service fee, and the reimbursement schedule does not mention it. The meal advance was recorded in a different account. It must not be added to the payable calculation or subtracted from it. It appears in the file because the clerk initially copied all amounts from the traveler’s expense summary onto a single worksheet.

The receipt summary has two figures that look like airfare. One is 640 units, labeled “ticket base.” The other is 655 units, labeled “ticket base plus seat selection.” The schedule specifically says to use the base fare and the fare ledger marks the 15-unit seat selection as a separate optional item. The approved reimbursement worksheet uses 640, not 655. This separate 15-unit note is not the 15-unit meal advance; the two entries have the same value but different descriptions and accounting categories. Neither is added to the base fare for this schedule.

The file also contains a supplier estimate for a 22-unit luggage service. The service was not selected and is not on the issued receipt. The estimate appears in a quotation printed before ticket issue. It is not a charge and is not reimbursable in this example. The presence of an amount on a quotation does not change the fare base. This is why the review separates estimated, issued, and paid amounts in the ledger.

The booking confirmation says the hotel portion was 120 units for the stay. A hotel summary in an earlier draft shows 102 units because the clerk transposed the final two digits. The supplier confirmation and the payment ledger both show 120. The 102 figure is a transcription error and was not used in the corrected calculation. Even if it were used to reconstruct a gross package line, it would not become part of the eligible base, because the rule excludes the hotel portion altogether.

A manager’s note says, “Reimbursement should be about four hundred and eighty, please confirm.” That note is a rough expectation, not a calculation rule. The desk uses the written schedule and verified ledger entries. The exact amount is obtained from the stated arithmetic rather than rounding the rough estimate. The rough note does not authorize changing the percentage or ignoring the service fee.

The reimbursement worksheet has four columns: source amount, category, eligible status, and calculation treatment. The 640-unit base fare is marked eligible. The 120-unit hotel is marked excluded. The 35-unit fee is marked deducted after percentage calculation. The 15-unit meal advance is marked separate account. The 15-unit seat selection is marked optional and outside the base. The 22-unit luggage service is marked estimate only. Each classification is supported by the schedule or the ledger; no amount is included only because it appears in the same document.

The ticket was paid by the department card. Esi did not send money to the desk, and this example does not describe a customer refund. The heading “reimbursement review” refers to the desk’s internal amount to reimburse under the sample schedule. A draft email used the word “refund” loosely, but the payment record shows a department reimbursement and not a supplier refund. This wording correction does not affect the numerical calculation.

The desk asked Tidewater Labs to confirm that its statement showed the base fare separately from the hotel. Tidewater Labs replied that the ticket ledger amount was 640 units and the hotel ledger amount was 120. The supplier did not combine them for the reimbursement formula. The reply confirms the two component amounts, while the written schedule determines which component is eligible.

The corrected spreadsheet was reviewed by a second clerk. The reviewer multiplied 640 by 80 percent, checked the product as 512, and then subtracted 35 to reach 477. The reviewer also checked that the hotel amount had not been added before the multiplication. The signed review note says “477 payable under this sample rule,” not “477 total trip cost.” The full package and fee figures remain 795 when all listed charges are included.

Case B reconciliation table

Entry one: base fare, 640 units, issued and paid, eligible for the percentage. Calculation: 640 × 0.80 = 512. Entry two: hotel portion, 120 units, issued and paid, excluded from eligible base. Entry three: service fee, 35 units, fixed deduction after percentage. Calculation: 512 − 35 = 477. Entry four: meal advance, 15 units, separate account, no calculation treatment in this schedule. Entry five: seat selection, 15 units, separate optional item, not part of the base fare. Entry six: luggage service, 22 units, estimate only, not issued. Gross package line before fee: 640 + 120 = 760. Total including fee: 640 + 120 + 35 = 795.

This table was entered in two systems, and a copy in the archive is missing the heading over the final column. The numbers themselves are intact. The final column states whether an entry belongs in the particular reimbursement calculation. It is not a list of all items that were paid. An item may be paid but still excluded from the eligible base, as with the hotel portion.

The archived sheet lists a 35-unit service fee below the table and a second 35-unit note in the comment field. There is only one service fee. The comment repeats the amount to explain the deduction; it is not an additional charge. If both appearances were added as charges, the total would be overstated by 35 units. The payable calculation subtracts the single fixed fee once.

The desk checked that the payment ledger did not record a second hotel night or any additional hotel tax. The confirmed hotel entry remains 120 units. A preliminary planning sheet mentioned 12 units for a possible local tax, but the supplier did not charge it in the final ledger. That planning figure is not part of the gross package line or eligible base. It is retained in the appendix solely to explain why an old draft had a different total.

A further note on the worksheet says “80% after fees?” with a question mark. That was a question from the first reviewer, not the applicable instruction. The attached schedule resolves the order: apply the percentage to the base fare, then subtract the fee. The final worksheet follows that order. The presence of the question does not create a second possible rule.

The reimbursement was approved for the sample amount of 477 units. This approval does not state that the traveler received 477 units in cash on the same day. The payment queue showed the amount awaiting routine processing. For the numerical check in this report, approval is the relevant endpoint; timing of transfer is outside the calculation. A later bank posting would not change the amount due under the formula.

Case C — sample supplier statement and component addition

The training statement uses reference HS-TL-9936 and is not connected to either Ines’s group itinerary or Esi’s reimbursement. It is a fictional statement assembled to test itemization. The supplier line for the issued ticket contains three components: 275 units for the principal fare, 148 units for the route supplement, and 87 units for the seat charge. The statement marks each of those three entries “issued.” A line for 60 units appears below them, labeled “possible lounge add-on — estimate, not selected.” The estimate is not issued and not included in the supplier’s paid total.

The correct issued ticket-component total is 510 units. The addition is 275 plus 148, which equals 423; 423 plus 87 equals 510. The 60-unit possible lounge add-on is not part of the issued components. Adding it would produce 570, but that would answer a different question about issued components plus an unselected estimate. The supplier’s displayed ticket total of 510 agrees with the three issued rows.

A training clerk first wrote 570 on a sticky note because the clerk added every number visible in the statement. The supervisor crossed it out and wrote 510 beside the three issued lines. The sticky note remains in the file so the training review can see the common arithmetic error. It is not a supplier correction, and it does not change the status of the estimate.

The ticket has no hotel component in this training statement. A separate itinerary preview mentions that a hotel could be reserved for 90 units per night, but no hotel was selected in the training booking. The preview is not on the supplier statement and is not a ticket component. A second preview mentions a transfer for 18 units, also not selected. Neither amount belongs in the 510-unit issued ticket total.

The statement’s total line is described as “issued ticket components.” It is not a total for all proposed travel options. The ledger displays the three issued rows and the 60-unit estimate in distinct sections. A reader who looks only at the number of rows may assume there are four charges, but the labels and status column distinguish three issued components from one estimate.

This sample was reviewed after an agent asked whether the route supplement might already include the seat charge. The statement lists the entries separately and provides a total that matches their addition. There is no instruction in the statement to net one row against another. The verified component total is therefore the arithmetic sum of all three rows marked issued.

The daily log records that the booking was ticketed on the supplier system. It does not indicate that the lounge add-on was selected. The customer did not ask the desk to add it after issue, and the supplier did not post a later charge for it. The estimate remains unselected at the time of this report. The question in the manager’s checklist refers to the issued ticket components, not to what might be added later.

Training note: component totals and booking totals

Staff should not assume that every table uses the same definition of total. In Case A, “displayed package line” includes fare and hotel, while the separate service fee sits outside that line. In Case B, “gross package line” includes fare and hotel but excludes the fee, while “total including fee” includes all three. In Case C, “issued ticket components” includes only the rows marked issued. The question being answered determines which line is relevant.

The accounting unit is printed beside the column heading, not beside every value. All figures within a single sample case use that unit. There is no need to convert the 480-unit fare in Case A into the 640-unit fare in Case B; they are separate fictional examples. A copied number should remain tied to its own reference label. The same caution applies to 15, which appears as both a meal advance and a seat selection in Case B, and to 60, which appears as a possible add-on in Case C.

An old training card advised the reader to “sum visible values.” That card was withdrawn because it ignored status and category. The current method is to read the requested total, identify qualifying rows, and add only those rows. The training statement gives one possible wrong sum of 570 because it includes the unselected estimate. The correct sum of issued ticket components is 510.

The schedule in Case B similarly requires selecting a base before applying the percentage. It is not enough to add every paid component and multiply the total. The rule’s phrase “base fare only” controls the calculation. Staff can verify the computation with a calculator, but they still must select the correct inputs first. A perfectly accurate multiplication using the wrong subtotal remains an incorrect application of the rule.

The handover template now has a field titled “calculation inputs used.” For Case B, that field reads “640 base fare; 80%; subtract one 35 fee.” It does not read “760 gross line” or “795 including fee.” For Case C, it reads “275 + 148 + 87 issued rows.” It does not read “all printed values.” This wording lets a second reviewer reproduce the result without guessing what the original clerk included.

There is no rounding in either principal calculation. In Case B, 0.80 multiplied by 640 produces the integer 512, and subtraction gives the integer 477. In Case C, the sum of the three issued values is the integer 510. The report does not apply a percentage to Case C, and it does not add Case C’s estimate to the issued total. No exchange-rate table is needed.

The manager asked that the final handover use short statements for the review questions. The longer discussion remains here to explain the component selection. An agent answering from the file should not use the rough draft figure simply because it is repeated in a comment. The authoritative rule and the verified ledger values are stated in the relevant case sections.

Supplier statement details for Case C

Header: sample ticket HS-TL-9936. Currency unit: training units. Ticket state: issued. Row 1, principal fare, 275, status issued. Row 2, route supplement, 148, status issued. Row 3, seat charge, 87, status issued. Sum of issued rows, 510. Row 4, possible lounge add-on, 60, status estimate only; selection field blank. Supplier amount collected for the ticket rows, 510. The estimate is shown in a separate advisory area and is not included in the collected amount.

The supplier statement also includes a harmless printing note: “For reference only, a lounge option can be priced later.” The note is not a charge, and no amount is due for the option unless it is selected and issued. The selection field is blank. The statement does not say that the option was included in the seat charge or that it was later added to the ticket.

A second copy of the statement has a total of 510 printed at the bottom and a handwritten 570 in the margin. The handwritten figure was made during an initial review and is crossed out. The printed total agrees with the issued rows. The margin note is not a supplier entry. This duplicate copy is retained because the training clerk asked how the mismatch was resolved.

The route supplement has a similar name to the transfer estimate in Case A, but the items are not the same. The 148-unit route supplement is an issued ticket component in Case C. The 45-unit transfer in Case A was an estimate that was removed from the second itinerary alternative. The shared travel vocabulary is not a reason to move an amount from one case to another.

The seat charge in Case C is 87 units. The 15-unit seat selection in Case B is a separate item in another booking. The two values refer to different sample records. The training statement’s 87-unit row is marked issued and should be included in its component total. The 15-unit row in Case B is excluded from the base-fare reimbursement formula, although it appeared in the expense summary. Those decisions follow the labels and rule attached to each file.

Daily handover log, selected entries

Monday, 09:10: The manager requested a review of the new reimbursement worksheet. Esi O'Neill’s base fare was checked against the Tidewater Labs ledger. The first draft used a gross amount. The reviewer asked that the schedule wording be placed beside the calculation so the fee order is not guessed from the spreadsheet layout.

Monday, 10:25: Ines Castillo’s itinerary comparison was moved from “issued” to “comparison requested.” The coordinator had not selected either option. The transfer entry was confirmed as an estimate in alternative one, and it was absent from alternative two. The package display for alternative two remains 690 before the separately shown fee.

Monday, 11:40: The training statement for HS-TL-9936 was checked. Three rows are issued. The 60-unit lounge item remains estimate only. A clerk’s 570 sticky-note sum was crossed out, and 510 was written as the issued-component total.

Monday, 13:05: The review clerk confirmed that the hotel amount on Esi’s final ledger is 120, not the transposed 102 shown on an early worksheet. The 12-unit possible local tax does not appear on the final supplier ledger. Neither the transposed entry nor the possible tax changes the base-fare calculation.

Monday, 14:20: Finance asked whether the 35-unit service fee appears twice in the archive. It appears once as a charge and once as a calculation note. The fee is deducted once. The duplicate notation is explanatory and is not another fee.

Tuesday, 08:50: The manager received the corrected worksheet. The payable amount under the sample schedule is 477. The gross package line before fee is 760 and the total with the fee is 795. Those two package figures are for context, not alternative eligible bases.

Tuesday, 09:30: The supplier statement printout was checked against the training ledger. The three issued components total 510. The possible lounge amount remains 60 and is not collected. No hotel or transfer was selected for the training case.

Tuesday, 10:15: The manager asked the desk to retain the comparison case because its separate-fee display had caused confusion in a previous review. The report now states the package subtotal and full amount including fee separately. The group coordinator has not made a final booking choice.

Tuesday, 11:45: A staff member noticed that two separate entries in Case B both have a value of 15. The categories were checked: one is a meal advance and one is a seat selection. Neither is included in the formula. They are not duplicate records of the same payment.

Tuesday, 13:10: The training coordinator asked whether the 87-unit seat charge could be omitted as optional. The supplier statement status is issued, so it is included in the question’s issued-component total. Optionality in another file does not override the status of this row.

Tuesday, 15:00: The manager asked that the final review questions be phrased as verifiable statements. The questions below refer only to the named calculation and use the values supplied in the report. They do not ask whether a traveler is satisfied, whether a booking should be approved, or whether an estimate might become a charge.

Quality-control checklist

For every calculation, the reviewer must first match the traveler or sample reference. The reviewer must then identify the applicable rule. The reviewer must distinguish a confirmed amount from an estimate. Finally, the reviewer must write the arithmetic and compare it with the question’s exact scope. This checklist is not a substitute for the schedule; it is a way to prevent values from one case leaking into another.

Case A checklist: reference HS-TL-4401; no ticket issued; alternative two package subtotal contains 480 base fare and 210 hotel; transfer estimate absent; 480 + 210 = 690; service fee of 25 separately shown; if the fee is asked for as part of an all-in figure, 690 + 25 = 715. No reimbursement schedule applies.

Case B checklist: Esi O'Neill; reference in the Tidewater Labs ledger; base fare 640; hotel 120 excluded; percentage 80%; fee 35 deducted afterward once; 640 × 0.80 = 512; 512 − 35 = 477. The gross package line is 640 + 120 = 760; including the fee gives 795. Neither package total is the eligible base.

Case C checklist: reference HS-TL-9936; issued rows 275, 148, and 87; 275 + 148 = 423; 423 + 87 = 510. The 60-unit estimate is unselected. The printed total of 510 matches the issued rows. The 570 margin calculation includes the estimate and is not the issued-component total.

The reviewer should not rely on the phrase “near five hundred” when an exact amount can be calculated. In Case B, the exact amount is 477 under the formula. Nor should the reviewer round 510 to an approximate value in Case C, since the question is whether the component rows equal the stated total. Both calculations have whole-unit results.

The desk’s sample files have been prepared for internal reading practice. They do not define the price of any current Harbor Software trip. A live booking can include different service fees, percentages, supplier rules, or eligible components. Staff must read the current record rather than assume that the sample values repeat. This report makes no claim about an actual customer’s entitlement.

Appendix: definitions and examples of status wording

“Estimate” means the amount is proposed but not posted as an issued charge. “Issued” means the supplier has placed the item on the booking statement. “Paid” means the ledger records payment. “Eligible” means a specific rule allows the item to enter a particular formula. A paid amount can be ineligible, and an estimate can be visible without being payable. These words describe different properties and should not be used as synonyms.

“Package line” in Case A and Case B refers to the fare and any included lodging shown on the package screen before the separately displayed desk fee. “Full amount including fee” adds the fee to that package line. “Issued ticket components” in Case C refers only to supplier rows marked issued. These definitions are local to the sample files. If another form uses the words differently, its own headings must be checked.

The word “customer” in the manager’s generic reporting template does not mean every person in this report asked for a refund. Ines’s coordinator asked for a comparison. Esi’s file concerns an internal reimbursement calculation. The training statement is a sample. The report contains no customer request to refund the Case C estimate, and it does not state that the lounge add-on was bought.

A line that says “possible,” “could,” or “estimate” must not be treated as an issued purchase without a later status entry. The Case A transfer amount is an estimate in one alternative and absent in the other. The Case C lounge amount remains an estimate. The possible local tax in the Esi planning sheet was not charged. The desk uses final ledger entries where the question concerns issued or paid amounts.

The question about Esi’s payable figure uses the exact schedule attached to Esi’s file. It is not a question about the amount of the trip as a whole. The question about the training statement uses only the issued ticket rows. It is not a question about all travel options shown in an itinerary preview. A reader should avoid substituting a nearby but broader total.

Appendix: reviewer comments

Reviewer A: “The 573 draft looked plausible because it uses 80 percent and subtracts 35. The error is not the subtraction; the error is starting with 760, which includes hotel. The schedule says base fare only. We need to show 640 × 0.80 = 512, then 512 − 35 = 477.”

Reviewer B: “The 485 calculation also looked plausible because the fee was taken off before the percentage. The order matters in the written rule. First calculate the percentage of 640; then subtract 35. Do not use 605 as the percentage base.”

Reviewer C: “On the sample ticket sheet, 570 is the sum of the three issued rows plus the 60 estimate. It is a valid sum of four printed numbers but not the issued ticket-component total. The requested sum is 510.”

Reviewer D: “The 690 figure in the group comparison is a package subtotal for alternative two. If someone asks for the amount including the service fee, the calculation is 690 plus 25, or 715. Do not call 690 an all-in amount.”

Reviewer E: “The same number can appear in different categories. There is a 15-unit meal advance and a 15-unit seat-selection entry in Esi’s file. The schedule uses neither. Matching values do not mean the entries should be merged.”

Reviewer F: “Keep the 45-unit transfer estimate tied to alternative one. Alternative two has no transfer. Adding the estimate into both alternatives would double count it.”

The reviewer comments are explanations of calculations and classification, not new amounts or new rules. The manager approved the edits that made the arithmetic explicit. The final schedule remains the quoted rule in Case B, and the final supplier statement remains the itemized record in Case C.

Appendix: file separation and cross-checks

The archive contains one folder for each reference. HS-TL-4401 belongs to the Ines Castillo comparison; the Tidewater Labs reimbursement folder belongs to Esi O'Neill; HS-TL-9936 is a training statement. The references are different even though they were reviewed on the same day. Their amounts should not be pooled into a single trip total.

A cross-check of the folder index found no additional fare line for Esi beyond the 640-unit base fare. The 655 figure in the receipt summary is the base plus the separate 15-unit seat selection, not a revised base. The 120-unit hotel is confirmed in the final ledger. The 102-unit worksheet entry is a transposition. The 12-unit local-tax possibility was not issued. The 22-unit luggage amount was an estimate. The two 15-unit items are separate categories.

A cross-check of the training folder found exactly three issued components. There was no later update adding the lounge option. There was no hotel charge and no transfer charge in that booking. The itinerary preview’s 90-per-night hotel possibility was never selected, and the 18-unit transfer possibility was never selected. The statement’s issued total remains 510.

A cross-check of the comparison folder found no payment and no ticket issue. Alternative one had an estimate for transfer, and alternative two did not. The hotel amount was 210 in both alternatives. The base fare was 480. The service fee was 25 and shown separately. These values explain the comparison display, but they do not change the Esi calculation or the training-statement sum.

When a reviewer sees a number repeated in a narrative, table, and comment, the repetition should be understood as corroboration unless the file marks a second transaction. The 35-unit service fee appears as a ledger item and in a note describing the deduction, but only one fee was charged. The 510-unit total appears in both the supplier printout and the checked calculation; it is one total, not two charges. The repeated 45-unit estimate in a duplicate printout is the same estimate, not an extra transfer.

Closing manager note

The report is ready for handover. The manager’s requested checks can be answered using the exact values and rules above. The relevant computations are set out in the case sections and repeated in the quality-control checklist to make them easy to verify. The surrounding examples are retained to show why gross totals, estimates, and category labels should not be confused with the requested amount.

The desk will keep the comparison example, reimbursement worksheet, and training statement in separate folders. A later reviewer may use the same arithmetic checks as a reading exercise but should not apply the example schedule to another traveler without a matching policy. If a supplier changes an issued amount, the ledger must be updated before any new calculation is made. The current report records the values verified for this handover only.

The manager requested no further reconciliation. The travel team will continue using the itemized component method for subsequent sample reviews. Any future report should show the amount, the category, the status, and the calculation step that includes or excludes it. This is sufficient to make the result reproducible and to avoid relying on a rough note or an unqualified “total.”
