This is the customer’s present position; it is not a statement that a refund has already been granted.

Reference details supplied by the dispatch desk:

The local depot uses four status families. “Manifested” means a label exists; it does not mean that the carrier has physical possession. “Accepted” means the carrier scanned the parcel at an intake point; it does not prove delivery. “Out for delivery” means a parcel is assigned to a route; it does not establish a completed handover. “Delivered” is a carrier event and must be evaluated against the customer’s delivery instructions and Tidewater Studio’s evidence rule. These definitions are included to prevent a status word from substituting for the underlying evidence.

For a split shipment, each carton receives a distinct label and can travel on a different vehicle. A problem with one label does not automatically affect the other labels. In this case, the manifest records three cartons, and the customer’s descriptions consistently refer to A, B, and C. The routing system’s duplicate image export briefly suggested a fourth piece; the corrected count is three. Neither the duplicate image nor the extra row represents a fourth item billed to the customer.

The freight allocation rule was in effect when this order was placed. It says shared freight is divided evenly among the cartons unless the labels contain a different allocation. None of the three labels records a different split. Finance rounds only when posting the final amount, and the system determines which carton receives any rounding remainder. Thus the customer’s provisional figure is a request to apply the written allocation, not a binding finance calculation. No one should multiply the full $22.40 by the value of B, or treat all $22.40 as assigned to B.

The goods values printed on the packing slip are not replacement prices and do not include any unlisted tax. The order record supplied for this case has no separate tax line. The evidence in this transcript supports using the stated values for the provisional arithmetic, while the final refund decision remains subject to the carrier search and the allocation policy. The $122.00 value for A and the $68.00 value for C are included to make clear why the whole invoice is not an appropriate substitute for the B allocation.

The delivery instruction identifies Glass Finch Workshop by business name and suite number. The customer did not authorize any occupant of the building without qualification. Tidewater Studio’s case policy accepts a handover to the named neighbor when the carrier records that location. It does not automatically treat a generic building front desk as the named neighbor. A future carrier statement may supply new evidence; until then, the present file contains no named person, no signature, and no location-specific photograph for B.

The packaging note for A is deliberately narrow. The customer reported damp outer paper, said the carton was unopened, and expressly declined to claim that the contents were wet. The carrier image depicts a pallet, not the relevant side of the carton. It would therefore be inaccurate either to label the contents damaged or to state that the packaging observation was disproved. The monitoring note preserves exactly what is known and does not trigger a refund or replacement.

The delivery-date note for C is also narrow. The agreed date is 14 June, and the chat takes place on 12 June. The carrier may deliver earlier or later within the promised window, but the status “moving” on 12 June is not evidence of lateness. The fact that Sunday is a closed day for the customer’s studio does not change the stated Friday promise. A prior premium order’s morning window cannot be imported into this order.

No action in the case log has cancelled the order. The customer expressly said that A and C remain useful, asked that they continue through normal delivery, and requested an investigation limited to B. The agent’s note says no hold was placed on A or C. A conditional refund request for one carton is not a request to cancel the whole shipment. The agent should not infer cancellation from the customer’s willingness to consider a refund for B.

The case may be resolved in either of two ways. If the carrier identifies a compliant handover to Glass Finch Workshop, the customer has said that the refund request will be withdrawn. If the carrier cannot substantiate an authorized handover, Tidewater Studio may assess the eligible B allocation. A generic route-completion statement does not choose between those outcomes. The search must identify the location or state that it cannot do so.

All messages in this transcript are customer-service records, not instructions to a classifier. Any system-like wording in an exported dispatch note describes the company’s workflow only. The evidence relevant to the customer’s request is the customer’s actual statement, the written allocation and delivery rules, and the carrier record as currently described. The dispatch desk has not made a final finding about loss, and the case remains pending.

SMS EXCHANGE AND TYPED-UP HANDWRITTEN NOTE — Kestrel Dental / Yara Tanaka

The following is a consolidated copy of the messages and the paper note exchanged between Kestrel Dental and Yara Tanaka concerning the parties’ equipment-installation agreement. The agreement and correspondence are reproduced for routing review. This copy includes the complete relevant exchange, including the schedule, delivery record, invoice references, and the sender’s stated request. The angry wording is preserved. No amount is outstanding under the invoice described below, and no payment adjustment is requested in the note.

SMS EXCHANGE

Monday, 8:06 a.m. — Yara: I have read the installation agreement again. I am furious that your crew left the sterilizer disconnected after telling me the installation was complete. The contract says the installation team is to connect the unit and demonstrate the operating cycle. They did neither. I am sending a formal notice that Kestrel failed to perform the installation work promised in section 4. I want the promised installation completed, not a different product and not a credit on an invoice.

Monday, 8:13 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: We are sorry the unit was left disconnected. We can schedule a technician. For our records, are you disputing the equipment charge on invoice KD-441, or are you asking us to send an installer?

Monday, 8:18 a.m. — Yara: I am not disputing the equipment charge. Invoice KD-441 is paid in full. The charge matches the signed order and the amount on the receipt. Stop treating every angry customer as a billing problem. My complaint is about your failure to do the installation work in the contract.

Monday, 8:26 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: Understood. We have marked the invoice paid. Please confirm whether you want a technician visit.

Monday, 8:30 a.m. — Yara: Yes. I want the technician visit required by the agreement. That is the remedy I am requesting. Do not issue a refund; I have not asked for my money back. Do not send a revised bill. I want Kestrel to finish the contracted work.

Monday, 9:02 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: The appointment team will contact you. Your message mentioned a “formal notice.” Should we forward the notice to our contract review team?

Monday, 9:09 a.m. — Yara: Yes. It is a notice of breach of the installation obligation. You may forward it to contract review. I am angry because this is the third time I have had to repeat what the signed agreement says. This is not a claim that the price was wrong, the tax was wrong, or the payment was duplicated. The correct invoice is not the problem.

Monday, 9:17 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: Our system has a “billing” word alert because the message mentions an invoice and payment. A routing rule says messages containing “invoice” may be copied to billing. That alert does not decide what you are asking for. We will include your clarification that the invoice is paid and undisputed.

Monday, 9:24 a.m. — Yara: Good. The actual notice is about failure to perform. I do not want an account credit, a refund, a collection hold, or an explanation of the invoice. I want the contract team to review whether Kestrel must complete the installation under section 4. I want the service team to arrange the visit after review.

Monday, 10:40 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: We have logged a service request and a contract notice. The billing alert remains visible in the system because the message contains the word “invoice.” It is only a keyword alert. We are not recording a billing dispute.

Monday, 10:46 a.m. — Yara: Then make sure no one mistakes a keyword for my request. I have already said the invoice is correct and paid. The legal notice concerns the missing installation and the remedy is completion of the agreed work. I am not asking for money back.

Tuesday, 11:12 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: The contract review team has asked us to confirm whether the installation obligation remains open. The work order shows delivery on Friday and a technician visit marked “attempted.”

Tuesday, 11:20 a.m. — Yara: “Attempted” is not completed. The technician left a carton and did not connect the unit. Your own work order says “connection not performed.” The contract calls for connection and demonstration, not merely delivery. Please do not close the notice based on the delivery record.

Tuesday, 11:31 a.m. — Kestrel service desk: We have added that note to the contract file. To avoid confusion, the amount paid under KD-441 remains unchanged, and we have not opened a request to recalculate or return it.

Tuesday, 11:37 a.m. — Yara: Correct. I am not asking you to calculate anything. I am asking you to honor the written installation clause. I expect a written response from the contract review team, not a billing statement.

TYPED-UP HANDWRITTEN NOTE, received with the SMS export

“Please attach this to my notice. I am angry, and I do not want another generic answer about invoices. I paid the exact agreed equipment price; the receipt and invoice agree. The contract is not a receipt-only arrangement: section 4 also requires Kestrel to connect the sterilizer and show the operating cycle. Your installer did not do that. I ask Kestrel to perform the installation it promised. This note is not a request for a refund, discount, reimbursement, or billing correction. Please route the notice for review of the written contract obligation and tell the appointment team to arrange completion if the obligation is confirmed. I am not withdrawing the notice just because the unit was delivered. Delivery and installation are different things.”

ATTACHMENT A — EXCERPTS COPIED FROM THE SIGNED ORDER

Order KD-441 identifies one sterilizer, the agreed equipment price, and the installation service. The order states that the equipment charge is payable upon delivery. The installation clause states: “Kestrel Dental will connect the sterilizer at the customer’s premises and demonstrate one operating cycle. Delivery of the equipment alone does not constitute completion of the installation service.” The order contains no condition that a customer must dispute an invoice before requesting performance of the installation obligation. The signed order is attached only to establish the promised work; it does not show a disagreement over the equipment price.

The copy of the order included in the file has the customer’s signature, Kestrel’s acceptance mark, and the delivery address. Its price entry matches invoice KD-441 and the payment receipt. There is no handwritten change to the amount, no note requesting that the charge be reversed, and no later amendment changing the installation clause. The service desk has checked the signed copy against its archived order and recorded that the payment was received. The discrepancy described in the notice concerns what the installer did, rather than what the customer paid.

ATTACHMENT B — INSTALLATION RECORD

The delivery entry says the equipment was brought to the premises on Friday. A separate line states, “connection not performed; no demonstration.” The technician’s note says that the visit ended before connection because the correct fitting was not in the vehicle. The customer’s messages do not deny delivery. They distinguish delivery from the installation service and ask Kestrel to complete the latter. The appointment record has not yet been amended to show completed work. No record in this packet says that the customer accepted an alternative remedy or agreed to cancel the installation obligation.

ATTACHMENT C — ROUTING HISTORY

The service desk’s intake screen contains a general keyword alert titled “billing words present.” The alert is generated when a message contains such words as “invoice,” “paid,” “charge,” or “refund.” It does not establish that the sender has a billing request. In this instance, the alert was generated by the customer’s explicit statement that the invoice was paid and that no refund or correction was sought. The desk has preserved the alert for audit purposes but has not opened a billing case. The separate contract-notice entry records the alleged failure to perform section 4. The service entry records the requested technician visit. The sender’s repeated clarification remains in the file so that the recipient of the notice does not confuse vocabulary mentioned in a denial with the sender’s actual request.

The review copy is intentionally complete enough to show the sequence, rather than presenting isolated words from one message. The opening complaint identifies the failure alleged. The service desk asks whether the customer disputes an invoice; the customer answers no. The customer then states the affirmative request: performance of the installation term. The later note repeats the same distinction in plain language. The records of delivery, payment, and the failed connection are included to describe the subject of the dispute, not to create a separate request for money. The notice is still open pending contract review and scheduling.

ATTACHMENT D — INTERNAL FILE NOTE

The service desk records that a message can contain financial vocabulary without seeking a financial remedy. The customer’s phrase “I am not disputing the equipment charge” is a denial of a billing dispute, not an assertion of one. The sentence “I have not asked for my money back” likewise disclaims a refund request. The notice asks Kestrel to perform a particular contractual service. For routing purposes, the presence of “invoice,” “payment,” and “refund” should not override the stated subject and requested action. The company has not concluded whether a breach occurred; that determination is for contract review. The packet does not ask the reviewer to decide liability, only to route the incoming notice according to its subject.

END OF CONSOLIDATED COPY

VOICEMAIL TRANSCRIPT AND ATTACHED ROUTING MEMORANDUM — Saltmarsh Freight / Amara Novak

This packet contains the voicemail left by Amara Novak, the transcription checked against the audio, and the intake memorandum prepared from the attached contract notice. Amara’s voice is angry throughout. The transcript preserves her wording, including repeated references to freight charges and invoices, because those words were part of her explanation of what she is not disputing. The principal request is stated in the voicemail and repeated in the handwritten-style note typed up by the intake clerk. The file includes contract excerpts and a chronological index so the request can be routed without relying on a keyword hit.

VOICEMAIL TRANSCRIPT

“Saltmarsh Freight, this is Amara Novak. I am leaving this message because your notices keep talking about the freight invoice as if that were the problem. It is not. I paid invoice SF-208 exactly as the signed agreement says, and I am not asking for a refund or a billing correction. I am furious that your company has failed to give me the signed delivery record required by the contract. The goods arrived; I am not saying they did not. What I have not received is the carrier-signed proof of delivery that section 7 requires you to provide within five working days after delivery. I want the company to provide that document and answer my written contract notice. Please send this to whoever reviews contract compliance. Do not send me another invoice.”

The voicemail continues: “I know your recording system may hear the words ‘invoice,’ ‘paid,’ ‘freight charge,’ and ‘refund.’ I am using those words to explain that I have no dispute about them. The charge matches the agreed amount. I am not asking anyone to recalculate a fee. I am not asking for money back. I am demanding the missing signed record. Your customer service representative told me the system had sent my first message to billing because it contained the word ‘freight.’ That is ridiculous. A word in the explanation is not the request. I need someone to review the clause and tell me when the document will be sent.”

Amara then says: “The contract says you will provide the signed delivery record. Your tracking page says delivered, but it is not the signed record. A tracking status and a carrier-signed document are not interchangeable under the text we signed. I have attached the notice again. This is not a claim about the amount charged, whether a payment cleared, or whether I should receive a credit. It is a request that Saltmarsh Freight perform the document-delivery obligation in our agreement. I am angry because I have asked twice and received a payment summary instead. Please route the notice correctly.”

The last portion of the voicemail says: “If you need to check the agreement, check section 7. If you need to check whether I paid, the receipt is attached, but that is not why I called. Do not treat the receipt attachment as a refund request. I want the signed proof of delivery and a response to the contract notice. I am not asking for legal advice from the person answering the phone. I am asking for the notice to reach the contract-compliance reviewer and for the missing item to be produced.”

INTAKE MEMORANDUM — prepared after listening to the recording

Caller: Amara Novak. Company named in notice: Saltmarsh Freight. Call purpose as stated by caller: obtain a contract-required signed delivery record and a response to a written notice concerning that document. Caller explicitly disclaims an invoice dispute, a request for a refund, and a request to recalculate the freight charge. Caller says the goods were delivered and does not dispute the tracking status. The distinction emphasized by the caller is between a tracking-page delivery status and the separate carrier-signed record specified by the contract. The requested routing is contract compliance or contract review.

The memorandum does not decide whether the company has breached the agreement. It records only what the caller says the agreement requires and what she wants the company to do. The voicemail contains financial terms because the caller anticipates a mistaken keyword route. The intake system’s “freight / invoice” alert is not evidence that she seeks a billing adjustment. The requested action is documentary performance under a written contract. The attached receipt is offered to prevent confusion about payment, not to challenge it.

ATTACHED NOTICE, typed up from the caller’s handwritten-style original

“To Saltmarsh Freight: I am giving formal notice that I have not received the signed delivery record required by section 7. The delivery itself is not disputed. The online tracking page is not the carrier-signed proof described in our agreement. Please provide the signed record and give me a written response explaining when it will be supplied. I am angry that my earlier request was answered with a payment summary. The freight invoice is correct and paid. This notice does not ask for repayment, a credit, or a corrected charge. I ask Saltmarsh Freight to perform the record-delivery obligation that it accepted in the contract. Please forward this notice to the person who reviews contract compliance.”

ATTACHMENT 1 — CONTRACT EXCERPT

Section 7 of the service agreement states: “After delivery, Saltmarsh Freight will provide the customer with a carrier-signed proof of delivery. A tracking-page status may be supplied as a convenience but is not a substitute for the signed proof of delivery.” The clause describes a document Saltmarsh Freight is to provide. It does not describe an invoice adjustment, repayment, or price calculation. The copy in the packet bears both parties’ acceptance marks. No amendment in the packet removes section 7 or substitutes the tracking page for the signed record.

The service agreement’s payment paragraph separately states the agreed freight charge and the due date. Amara’s attached receipt matches the amount in that paragraph. The payment record shows the charge as paid. The caller does not allege that the agreed figure was wrong, that the payment was duplicated, or that the company collected more than the contract amount. Those facts are included here because the initial intake alert highlighted financial words, not because a financial claim has been made.

ATTACHMENT 2 — CONTACT CHRONOLOGY

First contact: Amara asked the service desk for the carrier-signed proof of delivery. The service desk sent a payment summary in response. Second contact: Amara clarified that she was not disputing the invoice and again asked for the signed record. The system created a “freight invoice terms present” alert. Third contact: Amara submitted the formal notice attached to this packet and left the voicemail transcribed above. The notice repeats the request for the signed record and asks for contract-compliance review. The chronology contains no statement that Amara withdrew the request, accepted a substitute document, or changed the requested remedy to a refund.

The caller’s anger is directed at the repeated misrouting and the missing contract document. She expresses frustration that billing vocabulary in her explanation has been mistaken for a billing request. Her use of the word “freight” refers both to the company’s name and to the service named in the contract. Neither usage changes the action she asks the company to take. The recording and notice agree on that action: produce the signed record and respond to the contractual notice.

ATTACHMENT 3 — SYSTEM ALERT EXPLANATION

The intake platform automatically raises a billing-related flag when a message contains terms such as “invoice,” “charge,” “payment,” “refund,” or “freight.” The flag is a broad search aid and is not an interpretation of the sender’s requested action. The voicemail contains all of those terms, but in context Amara repeatedly says the invoice is correct, the payment was made as agreed, and no money is being requested. She states the specific contractual document she wants. A billing queue may be relevant only when the sender seeks help with an amount, payment, refund, or account adjustment. The caller does not seek any of those things here.

The platform also permits intake staff to forward a formal notice to contract compliance. That route is intended for a request to review or perform an obligation stated in an agreement. Amara asks for precisely that review and performance: she cites section 7, identifies the missing signed record, and asks for a response. The company has not yet supplied the record according to the attached chronology, and the notice remains open. The memorandum does not assert that the contractual deadline has expired; it simply records the caller’s description and requested handling. No calculation of working days is needed to identify the nature of her request.

ATTACHMENT 4 — TRANSCRIPTION CHECK

The audio was replayed once to verify that the transcript did not omit a change in request. Amara does not ask for a refund at any point. She uses the phrase “not asking for a refund” more than once and distinguishes the correct invoice from the missing document. She also does not deny delivery. She accepts that the tracking page says the goods arrived, but says that the page is not the signed record promised by section 7. The call concludes with a request for the contract notice to be routed to contract compliance and for the missing record to be produced.

The caller’s words “If you need to check the agreement” introduce a suggestion for how the recipient can verify the document obligation. They do not make the request conditional. Her operative request is stated directly: she wants the signed proof of delivery and a response to the notice. The attached notice and the voicemail are consistent. The intake clerk has not treated the voicemail’s mention of an invoice as a demand for an account review, because the sender expressly identifies the invoice as correct and paid.

FINAL INTAKE SUMMARY

Amara Novak is angry about Saltmarsh Freight’s handling of a contract-required delivery document. She says the carrier-signed proof of delivery has not been provided, while acknowledging that the goods themselves were delivered and that the tracking page shows delivery. She asks the company to provide the signed document and answer her written contract notice. She explicitly says the freight invoice is correct and paid and disclaims any refund or billing correction. The references to invoice, payment, freight charges, and refund occur in explanations that negate a financial request. The subject and requested remedy are stated consistently in the voicemail, notice, contract excerpt, and chronology. The packet is ready for routing; no liability determination is requested from intake.

Document control
This manual is issued by Harbor Foods for the administration of supplier invoices, payment records, and routine accounts payable enquiries. It applies to invoices submitted to Harbor Foods by Granite Supply, Tidewater Labs, and Saltmarsh Studio, and to the staff who record, review, and process those invoices. The manual is an administrative description of the current procedure. It does not change an amount agreed in a separate purchase order or contract. If a purchase order states a specific price or quantity, the staff member reviewing the invoice checks that document as part of the ordinary review.

The manual is arranged as follows: general service terms; supplier submission instructions; receipt and logging procedure; invoice review procedure; payment administration; records and reporting; routine examples; and appendices containing sample forms and a summary of assigned responsibilities. The examples and appendices are included to make the procedure understandable. They do not establish a separate payment promise for an individual invoice.

Section 1. General service terms
Harbor Foods maintains an accounts payable function for the purpose of receiving supplier invoices, checking them against the related purchasing records, recording approved obligations, and arranging payment through the company’s finance process. The accounts payable function is not a purchasing department. It does not place orders, approve delivery quality, or independently authorize a new supplier relationship. Those actions remain with the staff members identified in the relevant purchase record.

A supplier invoice is a request for payment for goods or services supplied to Harbor Foods. Receipt of an invoice does not by itself mean that the invoice has been approved, that the goods have been accepted, or that payment has been released. An invoice is recorded as received when the designated accounts payable mailbox or paper-mail address receives it. The receipt record is an administrative record and is not a confirmation that every item on the invoice is correct.

Harbor Foods asks suppliers to submit one invoice per email attachment where practical. A supplier may include supporting documents, such as a delivery confirmation or an agreed service record, with the invoice. If multiple invoices are sent in one message, each must be separately identifiable. The supplier should use a legible file format and should not send a password-protected document unless the password is provided through an agreed secure channel. The ordinary preferred format is PDF. A clear scanned copy is acceptable where an original paper document is not required by a separate agreement.

The supplier’s invoice should be addressed to Harbor Foods and should show the supplier’s legal or trading name, invoice number, invoice date, description of goods or services, amount requested, and any tax information that is applicable to the transaction. The invoice should identify a purchase order or other Harbor Foods reference when one has been provided. The supplier is responsible for supplying accurate billing details. Harbor Foods may ask the supplier to clarify information that is missing or difficult to read.

The routine payment term in this manual is payment within thirty calendar days after the date an approved invoice is entered into Harbor Foods’ payable schedule. A separate signed agreement may set another term for a particular supplier or transaction. Where a separate signed agreement applies, staff use the agreed term recorded in the supplier file. The general statement in this manual is not a substitute for checking that file. The payment term describes the routine schedule after approval and entry; it does not turn an unreviewed invoice into an approved invoice.

Payments are normally made by electronic bank transfer to the account details previously verified for the supplier. A supplier wishing to change its bank account must use the bank-detail change procedure in Section 6. An email that merely states new account details is not sufficient authorization for staff to change a verified account. This safeguard is intended to maintain accurate supplier records and to ensure that payment is sent to the intended recipient.

Harbor Foods may place an invoice on hold while a material discrepancy is reviewed. Examples include a difference in quantity, a price that does not match the purchase record, a missing delivery confirmation, or an unclear invoice reference. A hold means that review is incomplete. It does not mean that the invoice has been rejected or that the supplier has no right to payment. The accounts payable coordinator records the reason for the hold and, where appropriate, asks the relevant purchasing or receiving staff member for information.

Harbor Foods seeks to communicate in a clear and orderly manner. Suppliers may ask whether an invoice has been received, whether a missing item is needed, and whether a payment has been scheduled. The accounts payable function will answer based on the records available at the time. A status response does not amend a purchase order, a signed contract, or an agreed price. A request to change commercial terms is referred to the purchasing contact or the person authorized to make that change.

Section 2. Supplier submission instructions
Invoices should be sent to the accounts payable address listed in the supplier onboarding record. If the supplier has not received that address, it should request the current submission information from its Harbor Foods purchasing contact. An invoice sent to an individual employee may be forwarded for processing, but the supplier should use the designated address for later submissions. This reduces the risk that an invoice will be missed when an employee is away from work or when a team assignment changes.

The subject line of an invoice email should include the supplier name and invoice number. If a purchase order reference is available, the supplier may include it as well. The subject line is a practical sorting aid, not a replacement for the invoice itself. The content of the attached invoice remains the record used for entry. A message without an attachment may be treated as an enquiry rather than as a submitted invoice, unless the message contains a complete invoice in the body and the accounts payable coordinator can enter it accurately.

Suppliers should avoid combining unrelated account statements and individual invoices into one indistinguishable file. A statement can help identify outstanding items, but it is not necessarily a request for payment in place of the underlying invoices. If a statement lists several invoice numbers, the supplier should provide the invoice documents requested by the coordinator. The coordinator will compare the statement with Harbor Foods’ records and report any difference that can be identified from those records.

A corrected invoice should clearly indicate that it replaces or corrects an earlier invoice. The supplier should preserve a clear connection between the revised document and the earlier invoice number or transaction. Harbor Foods records the corrected document in a way that avoids treating the earlier and corrected versions as two separate payment requests. If the change concerns the supplier’s legal name, tax information, or payment details rather than a line-item correction, the supplier should also follow the applicable record-update procedure.

A credit note should identify the invoice or transaction to which it relates and state the amount credited. A credit note is recorded separately from an invoice. It may affect the open balance for an account, but staff do not infer a credit amount that is not shown in the document. If a supplier believes that an account statement has not reflected a credit note, the supplier should provide the credit note number and the related invoice reference in its enquiry.

Where Harbor Foods has provided a purchase order, the supplier should show that reference on the invoice. The absence of a purchase order reference does not allow accounts payable staff to invent one. The coordinator may ask the purchasing contact to identify the appropriate order. If the relevant purchasing contact confirms that no purchase order was issued, the invoice is reviewed using the other available records and the applicable authorization process.

The supplier should send a separate invoice for each agreed billing period when the contract or purchase record calls for periodic billing. The invoice should state the period covered and briefly describe the work performed or goods supplied during that period. If an invoice covers several sites, projects, or departments, the supplier should separate the lines sufficiently for the internal reviewer to identify the charges. The accounts payable coordinator does not decide how a supplier should allocate its commercial charges; the coordinator records the information provided and seeks clarification if it cannot be matched to the company’s records.

Section 3. Receipt and logging procedure
When a document arrives through the designated mailbox, the accounts payable coordinator records the date of receipt, the sender, the supplier name, the invoice number if visible, and the apparent invoice date. The coordinator also records whether the document is complete enough to begin review. If the attachment cannot be opened, is unreadable, or is clearly not an invoice, the coordinator records the issue and asks for a usable document or clarification.

The receipt log is used to track the document through review. It is not a final accounting determination. The log can show statuses such as received, awaiting information, under review, approved for scheduling, scheduled, or paid. These status terms describe administrative stages. For example, “received” means the document has arrived; “under review” means that staff are checking it; and “scheduled” means that it has been placed in the payment process. A supplier should not interpret “received” as a guarantee of payment on a particular date.

The coordinator assigns an internal reference where the record system requires one. The supplier’s invoice number remains the principal external reference for correspondence. If a supplier has reused an invoice number or sent two documents with the same number, the coordinator records the issue and requests clarification. Staff do not silently alter the supplier’s invoice number to make the records appear consistent.

The coordinator checks whether the supplier is present in Harbor Foods’ supplier register. If the supplier is not present, the invoice is referred for the ordinary supplier setup process. Supplier setup may require confirmation of the legal name, remittance address, tax information, and verified payment details. Receiving an invoice during setup does not remove those requirements. The document may be retained in the receipt log while the record is completed.

An employee who receives an invoice outside the designated mailbox should forward it to the accounts payable mailbox with the original attachment intact. The employee may add a brief cover note identifying the purchase contact or department, but should not edit the supplier’s document. The coordinator logs the document using the date it reaches the designated processing channel and retains the original message when required for the record. If the message is only a forwarded copy and an attachment is missing, the coordinator asks the forwarding employee or supplier for the complete document.

The coordinator checks for possible duplicate submissions by comparing supplier name, invoice number, invoice date, amount, and relevant purchase reference. Similarity between two documents is a reason to check, not by itself proof that one is a duplicate. If the supplier has sent a corrected version, staff record which version is current. If a document appears to be an accidental duplicate, staff do not enter it as a second payable item without resolving the question.

Section 4. Invoice review procedure
The first review is an administrative completeness check. The coordinator confirms that the supplier can be identified, that an invoice number and date are visible, that the requested amount can be read, and that the goods or services are described. The coordinator also checks for a purchase order or another internal reference where applicable. If a required piece of information is absent, the coordinator records what is missing and requests it from the supplier or the relevant Harbor Foods contact.

The next review compares the invoice with the supporting purchasing and receiving records. The purchasing contact confirms whether the transaction was authorized and whether the billed price is consistent with the purchase record. The receiving contact confirms the relevant receipt of goods or completion of services when that confirmation is needed. The coordinator does not replace those confirmations with an independent assumption based only on an invoice description.

A line-item difference may be caused by a typing error, a changed order, a partial delivery, or a genuine disagreement. The reviewer records the observed difference and sends it to the staff member who can explain or authorize it. If the supplier needs to issue a correction, the coordinator asks for the corrected document. If Harbor Foods needs to update an internal record, the authorized employee makes that update through the applicable procedure. The invoice is not marked approved merely because a difference has been reported to someone.

Where the invoice matches the purchase and receipt records, the appropriate reviewer records approval in the designated system. Approval confirms that the invoice is eligible to proceed through the payable schedule under the applicable authorization. The coordinator then checks that the supplier and payment information are available in the record. If required approval is absent, the invoice remains pending. The coordinator may remind the relevant reviewer that a document is waiting, but a reminder is not itself an approval.

If an invoice includes several line items and one is disputed, the reviewer documents the disputed item and follows the company’s process for deciding whether the undisputed portion may be processed separately. The accounts payable coordinator does not divide an invoice into new commercial obligations without authorization. If a supplier wishes to issue separate documents, it may do so after confirming the arrangement with the purchasing contact. The record should make clear which amounts are approved and which remain under review.

A tax line is checked against the information shown in the invoice and the supplier record. The coordinator records the stated amount and refers questions about tax treatment to the finance reviewer. The coordinator does not create a tax charge that is not shown or remove a charge on the basis of an informal assumption. If a corrected tax document is required, the supplier is asked to provide it through the ordinary correction process.

Any discount, credit, freight charge, service fee, or other adjustment should be identifiable in the invoice or a related authorized record. An amount described only in an accompanying message is not automatically entered as an invoice line. The reviewer checks that the adjustment is consistent with the purchase record or another authorization. If an adjustment is unclear, the invoice is held for clarification rather than assigned a guessed value.

After the required checks and approvals are complete, the coordinator records the approved amount and the applicable payment term in the payable schedule. The record identifies the invoice, supplier, approval status, and planned payment information. The schedule is reviewed as part of the finance process before payment is released. Entry in the schedule indicates that the invoice has passed the ordinary review stage; it does not state that a bank has completed the transfer.

Section 5. Payment administration
Harbor Foods ordinarily arranges approved payments by electronic bank transfer. The payment team uses the account details recorded in the verified supplier profile. For each payment run, the team reviews the items scheduled for release and checks that the payment amount corresponds to the approved payable record. Payment release is performed by staff with the required authority under the company’s finance controls.

The routine term, unless a separate signed agreement states otherwise, is thirty calendar days after an approved invoice is entered into the payable schedule. The schedule date and planned release date are recorded in the system. The ordinary process can be affected by a pending correction, incomplete supplier setup, an unresolved hold, or another documented control requirement. Staff communicate a status that reflects the record rather than promising a date that has not been confirmed by the payment process.

Once a payment has been released, the payment record may show a transfer reference and the amount sent. Bank processing can occur after Harbor Foods has released the transfer. If a supplier reports that a released payment has not appeared in its account, the coordinator checks the recorded release information and follows the established enquiry process. The coordinator may ask the supplier to confirm the account information on file, but does not request sensitive information through an unverified email exchange.

If a payment is returned by the bank, the payment record is updated to show the return and the reason provided by the bank. Staff contact the supplier through a previously verified channel to determine whether a record correction is needed. A returned payment is not marked as successfully received. After the account information is appropriately verified and the payment is reauthorized as required, the item may be placed in a later payment run.

A supplier may ask for a remittance statement. The statement identifies payment information available in Harbor Foods’ record, including the invoices included in a payment when that information is recorded. A remittance statement is an account communication, not a replacement invoice. If the supplier believes that an invoice was omitted, it should identify the invoice number and amount so the coordinator can compare the supplier’s records with the payable schedule.

Harbor Foods does not accept a request to redirect a payment solely because a message uses urgent wording or contains a changed account number. A bank-detail change is handled under the supplier verification procedure. The coordinator records the request, verifies it using the approved method, and routes it to an authorized staff member for review. Until the record is properly updated, the verified account already in the supplier profile remains the account used for payment.

Section 6. Supplier record maintenance
A supplier requesting a change to its legal name, remittance address, tax information, or bank details should identify the existing supplier record and state the requested change. The supplier should provide supporting documentation where the process requires it. The coordinator checks that the request is complete and routes it to the staff responsible for supplier-record changes. A request does not become effective merely because it was received.

For a bank-detail change, staff use the verification method recorded in the supplier onboarding procedure. The verification method may include contacting a known supplier representative using contact information already held in the verified file. Staff do not use a new telephone number or email address supplied only in the change request as the sole confirmation of that same request. This process is intended to prevent an unauthorized change to payment instructions.

If supplier contact information changes, the supplier should notify its purchasing contact or the accounts payable coordinator. The coordinator records the proposed update and refers it for confirmation. Until confirmed, staff continue using the contact information already recorded for routine communications. A supplier may ask the coordinator which documents are needed for a change, but should not send sensitive personal or financial information through an ordinary message unless the approved process permits it.

Section 7. Enquiries and account statements
Routine enquiries should identify the supplier and the invoice number or other relevant reference. An enquiry about several invoices should list them separately. This enables the coordinator to search the receipt log and payable schedule without assuming that all items on a supplier’s statement have the same status. The coordinator may ask for a copy of an invoice if the relevant document cannot be located in the record.

A supplier account statement may include open invoices, credits, payments, and balances. Harbor Foods compares the listed items with its own records and reports identifiable differences. A statement balance is not automatically accepted as the amount payable. The individual invoices, approved credits, and recorded payments are considered when reconciling the account. If an item is absent from Harbor Foods’ records, the coordinator may request the original invoice or other relevant document.

If a supplier disputes a recorded amount, the coordinator refers the issue to the purchasing contact or finance reviewer as appropriate. The response should state the record basis for the current status, where that basis can be shared. The coordinator does not change an approved amount simply to make two statements agree. A change is made only after the relevant supporting information and authorization are recorded.

A request for confirmation of payment should specify the invoice or payment reference. The coordinator checks whether the item is awaiting review, scheduled, released, returned, or otherwise recorded. Where no payment has been released, the coordinator says so based on the available record. Where a payment has been released, the coordinator provides the information authorized for supplier communication. The supplier can then compare the remittance information with its own bank records.

Section 8. Record retention and access
The accounts payable record may include the supplier invoice, supporting documents, approval records, correspondence needed to explain a decision, and payment information. Staff retain records according to Harbor Foods’ record-retention schedule. Documents are stored in the designated company system and are available to staff whose duties require access. A supplier request for a copy is routed to the appropriate contact and handled under the applicable business process.

The coordinator should record material status changes in a manner that allows another authorized staff member to understand what has occurred. A useful note identifies the action taken, the date, the responsible role, and any outstanding item. Notes should be factual and should distinguish a supplier’s statement from a verified internal record. For example, a note may say that the supplier reports delivery on a particular date while separately recording whether Harbor Foods’ receiving record confirms it.

If a document is replaced or corrected, the record should retain an appropriate link to the prior version. This makes it possible to understand why the payable amount changed and prevents an obsolete document from being mistaken for the current version. Access to obsolete copies remains subject to the ordinary record controls. Staff should not delete an audit-relevant document merely because a newer invoice was supplied.

Reports may summarize received invoices, pending approvals, scheduled payments, and completed payments. Each report should identify its reporting date and the status definitions used. A report is a view of recorded information at that time. Later corrections may cause a status or amount to change. Staff should avoid describing a draft report as a final account settlement.

Section 9. Roles and responsibilities
The accounts payable coordinator receives documents, maintains the receipt log, checks administrative completeness, requests missing information, routes discrepancies, and records approved invoices for scheduling. The coordinator may answer routine status questions from the company’s records. The coordinator does not independently authorize a purchase, certify receipt of goods, approve a disputed price, or approve a supplier bank-detail change without the required review.

The purchasing contact confirms the relevant commercial arrangement and purchase reference. The purchasing contact may explain an authorized order change or refer a supplier question to the person empowered to decide it. The purchasing contact does not replace the finance controls for payment release. If the purchasing contact is unavailable, the coordinator routes the question to the designated alternate rather than assuming that approval has been given.

The receiving contact confirms delivery or service completion when that confirmation is required. A receiving record should identify the relevant goods, service, site, or period sufficiently for the invoice reviewer to make a comparison. If the record is incomplete, the coordinator asks for clarification. A supplier’s delivery note may support review, but the internal confirmation process remains applicable.

The finance reviewer checks the payable record and applicable accounting information. The payment approver authorizes release according to the company’s internal controls. Where the same staff member is not permitted to perform more than one control step, the system assigns the tasks to separate authorized users. A status entered by one role is not treated as another role’s approval unless the control procedure explicitly provides for that action.

Suppliers are responsible for issuing accurate invoices and providing requested supporting information. Suppliers should promptly identify a correction, credit, or change to their contact or remittance details. A supplier should retain its own copies of invoices and remittance information. Harbor Foods’ procedure for recording a document does not remove the supplier’s responsibility to maintain its own business records.

Section 10. Routine examples
Example A: A supplier emails a complete invoice to the designated mailbox. The coordinator records the date and invoice number, checks the supplier record, and routes the invoice to the relevant purchasing and receiving contacts. Once the required confirmations and approval are entered, the coordinator adds the approved invoice to the payable schedule. The payment team processes it according to the applicable term and release controls.

Example B: An invoice arrives without a purchase order reference, although the supplier record shows that the transaction is normally associated with an order. The coordinator records the document and asks the purchasing contact to identify the relevant order. The coordinator does not create a reference. If the purchasing contact confirms the correct order, review proceeds using that information. If the reference cannot be established, the invoice remains pending clarification.

Example C: A supplier sends a statement showing three invoices, but Harbor Foods’ record contains two. The coordinator asks for the missing invoice document and checks whether it may have been sent to another address. The statement is not entered as a third invoice. Once the document is received, it is logged and reviewed in the ordinary way.

Example D: A supplier submits a revised invoice with the same invoice number and a corrected description. The coordinator links the new version to the prior version and asks the reviewer to confirm the change. The obsolete version is not entered a second time. The record identifies which document is current and why the review was repeated.

Example E: A supplier asks whether an invoice has been paid. The coordinator searches by supplier and invoice number. If the record shows that the invoice is approved but not yet released, the coordinator reports that status. If the record shows a released transfer, the coordinator provides the permitted remittance reference. The coordinator does not state that a bank has credited the supplier unless that information is available and verified.

Example F: A message requests a change to a supplier bank account and asks for immediate processing. The coordinator records the request and follows the established verification procedure. The requested account is not used simply because the message contains a complete account number or states that payment is urgent. The current verified account remains in place until the authorized change is completed.

Example G: A supplier invoice contains a service charge that is not shown in the related purchase record. The coordinator identifies the line and routes it for review. If the purchasing contact confirms the charge under an authorized arrangement, that confirmation is recorded. If not, the supplier is asked to clarify or correct the invoice. The coordinator does not decide the commercial issue by silently deleting the line.

Example H: A supplier reports that a payment was returned. The coordinator checks the payment record and confirms whether a return notice is recorded. If a return is confirmed, the supplier is contacted through the verified channel and asked to follow the account-update process if needed. The payment is not reported as successfully completed merely because it was released earlier.

Example I: A complete invoice is forwarded by an employee with a short note naming the purchasing contact. The coordinator preserves the attachment and logs the invoice. The employee’s note helps routing but does not approve the invoice or certify receipt. The ordinary purchasing, receiving, and finance review still takes place.

Example J: A supplier asks Harbor Foods to pay a statement balance without providing the individual invoices that support several listed items. The coordinator compares the statement with the account record and requests the underlying documents for items that cannot be matched. The statement can assist reconciliation, but the payable record must identify the underlying approved obligations.

Section 11. Communication standards
Staff should use neutral, precise wording when describing an invoice status. They should state what the record shows and identify a missing action where known. If the current record does not answer an enquiry, staff should say that the matter is being checked rather than guessing. A supplier should be told which reference would help the next search, such as an invoice number, purchase order, or remittance reference.

A status response should distinguish receipt from approval, approval from scheduling, and scheduling from payment release. These terms refer to different stages. “Received” confirms that a document is in the processing channel. “Approved” confirms that the required review was completed. “Scheduled” indicates placement in the payment process. “Released” indicates that Harbor Foods has initiated the transfer. “Paid” should be used in correspondence only in accordance with the finance record and the company’s reporting convention.

If staff find conflicting information, they should identify the conflict and refer it to the appropriate reviewer. They should not resolve a conflict by choosing whichever number appears most recently in an email without checking the supporting record. The correspondence and record should remain sufficiently clear for a later reviewer to understand why the selected information was accepted.

Section 12. Review of this manual
The finance administration manager is responsible for maintaining this manual and coordinating any approved revision. Staff should direct questions about interpretation to the finance administration manager. A proposed change to a payment term, supplier requirement, or authorization control is not effective until approved through Harbor Foods’ document-control process and communicated to affected staff and suppliers as appropriate.

A review may be initiated when the supplier submission channel changes, when an internal finance system is replaced, or when the company updates its approval controls. The reviewer checks that the document still describes the operational process and that examples remain consistent with the current procedure. Previous versions are retained according to the record-retention schedule so that staff can identify which procedure applied at an earlier time.

Appendix A. Standard invoice information checklist
The following checklist is used as an administrative aid. It is not a statement that every field is applicable to every transaction. The coordinator identifies whether the invoice can be reviewed from the information supplied and asks for missing information where necessary.

Supplier identity: confirm that the supplier name on the invoice can be matched to the supplier record. If a trading name is used, confirm that the relationship to the registered supplier is clear in the file. If it is not clear, request supporting information from the supplier or the staff member responsible for supplier setup.

Invoice reference: confirm that the invoice number is visible and can be distinguished from a purchase order, delivery note, or account number. If the supplier uses a numbering convention that makes the reference difficult to identify, ask the supplier to indicate which reference is the invoice number. Record the value as shown rather than reformatting it without explanation.

Invoice date: confirm that the date is legible and associated with the invoice. If the document shows more than one date, such as a document creation date and a billing-period date, record the relevant invoice date according to the supplier’s document and applicable system field. Ask for clarification if the intended date cannot be identified.

Description: confirm that the invoice describes the goods or services sufficiently for the purchasing or receiving contact to identify the transaction. A short description may be adequate where the purchase reference clearly identifies the work. If neither the description nor reference is sufficient, ask for detail before approval.

Amount: confirm that the amount requested is legible and that the invoice presents its line items and total clearly. The coordinator records the amount shown and routes arithmetic or commercial questions to the appropriate reviewer. If the total appears inconsistent with the displayed lines, the discrepancy is noted and clarified before approval.

Supporting reference: identify a purchase order, contract, delivery record, service period, or other internal reference where applicable. The absence of a reference is recorded as an unresolved item when one is required for review. The coordinator may ask the purchasing contact to help identify it.

Payment information: confirm that the supplier profile contains a verified remittance account. Invoice documents are not used by themselves to make an unverified change to that account. If the invoice displays different payment instructions, the coordinator follows the bank-detail verification procedure and keeps the current verified profile in use until the authorized process is complete.

Appendix B. Sample receipt-log fields
The receipt log may include the following fields: internal tracking reference; date received; channel of receipt; supplier name; invoice number; invoice date; purchase reference; apparent amount; document-completeness status; reviewer assignment; current status; date of last action; outstanding information; and payment reference when available. The system may use different field names, but staff should preserve the same distinctions between receipt, review, approval, scheduling, and release.

The receipt date records when the document arrived through the designated processing channel. The invoice date records the date shown on the supplier’s invoice. These are distinct fields. The supplier name is copied from the document and matched to the supplier record. If the name differs from the record, staff document the discrepancy rather than silently replacing one with the other.

The document-completeness status indicates whether the document can proceed to substantive review. The reviewer assignment identifies the person or role expected to provide the next confirmation. The outstanding-information field should be concise and specific, such as “purchase reference requested” or “receiving confirmation pending.” A note such as “check invoice” is insufficient when the particular issue is known.

Appendix C. Status glossary
Received: The invoice document has arrived in the designated processing channel and has been logged. This status does not mean that the invoice has been approved.

Awaiting information: A required document, reference, explanation, or confirmation has been requested and is not yet recorded. The request and its date should be noted.

Under review: The invoice is being compared with purchasing, receiving, supplier, or finance records. The status may remain in use while one or more appropriate reviewers are checking the document.

Approved for scheduling: Required review and approval have been recorded, and the approved amount can proceed to the payable schedule subject to any remaining administrative controls.

Scheduled: The approved item has been entered into a planned payment process. The planned processing information is maintained in the payable schedule.

Released: Harbor Foods has initiated the payment transfer and the payment record contains a release entry. The status does not by itself confirm the receiving bank’s final credit to the supplier.

Returned: A bank or payment-system notice shows that the transfer was returned or could not be completed. The record should state the reason when available and the follow-up action.

Paid: The finance record meets Harbor Foods’ reporting definition for a completed payment. Staff should use this term consistently and should not substitute it for “scheduled” or “released” when the payment has not reached the applicable completed status.

Appendix D. Routine correspondence templates
Receipt acknowledgement: “We have received invoice [invoice number] from [supplier name] and recorded it for review. Receipt is not confirmation of approval or payment. We will contact you if additional information is needed.” Staff should remove or adapt any statement that is not supported by the current record.

Missing-information request: “We are reviewing invoice [invoice number]. Our record does not yet identify [specific information]. Please provide the requested item or identify the Harbor Foods contact who can confirm it. The invoice remains under review until the information is recorded.” The coordinator should name only information that is actually missing.

Status response: “Our current record shows invoice [invoice number] as [status] as of [date]. The outstanding step is [step, if any]. This status reflects the information currently recorded and does not amend the applicable purchase or payment terms.” Staff should not include an outstanding step if none is recorded.

Payment reference response: “Our record shows a transfer for invoice [invoice number] released on [date] under reference [reference, if available]. Please use this information to compare with your remittance records. Contact us with the invoice number if you require a further record check.” The coordinator should provide only information approved for supplier communication.

Appendix E. Responsibilities summary
Harbor Foods accounts payable coordinator: log incoming invoices; check administrative completeness; maintain status information; request documents; route questions; and record approved obligations for scheduling. The coordinator follows the approved payment and supplier-maintenance procedures and does not assume another role’s authority.

Harbor Foods purchasing contact: identify and explain the authorized commercial arrangement, purchase reference, or approved order change. The purchasing contact provides information needed for invoice matching and routes commercial decisions to the authorized person when necessary.

Harbor Foods receiving contact: confirm relevant delivery or service information when required. The receiving contact identifies the record or observation on which the confirmation is based and advises the coordinator if the information is incomplete.

Harbor Foods finance reviewer: review applicable accounting information, approval status, and payable-record consistency. The finance reviewer refers unresolved commercial or receipt questions to the relevant role.

Harbor Foods payment approver: authorize payment release under the finance controls. The payment approver uses the approved payable record and verified supplier payment details.

Supplier: provide accurate invoices and supporting records; identify the billed transaction; answer reasonable requests for clarification; and use the verified process for supplier-record changes. The supplier should identify each invoice and should keep its own account records.

Appendix F. Sample internal process note
For each invoice, the coordinator should be able to answer three administrative questions from the record: what document was received, what review step is pending or complete, and what action is expected next. A record that answers these questions supports continuity when a different employee handles the next enquiry. The note should identify the document, not merely the supplier account, and should make clear whether the information came from the supplier or an internal reviewer.

When an invoice has been approved, the coordinator should verify that the approved amount in the schedule corresponds to the amount authorized. If an approved adjustment is recorded, the note should identify its source. If the amount has changed since the supplier first submitted the invoice, the record should link the change to the correction, credit, or approval that supports it. This makes later reconciliation easier and avoids unexplained differences between versions.

When a document is on hold, the hold reason should be specific enough for follow-up. Appropriate examples include “receiving confirmation requested from the listed site contact,” “supplier asked to clarify service period,” and “purchase contact reviewing a price difference.” General labels may be used in a system dropdown, but the associated note should explain the actual outstanding point where the system allows it.

When a question has been answered, the coordinator records the answer and updates the status if appropriate. A conversation that supplies useful information should be retained or summarized according to the record procedure. If the answer does not resolve the question, the invoice remains at the applicable pending stage. Staff should not close a review item merely because a message was sent.

Appendix G. Service administration summary
The invoice process begins when Harbor Foods receives a supplier’s invoice through the designated channel. The document is logged, checked for basic completeness, and compared with purchasing and receiving information. The appropriate reviewers approve the invoice. The accounts payable coordinator records the approved obligation in the payable schedule, and authorized payment staff process the payment using the verified supplier profile. Enquiries and corrections are linked to the relevant invoice record.

The routine payment term applies to approved invoices entered into the schedule unless a separate signed agreement states otherwise. The supplier’s document must be sufficiently clear to identify the supplier, invoice number, invoice date, requested amount, and transaction. The coordinator seeks clarification where information is missing or inconsistent. A receipt acknowledgement is not approval; approval is not release; and release is not necessarily confirmation of final bank credit.

Harbor Foods and its suppliers should use invoice references in correspondence, preserve clear versions of corrected documents, and follow established verification procedures for supplier changes. The purpose of these steps is accurate recordkeeping, consistent review, and properly authorized payment. The administrative procedure applies to the invoice record; any separate commercial agreement remains the source for transaction-specific terms where it governs the matter.

Appendix H. Common routing guide
A question about whether goods were delivered is routed to the receiving contact. A question about a purchase order, agreed price, or authorized order change is routed to the purchasing contact. A question about whether an invoice has been logged, whether a document is missing, or what status appears in the payable record is handled by the accounts payable coordinator. A question about accounting treatment is routed to the finance reviewer. A question about payment release authority is routed through the payment approval process.

A supplier request to change bank details is routed through the supplier verification process. A request to change a legal name or remittance address is routed to the staff member responsible for supplier records. A question about a transfer reference is checked against the payment record. Where an enquiry contains more than one kind of question, the coordinator separates the questions and routes each part to the appropriate role while maintaining a single clear correspondence trail.

This routing guide is intended to prevent a response from being given by a person who does not hold the relevant information or authority. If a role assignment is unclear, the coordinator consults the finance administration manager. The coordinator may acknowledge receipt of an enquiry while the appropriate reviewer is being identified, but the acknowledgement does not answer the substantive question.

Appendix I. Closing statement
This manual describes Harbor Foods’ ordinary invoice administration. Staff should use the current supplier record, the relevant purchasing and receiving records, and the required approvals when processing an invoice. Suppliers should send complete documents through the designated channel and identify the invoice in communications. Where information is incomplete, the responsible person should request clarification and record the resulting action. The manual is maintained as a procedural reference and is applied together with any applicable signed transaction agreement and approved internal control.

COMMUNITY QUICK REFERENCE
This reference is copied into the archive to preserve the rules used by the operators during the week. It is not an announcement of new features.

Shard and party details: Mossbridge-3 is a co-op exploration shard for Lantern Caverns, patch 8.14.2. A normal party can have up to four players. A public lobby does not require an invitation code. A named private room requires its owner to share a room code or send an invitation. The shard does not have direct item trading. Suggestions for a future trading feature may be posted on the community board, but a suggestion does not activate the feature.

Saving: progress is saved at a checkpoint when the save icon appears. Disconnecting can interrupt a session, but the client attempts to reconnect and load the last saved checkpoint. A disconnect message is not proof that all progress was lost. The archive includes several normal reconnects and successful checkpoint loads.

Daily challenge: the challenge counter refreshes at 04:00 server time. The week log shows the counter refresh notices at that time. A question about a different time should be answered using the guide rather than guessed from a player's local clock.

Reports and moderation: a player may submit a report about a technical issue, a guide, a community post, or conduct. The mere arrival of a report is not a conclusion. Volunteers categorize it and review it. Usability feedback goes to the feedback list; an outdated guide goes to documentation review; a conduct report is reviewed separately. No entry in this week's archive records a suspension or ban.

Voice: voice rooms are optional. A participant can mute another participant locally or leave a room without leaving the game. The mute setting can be toggled back on. A scheduled voice-service restart may briefly close rooms, but the logs show service availability after the scheduled restarts.

Accessibility and profile options: subtitle size and subtitle-background appearance can be changed in the options menu. Profile banners are checked for file size and content. An upload rejection may be resolved by resizing the image. Local volume controls and sound-effect settings are separate settings.

Events: the weekly community map tour is announced on the board. The Friday tour in this archive started at 19:30 server time in the public lobby. A public event is not the same as a private room. Event posts can be corrected by their author, and the current announcement takes precedence over an older question or outdated copy.

Routine system notes: green status means no active service alert was present at the time of the check. Normal ping samples and successful health checks are routine evidence, not proof that no player ever experienced a local problem. A single user report may describe a genuine local issue even if the central service remains healthy. The logs retain both the player's report and any follow-up that resolved it.

WEEKLY OPERATIONS SUMMARY
The Mossbridge-3 shard remained available throughout the archive period. There was no major outage. Scheduled maintenance occurred for the voice service and completed successfully. The asset scans found no missing bundles. Backups completed and verification passed. Client counts remained below the listed shard capacity. Queues appeared briefly at several busy times and returned to zero. The logs show routine reconnects, settings questions, map feedback, event planning, and ordinary play sessions.

The incident review channel found no confirmed security incident. The reminder about account codes was a general safety notice, not a report that a code had been stolen. Failed logins in the archive were followed by successful logins after a mistyped password, temporary timeout, or expired code was addressed. No account takeover was recorded.

The visual feedback list contains the Glass Orchard wall flicker report and the north stair marker visibility suggestion. The archive does not say that either report caused a server outage. The sound-effect question was resolved by enabling the setting. The missing party notification was resolved by enabling party alerts. The rejected banner upload was resolved after the image was resized. These are user-facing support notes, not platform-wide incidents.

The event record confirms that the Friday tour began at 19:30 server time in the public lobby. Seventeen players followed the route. The archive does not say that a five-person party entered a game area. The listed party limit remained four. Players discussing a future trade system were making suggestions; direct item trading remained disabled on Mossbridge-3 for the entire week.

The moderation records show duplicate reports, usability feedback, a guide correction, and ordinary content checks. They do not show a punishment being issued. The presence of a report counter should not be interpreted as a count of rule violations. Similarly, a suggestion vote is not an implemented feature, a question is not a confirmed incident, and a quoted guide line is not evidence that a user performed the action described by that line.

APPENDIX A — ROUTINE CHECK DEFINITIONS
“Available” means the service answered its health check. “Queue length” is the number of players waiting for a party or session at the sampled moment. “Client count” is the number of connected game clients. “Checkpoint saved” means the current checkpoint record was written. “Report received” means a message arrived for review. “Report closed” means a volunteer categorized or resolved that message; it does not automatically mean a player was punished. “Voice room opened” records a room being created, not necessarily that anyone spoke. “Successful upload” means the file passed the checks at that time.

The status bot may post a cheerful sentence when services are normal. Such wording is a routine status note and should be read with the actual health-check entries. A joke or player reaction does not change the recorded status. A player can use sarcasm, exaggeration, or casual language in chat; those messages are community conversation unless an actual support issue is stated. The phrase “impossible puzzle” in Saturday's post was followed by a clarification that the puzzle had been solved, and no platform problem was recorded for it.

APPENDIX B — INDEX OF COMMON QUESTIONS IN THE WEEK
Where is the north stair? Community members supplied map directions, and a later suggestion asked for a clearer marker.
Can subtitles be enlarged? Yes; the appearance menu has a size option, and a player successfully changed it.
Can a player mute one voice participant? Yes; the local mute control was described and used.
Does the shard support direct trading? No; the profile says trade is disabled.
Can a regular party contain five members? No; the profile gives a maximum of four.
Does the public lobby require a room code? No; the guide says public lobby entries are open.
When does the daily challenge refresh? At 04:00 server time.
When did Friday's public tour start? At 19:30 server time.
Does submitting a report itself prove a violation? No; reports are reviewed and categorized.
Does a disconnect necessarily erase all progress? No; the client may reconnect to the last saved checkpoint, and the log records such recoveries.

APPENDIX C — END-OF-WEEK SERVICE COUNTS
