FAQ excerpt: Sorting out appointment changes without making a meal of it

People ask whether moving a visit means they have cancelled it, and, honestly, the calendar makes that look more dramatic than it is. If you ask the desk to move your appointment to another available time, the original slot is released but the appointment remains active under the new time. A cancellation is different: you have to say you do not want the visit at all, and the desk records it as cancelled. Please don’t assume that a message saying “I can’t do Tuesday” is enough to cancel; staff will ask whether you want to reschedule.

For this FAQ, a request counts as a cancellation only when the patient explicitly says they no longer want the appointment, not when they decline one proposed time or ask for a different one. If a patient says, “I do not want to cancel; I just need Thursday instead,” record a reschedule. We know the wording can feel a bit circular, but the distinction matters when reminders go out.

A separate question is whether the visit is confirmed. A visit is confirmed when the patient or authorized contact replies affirmatively to the offered time. If the person says they have not confirmed, staff must leave it pending. An unanswered reminder is not a confirmation, and a note that says “no response yet” is not a sneaky yes. The system may still display the reserved time while pending, which is why people sometimes think it has been settled.

Finally, an appointment is marked as a telehealth visit only if the booking record explicitly says video or telephone. A patient asking whether video is available does not make the visit telehealth. That’s the whole thing; easy to mix up when reading a busy schedule, but staff should follow what the record actually says rather than guessing from a question or a tentative message.

FAQ excerpt: A few less obvious bits about reminders

The reminder service is useful, but it isn’t a mind reader, so please don’t treat a message sent by the service as proof that a patient agreed to anything. A reminder can be generated while an appointment is still pending. The booking becomes confirmed only after the patient replies yes, or an authorized contact accepts on the patient’s behalf. A reply saying “I have not agreed to this time” leaves the booking unconfirmed even if the reminder screen turns green for some unrelated reason.

Rescheduling has its own little wrinkle. If someone says, “I don’t want to cancel, but I need a different day,” staff should keep the visit active while searching for a new slot. If a new time is not available right away, the record may say “reschedule requested,” not “cancelled.” A patient who says they no longer want care is different; staff should ask once to make sure the request is intentional, then record the cancellation if confirmed. Don’t infer that from “Tuesday won’t work.”

We also get questions about reminder preferences. A patient can ask not to receive text reminders without asking to stop all reminders. The preference is specifically about text messages unless the patient says they do not want reminders by any channel. If they say “Please don’t text me; email is fine,” email reminders remain allowed. This is one of those details that seems obvious until someone reads only the first half of a note.

For chart status, “not completed” means the visit has not yet taken place, or the clinician has not marked it done; it is not a synonym for cancelled. Likewise, “not cancelled” does not mean confirmed. These are separate fields, and a record can be active but still awaiting the patient’s answer. Staff should preserve those distinctions even when the schedule is crowded and someone is asking for a quick answer at the desk.

People Operations — Quarterly staffing meeting notes
Date: 14 May
Chair: Wanjiru Mensah
Recorder: People Operations

The meeting reviewed the process for temporary schedule adjustments, the status of several requests, and the wording to be used in the revised manager guide. Attendees were reminded that a request is not an approval and that informal coverage arrangements do not amend an employee’s recorded schedule. The group agreed to keep the existing distinction between a manager’s acknowledgement and a formal authorization by People Operations.

Policy excerpt read aloud: “A temporary schedule adjustment is authorized only when People Operations records an approval in the case register. A manager may propose an adjustment but cannot authorize it. An entry marked ‘not declined’ is not, by itself, an approval; the register must say approved.” Wanjiru asked that the phrase “not declined” be retained because staff had repeatedly treated it as equivalent to approval. The group confirmed that the phrase was intended to describe an unresolved or non-rejected request, not to grant permission.

Case review, item 17: A laboratory coordinator asked to shift the start of her Thursday shift from 8:00 to 9:00 for four weeks. Her supervisor replied, “I have no objection to discussing this, and I am not opposed to a temporary trial if People Operations signs off.” The coordinator then wrote, “Thanks, I understand that you are not refusing the proposal.” The supervisor entered “not declined” in the local team tracker. The People Operations register, checked during the meeting, showed the case as “awaiting review”; there was no approval entry. The schedule therefore remained unchanged. No one disputed that the request had been made, but the group explicitly separated the existence of a request from its authorization.

Case review, item 18: A different employee had asked whether a shift change might be possible later in the summer. The manager’s note said, “No change requested for the current roster; do not treat this inquiry as a submitted request.” The register contained no case. The meeting agreed not to infer an active request from a hypothetical question about a future possibility. The guide should say that a request must identify a proposed change and a period, but this item was not treated as a current application.

The team also reviewed status labels in the shared tracker. “Not closed” means that the case has not been closed; it does not mean that the request was accepted, rejected, or fully assessed. “No objection recorded” means only that no objection appears in the manager’s comments. Neither label substitutes for the register’s decision field. Wanjiru noted that the combination of a positive-sounding phrase and a missing decision had led to confusion in two earlier audits. The revised guide will state the status labels in full rather than relying on shorthand.

Administrative follow-up: People Operations will publish a one-page explanation of the register fields. Managers will be asked to avoid writing “approved unless someone objects,” because silence is not approval under the quoted rule. The register administrator will retain the date and author of every formal decision. The group declined to make retroactive entries based on recollections of hallway conversations; if a decision was not recorded, the administrator must refer it for review rather than infer that it occurred.

The meeting closed with a reminder that an employee may still submit a request while the status is pending. A pending request is not an authorized schedule change, and a manager’s lack of refusal does not change that outcome. No general policy change was adopted at this meeting.

The monthly maximum is payable when eligible costs meet or exceed the cap; for example, a 258-credit eligible total is capped.

No listed amount is supported; for example, the policy provides no applicable amount.

People Operations — meeting record and action register
Meeting date: 22 November
Subject: Access badges during extended absences
Chair: Tomasz Sorensen
Recorder: Workplace Services

The meeting was convened to clarify when a staff access badge must be suspended during a leave of absence. The attendees reviewed the current access policy and recent questions from team administrators. The policy excerpt circulated in advance states: “A badge is suspended when an employee begins an approved absence lasting more than ten consecutive calendar days, unless the absence is designated as an approved remote-work period. The threshold is more than ten days, not ten days or more. A manager’s reassurance that access is unnecessary does not itself create a remote-work designation.” The policy administrator confirmed that the quoted text is the current version.

The group first reviewed the calendar-day count method. The first day of the approved absence counts as day one. Weekends and holidays are included. A separate medical appointment or a non-working day does not pause the count unless the case system records a return to active work. The group rejected a proposal to count only scheduled workdays because that would contradict the written rule. The ten-day threshold and the exception must both be checked before the access status is changed.

Case Alpha: The case register shows an approved absence beginning 2 October and an approved return to active work on 12 October. The record therefore covers 2–11 October as absence days: 2 October is day one and 11 October is day ten. A team note says, “The badge need not be suspended, since the employee was not away for more than ten days.” The register has no remote-work designation. The access administrator confirmed that the note is consistent with the threshold: an absence of exactly ten consecutive days does not exceed ten days. No badge suspension was entered for this case.

Case Beta: Another register entry shows an approved absence beginning 3 October, with return to active work recorded for 14 October. The absence days are 3–13 October inclusive: 3 October is day one and 13 October is day eleven. The employee worked remotely for two days during the period, but the case system does not designate the period as approved remote work. The manager wrote, “We did not need to suspend access because the employee could connect from home.” The group noted that the policy exception depends on an approved remote-work designation, not on informal ability to connect. The badge remained active by mistake and was referred for correction.

Case Gamma: A third employee had an absence period longer than ten days, but the register explicitly marks the entire period as an approved remote-work period. The badge was not suspended. The chair emphasized that this is the stated exception, rather than evidence that every extended absence can remain active. The entry contains both the approval and the remote-work designation; no inference from a manager’s comment is needed.

During discussion, someone proposed treating the phrase “not ineligible for continued access” as meaning that access was automatically permitted. The policy administrator clarified that this wording only indicates the absence of a stated disqualification; the actual threshold and exception still control. Likewise, a note saying “no suspension request received” does not establish that suspension is unnecessary. Access decisions are generated from the recorded absence dates and designation fields, not from whether a supervisor objects.

Action register: Workplace Services will correct the Beta badge record after confirming the dates and notify the manager. The administrator will leave Alpha unchanged and retain the day-count calculation in the audit entry. Gamma will remain active under the approved remote-work exception. No general exception was adopted. The meeting also directed staff to stop using “not away long enough” without listing the dates, because that shorthand has produced inconsistent interpretations. The minutes do not alter the policy or authorize retroactive remote-work designations.

questions.instruction: A badge suspension is required for an absence longer than ten days without approved remote work. Does Case Beta meet that rule?
questions.notes: 3–13 October inclusive is 11 days; no approved remote-work designation exists.

questions.instruction: A badge remains active under an exception only for an approved remote-work period. Which cases qualify for that exception?

candidates.description: A ten-day absence does not exceed the threshold; for example, 2–11 October counts as ten days.
A period longer than ten days is formally designated approved remote work; for example, the case register records that designation.
A period longer than ten days has an approved remote-work designation; for example, the register explicitly marks the whole period.
No case qualifies for the exception; for example, no approved remote-work period is recorded.

questions.notes: Only Gamma has the approved remote-work designation. Alpha is exactly ten days; Beta’s remote work was not formally designated.

Harbor Studio — Human Resources Operations Handbook and Implementation Record
Document owner: People Operations
Status: Approved for internal use
Effective date: 1 April 2025
Purpose: This document records the routine procedures used by Harbor Studio staff and managers for attendance, leave, workplace access, staff records, equipment, training, and employee support. It is intended to make ordinary administrative decisions consistent across departments. It does not replace an individual employment agreement. Where an individual agreement gives a more specific entitlement, People Operations must refer the matter to the appropriate HR lead rather than assume that this handbook changes that agreement.

Section 1. General administration

Harbor Studio maintains one central People Operations desk. The desk receives ordinary questions about schedules, leave forms, contact details, required training, equipment requests, and access badges. Staff may submit a request in person, by internal email, or through the company’s staff portal. A request is not considered approved merely because it has been submitted. Approval is recorded in the relevant portal field or in a written message from the assigned manager. Staff should retain the confirmation for their own records.

The People Operations desk is staffed on business days from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The desk may acknowledge a request outside those hours, but the acknowledgment does not mean that a review has occurred. Urgent building-safety concerns should be reported to the facilities contact listed on the staff portal. Urgent medical concerns should be handled through the company’s emergency procedure, not through an ordinary leave form. Routine questions should include the employee’s department and a brief description of the request so that the desk can route it correctly.

Managers are responsible for reviewing routine requests from their direct reports. People Operations maintains the records and advises on the procedure, but it does not silently approve a manager’s decision. When a manager is unavailable, the manager’s designated acting supervisor may review a request. Staff should not assume that a colleague’s informal opinion is an approval. If a record appears incomplete, the employee or manager should ask the desk to correct it rather than creating a second, conflicting record.

The handbook uses the phrase “business day” to mean Monday through Friday, excluding a Harbor Studio closure shown on the official calendar. A calendar day is any day on the calendar, including weekends and closures. Unless a section expressly states otherwise, deadlines in routine forms are calendar-day deadlines. Dates and times in the portal use the local time zone shown in the employee’s profile. If an employee is traveling, the profile time zone remains the time reference for submitting a request.

Section 2. Attendance and schedule records

Employees should record their scheduled work hours using the timekeeping procedure assigned to their team. A time entry should reflect the hours actually worked, not the hours an employee intended to work. If an employee makes an entry error, the employee should submit a correction request and explain the difference. A manager reviews the correction. The original entry is preserved in the audit record, and the corrected entry is displayed with its approval status.

A missed time entry does not, by itself, mean that an employee was absent. Managers should check the team calendar, work record, and any message from the employee before making an attendance determination. Conversely, a calendar entry that says “working” does not by itself establish that work was performed. Attendance records are administrative evidence and should be interpreted with the relevant context. Staff should not ask a coworker to enter hours on their behalf unless the team’s documented contingency procedure applies.

For a planned schedule change, an employee should notify the manager before the changed schedule begins whenever practicable. The manager records whether the change is approved, declined, or awaiting information. If an employee is unable to provide advance notice, the employee should notify the manager as soon as reasonably possible. The employee may use the normal contact method for the team. A later explanation can complete a record, but it does not rewrite the time at which the initial notice was sent.

Employees working remotely remain responsible for recording working time under their team’s ordinary procedure. A remote-work location must be approved separately if the employee’s agreement or team procedure requires approval. An employee’s presence at a location on a calendar or a travel itinerary does not itself constitute approval to work from that location. Managers should direct uncertainty about an arrangement to People Operations instead of making assumptions based on a prior arrangement for another employee.

Section 3. Leave requests

All planned leave requests should be entered in the staff portal. The request should identify the requested dates and the relevant leave category. The employee should submit the request to the direct manager for review. The manager records a decision in the portal. People Operations may assist with a question about the form or the employee’s available balance, but the desk does not approve a request on the manager’s behalf.

For an unexpected absence, the employee should notify the manager using the team’s designated contact method as soon as practicable. The employee should then complete any required record when able to do so. A message saying that an employee may be absent if a condition arises is not a report that the employee is absent. Similarly, a statement that an employee would have taken leave under different circumstances does not create a leave request. The actual request and the actual dates should be recorded.

Managers should review requests consistently and should not treat the submission of a request as proof that it has been approved. If the manager needs additional information, the manager should identify what is needed and leave the request marked as pending. An employee should not book a nonrefundable trip on the assumption that a pending request will be approved. If the requested dates change, the employee should amend the existing request where possible, rather than submit multiple copies without explanation.

The leave balance displayed in the portal is an administrative summary. Employees who believe that the balance is incorrect should ask People Operations to review the record. A balance inquiry does not itself request leave. A manager should not infer an employee’s intended dates from a balance inquiry or from a discussion about a future possibility. The approved dates are those recorded in the decision field, unless a later correction is documented.

Section 4. Workplace access and facilities

Employees receive a building access badge after the required identity and onboarding checks have been completed. The badge is assigned to one employee and must not be lent to another person. A visitor should be checked in under the visitor procedure. An employee who loses a badge should notify Facilities promptly so that access can be reviewed. The badge record identifies the badge assigned; it does not, on its own, prove that the employee entered the building on a particular day.

The main office has shared meeting rooms, quiet rooms, and individual work areas. Room reservations should be made through the shared calendar. A reservation indicates that a room has been requested for a time; it does not guarantee access if the room is unavailable for a safety or maintenance reason. When a reservation is cancelled, the person who made it should update the calendar so that other staff can use the room. The facilities team may correct a calendar entry to reflect a closure.

Employees should report hazards, broken equipment, and access problems through the facilities form. The form asks for the location, a concise description, and whether the issue presents an immediate safety concern. A facilities acknowledgment means that the report was received. It does not necessarily mean that repairs are complete. Facilities records the work status separately. Staff should avoid placing sensitive employee information in a general facilities report unless it is necessary to describe the issue.

Harbor Studio’s office does not have a staffed reception desk outside the hours listed on the portal. Employees should not promise a visitor that an after-hours entry will be available unless an authorized contact has confirmed the arrangement. If a visitor arrives without a booking, the employee responsible for the visit should follow the current visitor procedure. A message to a colleague asking whether a visitor might arrive is not itself a visitor registration.

Section 5. Staff records and privacy

People Operations maintains employment records in the restricted staff system. Employees may ask to review information about their own record through the designated process. Managers may access information required for their management responsibilities, subject to the access controls assigned to their roles. A manager should not circulate an employee’s private record to a team mailing list merely because the manager has access to it.

A request to update a contact detail should specify the new detail and the date on which it should take effect. People Operations may ask the employee to confirm the change through the secure portal. A draft message containing a proposed address is not necessarily a completed update. Staff should report an incorrect record rather than assume that a prior conversation changed the system. The record history shows the submitted change and the time it was verified.

The company retains routine administrative records according to its retention schedule. Staff should not make informal copies of restricted records for convenience. If a record is needed for a documented business purpose, the employee should use the approved access process. A record’s presence in an archive does not mean that it is currently approved for broad access. When a message includes a forwarded excerpt from an older exchange, the sender and context of the excerpt should be considered before attributing a request to the person who forwarded it.

Staff should use the internal reporting channel for a concern about workplace conduct. The report should describe what the reporting employee observed or experienced and should distinguish direct observations from information received from another person. A report may be submitted even if the employee is uncertain about the appropriate category. People Operations will route it for review. The existence of a report does not establish that every claim in it has been confirmed.

Section 6. Equipment and purchasing

Routine equipment requests are entered in the staff portal and routed to the employee’s manager. The request should state the item, the work need, and whether the item is replacing equipment that is no longer serviceable. The manager records approval or decline. Purchasing may then check stock and arrange the order. A request marked “submitted” is not an order confirmation. The purchase record is updated when Purchasing confirms the order.

Employees should return company equipment when a manager or People Operations asks for it, or when the employment relationship ends, following the return instructions provided. If equipment is damaged, the employee should report the damage promptly and describe what happened. The report should not assign blame without evidence. The equipment team determines whether repair or replacement is appropriate. A device listed in the equipment register is assigned to the named employee, but the register may require updating after a transfer or approved reassignment.

Purchasing requests should not be divided into multiple entries merely to avoid a review step. If several items support one work need, the employee should list them together and explain the request. The system may show estimates, quotations, and final costs in separate fields. An estimate is not a final charge. The approver should use the amount and status identified in the applicable field rather than adding unrelated figures from another request.

Section 7. Training and internal communications

Required training is assigned through the learning portal. An employee should complete the assigned module and confirm completion using the portal’s completion control. Opening a module does not count as completion. A manager may view the completion status for the manager’s team. People Operations may correct a record when a technical issue prevented a completed course from appearing properly, after confirming the relevant evidence.

Internal communications should be clear about whether a statement is an instruction, a request, a draft, or a quotation from another person. A line included in a forwarded message does not automatically become the forwarding employee’s instruction or position. Employees should preserve enough context to show who wrote the original message and what response, if any, followed it. If a communication includes a proposed policy change, staff should not treat it as effective until the authorized owner has approved and published it.

Team announcements should use the current approved templates where available. A draft announcement may contain placeholder dates or example names. The author should remove placeholders before sending a final notice. Recipients who spot an apparent error should ask the sender to verify it. The company does not infer an employee’s consent to a change merely because the employee received or opened an announcement.

Section 8. Employee support and escalation

Employees may contact their manager, People Operations, or the relevant specialist team when they need assistance. The correct contact depends on the subject of the request. People Operations can explain routine HR steps, but it does not provide facilities repairs, purchase approvals, or emergency response. The staff portal lists the appropriate contact points and the ordinary response expectations.

If an employee disagrees with a routine decision, the employee may ask the decision-maker to explain the recorded outcome or may request review through the stated escalation route. The employee should identify the decision and provide any relevant information not previously considered. An escalation request does not automatically suspend a decision or change its status. The reviewer records the outcome and the reason for any change.

Managers should handle employee questions respectfully and maintain a factual record of decisions. A manager should not promise an outcome that another authorized person must approve. Where a question concerns a policy exception, the manager should identify the exception requested and send it to the policy owner. Until an exception is approved in writing, the ordinary procedure remains in effect. A past exception for a different person does not establish that the same exception applies to every later request.

Section 9. Roles and responsibility summary

The employee submits accurate information and follows the applicable request procedure. The direct manager reviews the employee’s routine request and records a decision where manager approval is required. People Operations maintains HR records, advises on HR procedures, and routes matters that require specialist review. Facilities handles building access and workplace maintenance. Purchasing handles confirmed orders after the required approval. The learning portal records training status. These responsibilities are separate even when one matter involves more than one team.

A person who receives a forwarded message should distinguish the original writer from the person forwarding it. The forwarding employee may be asking for advice, providing background, or requesting action; the original message may have been written by someone else. The record should make clear whose request is being reviewed. The same principle applies to a quoted policy excerpt: the excerpt describes the policy text, not necessarily the current status of the particular request being discussed.

Section 10. Record correction and audit trail

When an employee or manager identifies an administrative error, the person should submit a correction request that identifies the field, the existing entry, and the proposed correction. The correction should include a concise reason. The record owner reviews the request and either makes the correction or explains why the existing record remains. The system retains an audit trail so that later reviewers can distinguish an original entry from an approved correction.

A correction does not erase the fact that an earlier entry was made. For example, correcting a mistaken schedule field changes the current displayed information after approval, while the audit history still shows the original entry and correction time. Staff should not interpret the existence of an earlier incorrect entry as proof that the corrected information is also wrong. Where two records conflict, the responsible owner should identify which record is authoritative for the question at hand.

The audit trail is intended to support accountability and continuity. It is not a substitute for a clear explanation. A reviewer should read the relevant entry, any linked decision, and the correction history. A notification that a record was changed indicates that an update occurred; the reviewer should inspect the updated field to understand what changed. A notification that an update was requested does not prove the requested change was approved.

Section 11. Calendar and meeting practices

Employees should use the shared calendar to record work-related meetings and planned absences that have been approved. Calendar entries should be concise and should not expose private information unnecessarily. A tentative entry should be marked as tentative. A meeting invitation is not evidence that the invited person accepted. The calendar’s response field records acceptance, decline, or no response.

If a meeting organizer changes the time, the organizer should send an updated invitation. A message proposing a time does not change an existing appointment until the organizer updates the invitation or the participants clearly confirm an alternative. If the meeting is cancelled, the organizer should mark it cancelled so that recipients do not rely on an outdated entry. A cancelled meeting does not cancel a separate appointment unless the record expressly links the two.

Teams should avoid using calendar labels as substitutes for formal HR records. A calendar note such as “appointment,” “remote,” or “out” may provide context, but any required leave or schedule approval must also be recorded through the applicable procedure. Managers should avoid drawing a conclusion from a calendar label alone when the employee’s formal record says something different. If the mismatch matters, the manager should request clarification and allow the record owner to resolve it.

Section 12. Onboarding and departure administration

During onboarding, People Operations assigns the required forms and identifies the tasks that must be completed before access is granted. The employee should complete each required task and report any technical obstacle. A welcome message is not a substitute for completion of a required form. The manager confirms the employee’s role, team contact, and ordinary reporting arrangements. Facilities handles the badge after the stated checks are complete.

When an employee changes teams, the former and new managers should coordinate the transfer of work responsibilities. People Operations updates the staff record after receiving the approved change. Access should be reviewed according to the new role. The employee should not assume that every prior permission remains appropriate, nor that every prior permission has been removed, without checking the access record.

For a planned departure, the manager and employee should follow the departure checklist. The checklist identifies equipment return, access review, record handoff, and final administrative steps. A manager may assign work handoff tasks, but should not ask the departing employee to disclose personal account credentials. People Operations records the relevant employment dates in the staff system. A draft departure date in a planning document is not final until the authorized record has been confirmed.

Section 13. Respectful workplace procedure

Harbor Studio expects staff to communicate respectfully and to raise concerns through an appropriate channel. A person who receives a concern should listen, record the essential facts, and explain the next procedural step without promising a particular finding. If immediate safety is involved, the person should use the emergency or safety procedure. Other concerns should be routed to People Operations or the designated reviewer.

A concern may describe conduct that is disputed, incomplete, or reported secondhand. The reviewer should identify the source of each statement and seek relevant information before reaching a conclusion. A preliminary note is not a final finding. A person named in a report should be given the appropriate process under the applicable procedure. Staff should not retaliate against a person for raising a concern in good faith or for participating in a review.

Where a concern involves a manager, the employee may use the alternate contact listed in the staff portal. If an employee is unsure which route applies, People Operations can direct the employee to the right channel. Sending a concern to the wrong inbox does not make the concern invalid; the recipient should route it appropriately and preserve the date it was received. The recipient should avoid forwarding sensitive details to people who do not need them.

Section 14. Internal forms and status labels

The staff portal uses a limited set of status labels. “Draft” means that the form has not been submitted. “Submitted” means that the form has been sent for review. “Pending” means that review is not complete or that additional information is needed. “Approved” means that the authorized reviewer recorded approval. “Declined” means that the authorized reviewer recorded a negative decision. “Closed” means that the administrative workflow has ended; it does not necessarily mean that the request was approved.

Users should read the status together with the decision field and any reviewer comment. A submitted form may be awaiting review. A pending form may be awaiting the employee, manager, or another owner. A closed form may have been completed, withdrawn, or declined, depending on its recorded outcome. If the status and decision field appear inconsistent, staff should contact the record owner rather than select the more favorable interpretation.

The portal may send automatic notifications when a status changes. Notifications are informational and may arrive after the change has already occurred. The current portal record is the authoritative source for the workflow status. A saved screenshot or printed copy can help the employee keep track of a request, but it does not override a later corrected record. The record owner should explain any material change that affects the employee’s understanding of the outcome.

Section 15. Routine review calendar

People Operations reviews this handbook periodically and may issue a revision when an administrative procedure changes. The document owner identifies the revision date and summarizes material changes in the change log. A proposed edit in a working draft does not modify the approved handbook. Managers should refer staff to the published version rather than circulate an unapproved copy. If a staff member finds two published copies with different wording, the staff member should report the discrepancy to People Operations.

A revision does not automatically change an individual’s existing record. For example, a procedural change may alter how future requests are submitted while leaving an already recorded decision intact. If a revision is intended to affect pending requests, the change notice should say so and identify the effective date. Staff should not infer a retroactive change from a general announcement that does not state one.

The document owner maintains the revision log and archives prior approved versions. Archived versions are retained to clarify what wording applied at an earlier time. Staff should use the current approved version for a current question unless the question specifically concerns an earlier decision. In that case, the relevant date and applicable version should be identified before a conclusion is recorded.

Section 16. Department-specific notes

Each department may maintain a local guide for practical matters such as team communication channels, routine meeting cadence, and equipment preferences. A local guide must not contradict an approved company-wide procedure. The department manager is responsible for keeping the local guide current. People Operations can review a proposed local procedure when the proposal affects employee records, leave, attendance, or another HR process.

A local custom is not automatically a policy exception. If a department has routinely handled a matter in a particular way, the manager should still check whether the practice is consistent with the current handbook. Staff who encounter inconsistent instructions should ask the manager or People Operations to clarify the controlling procedure. The clarification should be recorded where it is likely to affect later decisions.

Section 17. Employee questions and response records

Employees should include enough information for the recipient to understand the question, but should avoid sending unnecessary personal details. The recipient should acknowledge receipt when appropriate and state whether the matter is being answered, referred, or held pending more information. An acknowledgment should not be phrased as a final decision unless the recipient is authorized to make that decision and has completed the review.

If a question is referred to another team, the referring person should identify the destination where practical. The employee may follow up if no response arrives within the ordinary service period shown on the portal. Follow-up messages should refer to the existing request number so that staff can locate the record. A repeated question does not create a second approval or cancel the first request; the record owner should link related communications where possible.

When a response contains a summary of policy, staff should distinguish the policy text from the response writer’s interpretation. If the summary appears inconsistent with the published procedure, the employee may ask for clarification. A short informal message may be useful for directing a question, but a formal decision should be entered in the designated record when the procedure requires one.

Section 18. Operational continuity

If the staff portal is unavailable, employees should use the temporary procedure announced by People Operations. The temporary procedure should identify how requests are received, where supporting information is stored, and how the system will be updated when service returns. Staff should not create unofficial copies in a shared location unless the temporary notice directs them to do so. Once the portal is restored, the responsible team should reconcile temporary submissions against the official record.

If an employee cannot reach a manager, the employee should use the designated acting supervisor or the alternate contact listed for the department. The employee should retain the time and content of the attempted contact. A failure to receive an immediate response does not itself indicate approval or denial. The decision should be recorded by the person authorized to make it when that person is available or when the documented alternate procedure applies.

Section 19. Plain-language reminders

A request is not an approval. A draft is not a submission. A submission is not a completed review. An acknowledgment is not a decision. A proposal is not an effective policy. A calendar entry is not a formal leave record. A forwarded quotation is not necessarily the sender’s own statement. A displayed balance is not a leave request. A badge assignment is not proof of entry. These distinctions are intended to help staff read administrative records accurately and avoid attributing actions or decisions to the wrong person.

Employees and managers should use the designated form, identify the relevant dates, and check the recorded status. If the record is unclear, they should ask the responsible owner. The goal is not to add unnecessary steps; it is to ensure that requests are reviewed by the correct person and that the final record states what actually happened. Where the procedure is silent, staff should seek guidance rather than invent an approval rule.

Section 20. Example reference cases

The following examples are included to explain ordinary record handling. They do not create additional policy requirements. In the first example, an employee enters a planned absence request, and the manager marks it pending while asking for a date clarification. The request remains pending until the manager records an outcome. The employee should not treat the initial submission as approval.

In the second example, an employee writes to People Operations asking whether the displayed leave balance is correct. That message is a balance inquiry, not a request to take leave. If the employee later wants specific dates off, the employee must submit the dates through the leave procedure. The two matters may be related, but they are recorded as separate requests.

In the third example, a manager forwards an older message written by an employee and asks People Operations to advise on the process. The original employee is the writer of the quoted request; the manager is the person seeking procedural advice in the forwarding message. The reviewer should preserve both roles in the record and should not attribute the original request to the manager.

In the fourth example, a team member writes, “If the equipment fails again, I may ask for a replacement.” This is a statement about a possible future request, not a current replacement request. If the equipment later fails and the employee wants a replacement, the employee should submit the ordinary equipment form and describe the actual problem.

In the fifth example, an employee sends a message saying that a training module has been opened. The learning portal still shows “not completed.” The employee should complete the module and use the completion control. Opening the module alone does not satisfy the completion requirement. If the employee completed it but the portal did not record the result, the employee may request a record review.

In the sixth example, a staff member finds a draft procedure that says a new form may be introduced next quarter. Unless the authorized owner approves and publishes the revision, the current procedure remains in effect. Staff should not change their submissions based only on the draft. The document owner should publish the final procedure with its effective date.

Section 21. Publication and acknowledgments

The approved handbook is available in the staff portal under People Operations documents. The portal listing identifies the document owner, effective date, and current revision. Employees may acknowledge that they have accessed the handbook where the portal requests acknowledgment. The acknowledgment confirms receipt or access according to the portal wording; it does not create a separate approval of every future decision made under the handbook.

Managers should direct questions to the relevant owner and should not distribute obsolete copies as current guidance. A locally saved copy may be out of date. Before relying on a passage, the employee should check the portal’s current version and effective date. If the portal is temporarily unavailable, the employee may ask People Operations to confirm the current version once service is restored.

Section 22. Closing statement

This handbook is an administrative reference for ordinary Harbor Studio processes. Its sections should be read together with the record associated with a particular request. The responsible person should use the information actually recorded, distinguish a completed action from a possibility or proposal, and avoid treating an informal comment as a formal decision. Questions about interpretation should be directed to People Operations. Questions about facilities, purchasing, or urgent safety matters should be directed to the appropriate specialist contact listed in the staff portal.

End of document. Change log: 1 April 2025, initial publication for internal use. No additional revisions are recorded in this copy.
