Classification: Internal operational record
Review period: 12–18 May
Prepared by: Operations Coordination Office

Executive summary

On 14 May, the dining room at the fictional Saltmarsh Foods hotel, the Juniper Quay Hotel, opened its evening service at 18:00 as scheduled. The restaurant served dinner to hotel guests and local diners. The service was completed without a safety incident, a payment-system outage, or a building closure. One operational issue was recorded: the printed dessert menu listed the pear tart at $8, while the point-of-sale system displayed $9. The duty manager authorized the lower printed price for guests who had already received that menu. The menu record was corrected for the following service. This report records the event, the review process, the supporting material, and the routine controls that were checked.

The purpose of this document is to preserve an accurate operational account rather than to assign individual blame. It describes what staff observed, what actions they took, which records were inspected, and which follow-up activities were completed. The report distinguishes the dessert-price discrepancy from unrelated matters discussed during the same operating period. In particular, a breakfast reservation count, a room-service charge, a supplier delivery, and a maintenance request were reviewed as separate records and did not change the finding about the printed dessert price.

The incident was limited in scope. The evening shift supervisor identified the difference between the printed menu and the point-of-sale listing at 18:12. The printed menu was the version placed at tables for that service. The point-of-sale listing was the amount shown when a server selected the pear tart. The supervisor consulted the duty manager, who instructed staff to honor the price printed on the menu already presented to guests. The restaurant continued service. Staff recorded the discrepancy, removed the remaining copies of the incorrect menu after the first seating, and used a corrected menu for the next service. The corrected menu and the point-of-sale listing both showed $9 for the pear tart.

The review found no evidence that guests were charged more than the price they had been shown for the affected orders. The shift record lists three pear tart orders placed before the menu was replaced. Each was charged at $8. There were no pear tart orders recorded after the corrected menu was introduced on 15 May until the point-of-sale and menu records had been reconciled. The price difference was therefore a menu-control issue, not a payment-system failure. The records in this report use the hotel's local operating date and local currency notation.

Scope and method

The review covered the dinner service on 14 May and the correction process completed on 15 May. The review coordinator examined the printed menu proof, the point-of-sale item listing, the manager's shift log, the restaurant reservation sheet, the service team's written handover, and the daily revenue summary. The coordinator also spoke with the staff members who had handled the menu and the three affected orders. The review did not examine the hotel’s general pricing policy beyond the controls relevant to this event. It did not evaluate the quality or presentation of the pear tart, because no complaint about the food itself was recorded.

The documents were compared in the order in which they were created or used. The menu proof showed $8. The point-of-sale listing showed $9. The shift log documented the discovery at 18:12 and the manager's instruction to honor the printed amount. The order records showed three affected purchases at $8 each. The next day's corrected menu proof showed $9, and the point-of-sale listing continued to show $9. These records agreed on the sequence of events.

The review uses “printed menu” to mean the paper menu placed on tables at the beginning of the 14 May dinner service. It uses “point-of-sale listing” to mean the price selected by staff in the restaurant sales terminal. “Corrected menu” means the version printed for service beginning 15 May. These labels are used consistently throughout the report so that staff can distinguish the paper copy from the electronic listing.

No external assumptions are required to interpret the findings. Times and dates are copied from the hotel records. Prices are in the local currency represented by the dollar sign in the records. A reference to a guest order identifies a transaction recorded by the restaurant, not a reservation or a room charge. The report does not infer guest intent from the fact that an order was placed; it records only the menu, price, and transaction information present in the examined material.

Hotel and restaurant context

The Juniper Quay Hotel is operated in this scenario by Saltmarsh Foods. Its restaurant serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner. The restaurant uses a paper menu at tables and a point-of-sale terminal for order entry and payment. The paper menu is prepared from a menu proof approved by the restaurant manager. Prices are also entered into the point-of-sale system. The two records are intended to match before service begins.

The restaurant shift team on 14 May included the evening shift supervisor, two servers, one host, and the kitchen team. The duty manager was responsible for operational decisions during the shift. The restaurant manager was not on the floor at the moment the difference was discovered, but was available by telephone and reviewed the correction on the following morning. The shift supervisor recorded the event and passed it on in the regular handover.

The evening service was scheduled to begin at 18:00. The first seating included hotel guests and diners with reservations. The restaurant remained open through its normal dinner period. No change to the opening time, closing time, or reservation schedule was made because of the menu issue. The host continued to seat guests, and the kitchen continued preparing orders. Staff did not suspend service or close the dining room.

The pear tart was one item in the dessert section. The dessert section also included a lemon cake, a chocolate pudding, and a fruit plate. Those items were listed at the same prices on the paper menu and in the point-of-sale system. The review checked those neighboring entries because a broader transcription error could have affected several items. The comparison found that the pear tart was the only dessert whose price differed between the paper menu and the sales terminal on 14 May.

The restaurant's normal practice is to honor the price on a menu a guest has already been given when a discrepancy is noticed during service, while promptly correcting the underlying records for later guests. The duty manager applied that practice. The report records the manager's instruction as an operational decision and does not treat it as a change to the general listed price. The listed price for later service remained $9 after the corrected menu was issued.

Chronology

At 16:40 on 14 May, the restaurant team completed its pre-service checks. The shift supervisor reviewed table settings, staffing, and the printed menus. The check was recorded as complete. The menu check at that point did not identify the difference in the pear tart price. The point-of-sale terminal had been checked earlier in the day by the restaurant manager, and its dessert listing showed the pear tart at $9.

At 18:00, the host began seating dinner guests. Servers placed the paper menus on tables. The restaurant opened according to its normal schedule. No issue with the menu was reported during the first few minutes of service. The kitchen ticket system and payment terminal were operating normally, according to the shift log.

At 18:12, a server asked the evening shift supervisor to confirm the price of the pear tart. The server had read $8 on the paper menu and saw $9 on the point-of-sale screen. The supervisor checked both records and confirmed the mismatch. The supervisor wrote down the time and informed the duty manager. The discrepancy was not discovered by a guest complaint; it was raised internally by a member of the service team.

At 18:16, the duty manager instructed staff to honor the $8 price printed on the menu already presented to guests. The manager asked the supervisor to make sure that servers did not charge a guest $9 when that guest had been shown the $8 menu. The manager also asked the supervisor to set aside the remaining copies of the printed menu and to record the affected orders. Service continued while staff followed those instructions.

At 18:20, the supervisor informed the servers. The servers acknowledged the instruction and continued to take orders. The host was asked not to put additional copies of the incorrect menu on tables after the existing first seating was complete. Guests who had already received the menu could continue to use it during their meal. The supervisor did not announce the discrepancy to the dining room because staff could resolve it at the point of sale without interrupting guests.

Between 18:20 and 19:05, three pear tart orders were entered. The order records show that each was charged at $8. The supervisor compared each order with the table check before it was closed. The checks did not show a $9 pear tart charge for any of these three orders. The staff did not alter the point-of-sale listing during the busiest part of the service because the duty manager wanted the record of the system price to remain unchanged until the existing menus had been collected and the correction could be verified.

At 19:10, the first seating had substantially finished. The host collected the remaining incorrect menu copies from the tables that had turned over. The supervisor counted and set aside 18 copies. The count was entered in the shift log. The count describes copies removed from use; it is not the number of guests who saw a menu and is not a count of dessert orders.

At 19:25, the restaurant manager was contacted and informed of the discrepancy and the temporary instruction. The restaurant manager confirmed that the printed price should be honored for guests who had received the menu. The manager requested that the next print run show $9 and that the paper proof be compared with the point-of-sale listing before distribution. The manager did not direct staff to change the price of the three orders already entered at $8.

At 20:00, dinner service continued with the remaining menus managed by the host and servers. No further copies of the incorrect menu were placed on new tables. The supervisor recorded that no additional pear tart orders were placed after the three recorded orders. This statement refers to the remainder of the service on 14 May, as shown in the sales record.

At 21:35, the restaurant closed the dinner service. The shift supervisor completed the handover entry, noting the mismatch, the manager's instruction, the 18 copies removed, and the three orders charged at $8. The supervisor also recorded that there had been no guest complaint about the price and no refund request. The absence of a complaint is documented as a fact in the shift record; it is not used as a substitute for checking the transaction amounts.

At 08:15 on 15 May, the restaurant manager reviewed the incident record and asked the menu coordinator to prepare a corrected proof. At 09:00, the coordinator changed the pear tart price on the paper menu proof from $8 to $9. The other dessert prices were left unchanged. At 09:20, the manager compared the proof against the point-of-sale listing. Both showed $9 for the pear tart. The manager initialed the proof and approved it for printing.

At 10:05, the corrected menus were printed. At 10:25, the host and supervisor checked a printed copy against the approved proof and the terminal. The check confirmed the pear tart price was $9 in all three places. The corrected menus were placed into service for the next meal period. The remaining 18 incorrect copies were marked obsolete and placed in the recycling container. The shift record notes this disposition.

At 11:00, the restaurant manager reviewed the three affected transaction records. The records showed $8 for each pear tart. The manager confirmed that the amounts followed the instruction given during service. The manager found no $9 charge for those orders and no separate adjustment or refund entry. The manager closed the operational follow-up as complete.

Evidence reviewed

The menu proof used for the 14 May print run was retained in the restaurant shared folder. It showed the pear tart listed at $8. The proof was dated 13 May and contained the manager's approval mark. No other dessert price differed from the point-of-sale listing in the comparison performed for this review. The approval mark demonstrated that the proof had been approved, but it did not establish that the price had been compared against the terminal before printing.

The point-of-sale item listing was inspected on 15 May. It showed the pear tart at $9 during the 14 May service and after the correction. The system history showed no price change during the service period. The listing for the lemon cake, chocolate pudding, and fruit plate matched their printed prices. The evidence therefore supports a single-item paper-menu discrepancy rather than a terminal outage or a general pricing change.

The restaurant shift log was completed by the evening shift supervisor. It recorded the time of discovery as 18:12, the instruction from the duty manager at 18:16, the removal of 18 menus after the first seating, and the three pear tart orders. The log also stated that staff continued service. The review found no conflicting time in the handover or manager's follow-up note.

The transaction records were checked individually. Each of the three pear tart orders on 14 May showed a price of $8. The total recorded for these three items was $24. The calculation is three orders multiplied by $8 per order, which equals $24. The report includes the total for reconciliation purposes only. It does not imply that all 18 removed menus resulted in an order or that every guest who saw a menu purchased dessert.

The reservation sheet listed 26 dinner covers for the evening. A cover is a restaurant seating count and does not indicate how many people ordered a particular item. The number of reservations was not used to calculate the number of affected pear tart transactions. The transaction records, rather than the reservation sheet, establish the three pear tart orders.

The daily revenue summary was compared with the transaction records. It showed the three pear tart items at $8 each. No unexplained difference was identified for the pear tart line. The summary did not show a payment-system outage or a restaurant-wide discount. The discrepancy was limited to the difference between the printed price and the terminal price, with the manager's instruction determining the amount charged to guests who had received the incorrect menu.

The service team's handover confirmed that the remaining menus were collected after the first seating. It also confirmed that the team used the corrected menu for the following service. The handover contained no report of a guest being charged $9 after being shown the $8 menu. The review did not treat the absence of such a report alone as proof; it also examined each transaction record.

A maintenance log was examined because a staff message from the same evening mentioned the restaurant printer. The log concerned a paper-feed issue at the front desk printer on 12 May. It did not concern the restaurant's menu printing on 14 May. The restaurant menus were printed successfully, and the discrepancy was the price text on the menu, not a printer malfunction. This unrelated maintenance note did not alter the incident finding.

A supplier delivery note was also reviewed because it included the word “pear.” The note recorded delivery of fresh pears to the kitchen on 14 May. It listed a quantity of 12 kilograms and a receiving time of 10:30. It did not list a retail price for the pear tart and did not determine the restaurant menu price. The delivery record was a purchasing document, not evidence of a guest charge.

The breakfast reservation sheet for 15 May listed 31 breakfast covers. This count was not related to the dinner menu discrepancy. The breakfast menu did not include the pear tart, and breakfast service used its own menu. The record was retained in the daily operations folder but was not used to assess the 14 May dinner transactions.

The room-service ledger contained one separate entry for a dessert order on 14 May. That order was for chocolate pudding, not pear tart, and it was charged at the amount printed on the room-service menu. It was not a Juniper Quay dining-room transaction. It did not add to the count of three pear tart orders and was not included in the $24 reconciliation total.

The front desk report noted that one guest had requested a copy of a dinner receipt. The request was fulfilled and the receipt matched the point-of-sale record. The receipt request did not concern an incorrect charge, and no complaint was recorded. The front desk report was checked to ensure that a separate guest contact had not been overlooked.

The manager's follow-up note dated 15 May documented the corrected proof and the comparison with the terminal. The note stated that the menu showed $9 and the point-of-sale listing showed $9. It also stated that the manager approved the proof before printing. The printed copy reviewed by the coordinator matched the approved proof. The records therefore establish that the correction was completed before the next service.

Finding

The review finds that the printed dinner menu on 14 May listed the pear tart at $8, while the point-of-sale listing showed $9. The difference was identified by a server and confirmed by the evening shift supervisor at 18:12. The duty manager instructed staff to honor the printed $8 price for guests who had already received that menu. Three pear tart orders were recorded at $8. The paper menu was corrected for the following service, when both the printed menu and point-of-sale listing showed $9.

The event did not involve a guest being charged more than the printed price on the affected orders. It did not involve a confirmed guest complaint, a payment-system outage, or a change to the restaurant's opening schedule. The issue was a mismatch between two price records. The corrective action brought the paper menu into agreement with the existing point-of-sale listing.

The review does not conclude that the $8 price was the intended ongoing price. The menu proof and the sales terminal differed, and the manager's instruction was specifically to honor the menu already shown to guests. The corrected menu and terminal both showed $9 for later service. This distinction prevents the temporary guest-facing accommodation from being mistaken for a permanent price change.

The review also does not conclude that all diners were affected. The evidence identifies three pear tart transactions and 18 paper copies removed from use. The count of removed copies is not a count of transactions. No evidence in the examined records supports a larger number of pear tart orders during the affected service.

The cause was a failure to reconcile the approved paper menu proof with the point-of-sale listing before the 14 May menu was printed. The proof had been approved, but the available records do not show a documented comparison against the terminal before distribution. The review does not attribute the error to a specific individual's intent. The immediate correction was to update the proof, check it against the terminal, and replace the paper menus.

Contributing conditions

The paper menu and point-of-sale listing were maintained in separate records. The price could therefore be correct in one record and incorrect in the other without an automatic warning. The pre-service checklist included a general menu check, but its entry did not require staff to initial a side-by-side price comparison. The team completed the checklist, yet the mismatch remained undetected until a server encountered the item on the terminal.

The menu proof was approved before the next service, but the approval process did not require the approver to record the corresponding point-of-sale amount. The manager had reviewed the proof for presentation and wording. The records do not show that a second person independently compared every price. These conditions explain how the discrepancy could pass through normal preparation without suggesting that the staff knowingly distributed inconsistent information.

The discovery occurred early in the service and was communicated promptly. The supervisor and duty manager made a clear decision about the price to honor, and the team received the instruction before the recorded pear tart orders were completed. Staff had a straightforward process to follow. The remaining menus were removed when tables turned over, avoiding unnecessary interruption to guests already seated.

The restaurant did not make an electronic price change during the dinner rush. That decision preserved the original system record and avoided introducing a second change while staff were resolving the discrepancy. It also made it possible to compare the actual point-of-sale amount with the printed amount after service. The manager then made the paper record match the existing terminal listing for the next service.

No evidence suggests that the supplier's pear delivery, the front desk printer issue, the breakfast cover count, or the room-service order contributed to the menu discrepancy. Those records were reviewed because they appeared in the same operational folder or included similar terminology. Their subject matter and transaction details were distinct from the restaurant dinner menu.

Actions completed

The duty manager told staff to honor the $8 amount shown on the paper menu already presented to guests. The supervisor relayed that instruction to the servers. The transaction records confirm that the three pear tart orders were charged at $8. The manager reviewed those transactions the next morning and found no conflicting charge.

The supervisor removed 18 remaining copies of the incorrect menu after the first seating. The copies were not reused for the next service. They were marked obsolete and recycled after the corrected menus were checked. The count and disposal were recorded in the shift log.

The menu coordinator changed the pear tart amount on the proof from $8 to $9. The restaurant manager compared the corrected proof against the point-of-sale listing and approved it. A printed copy was checked again before distribution. The new paper menu and the sales terminal both showed $9. These actions were completed on 15 May before the next service period.

The manager reviewed the transaction summary, menu proof, and shift log. The review established that the price difference was limited to the pear tart and that no other dessert price required correction. The manager closed the follow-up after verifying the corrected documents and the three affected transaction amounts.

The service team received a reminder that any difference between a paper menu and the terminal should be raised with the supervisor before the transaction is closed. The reminder did not change the manager's instruction for the 14 May guests. It was intended to ensure that future differences are documented promptly and that staff do not make an independent price decision without authorization.

Preventive follow-up

The restaurant manager added a line to the pre-service checklist requiring the checker to compare menu prices with the point-of-sale listing. The revised line includes a space for the checker’s initials and the time of the comparison. This is a recordkeeping measure. It makes the comparison visible rather than relying on a general statement that the menus have been checked.

The manager also assigned one person to maintain the approved price list used for both the paper menu and the terminal. When a price is changed, the person preparing the paper proof must compare the proof with that list, and a second person must verify the final copy against the terminal. The records should show the date and the names or initials of the preparer and checker. The purpose is to make the approved amount easy to identify and to prevent a menu proof from being treated as verified solely because it has been reviewed for layout.

The restaurant will retain one dated copy of each approved menu proof and one sample of each printed menu version. If an error is found, the obsolete version will be marked and stored or disposed of according to the records schedule. The restaurant manager will be able to identify which version was in service on a particular date. The 14 May proof and the corrected 15 May proof have both been retained with the incident record.

The shift supervisor will include price discrepancies in the handover even when they are corrected before closing. The handover should state the menu item, the paper amount, the terminal amount, the instruction given, the number of transactions involved if known, and whether a corrected menu has been issued. The handover should distinguish confirmed transaction counts from menu-copy counts or reservation counts.

The manager will review the revised checklist at the end of the next seven dinner services. The review will confirm whether the comparison was completed and whether the paper and electronic prices matched. This follow-up is intended to test whether the control is being used, rather than to reopen the already completed 14 May transactions. The report records the planned review as a preventive action; it does not claim that the seven-service review has already occurred.

The team will continue to use the established instruction to honor a price shown on a menu already presented to a guest, subject to the duty manager's direction. If the discrepancy affects more than one item, staff should contact the duty manager and pause entry of the disputed item until they receive guidance. For a single item with a clear printed amount, staff should not make an unauthorized change in the point-of-sale system during service. The manager will determine the correction and document it.

Communication and handover

The shift supervisor communicated the discrepancy first to the duty manager, then to the servers and host. The restaurant manager was notified later in the evening. The communication sequence was recorded in the shift log and confirmed in the manager's note. The staff involved understood the instruction as applying to guests who had received the $8 menu. No record indicates that the team told guests the pear tart had a permanent $8 price.

The host's role was to stop placing additional incorrect copies on newly seated tables and collect copies as tables turned over. The servers' role was to follow the price instruction for orders. The supervisor's role was to confirm the checks and document the transactions. The duty manager's role was to decide how to handle the mismatch during the service. The restaurant manager's role was to approve the corrected proof and oversee the next-day reconciliation.

The handover language was reviewed for clarity. It identified $8 as the printed amount on the 14 May menu and $9 as the terminal amount. It recorded that the manager directed staff to honor $8 for affected guests. It did not describe $8 as the ongoing menu price. The distinction was preserved in the next-day correction note, which recorded $9 on both the proof and the terminal.

The report does not include personal opinions about which employee should have noticed the issue first. The service team followed the direction issued after discovery, and the documents show that the correction was completed. The process improvement is focused on making the comparison routine and verifiable before service begins.

Operational impact

The restaurant remained open for its scheduled dinner service. The kitchen and dining room continued operating. The issue required staff time to compare the menu and terminal, communicate the instruction, collect obsolete paper menus, record the affected orders, and prepare a corrected proof. The records reviewed do not identify a delay to the opening time or a reduction in the number of reservations served.

Three pear tart orders were charged at $8 rather than the $9 amount shown in the terminal listing. The recorded difference per order was $1. The total difference between the terminal listing and the three charged amounts was 3 multiplied by $1, or $3. The report records this arithmetic to describe the price difference, not as an additional charge to guests. The guests were charged the printed amount, and the manager directed staff to honor that amount. No payment-system failure is implied by the difference.

The restaurant did not record a refund, because the examined orders were charged at the printed menu price. It did not record a price complaint, although the staff member's discovery was documented. There is no evidence in the reviewed records of an unrecorded charge or of a guest being asked to pay the higher terminal amount after receiving the $8 menu.

The menu correction required a new print run and the disposal of 18 outdated copies. The report does not assign a monetary value to the printing because no cost figure for that work appears in the records. The operational impact is therefore described in terms of the work completed rather than an unsupported financial estimate.

The restaurant's other services were not affected. The breakfast menu for 15 May did not contain the pear tart, and room service used a separate menu. The hotel continued its normal front-desk and kitchen operations. These details are included to delimit the event and not to suggest that every hotel department was part of the incident.

Records and limitations

The review relied on records created at the time or during the next-day correction. The shift log, transaction details, printed menu proof, point-of-sale listing, and corrected proof provided consistent information about the price difference and its resolution. The manager's follow-up note supported the timing of the correction. The review did not identify a discrepancy among those records.

The review did not interview guests. The transaction records show the amounts charged, and no complaint or refund request appears in the examined guest-contact records. The report therefore does not make claims about what individual guests remember or whether they noticed the menu price. It states only that the paper menu presented for service showed $8 and that three recorded pear tart orders were charged at $8.

The 18-copy count is based on the supervisor's shift entry. The review did not count every menu that had been printed at the start of the service. It therefore cannot use the 18 remaining copies to calculate how many total copies were distributed or how many guests viewed the menu. The order count of three comes from the restaurant transaction records and is separately supported.

The reservation count of 26 covers is a service-planning figure. It is not a count of guests who ordered dessert. The breakfast count of 31 covers belongs to a different meal period. Neither figure was substituted for the transaction count. The report includes these adjacent figures because they appeared in operational records reviewed during the investigation, but they do not change the finding.

The supplier delivery note establishes that pears were delivered to the kitchen. It does not establish the cost, recipe, or retail price of the tart. The report makes no claim about food cost or menu profitability. The incident concerned the difference between a printed price and a point-of-sale price, and the available records are sufficient to determine those amounts.

The report uses the term “incident” in the operational sense of a documented discrepancy requiring a manager decision and correction. It does not classify the event as a safety event, a guest injury, fraud, or a system outage. No evidence reviewed supports those classifications.

Lessons for service controls

A completed checklist is useful only when its entries describe the control that was actually performed. The previous general menu check did not show that prices had been compared with the sales terminal. A specific check creates a clearer record and makes omissions easier to detect. The revised checklist therefore names the price comparison directly.

A menu proof and a point-of-sale listing can each be internally correct as records while disagreeing with one another. The control must compare the two sources rather than assume that approval of one automatically validates the other. The restaurant manager's correction process did this on 15 May and established $9 as the price for the next service.

Clear communication during service prevented the mismatch from becoming an inconsistent charging practice. The duty manager gave one instruction, and the supervisor passed it to the relevant staff. Staff did not choose different prices independently. The transaction review confirmed that all three affected orders followed the same instruction.

Counting objects and counting transactions answer different questions. The 18 removed menus show how many copies were collected at the time recorded. The three orders show how many pear tarts were sold during the affected period. The reservation total shows how many dinner covers were planned. Keeping those categories distinct prevents a numerical report from overstating or understating the impact.

A temporary instruction for a particular service should be recorded separately from the normal listed price. The manager's instruction to honor $8 addressed guests who had received the paper menu. It did not establish that $8 was the intended ongoing price. The following day's correction retained $9 in both the paper and electronic records. The shift log and corrected proof make that sequence clear.

The restaurant will use the post-incident checklist review to confirm that the improved comparison is practicable during ordinary pre-service preparation. If staff find that the check cannot be completed in the available time, the manager will adjust the work assignment rather than remove the comparison. Any later adjustment will be documented separately and will not alter this incident record.

Conclusion

On 14 May, the Juniper Quay Hotel restaurant's paper dinner menu listed the pear tart at $8, while the point-of-sale listing showed $9. Staff identified the mismatch at 18:12. The duty manager instructed staff to honor the paper menu amount for guests who had already received it. Three pear tart orders were charged at $8. The restaurant removed the remaining incorrect menus, corrected the proof, compared the corrected version with the terminal, and placed menus showing $9 into service on 15 May.

The review found no evidence that the three guests were charged above the amount printed on the menu, and no evidence of a payment-system outage. The issue was a single-item mismatch between paper and electronic price records. The immediate correction was completed, and the preventive action is a documented comparison of menu prices with the point-of-sale listing before distribution. The follow-up review of that control is planned after seven dinner services.

Appendix B: record distinctions

A menu copy is a printed document. A menu copy is not a guest, a reservation, or a transaction. The 18 copies counted in the shift log were the remaining incorrect copies collected after the first seating. That count does not show how many copies were originally printed or how many diners read them.

A cover is a restaurant seating count. The 26 dinner covers recorded on the reservation sheet are not the number of pear tart orders. The count of pear tart orders comes from the transaction records and is three.

A point-of-sale listing is the electronic item price used by staff when entering an order. It displayed $9 for the pear tart. The paper menu used at tables displayed $8. The two amounts differed on 14 May and matched at $9 on 15 May.

A manager instruction is a direction for staff to follow in the circumstances described. The duty manager directed staff to honor the printed price for guests already shown the $8 menu. That instruction explains why the three transactions show $8, even though the point-of-sale listing displayed $9.

A corrected menu is the version issued after the proof was updated and checked. It showed $9 and matched the terminal. It was used for the following service. It should not be confused with the paper copy in use at the beginning of the 14 May dinner service.

Appendix C: separate records considered

The breakfast reservation sheet for 15 May recorded 31 covers. It was not used to count dinner dessert orders. The breakfast menu did not list the pear tart.

The room-service ledger recorded a chocolate pudding order. It was a separate service and a different dessert. It was not included in the three pear tart orders.

The supplier note recorded delivery of 12 kilograms of pears at 10:30. It was a kitchen receiving record and did not state the retail price of the pear tart.

The maintenance note concerned a front desk printer on 12 May. It did not concern the restaurant menu print run on 14 May.

The front desk report recorded a receipt-copy request. The receipt matched its transaction record, and the report did not describe a complaint about the pear tart price.

These records were considered because they appeared near the incident material or shared a word with the item under review. They describe separate activities. None changes the confirmed comparison of the paper menu and the point-of-sale listing.

The checker compares the listed prices with the point-of-sale listing, including each dessert item. The checker records initials and time beside the price-comparison line. A second assigned staff member confirms that the printed sample matches the approved proof. If any amount differs, the staff member reports the item to the supervisor and duty manager before the restaurant opens or before the item is sold, whichever occurs first.

The checklist does not authorize staff to change the terminal price without approval. It does not replace the duty manager's decision when a mismatch is found during an active service. It records that the comparison was made and identifies who completed it. If the paper menu and terminal agree, the checker records that result. If they do not agree, the restaurant manager or duty manager documents the approved resolution and the version to be used.

For a mismatch discovered after guests have received a menu, the staff member identifies the amount shown to the guest, informs the supervisor, and follows the manager's instruction. The supervisor records the time of discovery, the item, both listed amounts, the decision, and the transaction count if it can be established from the sales record. Menu-copy counts are recorded separately from transaction counts. The distinction is included in the revised procedure because the two numbers describe different things.

Appendix E: review sign-off

The restaurant manager reviewed the incident documentation on 15 May. The manager confirmed that the corrected paper menu and the point-of-sale listing both showed $9 for the pear tart. The manager also confirmed that the three affected transactions showed $8 each, in accordance with the instruction given during the 14 May service. The manager recorded the immediate follow-up as complete and assigned the checklist review after seven dinner services.

The Operations Coordination Office reviewed the wording of this report to ensure that the finding remains limited to the evidence examined. The report distinguishes the 14 May printed amount, the electronic listing, the manager's temporary instruction, and the corrected menu for later service. It does not state that a guest paid $9 for an item shown as $8, because no such transaction appears in the records. It does not state that $8 became the ongoing listed price, because the corrected menu and terminal both showed $9.

The review record is closed for the purpose of documenting the 14 May event. The preventive checklist review remains a scheduled action. Completion of that future review will be recorded in the ordinary operations log and will not require a change to the established facts in this report.

SECTION TWO: PRODUCT REVIEW OF THE EVENT KIT

Review submitted April 14 by Kwame Novak, committee volunteer
Product: GatherMate Folding Registration Kit, standard edition
Rating selected by reviewer: four out of five stars

I am pleased to offer a careful review of the GatherMate Folding Registration Kit after using it for our small planning-session rehearsal. We purchased one standard kit for the Spring Gathering, principally for check-in at the entrance. The carton arrived in good condition, and the printed packing list was clear. The kit includes a folding tabletop sign holder, a set of blank tent cards, a small clipboard, and a soft carrying sleeve. It does not include a printed welcome sign, a tablet, a printer, or decorative banners. Those distinctions were easy to understand from the product description and were confirmed by the packing list.

The sign holder was simple to unfold, and it stood steadily on the registration table during our rehearsal. The clear panel is suitable for a single sheet of paper. We placed a plain welcome sheet in it, and guests could read it from the doorway. The holder is not intended to be attached to walls or used outdoors. The supplied instructions very politely recommend a flat indoor surface, and that is exactly where we used it. It took less than a minute to set up, even though I was reading the instructions as I went.

The tent cards are blank, which worked well for our purpose because we intend to print names ourselves. They are not preprinted badges, and they do not arrive with guest names filled in. I mention this because a picture in the online gallery shows sample names on cards. The picture is an example of how a customer might use the cards; it does not mean that personalized cards are included. Our committee was comfortable preparing its own cards, so this was not a problem for us.

The clipboard is lightweight and holds a few sheets of paper securely. We used it for a rehearsal attendance list, not for collecting payments. The product description does not claim that the clipboard is a cash box or a secure records cabinet, and I would not treat it as either. It is an ordinary clipboard. The carrying sleeve is useful for keeping the components together between meetings. The kit itself does not supply pens; we brought our own.

The instruction leaflet is short and courteous. It explains how to open the holder, how to insert a sheet, and how to fold the kit for storage. It does not provide event-planning advice, guest-list software, or a schedule template. Those are outside the product's purpose. We already had a schedule prepared by our team, and the kit did not need to replace it. The listed dimensions matched the item we received, and no part was missing.

During the rehearsal, we placed the sign holder beside the entrance registration area. We also laid the blank cards in a shallow stack and placed the clipboard on the table. That arrangement looked neat without requiring extra decoration. The product does not provide a table, table covering, chairs, refreshments, microphones, or a projector. These are venue or organizer arrangements, rather than parts of this registration kit. Our venue booking separately includes the furniture and basic drinks, and our team is supplying the printed materials.

The kit's materials feel adequate for occasional indoor use. I would not describe them as heavy-duty equipment for daily commercial handling, because the maker does not make that claim. The folding joints operated smoothly in our rehearsal. The sleeve is fabric and has no lock. It is useful for carrying the kit, but it should not be considered a secure case. The instruction leaflet asks users to store the components dry and flat, which is a sensible request.

I was particularly glad that the product arrived without extra promotional inserts or unrelated items. The packing list clearly named the four included components: one folding sign holder, blank tent cards, one clipboard, and one carrying sleeve. There were no preprinted signs, name badges, pens, or electronic devices in the carton. Nothing in the listing promised those things, so their absence is not a defect. In fact, the clear list made it easy for our team to check the package before putting it away.

For a small gathering, this is a practical kit if the organizer already has paper, pens, and a registration table. It is not a complete event package, and it does not claim to be one. Someone expecting a full check-in station with a tablet, printer, customized guest cards, and a large floor-standing sign would need to acquire those items separately. Our expectations were modest and matched the listing. We are supplying our own printed welcome page, place cards, name badges, and projector, while the venue supplies the screen and microphones under a separate room booking.

The online product page also included an optional upgrade for a larger floor stand. We did not select that upgrade. The standard kit we received is the tabletop edition. The floor stand appears in one demonstration photograph, but the product caption labels it as an optional accessory. I want to be especially clear that our review concerns the standard tabletop kit and not the optional floor stand. The standard edition was all we needed for a sign placed on a registration table.

The checkout confirmation was polite and easy to follow. It showed one standard edition kit and no add-ons. We were not billed for an upgrade, rush handling, or personalization. The delivery note stated that the parcel had been left at our office reception, and our volunteer collected it the same afternoon. The packaging was not excessive, and the parts were protected from bending. The product did not arrive late for our rehearsal, and no replacement was required.

I also appreciated that the seller's customer-service note explained how to contact them if a part was missing. We did not need to contact them. The note did not promise a refund automatically, nor did we ask for one. We received the item we ordered and are satisfied with it. A four-star rating reflects that the product is useful and clearly described, although a slightly thicker sleeve would be welcome for frequent transport. That small preference does not change what was included in the standard edition.

To summarize the practical experience, setup was quick, the sign holder was stable on a tabletop, the cards were blank as described, and the clipboard did its ordinary job. The kit was suitable for our entrance rehearsal. It is best viewed as a modest registration aid rather than a complete event-planning solution. The product description was sufficiently clear about the included components and the optional floor stand. We are pleased to have purchased the standard edition, and we expect to use it again at the gathering.

A few colleagues asked whether the kit could be used for meal tickets. It could hold a small stack of paper tickets on the table, but it does not print or validate tickets. Another colleague asked whether it included a digital guest list. It does not. We are using a separate spreadsheet prepared by our committee. Neither of these features was advertised as included. The kit's purpose is to help organize a basic physical check-in area, and within that limited purpose it performed well.

We tested the folding action twice and found it easy to operate. We wiped the tabletop sign holder with a dry cloth after the rehearsal and returned all pieces to the sleeve. We did not use adhesive, tape, or wall fasteners. The maker's instructions do not recommend attaching the holder to a wall, and there is no reason to do so when it is designed to stand on a tabletop. Our setup remained neat and did not obstruct the doorway.

The product's name includes the word “registration,” which might lead a shopper to imagine that all registration supplies are bundled. The listing avoids that confusion by naming the actual contents. In our case, the blank cards were exactly what we wanted because we plan to print our own names. The sign holder accepts a page that we prepare. The clipboard accepts forms that we prepare. The sleeve carries the components. No personalized service or printing is part of the standard purchase.

Overall, I would recommend the standard GatherMate kit to a polite, organized volunteer who needs a small, reusable tabletop setup and understands that printed materials are their own responsibility. I would not recommend buying it as a substitute for a room booking, catering order, audiovisual package, or complete conference registration system. Those services are not part of the item. Our event arrangements are documented separately, and the kit complements rather than replaces them. Thank you to the seller for presenting the contents plainly and for packing the order with care.

APPENDIX A: COMMITTEE CHECKLIST

The committee's checklist records: confirm the north room; bring laptop and projector; bring printed welcome sheet; prepare place cards and badges; pack the GatherMate standard kit; bring pens; confirm basic tea and coffee for thirty-eight; and send the final program to the host. The venue supplies the standard screen, two microphones, tables, chairs, and plain coverings. The committee brings the sign and printed materials. The premium dessert tray remains unselected. These are checklist reminders, not additional orders.

APPENDIX B: REHEARSAL OBSERVATION

At the rehearsal, the tabletop sign holder was placed beside the clipboard, with blank cards arranged in a neat stack. The sign was printed by the committee on ordinary paper. A volunteer stood behind the table and greeted the practice guests. No projector was connected during the check-in rehearsal. The registration kit was packed away afterward in its carrying sleeve. The room used for rehearsal was a committee office and was not the venue reserved for May 18.

APPENDIX C: ORDER DETAIL

Purchase record: one GatherMate Folding Registration Kit, standard edition. Quantity: one. Included components: tabletop folding sign holder, blank tent cards, clipboard, carrying sleeve. Not included: printed sign, personalized badges, pens, tablet, printer, floor stand, table, chairs, food, drink, projector, or screen. Optional floor stand: not selected. The purchase record contains no refund request. The committee marked the item received and in satisfactory condition.

APPENDIX D: FRIENDLY REMINDER

All colleagues are kindly asked to use the committee's current checklist rather than an early draft. Early drafts mentioned possible banners, a dessert option, and alternate seating. Those possibilities were discussed but were not added to the confirmed order. The current arrangements are the ones expressly listed in the messages and order details above. We are grateful to everyone for taking a moment to distinguish confirmed items from ideas that were merely considered. This small courtesy will help the event proceed smoothly.

APPENDIX E: FINAL PREPARATION NOTE

The registration table will be near the north-room entrance. The welcome sheet will sit in the tabletop holder, and the volunteer will use the clipboard for the attendance list. Blank tent cards will be filled in by the committee. The GatherMate kit has no built-in electronics, and the team will not rely on it for printing or storing digital information. The laptop and projector are separate items brought by the organizer. The room's screen and two microphones are supplied under the venue booking, not by the kit seller. All components have been checked and are ready for the gathering.

Meridian Foods Community Harvest Dinner — Event Service Guide and Terms

A very warm welcome to everyone assisting with the Community Harvest Dinner, scheduled for September 12 at Willowglass Hall. Meridian Foods is grateful for the generous help of its staff, suppliers, volunteers, and invited community partners. This document has been prepared with the greatest care to make the event arrangements straightforward. It includes the applicable service terms, a planning overview, venue notes, and routine appendices. The confirmed arrangements are written plainly, and ideas that were discussed but not selected are identified as such. Please do not hesitate to use this guide as the convenient reference for the event.

PART ONE: CONFIRMED EVENT OVERVIEW

The Community Harvest Dinner is an evening gathering for invited guests. The hall booking begins at 3:00 p.m. and ends at 10:00 p.m. on September 12. Guests are expected from 5:30 p.m. The welcome remarks begin at 6:00 p.m., dinner service begins at 6:30 p.m., and the program is scheduled to conclude at 9:00 p.m. The organizing team expects to clear the hall by 9:30 p.m. The later booking end time allows a comfortable buffer for packing and departure.

The confirmed room is the glass hall, not the garden room. The glass hall has movable banquet tables, chairs, a small lectern, and an indoor reception area. The garden room was considered during early planning but was not reserved. The hall's standard sound system and one lectern microphone are included in the confirmed room package. A portable second microphone is not included. If an organizer decides that a second microphone is needed, an explicit written request and separate confirmation are required. No second microphone appears in the current order.

The confirmed food service is the standard harvest supper for forty-eight guests. It includes a soup course, a vegetable main course, bread, and a fruit dessert. Water is provided at the tables. A tea-and-coffee station is included for the same forty-eight guests. The dinner package does not include an open bar, a premium pastry station, or a late-night snack. Those optional services were mentioned in an early planning outline, but they were not selected in the approved order. The service count is based on forty-eight attending guests, not on the larger number of people who received invitations.

The organizer will supply place cards, printed menus, and a freestanding welcome sign. The venue will supply tablecloths, ordinary place settings, and the lectern. The venue does not print personalized materials under the standard dinner package. A laptop and a presentation projector are not included in the room package; the organizer has not asked the venue to supply either one. The standard room screen is available, and the organizer has confirmed that the screen is sufficient for the short presentation.

The committee is responsible for its own guest list and invitations. An early draft estimated fifty-two guests, but the approved count is forty-eight. This change was confirmed before the final food order. The venue's staff will prepare forty-eight dinner places and forty-eight servings of tea and coffee. The four people removed from the earlier estimate are not to be counted as additional guests. The final number is repeated here for convenient confirmation.

PART TWO: TERMS OF SERVICE — EVENT BOOKINGS

1. Scope of service. These terms apply to the room, food, beverages, and equipment expressly identified in the written confirmation for an event. A service discussed in an email, draft agenda, planning note, or sample package is not part of the booking unless it appears as a selected item in the final confirmation. This distinction is intended to be helpful and is applied consistently. The names of optional services may appear in the planning materials without constituting an order.

2. Confirmed selections. The written confirmation identifies the selected hall, date, access period, guest count, food package, and included equipment. If a description says “not selected,” “not ordered,” “considered only,” or “awaiting a separate request,” the item is not included in the current service. Empty lines on a planning worksheet are informational and do not create an order. The confirmation for the Community Harvest Dinner lists the glass hall, forty-eight standard harvest suppers, forty-eight tea-and-coffee servings, the standard room sound system, one lectern microphone, and one screen.

3. Optional equipment. A second microphone, portable speakers, a projector, or other additional equipment must be requested in writing and accepted in a revised confirmation before the event. A general question about availability is not a request to add equipment. A statement that the organizer will bring an item is not a request for the venue to provide that item. The venue will not infer an order from a draft program, a sample photograph, or a list of possible equipment. For the Community Harvest Dinner, the organizer brings its laptop and projector, while the venue supplies the screen and one lectern microphone.

4. Food and beverage counts. The final guest count recorded in the written confirmation determines the number of standard food and beverage servings. An earlier estimate does not override a later confirmed count. The venue prepares servings for the confirmed number and does not add people who were removed from a prior estimate. If the confirmed count is forty-eight, the standard package is prepared for forty-eight guests. The inclusion of water at the table does not imply an open bar, and inclusion of tea and coffee does not imply a premium pastry station or other optional menu item.

5. Optional menu services. Premium pastries, late-night snacks, specialty drinks, and bar service require separate selection in the final order. Mentioning an option while comparing packages does not select it. A draft agenda that says “possible dessert station” is not a confirmed order. If an organizer later wishes to add an option, the organizer must make an explicit written request and receive a revised confirmation. Until that exchange is complete, the item remains unselected. The Community Harvest Dinner has no premium pastry station, open bar, or late-night snack in its approved order.

6. Organizer-supplied materials. An organizer may bring printed menus, place cards, signs, and presentation materials, provided they are used in a safe and orderly manner. A freestanding sign may be placed in an approved indoor area without blocking an entrance. The venue does not produce personalized menus or place cards unless such a service is expressly added. The organizer remains responsible for checking the accuracy of any materials it prints. The hall's ordinary table settings and tablecloths are supplied by the venue under the confirmed dinner package.

7. Room access and timing. Access starts and ends at the times in the booking confirmation. Program times do not silently extend or shorten the room booking. A planned conclusion before the room's booked end time is simply a program detail. Organizers should allow suitable time for setup and departure. For the Community Harvest Dinner, access starts at 3:00 p.m. and ends at 10:00 p.m.; the program concludes at 9:00 p.m., and the team plans to clear the hall by 9:30 p.m.

8. Changes. A change is effective only when it is recorded in a revised written confirmation. A courteous inquiry, preliminary estimate, or unapproved draft is not itself a change. The venue and organizer should identify the item being changed so that unrelated parts of the order remain clear. For example, changing the guest count does not change the reserved room, and selecting a food service does not automatically select optional equipment. The current written confirmation should be consulted for the active order.

9. Cancellations. A cancellation must clearly identify the booking and state that the organizer is cancelling it. Asking about cancellation terms, considering whether to cancel, or writing that a booking would be cancelled if circumstances changed does not itself cancel the event. A cancellation becomes effective when acknowledged under the applicable booking procedure. No cancellation request has been made for the Community Harvest Dinner. The booking remains confirmed for September 12.

10. Refund inquiries. A refund is not automatic merely because a customer asks a general question about payment or receives a copy of these terms. Any refund request must be clearly made by the customer responsible for the booking and is reviewed according to the applicable cancellation schedule. A forwarded message from a different customer is not the current organizer's request. The venue records requests by the person who sends them and the booking to which they refer. No refund request is recorded for this event.

11. Payment record. The booking summary shows a deposit received from Meridian Foods and a remaining balance due from Meridian Foods. A supplier's invoice for flowers is a separate transaction and does not alter the hall booking account. The venue does not owe the organizer a payment simply because the organizer has paid a deposit. If an adjustment is approved, it will appear in the account statement. No adjustment or refund is presently recorded.

12. Care and access. Guests and organizers are asked to treat the hall and its furnishings considerately. Decorations may not be attached to walls or fixtures without written permission. Freestanding items should not block doors, corridors, or emergency equipment. The organizer has described one small freestanding welcome sign for the indoor reception area. No wall banners, outdoor signs, or hanging decorations are included in the confirmed plan.

13. Sound and presentations. The standard room sound system and one lectern microphone are included. The organizer may use its own laptop and projector with the standard screen, subject to a brief setup check. The venue does not supply a presentation operator under the standard package. If extra equipment or staff support is desired, it must be requested and confirmed separately. A program listing two speakers does not automatically mean that two microphones have been ordered.

14. Final confirmation priority. If a preliminary note differs from the final written confirmation, the final confirmation governs the selected services. This rule is not a reason to disregard clear changes that were accepted later in a revised confirmation; such a revision becomes the latest written confirmation. In the absence of a revision, the active final confirmation controls. For this dinner, the latest confirmed count is forty-eight, and the latest confirmed menu is the standard harvest supper.

PART THREE: PLANNING CORRESPONDENCE EXCERPTS

August 1 — Event desk to committee: A very pleasant afternoon to you. We can offer either the glass hall or garden room on September 12. The glass hall is available for the requested evening schedule. Please let us know which room you prefer, and we will be glad to prepare the written confirmation.

August 2 — Committee to event desk: Thank you for your helpful options. We would be pleased to reserve the glass hall. The garden room is attractive, but it is not our selection. We expect the initial guest count may be about fifty-two, subject to final confirmation.

August 2 — Event desk to committee: Certainly. The glass hall is now held for your event. The approximate count is noted as fifty-two, and we will ask for a final number before the food order is prepared. The standard room package includes the screen, sound system, and one lectern microphone.

August 5 — Committee to event desk: We are considering whether to add a second microphone because two people may speak. Please let us know whether one is available. This is an inquiry only, and we are not yet asking you to add it to the order.

August 5 — Event desk to committee: We would be glad to check availability. A second microphone can be requested as an additional item. It will not be added unless you send an explicit request and we issue a revised confirmation. The current booking continues to include one lectern microphone.

August 6 — Committee to event desk: Thank you. We will use the one lectern microphone and will not request a second one. The two speakers can share it. Please keep the equipment order unchanged.

August 8 — Committee to event desk: We have seen the menu options and would like the standard harvest supper. The premium pastry station sounds pleasant, but we have not selected it. Please include the standard meal and leave optional dessert service off the order.

August 8 — Event desk to committee: With pleasure. The standard harvest supper is selected. The premium pastry station is not selected, and no open bar or late-night snack has been added. We will confirm the final guest count before service.

August 12 — Committee to event desk: The presentation will use our own laptop and projector. We would be grateful if the hall screen could be available. We are not requesting a projector from the venue.

August 12 — Event desk to committee: Certainly. The standard screen is part of the room package. Your laptop and projector are organizer-supplied, and no venue projector is listed. The room sound system and one lectern microphone remain included.

August 19 — Committee to event desk: We have now completed the guest list. Please change the count from fifty-two to forty-eight. We confirm that forty-eight guests will attend. Kindly prepare the standard supper and tea and coffee for that final number.

August 19 — Event desk to committee: Thank you for the timely confirmation. The final service count is forty-eight. I have updated the standard supper and tea-and-coffee count to forty-eight. The room booking remains the glass hall on September 12.

August 20 — Committee to event desk: Our printed draft program says the dinner concludes at 9:00 p.m. We expect to clear the hall by 9:30 p.m. Please retain the room booking until 10:00 p.m., as confirmed.

August 20 — Event desk to committee: Certainly. The booking remains through 10:00 p.m. The 9:00 p.m. program conclusion and 9:30 p.m. planned clearance do not change the reserved access period.

August 22 — Committee to event desk: We will bring place cards, menus, and one freestanding welcome sign. The sign will stand indoors beside the reception area. We will not use wall banners or outdoor signs.

August 22 — Event desk to committee: That arrangement is noted. The venue supplies tablecloths, ordinary place settings, and the lectern. The committee supplies its own printed materials and sign. Please keep the sign clear of doors and walkways.

August 26 — Event desk to committee: Here is the current confirmation for your kind review: glass hall, September 12, access 3:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.; standard harvest supper for forty-eight; tea and coffee for forty-eight; screen; sound system; one lectern microphone; and ordinary hall furnishings. Not selected: garden room, second microphone, venue projector, premium pastry station, open bar, late-night snack, and wall or outdoor decorations.

August 26 — Committee to event desk: The summary is accurate and most helpful. Please leave the arrangements exactly as shown. We appreciate the care taken to distinguish the selected items from the options we discussed earlier.

PART FOUR: EVENT-DAY SERVICE NOTES

The room attendant will unlock the glass hall at 3:00 p.m. and will check the screen, sound system, and lectern microphone before the organizer arrives. The organizer may connect its own laptop and projector to the screen during setup. The venue's role is limited to providing the listed equipment; technical operation of the organizer's presentation remains with the organizer. The attendant can point out the ordinary controls but is not booked as a presentation operator.

The catering team will set forty-eight places. The standard harvest supper is served according to the confirmed schedule. The tea-and-coffee station is prepared for forty-eight guests. Water is placed on the tables. No separate bar service, pastry station, or late-night snack is scheduled. If a guest brings a personal dietary question to the event desk, staff will respond courteously using the information available in the confirmed menu; that interaction does not add a new menu service.

The host may place the committee's printed menus and place cards at the tables. The welcome sign may be positioned beside the indoor reception area. It should remain freestanding and should not obstruct the door. The venue's tablecloths and ordinary place settings are arranged before guest arrival. Additional decorative materials should not be assumed to be included simply because a sample event photograph shows them.

At the end of the program, the committee will gather its own printed materials, laptop, projector, and sign. The venue team will clear the standard catering items and furnishings as part of the service. The committee plans to be out by 9:30 p.m., while the room remains booked until 10:00 p.m. The later access end gives the group a reasonable opportunity to depart without rushing.

PART FIVE: ORDER SUMMARY AND ROUTINE RECORDS

Confirmed booking: Meridian Foods Community Harvest Dinner. Date: September 12. Venue: Willowglass Hall, glass hall. Access period: 3:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. Guest count: forty-eight. Food: standard harvest supper for forty-eight. Beverage: tea and coffee for forty-eight, plus water at tables. Room items: standard sound system, screen, one lectern microphone, tables, chairs, lectern, tablecloths, and ordinary place settings. Organizer items: laptop, projector, printed menus, place cards, and freestanding welcome sign.

Not selected or not included: garden room, second microphone, venue projector, premium pastry station, open bar, late-night snack, personalized printing, wall banners, outdoor signs, and presentation operator. These items may appear in an early outline or a sample description, but they are not in the approved order. The current confirmation contains no additional equipment or catering selection.

Account note: Meridian Foods paid the required deposit. The remaining balance is payable by Meridian Foods under the account schedule. A separate floral supplier invoice is not part of the hall account. No refund, account adjustment, or cancellation is recorded. The event remains confirmed. This note is provided for administrative clarity and does not create a new service selection.

PART SIX: COURTEOUS REMINDERS FOR THE COMMITTEE

Please bring the items that the committee has chosen to supply, including the laptop, projector, menus, place cards, and freestanding welcome sign. Please allow the venue team to provide the screen, one lectern microphone, room sound system, furnishings, tablecloths, food, and beverages listed in the confirmation. We are grateful for everyone's help in keeping the responsibilities clear. If a new item is desired, a written request followed by a revised confirmation will be the most reliable way to document it.

Please also use the final count of forty-eight rather than the early estimate of fifty-two. This will help the catering team prepare the correct number of meals and drinks. The earlier estimate is preserved in the correspondence only so that the planning history remains understandable. It has been superseded by the confirmed count and should not be treated as an additional four guests.

Finally, the committee's draft program and planning notes are welcome reference materials, but the confirmed order controls the services to be supplied. A possible option is not an order; an inquiry about availability is not an order; and a statement that the organizer will bring an item is not a request for the venue to provide it. The approved order is intentionally concise and is repeated above for the convenience of all participants. Thank you very much for reading and for helping the evening run smoothly.
