Tidewater Dental | Contract Administration Policy, revision 8.2, effective 14 May 2025

Purpose and routing. This page governs notices received under Tidewater Dental’s equipment-service agreements. Intake staff must route a notice according to the act the sender actually requests from Tidewater, not according to the subject line, an opponent’s quoted demands, or the department named in an attachment. The sender is the person or organization that transmitted the current message to Tidewater. A quoted speaker is not the sender unless that speaker separately transmitted the current message. The billing queue handles requests to refund, reverse, or explain a payment collected by Tidewater. The claims queue handles requests for compensation for damage or loss. The contract queue handles requests to interpret, enforce, or terminate an agreement, including formal notices of breach. A notice may describe more than one issue; route each actual request to the relevant queue.

How to read praise. Customers sometimes write, “Wonderful work; exactly what we needed,” when the surrounding details make clear that they mean the opposite. Intake staff should not classify a complaint as praise merely because its wording is positive. Conversely, direct praise without a contrary complaint is not a request for corrective action. The words “perfect,” “delightful,” and “excellent” do not independently establish satisfaction or dissatisfaction. Consider who wrote them and what outcome that person seeks.

Authority and quoted material. A forwarded clause, opposing counsel’s email, a vendor’s response, or a proposed draft is evidence of what that author said, not automatically a request made by the current sender. If a Tidewater customer forwards a vendor’s demand that Tidewater pay an invoice, that demand does not mean the customer is asking Tidewater to pay the customer. If Tidewater forwards a customer’s request to its own counsel, the customer remains the requester in the original communication, but the current sender is Tidewater. For intake, use the current sender’s express cover message to determine what action that sender wants. When the cover message explicitly says it is forwarding material only for recordkeeping and makes no request, do not treat quoted demands as the sender’s requests.

Examples of routing. A sender who says Tidewater charged a fee twice and asks for one charge back belongs in billing. A sender who reports a broken cabinet and seeks the cost of replacement belongs in claims, even if the agreement’s limitation clause is attached. A sender who says the service contract expired and requests written confirmation belongs in contract. A sender who asks only whether a payment was received belongs in billing only if the question concerns a Tidewater-collected payment; a request to confirm whether a contract notice was received belongs in contract. Do not infer a refund request from the mere presence of a receipt or a claim from a description of a damaged item when the sender expressly says no compensation is sought.

Recordkeeping. Preserve the original transmission, including the cover note and quoted chain, in the intake file. Record the actual sender, the requested action, any applicable agreement section, and the destination queue. If a message contains sarcastic praise, note the factual conduct that reveals its intended meaning. If sender identity is unclear, seek clarification rather than attributing another person’s request to the sender. An internal employee’s routing suggestion is not a customer request and does not override the sender’s words. A message asking Tidewater to send a matter to a particular queue is not, by itself, evidence that the underlying customer seeks the service associated with that queue. Route based on the requested substantive action, not merely the preferred destination.

Illustrative file TD-441: A technician left a sterilizer unsecured, and the customer wrote, “A truly brilliant installation.” If that same customer asks Tidewater to reimburse the repair invoice, classify the requested action as compensation for damage. If the customer instead asks Tidewater to reverse a duplicate service charge and mentions the installation only as context, classify the requested action as a payment reversal. The author and the requested remedy, not the technician’s description of the event, control. In either case, a technician’s later email saying “the customer owes us for the visit” remains the technician’s position, not the customer’s request.

Deadlines and routing do not alter substance. A notice delivered on a deadline remains a contract notice if it asks for contract enforcement; a late payment complaint remains a billing matter if it asks for a refund. Staff should not convert a notice into a different request because another party says that conversion would be convenient. When a sender expressly denies seeking a remedy, that denial controls over an opponent’s characterization of the sender’s motive, unless the sender separately requests the remedy elsewhere in the same current message.

This protocol applies to notices under Saltmarsh Foods’ wholesale supply agreements. A sender’s request determines routing. The billing desk handles a request to return money Saltmarsh collected or correct a payment it received. The claims desk handles a request that Saltmarsh compensate the sender for physical or financial loss arising from a product or service. Identity rules. In an email chain, the person who sent the current message is the sender for intake purposes. A sender’s request to archive a notice is not itself a request to carry out the relief demanded inside that notice. When text says that a phrase was sarcastic, or the surrounding facts plainly reverse its literal praise, classify the intended complaint rather than the surface compliment.

Incident review: Copperleaf Studio’s Tuesday green build

Prepared by: Ines Bergstrom, release engineering
Review date: 18 June
Tone note from the author: We have apparently achieved the rare engineering milestone of making a green checkmark look suspicious. Please enjoy the following account of how several independent systems all reported success while the people reading them learned to distrust the color green.

Executive summary

On Tuesday, the Atlas web client’s continuous-integration pipeline completed successfully for commit `c91a7d2`. The release candidate was not deployed to production. The build passed its configured tests, produced an artifact, and published that artifact to the staging registry. The production deployment job was manual and remained unapproved throughout the incident window.

The triggering event was not a failed production deployment. No production deployment was attempted. The triggering event was a review comment from a release coordinator who saw the green pipeline badge, assumed it meant production had received the candidate, and asked why the customer-facing behavior had not changed. The behavior had not changed because no production rollout had occurred. This is not a subtle distinction, but our systems have spent several quarters working very hard to make it look subtle.

A second source of confusion was a retry of the visual test shard. The first attempt failed because a screenshot comparison exceeded its configured pixel threshold. The retry passed after the test runner refreshed a stale browser profile. The retry result replaced the first attempt’s status in the compact dashboard. The detailed job history retained both attempts, because the detailed view is where information goes to be technically available and practically ignored.

The review also found a separate warning in a dependency audit. The warning concerned an optional package used by the local documentation preview, not a package included in the production bundle. It did not fail the pipeline and was not the reason the production job remained unstarted. The warning is included here because it attracted several theories, all of which were more dramatic than the evidence.

Scope and definitions

This report uses “build” to mean the CI workflow associated with one commit. It uses “artifact” to mean the packaged web client stored in the staging registry. “Staging” is the internal preview environment. “Production” is the public environment served to customers. A staging publication is not a production deployment, even if a dashboard places both nouns beside the same green circle.

A job marked `manual` requires an authorized person to approve or start it. A job marked `pending approval` has not run. A job marked `skipped` was not executed. A successful build does not imply that every downstream job ran. The pipeline definition intentionally separates validation, staging publication, and production deployment. This separation is documented in the repository, in the deployment handbook, in the runbook, and, apparently, in several places that we did not consult before asking whether production had changed.

The incident window begins with the first push of commit `c91a7d2` at 09:12 and ends with the release coordinator’s clarification at 11:46. Times in the log excerpts are local studio time on the date printed above. The pipeline uses UTC internally, but the interface converts timestamps to local time. No daylight-saving conversion is relevant to this report. The difference between the first push and the clarification is 154 minutes. That calculation is included because at least one chat message described the interval as “about an hour,” which is how precision is born in a group conversation.

Participants and systems

The release coordinator was Chiara Okafor. The CI administrator was Callum Mensah. Farid Mensah reviewed the client changes. The automated systems involved were the Copperleaf CI runner pool, the Atlas visual-test service, the artifact registry, and the deployment approval service. The names in this report identify roles in this incident; they do not imply that any one person caused the confusing display. The display was a collective achievement.

The CI runner pool comprised six Linux runners and two browser-test runners. The build at issue used three Linux runners and one browser-test runner. No runner was shared with a production deployment because no production deployment was running. The artifact registry accepted one staging artifact for the commit. There was no production artifact promotion event, no production rollout record, and no production health check associated with `c91a7d2`.

The deployment approval service had an open manual job for the production environment. Its state was `waiting`, not `running`, `succeeded`, or `failed`. The job had not been approved. The release coordinator had permissions to approve it but did not do so. The report explicitly records this because “the button was available” and “the button was pressed” have been treated as interchangeable concepts in earlier discussions. They remain different concepts.

Timeline

09:12 — Farid pushed commit `c91a7d2` to the release-candidate branch. The commit changed the Atlas settings panel and updated two test snapshots. It did not modify deployment configuration.

09:13 — The CI workflow started. The source checkout completed on the first attempt. Dependency restoration used the existing lockfile and cache. The cache hit rate was 82 percent, which the dashboard presented as a large number without telling anyone whether it was cause for celebration.

09:17 — Static checks passed. The formatter made no changes. The type checker reported no errors. The lint job emitted two existing advisory notices concerning documentation examples. They were not newly introduced by this commit and did not affect the job’s exit status.

09:24 — Unit tests passed: 486 tests, zero failures, nine skipped tests. The skipped tests were tagged as requiring an external identity provider. The test report did not claim that the skipped tests passed. It said they were skipped, which is the correct word and the less comforting one.

09:31 — The first visual-test attempt reported one snapshot mismatch in the settings panel. The comparison measured a changed region of 1.8 percent of the panel. The configured maximum was 1.5 percent. The screenshot included a browser profile with a stale font cache. The job failed, as configured.

09:34 — The visual-test retry started automatically under the retry policy. It used a clean browser profile. The comparison measured 0.4 percent difference, under the 1.5 percent threshold. The retry passed. The dashboard summary displayed the shard as passed and placed the failed attempt behind a small history control.

09:41 — The integration-test shard passed. It ran against the staging service emulator, not against production. Its environment label was present in the detailed job page. The compact board showed only “integration: green.”

09:49 — The build-and-package job passed. The artifact was named `atlas-web-c91a7d2.tar`. Its checksum was recorded in the registry. No production promotion label was attached.

09:53 — The staging publication job passed. The preview URL became available to authorized staff. Staging received the candidate. Production did not.

09:54 — The production deployment job appeared as `manual: waiting`. No approval event was recorded. No deployment runner was allocated to that job. The absence of an allocation is consistent with a job that has not started; it is not a mysterious second kind of deployment.

10:02 — Chiara opened the compact pipeline board. The board showed a green overall status and a staging publication badge. It did not show the manual production job in the initial viewport. Chiara later said that she inferred the candidate had been deployed because the board looked “finished.” The board did not say production had been deployed. It did, however, make the manual job less visible than the celebratory green status. We have chosen to describe this as a design flaw rather than a reading flaw because it is easier to fix a design flaw and less satisfying to hold a meeting about reading.

10:08 — Chiara posted in the release channel: “Looks green. Has the settings change reached customers yet?” This was a question, not an approval and not a deployment instruction.

10:11 — A build notification bot posted: “All required checks passed.” The bot’s definition of required checks excluded the manual production deployment job. The message was accurate according to its configuration, although not especially generous in helping a person distinguish “checks passed” from “release completed.” The bot did not claim that customers had received the change.

10:17 — Farid replied that the staging preview showed the updated settings panel. He did not say the production service had changed. He added, “If the preview looks right, I can ask for production approval after the release review.” The phrase was conditional and described a possible future request. It was not a request for approval, and it did not start a deployment.

10:22 — Callum checked the approval service. The production job still showed `waiting`. There was no approval event. Callum pasted a screenshot of the job state into the channel.

10:25 — Chiara said, “Ah. Green means it did the checks, not that it went to the public. Excellent use of color theory.” This was sarcasm. The sentence did not mean that production had been updated. The status screenshot, rather than the joke, is the evidence of the job state.

10:38 — A separate dependency-audit warning was raised in the release channel. It named a package used by the documentation preview. The package was a development-only dependency and was not in the production bundle. Callum confirmed the scope by comparing the lockfile’s runtime dependency list with the bundle manifest. The warning was not a deployment blocker under the written policy.

10:51 — Farid completed the release review. He noted that the changed settings labels matched the approved design. He did not authorize production deployment. His review comment said, “If the product owner confirms the wording, the release can proceed.” The product owner had not yet confirmed the wording. The condition was not met.

11:04 — Chiara checked the customer-facing environment directly. The old settings panel was still present. That observation was consistent with the production job remaining unstarted. It was not evidence of a failed deployment, because no deployment had been attempted.

11:19 — The product owner confirmed the wording in a separate review system. This confirmation removed one release-review condition but did not automatically approve the manual deployment job. The deployment workflow requires a separate approval action. No such action occurred during the incident window.

11:32 — Callum updated the pipeline board configuration in a test branch so the manual production job would appear in the compact view. This was a proposed interface change only. It did not alter the state of the production job or run a deployment.

11:46 — Chiara posted: “Confirmed, nothing went to production; I read the board as if green meant shipped. Please make the waiting job harder to miss.” This is the final clarification in the incident window. The production job remained waiting at that time.

Evidence inventory

The team collected the CI workflow record, job-attempt history, artifact registry record, staging publication event, production approval-service record, runner allocation log, customer-facing environment version, and channel messages. The records agree on the relevant point: the build and staging publication succeeded; the production deployment did not run.

The workflow record contains a top-level status of `success`. That status summarizes required validation jobs and successful staging publication. It is not a record of production deployment. The workflow schema allows a successful overall status while a manual downstream job remains waiting. This design is documented and intentional, though the presentation of that design is now under review.

The detailed attempt history shows visual-test attempt one failed and attempt two passed. The final shard status is passed because retry policy uses the successful final attempt. The first attempt is retained in the history and was not erased. The summary view collapses retries. This is relevant to understanding why a reviewer first saw a green board, but it does not change the deployment state.

The registry record shows the artifact checksum and a staging tag. It has no production tag. The staging publication event identifies the destination as `atlas-preview`. The production service’s currently served version remained `b48f0aa` throughout the incident window. The candidate’s commit was `c91a7d2`. There is no record that `c91a7d2` was served to production.

The approval-service record lists the production job as `waiting`. The approval event table contains no row for the job. The runner allocation log contains no production deployment runner allocation. The deployment log contains no start time, no completion time, no rollback, and no failed deployment attempt. These are not merely missing success records; together with the explicit waiting state, they establish that the deployment had not started.

The staging preview served the candidate artifact. The preview is accessible to staff with the correct permissions and is not the public customer environment. One screenshot in the review thread showed the updated settings panel. Its image metadata identified the staging preview URL. A second screenshot, taken from the customer-facing environment, showed the old panel. The images were initially posted without captions. We recommend captions, because asking people to infer environments from interface details is an elegant way to create a second incident.

The audit warning’s advisory status is independently documented. It concerned `doc-preview-helper`, present in the development dependency group. The production bundle manifest contains no entry for that package. The security scanner’s policy marks this category as “notify, do not block.” The warning neither caused nor prevented the production job from starting. The job remained manual and waiting because nobody approved it.

What happened, without the green tint

A commit entered the pipeline. Automated checks ran. One visual shard failed once and passed on retry. The candidate was packaged and published to staging. The pipeline’s required jobs finished successfully. The production job was available for manual approval, but nobody approved it. Therefore, production did not receive the candidate.

The system gave a green summary for a successful validation workflow. A person interpreted that summary as a completed release. The person asked whether the change had reached customers. The team checked the deployment record and answered that it had not. The team did not discover a hidden production failure, an unauthorized rollout, or a rollback. It discovered that the compact board makes “checks complete” visually resemble “release complete.”

No customer report was linked to this event. No customer account was changed. No production data was written. No emergency mitigation was needed. The incident’s operational impact was confusion and a delay in release coordination, not an outage. The report calls it an incident because the review process asks us to document confusing release state before it becomes a more expensive form of confusion.

Counterfactuals and tempting stories

Several people proposed plausible accounts that are not supported by the record. They are listed here so they do not become folklore by being repeated in later retrospectives.

One proposal was that the production deployment ran and then rolled back automatically. If that had happened, the deployment service would show a start event, a rollout identifier, and a rollback event. It shows none. The job remained waiting. The old production version is not evidence of a rollback when the candidate was never deployed.

Another proposal was that the dependency warning blocked the production job. If the warning had blocked the job, the workflow would show a policy failure or a dependency-gate state. It shows a manual waiting job. The warning’s policy category is advisory, and the package is absent from the production bundle. The warning is an unrelated near miss, not the cause.

A third proposal was that Farid’s message started the production process. He wrote that if the preview looked right, he could ask for approval after the review. This described a possible future action, subject to conditions. He did not ask for approval in that message. The approval record contains no event.

A fourth proposal was that the green badge itself meant the public site had changed. The badge meant the required checks passed. Its scope is defined by the workflow configuration. A visual indicator is not a deployment record. We say this with the solemnity of people who had to assemble six logs to establish what a missing button press looks like.

A fifth proposal was that the first visual-test failure meant the candidate was unsuitable for production. The failure was real, but it was an initial attempt that the configured retry policy followed with a passing attempt. The release review separately inspected the changed panel. Whether the retry policy should be changed is a valid engineering question; it is not evidence that production deployment occurred.

A sixth proposal was that the staging screenshot proved the candidate was public. It proved that the candidate was visible at the staging preview URL. The environment was named in the screenshot metadata and publication event. The customer-facing screenshot showed the old version. The distinction is supported directly by the records.

A seventh proposal was that the product owner’s 11:19 confirmation automatically released the candidate. The workflow does not connect that review system to the deployment approval service. The confirmation satisfied one review condition; it did not create an approval event. The production job remained waiting after 11:19 and at 11:46.

An eighth proposal was that the lack of a runner allocation meant the runner pool was exhausted. The runner pool had available capacity, and the job had not been approved, so it was not eligible for allocation. A job that is waiting for a human action does not need a runner. No capacity incident occurred.

A ninth proposal was that an unlabelled screenshot in the channel showed a production page. The image metadata identifies the preview URL. The confusion was understandable because the screenshot itself did not include a visible environment banner. It was still a staging screenshot. We can acknowledge why a mistake happened without changing what the evidence says happened.

A tenth proposal was that “all required checks passed” meant every job in the workflow, including the manual production step, had completed. The bot’s message described required checks, not all jobs. The manual job was not a required validation check. The message was accurate and incomplete for release status. Both can be true at once, which is inconvenient but not a paradox.

Why the display misled people

The compact board was designed for quick review of validation state. It placed the overall green badge at the top and rendered manual jobs below a fold. The board treated a manual production job as an optional downstream action, so it did not change the overall success color. That behavior was inherited from the prior pipeline template. The template was originally used for libraries that published artifacts but did not deploy services. Atlas later adopted it for a deployable client, and the interface conventions were not revisited.

The staging publication badge used the word “published” without showing “to staging” in the compact view. The detailed job page showed the destination, but the compact view did not. This was a poor information hierarchy. It is also true that the release handbook defines staging and production separately. A system should not rely on a handbook to counteract the impression created by its main status screen.

The retry summary was another contributor. The initial visual failure was hidden behind the attempt history, while the final pass was prominent. This is correct under the configured retry policy, but it leaves little indication that the pass depended on a retry. The team will evaluate whether to show “passed on retry” in the summary. That would communicate useful context without falsely implying that the final job failed.

The channel bot’s message was scoped to required checks. The phrase was not wrong, but the bot did not say “production has not been deployed” or “manual production approval remains pending.” We do not expect a bot to narrate every possible state, but we do expect it not to make a successful validation summary look like a finished release. A status message that can only be interpreted correctly by reading its configuration is a status message with an unusually demanding audience.

The people involved were working from different screens. Chiara saw the compact board. Farid saw the staging preview. Callum saw the approval service. Each screen displayed a true fragment of the process. The confusion arose because the fragments were not assembled in one place. No participant claimed to have seen a production deployment record. The mistaken inference came from combining a green summary with an expectation that the release process had completed.

Root cause and contributing factors

The direct cause of the mistaken belief was that the compact CI board presented a successful validation-and-staging workflow with a prominent green status while hiding the pending manual production job from the initial view. The production job itself behaved as designed: it waited for approval and did not run.

Contributing factor one was ambiguous status language. “Success” referred to the configured required jobs, while some users read it as “release complete.” Those meanings should not be left to a reader’s optimism.

Contributing factor two was the visual proximity of staging publication and production concepts elsewhere in the interface. The compact board used a single workflow card for both, even though the destinations and approvals differ.

Contributing factor three was the lack of a persistent environment label in preview screenshots. A screenshot can travel farther than the URL from which it was taken. The environment should travel with the image.

Contributing factor four was the hidden retry history. The retry was legitimate, but the summary omitted the fact that the first attempt failed. The omission did not cause the mistaken production inference, but it made the overall green display seem more authoritative than the underlying run history warranted.

Contributing factor five was that the team had not practiced the release flow recently. The last Atlas production rollout was six weeks earlier. People remembered the general shape of the workflow but not which steps were manual. The workflow should make its current state obvious rather than depend on episodic memory.

There was no evidence of a code defect causing the production environment to remain unchanged. There was no failed production rollout, no rollback, no runner shortage, no approval-service outage, and no policy gate triggered by the dependency warning. These alternatives were checked because each was proposed during the discussion, not because the logs suggested them.

Resolution

No operational repair was required because production had not changed. The candidate remained available in staging. The release team completed the normal review after the incident window and handled any later deployment through the standard approval process. This report does not treat that later process as part of the incident window, and it does not claim that the candidate was later deployed. The available incident evidence ends at 11:46, when the production job was still waiting.

The immediate communication fix was a channel clarification: the build was green for required checks and staging, while production approval was pending. The clarification prevented staff from repeating the assumption that the public site had changed. The status board configuration was changed in a test branch for review, not applied directly to the production CI configuration during the incident.

The team preserved the job-attempt history, approval record, and artifact metadata. The retention policy already covered these records, so no special forensic export was needed. The event did not require a customer notification because there was no production change, customer impact, or data exposure. The team did not issue a rollback notice because there was nothing to roll back.

Corrective actions

Action one: show the production deployment job in the compact pipeline view whenever it is waiting for approval. The display should use an explicit label such as “Production deployment: waiting for approval,” not a generic gray dot. Owner: CI interface team. Due date: 28 June.

Action two: distinguish validation success from release completion. The overall workflow summary should say “Checks passed” when required checks pass and should not use “Release complete” unless the deployment has completed. Owner: build-platform team. Due date: 2 July.

Action three: label staging publication with its destination in all views. Replace “Published” with “Published to staging” in the compact board and notification. Owner: Atlas maintainers. Due date: 25 June.

Action four: include a persistent environment banner in staging screenshots and preview pages. The banner should remain visible in captured images without obscuring the interface under test. Owner: visual-test team. Due date: 5 July.

Action five: expose retry history in the summary. A successful retry should be shown as “passed on retry,” with a link to the initial failure. Owner: test-infrastructure team. Due date: 9 July.

Action six: update the release handbook with a short state diagram that distinguishes check completion, staging publication, manual approval, production rollout, and post-deployment health checks. Owner: release engineering. Due date: 30 June.

Action seven: audit other repositories using the inherited library pipeline template. Identify any deployable service that may display a green summary while a manual production job is pending. This is a review, not an assumption that the same issue exists elsewhere. Owner: CI administrators. Due date: 12 July.

Action eight: adjust the notification bot to report pending manual deployment jobs alongside required-check status. The bot should not label a build “released” unless the production deployment record confirms completion. Owner: automation group. Due date: 3 July.

Action nine: document the dependency scanner’s advisory behavior and runtime-scope classification. The purpose is to reduce unrelated warnings being treated as release blockers. Owner: dependency stewardship group. Due date: 7 July.

Action ten: add a release checklist item requiring the approver to confirm the target environment shown in the deployment service before starting a rollout. This is intended to prevent a future staging-versus-production mix-up. Owner: release engineering. Due date: 30 June.

Action eleven: review whether the manual deployment job should be visually connected to the checks card or presented as a separate release stage. This is a design review, not a change to the approval policy. Owner: CI interface team. Due date: 15 July.

Action twelve: measure how often the compact board is used without opening the detailed workflow. If many release decisions are made from the compact view, the interface must carry enough state to support those decisions. Owner: developer experience group. Due date: 20 July.

Action thirteen: add a test for the state combination “required checks passed, staging published, production waiting.” The test should verify that the interface does not display a completed-production label. Owner: CI interface team. Due date: 4 July.

Action fourteen: preserve manual approval as a distinct event in audit records. This action is already satisfied by the current approval service, but the team will keep the record visible in the runbook because a green badge has now demonstrated that people can overlook a missing approval event. Owner: CI administrators. Due date: complete.

Action fifteen: conduct a short walkthrough for the release group after the interface change is ready. The walkthrough will use a staging test run and will explicitly demonstrate the difference between a successful build and a completed production rollout. It will not ask anyone to infer the difference from badge color. Owner: release coordinator. Due date: 22 July.

Verification plan

Corrective actions will be verified against a test workflow with five states: checks failing; checks passed but staging not published; staging published with production waiting; production approved and running; production completed with health checks passed. The compact view must communicate each state without requiring a reader to open hidden attempt history or infer the environment from context.

The interface test will include a successful required-check summary with a pending manual production job. It will assert that the production job is visible and labeled pending. It will also verify that no “released” label appears before a production deployment completion event. This is an interface correctness test, not a test of whether a human can guess what an ambiguous green circle was meant to imply.

The notification test will confirm that “all required checks passed” can coexist with “production approval pending” in one message. It will confirm that a staging publication is named as staging. The test will include a package-audit advisory to ensure the notification does not incorrectly say the production job was blocked by an advisory-only warning.

The retry test will create one failed visual attempt followed by a successful retry. The summary should indicate the retry and link to both attempts. The final shard status should remain passed if the configured retry policy considers a successful retry sufficient. The interface must not conceal the earlier failure or misrepresent it as a production deployment event.

The screenshot test will capture staging and production pages with environment labels visible. The metadata and visible label should agree. The test will use separate synthetic content so that the same interface can be recognized in both environments without relying on color or memory.

The release checklist change will be reviewed after two release cycles. The team will check whether approvers can identify the target environment and whether manual approval events correspond to deployment starts. A checklist confirmation alone will not count as proof of deployment; the deployment service remains the source of truth for whether a rollout occurred.

The audit-warning clarification will be verified against the lockfile and production bundle manifest. The scanner’s advisory category should remain non-blocking unless policy changes through the standard review process. No one should “fix” the misleading board by silently changing dependency policy. That would be a different change and, given our recent performance, it deserves its own explicit label.

Appendix A: selected job records

Workflow ID: `atlas-rc-1842`
Commit: `c91a7d2`
Branch: `release-candidate`
Overall workflow state: `success`
Required checks: `success`
Staging publication: `success`
Production deployment: `manual / waiting`
Production approval event: none
Production runner allocation: none
Production deployment start: none
Production deployment completion: none
Rollback event: none

Visual shard attempt 1: `failed`, comparison 1.8%, threshold 1.5%
Visual shard attempt 2: `passed`, comparison 0.4%, threshold 1.5%
Final visual shard state: `passed after retry`

Unit test summary: 486 passed, 0 failed, 9 skipped
Integration shard: passed against staging service emulator
Static checks: passed
Artifact: `atlas-web-c91a7d2.tar`
Registry destination: staging registry
Production tag: none

Appendix B: selected conversation excerpts

Chiara, 10:08: “Looks green. Has the settings change reached customers yet?”

Bot, 10:11: “All required checks passed.”

Farid, 10:17: “The staging preview has the new panel. If that looks right, I can ask for production approval after the review.”

Callum, 10:22: “Approval service says production is waiting. No approval event.”

Chiara, 10:25: “Ah. Green means it did the checks, not that it went to the public. Excellent use of color theory.”

Farid, 10:51: “If the product owner confirms the wording, the release can proceed.”

Chiara, 11:46: “Confirmed, nothing went to production; I read the board as if green meant shipped. Please make the waiting job harder to miss.”

These messages include conditional statements about actions that might happen later. They do not record those actions happening. A future request for approval is not an approval; a possible release is not a deployment; a preview that looks correct is not a production environment. We have written these distinctions several times because the interface failed to make them once.

Appendix C: checks against alternative explanations

Was production deployed and then rolled back? No. The production job has no start event, deployment identifier, or rollback record. Its state remained waiting.

Did the dependency warning block production? No. The warning was advisory, concerned a development-only package, and did not change the manual job state.

Did the visual-test retry deploy anything? No. It changed the final status of a test shard. The deployment job is separate and remained waiting.

Did a staging publication count as production publication? No. The registry destination and preview URL identify staging; the production environment served the prior version.

Did the product owner’s confirmation start deployment? No. It satisfied a review condition but was not connected to the approval service. No manual approval event followed during the incident window.

Was production unchanged because a production attempt failed? No. There was no production attempt. The environment remained unchanged because no deployment was started.

Did a lack of runner allocation indicate an infrastructure outage? No. A manual job waiting for approval had not become eligible to receive a runner. Available runner capacity was recorded.

Did the green summary assert that customers had received the update? No. It summarized required checks. The summary was easy to misread, but it did not state that production deployment had completed.

Appendix D: follow-up notes

The team has deliberately not proposed automatically deploying after a successful build. That would remove the manual approval step and alter the release policy, whereas this incident concerns the visibility of the existing state. Any proposal to change approval policy requires a separate risk review. If someone suggests that automatic deployment would make the badge less confusing, the answer is that it might make the badge simpler by making the operational consequences larger. That is not the same as solving the communication problem.

The team has also not proposed suppressing the dependency advisory. Its relevance was misinterpreted, but suppressing it would discard useful information. The right improvement is to show scope and blocking status accurately. Warnings should neither masquerade as blockers nor be hidden because someone once read one too quickly.

The team has not treated the first visual-test attempt as proof that the test is useless. The mismatch was real under the configured threshold, and the retry passed with a clean profile. We will review test stability separately. The pipeline’s decision to accept the successful retry was consistent with policy. Whether that policy should be stricter is open for review, but it does not alter the fact that production did not run.

The team has not stated that the release was rejected. No rejection event exists. It was awaiting a manual approval after review conditions were being resolved. “Not deployed yet” is the supported description. “Rejected,” “failed,” and “rolled back” would each add a fact that the records do not support.

The team has not stated that the release was eventually deployed. The incident window ends with the job still waiting. Later activity is outside this report’s evidence. If the candidate was deployed later, that would require a later deployment record. The report does not fill gaps with likely outcomes, even when the likely outcome would make the timeline feel tidier.

Appendix E: operational interpretation guide

A green required-check indicator means that the configured required checks passed. It does not, by itself, mean a package was published, a staging service was updated, a production job was approved, a deployment runner executed, or customers received a change. Each of those claims needs its own record.

A staging publication event means that the candidate was made available in the staging environment. It does not mean that the public production environment changed. A preview link may resemble the customer-facing site because it is built from the same application. Similar appearance does not erase environment boundaries.

A manual job in `waiting` state means that the workflow is waiting for an authorized human action. It does not mean the job is secretly running. It does not mean the approval service is broken. It does not mean an automatic deployment has happened. The job’s state and event record are direct evidence.

A failed test attempt followed by a successful retry means the test passed under the configured retry policy, with an earlier failed attempt retained in history. It does not mean the first attempt never happened. It does not imply that later deployment jobs ran. Test status and deployment status are separate dimensions.

An advisory audit warning means the scanner reported an issue under a non-blocking policy category. Its impact depends on the package scope and policy. Here, the package was development-only and absent from the production bundle. The warning was real; the claim that it blocked production was not.

A conditional statement such as “if the review is acceptable, I can ask for approval” describes an action dependent on a condition. It does not perform the action. The message from Farid recorded a possible future request. The approval system recorded no request or approval. The distinction is ordinary grammar supported by an event log, not a philosophical dispute.

A conditional statement such as “if the product owner confirms the wording, the release can proceed” describes a prerequisite. Once the product owner confirmed the wording, the separate manual deployment approval still remained necessary. Satisfying one condition did not satisfy every condition. The workflow does not infer an approval from a review comment.

Sarcastic remarks in the channel are retained as conversation, not treated as operational events. “Excellent use of color theory” was criticism of the board’s design. It was not a statement that the board accurately represented production. “Looks green” was a description of the interface and a question about deployment, not a record of a deployment.

Appendix F: evidence limitations

This report uses system records available for the incident window. The CI workflow record, approval-service audit, registry event, and environment version were retained and independently checked. The channel excerpts were exported from the release channel. The screenshot metadata was available for both images. No evidence suggests that records were deleted or altered.

The report does not infer the state of production after 11:46. It does not infer that the candidate was never deployed at any later date. It makes a narrower claim: during the recorded incident window, the production job did not start and production did not receive the candidate. That claim is supported by the waiting state, absent approval event, absent runner allocation, absent deployment record, and unchanged production version.

The report does not establish why the compact board was designed with its current hierarchy beyond the historical template information found in the repository. It does establish that the board hid the waiting job below the initial viewport and that the user interpreted the green summary as release completion. The interface change is based on those observable facts, not on speculation about what any person should have understood.

The report does not assess the security severity of the development-only package warning beyond the scanner’s recorded category and its absence from the production bundle. That warning is not necessary to decide whether production deployment happened. It is included as a distractor because it was discussed during the incident, not because it provides evidence about deployment status.

The report does not decide whether the visual test’s threshold is ideal. It records the measured comparisons and configured threshold. The first attempt exceeded the threshold; the retry did not. This is enough to explain the test history. A separate stability review may recommend a threshold or runner change, but that would not change the production job record.

Final finding

The Tuesday pipeline passed its configured required checks and published the candidate to staging. The manual production deployment job remained waiting for approval. No production approval, runner allocation, deployment start, completion, or rollback occurred during the incident window. Therefore, the customer-facing production environment did not receive commit `c91a7d2` during that window.

The confusing green board and the conditional messages prompted reasonable questions, but neither is evidence that a deployment happened. The available evidence supports one straightforward operational conclusion, despite our efforts to decorate it with retries, advisory warnings, and a color palette that seems to have opinions of its own.
