Granite Foods SaaS Operations Handbook and Service Desk Guide

Document purpose
This handbook explains the normal operation of the Granite Foods staff portal and the steps used by the operations team when a service problem is reported. It is written for staff who use the portal, the service desk, and the operations people who maintain the service. The descriptions here are the current instructions for this handbook. They are intended to be easy to follow, even when the person reading has not worked with the portal for a long time. Use the section that matches the question or work in front of you. If something is not clear, contact the service desk rather than guessing.

The portal is a hosted service for Granite Foods employees and approved business partners. It contains staff notices, order-status views, and an internal support request form. It is not the system that takes payment from customers, and it is not the system that controls warehouse equipment. A problem in the portal can make a page slow, prevent a user from signing in, or delay an internal request, but it does not by itself mean that an order has been lost or a payment has been taken twice. The operations team checks each reported symptom and gives an update about what is known.

For this handbook, “service desk” means the group that receives user reports and passes technical issues to the operations team. “Operations team” means the people responsible for monitoring and maintaining the portal. “User” means an employee or partner with an approved account. These words are used the same way throughout the document. A user should give the service desk a clear description of what happened and should not send a password in a message.

Service overview
The portal has three main areas. The Home area displays staff notices and links. The Orders area shows a read-only summary of order records that are already available to the portal. The Help area lets a user submit a support request and see the status of that request. The Help area is the approved way to ask the service desk for ordinary assistance. The service desk can also receive a report by email when the portal itself is not available.

The portal is intended for normal browser use on a supported computer or phone. The operations team tests the current browser versions listed on the staff technology page. The team cannot promise identical behavior in every browser, on every device, or when a user has disabled required browser features. If a page does not load, first check that the device has an internet connection and that the user is using the correct portal address. Do not repeatedly submit the same form while the page appears slow. A repeated submission can create more than one support request.

The service is monitored by automated checks and by operations staff during the published coverage hours. Automated checks can identify whether the portal responds, but they cannot tell whether every user’s task is working correctly. A green monitor is useful information but does not prove that a particular user has no problem. Similarly, one user’s report does not prove that the whole service is unavailable. The operations team compares reports, monitoring information, and recent service changes before it describes the scope of an incident.

Service status and incidents
The status panel on the portal Home area shows the current service condition. The panel uses the labels “Operational,” “Degraded,” “Unavailable,” and “Maintenance.” Operational means that the main portal functions are responding as expected. Degraded means one or more functions are responding slowly or are only partly available. Unavailable means the main portal cannot be used by the affected users. Maintenance means that planned work is in progress or about to begin, and that some functions may be temporarily unavailable.

An incident is a service problem that needs operations attention. A report becomes an incident record when the service desk or operations team has enough information to track it. The incident record has a short title, a description of the observed effect, the time the report was received, and an owner. The incident title should describe the service symptom, not guess at its cause. For example, “Help form will not submit” is a better title than “database failure” when the cause has not yet been checked.

The operations team makes the first status update after it has confirmed the reported effect or has found a monitoring alert that supports the report. The update states what is affected, what is not yet known, and when the next update is expected. A status update should not claim that a cause is confirmed when the team is still investigating. The next update can say that there is no new finding; this is still useful because it tells users the incident is being followed.

When an issue is resolved, the operations team updates the status panel and records a short resolution summary. The summary describes what users should now be able to do. If a temporary workaround was used, the summary identifies it as a workaround rather than a permanent correction. The team may keep reviewing an incident after service has returned, especially if it needs to determine why the issue happened or how to reduce the chance of a similar issue.

Reporting a problem
A user reporting a problem should include the portal area, the approximate time, the action attempted, and the message shown on screen. A screenshot can help when it does not include private information. The user should say whether the problem happened once or several times and whether another approved user saw the same result. This information helps the service desk distinguish a local browser problem from a broader service issue.

Do not include a password, a full payment-card number, or another person’s private information in a support request. If a screenshot contains information that should not be shared, remove or cover that information before sending it. The service desk may ask for more details, but it should not ask the user to send a password. If a person receives a message asking for a password, they should not reply with it and should report the message through the usual security contact route.

When the Help area is available, use its “New request” button and choose the closest topic. The topic helps route the request but does not determine whether the request is valid. If no topic seems right, choose “Other portal question” and explain the issue in the description. A user should not open several requests for the same problem just to get a faster response. If another symptom appears later, add a comment to the existing request when possible.

When the portal cannot be opened, send an email to the service desk address listed in the staff directory. The subject should begin with “Portal issue” and should include a few words about the problem. The email should include the same basic details as a Help request. The service desk will create or update an incident record if the report needs operations attention. An email report does not need to be copied to several teams; the service desk is responsible for routing it.

Support request handling
The service desk reviews new requests and assigns them to a queue. A request about access is sent to the account support queue. A request about a page that is not loading is sent to the portal operations queue. A request about the wording or accuracy of a staff notice is sent to the content queue. If the request contains more than one matter, the service desk can split it into separate records so that each matter has a clear owner.

A request is not the same as an incident. A request can be an ordinary question, an access change, or a request for information. An incident is a disruption or reduction in service that needs investigation. A user does not need to decide which type applies before contacting the service desk. The service desk records the request in the appropriate way and tells the user if more information is needed.

The service desk acknowledges a request by placing a reply in the Help area or by replying to the email that was used to contact it. An acknowledgement confirms receipt; it does not mean the issue is already solved. If a user does not see an acknowledgement, the user should check the original request details and then contact the service desk once with the request reference, if available. Repeated messages without new information may make it harder to keep the record clear.

A service desk reply should be understandable and should state the next step where one is needed. If the user must try a simple check, the reply should explain what to do and what result to report. If operations needs to investigate, the service desk should say that the request is being passed to operations. The user should not be told that a technical cause is certain unless that cause has been verified by the responsible team.

Incident priority
The operations team assigns an incident priority based on the effect on users and the number of users affected. A broad interruption of the main portal is more urgent than a minor display problem affecting one user. A problem that prevents the Help area from accepting reports can also need urgent attention, because it blocks the usual contact route. Priority is an internal routing aid; it is not a promise that every incident with the same label will have the same resolution time.

The incident record uses the labels “Critical,” “High,” “Normal,” and “Low.” Critical is for a widespread loss of the main portal or a serious security concern that requires immediate operations coordination. High is for a major function that is unavailable to a substantial group, or for a problem that blocks important staff work with no practical workaround. Normal is for a limited disruption where users can continue some work or use a reasonable workaround. Low is for a minor inconvenience, a question, or a cosmetic issue that does not prevent the main task.

A reporter may describe an issue as urgent, but the operations team assigns the priority after reviewing the effect. A user should explain why the issue matters rather than selecting a priority as if it were guaranteed. The team can change the priority when new reports show that more people are affected or when a workaround becomes available. The incident history records such changes so later readers can understand the handling.

A priority does not change the facts in the incident description. For example, a page can be slow for one person without being a widespread outage. A reported blank page should be investigated, but the team should not assume that all portal areas are unavailable until it checks them. The status panel should reflect the known service impact and be updated when the scope changes.

Account access
Accounts are issued to approved users. The account support queue handles ordinary questions about sign-in, account status, and approved access changes. A user should sign in with the account assigned to that user and should not share credentials with a colleague. Sharing one account makes it difficult to know who performed an action and can create a security problem.

If a user forgets a password, the user should use the password-reset link on the sign-in page. If the link does not work, the user should contact account support and include the account name and the error message, but not the password. Account support checks the request using the approved verification process. It does not ask the user to reveal the old password or to send a password in an email.

Access to the Orders area is provided according to the user’s approved work role. A user who believes that the Orders area is missing should report the account name and the expected work role. The operations team checks the access record before changing permissions. A user should not ask another person to sign in and display restricted information on the user’s behalf.

When a user changes team or no longer needs portal access, the responsible manager should send an access-change request through the established route. The request should identify the account and the required change. Access changes are made by the authorized account support staff and are recorded. A request to remove access is not the same as a report that the whole portal is unavailable.

Planned maintenance
Planned maintenance is work scheduled in advance to keep the portal reliable and secure. The operations team posts a notice on the status panel and, when appropriate, sends a notice to portal users. The notice describes the affected service area, the expected start and finish, and any user action that may be needed. The notice should not suggest that a precise finish is certain when the work may take longer.

During maintenance, the portal status panel displays “Maintenance.” Some functions may continue to work while others are paused. Users should follow the notice and avoid repeating an action that has not completed. If an action appears to have stopped, the user can check the relevant page again after the maintenance notice ends and contact the service desk if the result is still unclear.

Maintenance is different from an unplanned incident. Planned work is announced in advance when possible and is performed for an identified operational reason. If the work causes an unexpected problem, the operations team opens or updates an incident record and changes the status information as needed. The fact that maintenance was scheduled does not mean that every problem reported during that period is necessarily part of the maintenance.

The operations team keeps a record of completed maintenance. The record includes the work performed, the service areas checked, and any follow-up task. A maintenance record is not a user support request, though a user report can help the team discover an issue associated with the work. Staff should use the normal reporting route if they see a problem during or after maintenance.

Change handling
A change is a planned modification to the portal, its configuration, or its supporting service. Each change has a description, an owner, a reason, and a check plan. The owner records what was changed and how the team will confirm that the change worked. Changes that can affect users should be scheduled and communicated in a way that avoids unnecessary surprise.

Before a change is completed, the responsible team considers the possible user impact and the steps for returning to the earlier configuration if the change does not work. A change record should be clear enough that another operations person can understand what was intended. A technical note that only the person who wrote it can understand is not sufficient for a reliable handover.

After a change, the owner checks the relevant portal functions. A successful check means the tested function behaved as expected at that time; it does not mean every possible use has been tested. If a user reports a new issue after a change, the team compares the report with the change record, but it should not assume a connection until the facts support that conclusion.

Small text corrections to a staff notice may follow a lighter review route than a technical change to sign-in or data access. The person responsible for the content still checks that the correction is accurate and approved. The distinction between a content correction and a technical change is recorded so that later readers know what kind of work took place.

Monitoring and alerts
Automated monitoring checks selected portal functions and sends an alert when a check does not receive the expected response. An alert is a signal for review, not a complete diagnosis. The operations team checks the alert, verifies whether the condition continues, and compares it with other monitoring results and user reports. A single short alert can clear before it affects users, while a continuing alert may indicate a larger issue.

The monitoring dashboard includes service response information, recent check results, and the state of selected supporting components. The dashboard is for operations use and may contain technical details that are not helpful to users. User-facing updates should describe the practical effect rather than copying internal alert text without explanation.

If monitoring shows an error but users report that the portal is working, the team still records and investigates the signal according to its normal process. If monitoring is green but a user cannot complete a task, the user report also remains valid and should be checked. Monitoring and user reports provide different kinds of evidence; neither should be ignored just because the other looks normal.

Operations staff should not change an alert threshold merely to stop an alert from appearing. A threshold change needs a reason, an owner, and a record. The team should check whether the alert is noisy because of a short-lived expected condition or because the monitored behavior is not configured correctly. The purpose is useful warning, not a dashboard with no red marks.

Data handling and privacy
The portal displays information needed for its stated internal purposes. Users should only view records that relate to their approved work. A support request should contain enough information to investigate but should not include unrelated personal information. If a user accidentally sends sensitive information, the user should tell the service desk so the record can be handled under the appropriate procedure.

Operations staff use approved accounts and follow the access rules for the work they perform. They should not copy portal data into personal storage or send it through an unapproved channel. When a technical investigation requires an example record, the team should use the minimum information needed and follow the normal access and retention controls.

A user who believes information is visible to the wrong person should report the concern promptly through the service desk and identify the affected area. The user should not attempt to investigate by viewing other people’s accounts. Operations will assess the report and involve the designated security contact when the facts require it. The report should be treated carefully even when the user is not certain that information was exposed.

The portal’s Orders area is a read-only summary. A displayed order status is information made available from the relevant record; the portal itself does not confirm delivery, authorize a payment, or change the order. If the information appears incorrect, report the displayed value and the relevant reference to the service desk. The team will identify which group owns the source record and route the question appropriately.

User responsibilities
Users should keep their account information private, use the approved portal address, and report an unexpected sign-in prompt or unusual page. Users should read service notices that apply to the task they are doing. If a notice asks the user to wait while work is completed, the user should avoid repeated submissions that could make the result less clear.

Users should describe what they observed rather than state an unverified technical explanation. “The Orders page stays blank after I select the record” is useful. “The server database is broken” may be a guess unless the user has direct evidence. The operations team can investigate a symptom without requiring the user to know the internal design of the portal.

Users should respond to reasonable requests for clarification. If the user no longer needs help, the user can say so in the existing request. If the problem is still occurring, the user should explain what was tried and what happened. Clear follow-up helps prevent a record from being closed while the user still needs assistance.

Users should not use the support request form for unrelated announcements or personal conversations. The service desk may redirect such messages to a more suitable route. The purpose of the form is to record a portal question, an access matter, or a service issue so it can be reviewed and assigned.

Operations responsibilities
Operations staff review monitoring information, manage incident records, and keep the service status information consistent with the known impact. They assign an owner to active work and provide a handover when another person takes over. A handover should say what is known, what has been tried, what remains uncertain, and what the next action is.

When a technical change is made during an incident, the person making it records the action and the observed result. If the change does not improve the service, the record should say so. Recording an unsuccessful action is important because it prevents another person from repeating it without understanding the history.

Operations staff should keep user communication factual and calm. They should avoid blaming a user or another team before the cause is understood. If the service team needs help from another group, operations records the handoff and remains clear about which team is currently responsible for the next action.

When an incident is resolved, the owner checks that the stated user impact has ended or is reduced as described. The owner records any remaining limitation. If further review is needed, the incident can be closed with a linked follow-up record, provided the user-facing service has returned to the stated condition. A follow-up task does not mean that the original service issue is still active.

Closure and follow-up
A support request can be closed when the question has been answered, the requested action has been completed, or the user confirms that no further help is needed. The closing message should summarize the outcome. If a user replies with new information after closure, the service desk can reopen the existing record or create a linked one, depending on whether it is the same issue.

An incident can be marked resolved when the affected function is again available or an agreed workaround has restored the reported task. If a workaround remains in place, the incident summary says that it is a workaround and identifies any limitation. A resolved incident may still have a review action, such as improving monitoring or documenting a technical cause.

The team reviews selected incidents to identify useful service improvements. The review may consider what happened, how the team learned about it, how users were informed, and whether the response process could be clearer. The goal is to improve service handling, not to assign blame to a person who made a good-faith report or performed an approved action.

A review record should distinguish confirmed facts from possible explanations. If the team has not confirmed the cause, it should say that the cause remains unknown. A practical action should have an owner and an expected completion point recorded in the team’s normal tracking system. A review is not complete merely because a meeting was held; the useful outcome is a clear record and a tracked action where one is needed.

Service desk contact routes
For a normal portal question, use the Help area and choose the closest topic. For an access question, choose the account topic. For a suspected service interruption, submit a request if the Help area works, or email the service desk if it does not. The service desk address is listed in the staff directory and is also printed in the internal contact page.

For a security concern, use the security contact route shown on the internal security page. If the concern also stops the portal from working, the user may report the service symptom to the service desk as well. The user should avoid sending sensitive material to a broad distribution list. The designated teams can coordinate without unnecessary copies of private information.

The service desk is not an emergency medical, physical safety, or public emergency contact. If a matter concerns immediate physical danger, staff should use the established local emergency process. The portal support route is for portal and account matters only. This separation helps the correct response team receive the message without delay.

If a user is unsure which contact route applies, the user can send a short description to the service desk and ask for routing. The service desk will redirect the message if another internal team owns it. The user should not need to know the internal reporting structure before making an ordinary portal report.

Internal communication
Operations uses an incident channel for active service issues. The incident owner posts the current findings and the next action. Team members should keep technical discussion in the channel or incident record so that a person joining later can follow the history. Important decisions made by phone or meeting should be added to the incident record afterward.

The incident channel is not a replacement for user-facing status updates. Internal terms may be useful to engineers but confusing to users. The incident owner or communications delegate prepares a short public update that says what is affected and what users can do. Internal speculation should not be copied to the status panel as if it were a verified finding.

A staff member who notices an issue should share the observed facts and the time, even if another person has already started investigation. The incident owner can decide whether the report adds new information. Reports from different users can show that the impact is broader than first expected, and the team should not discard them only because the initial report is already recorded.

At shift change, the outgoing owner gives the incoming owner a concise but complete summary. It includes the incident status, affected functions, last user update, actions already attempted, and next expected check. If there is no new information, that should be stated directly. A silent handover can lead to duplicated work or an update being missed.

Service quality measures
The operations team reviews basic service measures to understand whether the portal is working reliably. Measures can include successful page checks, response behavior, incident counts, and time taken to acknowledge requests. A measure is useful only when its meaning and limitations are understood. A count of requests does not automatically tell the team how many users were affected, because several requests can describe one issue and one request can describe a problem affecting many users.

The team uses measures to find patterns and choose improvements. A sudden increase in sign-in questions may indicate a confusing instruction or an account process issue. A number of reports about one page may indicate that the page needs review. Before drawing a conclusion, the team checks the underlying records and considers whether reporting habits changed.

A service measure should not be used to discourage a user from reporting a genuine problem. The purpose of measurement is to improve service, not to make the number of reports appear small. Operations should preserve useful context when it combines related records, so the history remains understandable.

When the team reports service quality, it should say which period and which measure are being described. A statement such as “the portal was available” should not imply that every page and every individual account worked at every moment. The team should describe the measured scope and any known limitation in ordinary language.

Knowledge and documentation
The operations team keeps short knowledge notes for common user questions and repeatable checks. A note should have a title that describes the task, a last review date, and an owner. The steps should be tested before they are shared as instructions. If the service changes, the owner updates the note or marks it for review rather than allowing old instructions to remain unnoticed.

A knowledge note should separate what a user can safely do from what only an authorized operations person may do. It should not encourage users to change technical settings that they do not understand. If a safe self-check does not solve the problem, the note should tell the user how to contact the service desk.

The service desk can use a knowledge note to answer a repeated question, but it should consider whether the note fits the user’s exact situation. A general instruction is not proof that a particular report has been resolved. The service desk should ask a follow-up question if the observed behavior does not match the note.

When a note is retired, the owner removes it from the active list or marks it clearly as no longer current. Retired notes can be retained in the documentation history when needed, but they should not appear as current advice. Documentation should help people act consistently, not create another source of confusion.

Operational handover notes
A handover note is prepared when work passes between staff members or teams. It uses a clear date and identifies the service or record involved. It states the present condition, actions completed, open questions, and the next owner or action. It should avoid unexplained short forms when the reader may not know them.

Handover notes must not contain passwords or unnecessary personal data. If a secure reference is needed, use the approved record link rather than copying private content into a general channel. The next person should have enough context to continue the work while still following the access rules.

If there is no work to transfer, a handover can simply say that there is no active incident and identify any scheduled task that remains. A handover need not invent activity. Clear absence of pending work is better than leaving the next person to guess whether something has been missed.

When a handover is received, the new owner acknowledges it and asks for clarification if an important point is missing. The outgoing person remains available for reasonable questions during the transition where practical. This process helps keep service work continuous across different working periods.

Appendix A: Plain-language status examples
“Operational: The main portal functions are responding normally according to current checks.” This description does not promise that every personal device has no issue. If one user is unable to sign in, that user should still contact account support.

“Degraded: The Orders area is slower than normal for some users. Home and Help remain available. Operations is checking the cause.” This gives users an idea of the affected area without claiming that the entire portal is unavailable.

“Unavailable: The main portal cannot currently be opened by the affected staff group. Operations is investigating. Users should avoid repeated form submissions and check for the next status update.” This states the current impact and a practical instruction.

“Maintenance: Planned work is in progress. Some portal functions may not respond until the work is complete. Please follow the notice and contact the service desk if a problem remains afterward.” This tells users that the condition is planned while still allowing them to report a continuing issue.

“Resolved: The Help form is accepting requests again. If a request submitted during the interruption is missing, contact the service desk with the approximate submission time.” This is more helpful than simply saying “fixed,” because it tells users what function returned and what to do if their own request is not visible.

Appendix B: Example report contents
A useful report might say: “At about 10:20 this morning I opened the Orders area on my work laptop. The order summary page stayed blank after I selected reference GF-184. I refreshed once and got the same result. The Home area still opened. I do not know if another user has the same problem.” This includes an approximate time, location in the portal, action, observed result, and a check already tried. It does not claim a cause.

A report that says only “portal broken” may still be accepted, but the service desk will probably need to ask what the user was doing and what appeared. A user who cannot provide a reference should still report the symptom in ordinary terms. The service desk can begin with the information available and ask a simple follow-up question.

A report should not include a copied password, a full private record, or another user’s unrelated account details. If the user has a screenshot, the user should check it before attaching it. The goal is to show the problem without exposing more information than is necessary.

Appendix C: Common questions
Question: “The status panel says Operational, but my page does not open. Is my report still useful?” Yes. The status panel describes the current overall service checks, and a single user can still have a problem. Report the page, approximate time, and message shown so the service desk can check the specific case.

Question: “I clicked Submit twice because the first page seemed slow. Should I send another request?” First check whether a request reference appeared or whether the request is visible in Help. If there is a duplicate, tell the service desk which records appear to be repeated. Do not keep submitting the same form just to test it.

Question: “Does an acknowledgement mean operations has solved my issue?” No. It means the request was received. The reply should say whether the service desk needs more information or has passed the issue to another team.

Question: “Can I give my password to a colleague so they can check the same page?” No. Each approved user should use their own account. Ask the colleague to report what they see under their own account, or ask the service desk to check the access question.

Question: “Should I pick Critical when I submit a request?” A user can explain the impact, but the operations team assigns incident priority after reviewing the facts. Give the service desk a clear description of who is affected and which task cannot be completed.

Question: “If an issue happens during maintenance, should I ignore it?” No. Follow the maintenance notice and report a problem that remains or that appears unexpected. Planned work and an unplanned issue are different records, even if they occur at the same time.

Appendix D: Record quality checklist
Before an incident update is published, the owner checks that the service area is named, the impact is described in plain language, and uncertain details are not presented as confirmed. The owner also checks that the next update expectation is sensible. If the situation changes before that time, the owner can post earlier information.

Before a request is closed, the service desk checks that an answer or outcome is recorded and that the user has a clear next step if the issue continues. Before an incident is closed, operations checks the affected function and records any remaining workaround or follow-up. These checks are short, but they make later review much easier.

If a record has no clear owner, the person who notices this should assign or request an owner rather than leaving the record unattended. If two records appear to describe the same issue, the service desk can link them. The original reports should remain traceable so that each reporter’s information is not lost.

A record can contain a correction when an earlier detail was mistaken. The correction should explain what changed and why, without deleting the history needed to understand the investigation. Clear records support users, operations staff, and future service improvements.

Appendix E: Staff portal boundaries
The staff portal presents internal information, but it is not a substitute for the official system that owns a business record. If an order summary looks wrong, the user should report it for checking. The portal display alone does not change the underlying order. If a support request is submitted, the request records the question; it does not itself approve a business transaction.

The portal also does not replace the company’s standard communications for urgent business decisions. A staff notice can point to an approved process, but the user should follow that process when the task requires a formal approval. Operations staff maintain the portal and route technical reports; they do not decide every business question that appears in a support request.

These boundaries are included so that reports go to the right owner. A portal technical issue should go to the service desk or operations. An account permission question should go to account support. A question about the content of a business record should be routed to the group responsible for that record. The service desk can help direct a user when the correct group is not obvious.

Appendix F: Routine operations day
At the beginning of a working period, the operations person reviews the status panel, recent monitoring alerts, and open incident records. The person checks whether an incident has a current owner and whether a user update is due. If all checks are normal, the person records the routine review according to the team practice. A routine check is not a claim that no user can have a problem.

During the working period, new alerts and reports are reviewed as they arrive. The person records a time and a concise finding, then decides whether an existing incident should be updated or a new record should be opened. When several reports concern the same symptom, they can be linked to one incident while retaining the individual reports.

Before the end of a working period, the owner reviews open work and prepares any needed handover. An incident with no new information still receives a clear handover if it remains active. If there is no active issue, the person does not need to create an incident merely to fill the record; a routine operational review can be documented in its normal place.

The routine is meant to keep information current without making claims beyond what has been checked. A status panel, an incident record, and a support reply serve different readers, but they should not contradict one another. If a difference is noticed, the owner checks the facts and corrects the appropriate communication.

Appendix G: User communication examples
A useful acknowledgement is: “We received your report about the Help form. The service desk is checking whether the request was saved. Please do not submit the same form again for now. We will reply in this request when we have checked.” This confirms receipt and sets an immediate expectation without claiming that the cause is known.

A useful investigation update is: “Some users cannot open the Orders summary. Home and Help are responding in current checks. Operations is investigating the Orders area and will post another update when there is a change.” This identifies scope and avoids saying all portal functions are down.

A useful request for detail is: “Could you tell us the approximate time, the page you opened, and the words shown in the error message? Please do not send your password.” This asks for information the team can use and reminds the user of a privacy boundary.

A useful closure is: “The account support team restored access to your portal account. Please try signing in with your own account. If the same message appears, reply to this request with the time and wording.” This states the outcome and gives a clear route if the problem continues.

Appendix H: Keeping the handbook useful
The handbook owner reviews this document when the portal changes in a way that affects user instructions or when the service desk finds a section that causes repeated confusion. Staff can suggest a correction by sending the section name and the proposed clarification to the documentation owner. A suggestion is not automatically an approved policy change; the owner checks it with the relevant operations lead before updating the current instructions.

When an update is made, the owner identifies the changed section and records the revision in the document history. Small wording corrections can improve clarity without changing the process. A change to a contact route, access rule, status label, or operational responsibility should be reviewed by the team responsible for that subject.

The purpose of this handbook is to give consistent, practical guidance. It does not replace a specific approved instruction that is newer and directly relevant to a task. If staff find two current instructions that appear to conflict, they should ask the responsible owner to clarify and should not silently choose whichever instruction is easiest. The clarified instruction should then be reflected in the documentation so the same question does not remain unclear.

End of handbook. The normal portal problem contact route is the service desk, available through the Help area when the portal is working and by the service desk email listed in the staff directory when the portal cannot be opened. The main incident status labels remain Operational, Degraded, Unavailable, and Maintenance. The incident priority labels remain Critical, High, Normal, and Low.

Copperleaf Labs — fabrication agreement, amendment packet, and shop-floor notes

A slightly rambling file assembled by Beatriz Rahman, who says she prefers one untidy packet to twelve tidy ones that nobody can find. Copperleaf Labs is a small manufacturing shop making short runs of instrument brackets and enclosures. Saltmarsh Freight carries some of the finished cartons. The packet concerns order CL-481, placed by Wanjiru Haddad for a prototype line. This is a working copy; dates, quantities, and responsibilities below are part of the file, not assumptions about ordinary industry practice.

DOCUMENT A — ORIGINAL FABRICATION AGREEMENT, SIGNED 4 MARCH

1. Parties and work. Copperleaf Labs (“Shop”) will cut, deburr, and assemble 120 aluminum sensor brackets for Wanjiru Haddad (“Customer”). The drawing revision is C-7. Customer supplies two inspection gauges; Shop supplies stock and fasteners. The Shop’s quotation, Q-481, is attached only for unit price and estimated schedule. If the quotation conflicts with this agreement, this agreement controls.

2. Price and payment. Unit price is $38.00, for a total base price of $4,560. Customer pays a deposit of $1,200 on signing. The remaining base amount is due within 15 calendar days after delivery. A separate packing fee of $90 is due with the balance. A line on an early draft says “all freight prepaid by the Shop,” but the executed agreement’s paragraph 8 says freight is billed separately to Customer at carrier cost. The early draft is not incorporated.

3. Schedule. The scheduled ship date is 18 March. “Ship date” means the date the Shop tenders the cartons to the carrier, not the date Customer receives them. A delay of up to two business days caused by a documented machine outage does not by itself constitute a missed ship date. A delay outside that allowance may trigger the service credit in paragraph 7, but only if Customer sends the notice described there. Shop will not be liable for delays caused by a carrier after tender.

4. Acceptance. Customer has five business days after receipt to inspect. A written defect notice must identify the affected quantity and the drawing requirement allegedly missed. Silence is not deemed acceptance if Customer has sent a timely defect notice; otherwise, the shipment is accepted on the sixth business day. A scratched carton alone does not establish that the brackets are defective. Shop may replace confirmed nonconforming pieces, but replacement does not automatically waive a separately earned late-shipment credit.

5. Change requests. A drawing or quantity change is effective only when both parties approve a dated change order. Informal messages may explain a request but do not amend price, delivery date, or quantity. Shop must not treat a Customer’s inquiry as approval. The parties can, however, use email signatures to approve a change order if the email clearly identifies the changed term and says it is approved by both sides.

6. Inspection gauges. Customer is responsible for collecting its gauges from the Shop within ten calendar days after the last accepted delivery. The Shop must not discard a gauge unless it has first sent two written reminders, at least three calendar days apart, and Customer has not responded to either. “Not unresponsive” means Customer has replied in writing, even if the reply only says that collection is being arranged. The Shop is not required to ship gauges unless a written change order says so.

7. Late credit and notice. If the Shop tenders the complete order later than the scheduled ship date plus the permitted two-business-day outage allowance, Customer may claim a credit of $25 per calendar day, capped at $125. Customer must send a written claim within five calendar days after tender. There is no credit if the order was late solely because Customer approved a change order that moved the date. This clause was written in a hurry; the signed amendment below clarifies how to count the allowance and which delivery record controls.

8. Freight and risk. Customer pays the carrier’s actual charge. Risk transfers when the carrier signs the Shop’s pickup receipt. An internal packing slip is not proof of tender. If the carrier’s scan and the signed receipt differ, use the signed receipt unless the amendment expressly supplies a different rule. Shop will share the dispatch record on request.

9. Order of documents. This agreement controls over Q-481 and informal messages. A later bilateral amendment controls over an earlier paragraph to the extent it specifically changes that paragraph. An amendment does not silently change unrelated terms. If two provisions in this signed agreement remain inconsistent, the more specific provision governs. A clerk’s copied summary has no amendment force.

DOCUMENT B — AMENDMENT 1, BOTH PARTIES’ EMAIL APPROVAL, 11 MARCH

Subject: Approved date and pickup record for CL-481

Wanjiru: “I approve the change to the ship date to 20 March because the extra inspection fixture is arriving. No change to quantity or the price.”

Beatriz: “Copperleaf approves that date change. I also want the record to be clear: for this order only, use the carrier-signed pickup receipt as tender evidence, and count the two-business-day outage allowance after the revised date, excluding the ship date itself. Everything else in sections 1–9 stays put.”

Wanjiru: “Agreed to the entire change as stated. I am not disagreeing with the receipt rule.”

Beatriz: “Confirmed, amendment approved by both parties.”

The Shop’s document index calls this “Amendment 1.” A later handwritten note in the index says “date maybe 19th?” but no party approved that note. The amendment changes the scheduled ship date from 18 March to 20 March and clarifies the outage allowance and tender evidence. It does not change the five-calendar-day claim period, the daily amount, or the cap.

DOCUMENT C — DISPATCH LOG AND MACHINE LOG, COPIED 27 MARCH

17 March, 16:10 — Machine M-2 stopped after a belt alarm. Maintenance ticket opened.
18 March — Machine M-2 unavailable. No production entry for CL-481.
19 March — Technician log: belt replaced; machine run tested at 14:00. Production resumed. Beatriz’s informal note: “Probably two down days, unless the 17th is included?”
20 March — Scheduled date as amended. Packing and final count completed. No carrier signature that day.
21 March, 09:30 — Carrier scan in Saltmarsh Freight portal says “label created / shipment data received.” This is not a signed pickup receipt.
22 March, 08:15 — Carrier-signed pickup receipt: 120 cartons’ worth of brackets, one pallet, tendered at Copperleaf dock. Both the Shop dock worker and carrier driver signed. The freight portal later shows a separate “received at regional hub” scan at 18:42.
22 March, 10:05 — Beatriz emailed: “We are glad it got collected today; attached signed receipt.”
24 March — Carrier portal marks shipment delivered. Customer’s receiving clerk signed; no damage notation.

An older one-page dispatch summary says, “Tender 21 March; scan found.” It was generated from the portal’s label-created event and conflicts with the signed pickup receipt and Beatriz’s attached record. The dispatcher wrote in the margin, “Do not rely on old summary; it is not the actual handoff.” The amendment says the signed receipt controls. The machine record supports downtime on 18 March, and the repair was complete on 19 March; whether that counts as one or two business days is determined by the amendment’s counting instruction. Saturday and Sunday are not business days under section 3’s shop calendar. The shop calendar lists Monday through Friday as business days and makes no special holiday exception for this period.

DOCUMENT D — CUSTOMER EMAILS ABOUT INSPECTION AND GAUGES

25 March, 09:02, Wanjiru: “The cartons arrived yesterday. I have not found any defect in the brackets so far. I am not saying there are no possible issues; inspection is still in progress.”

26 March, 15:41, Wanjiru: “I do not dispute that all 120 were delivered. Two have a burr at the lower tab, which is not within the C-7 edge condition. Please record a defect notice for two pieces. The rest look fine.”

26 March, 16:03, Beatriz: “I read that as no defect report because you wrote ‘do not dispute delivery.’”

26 March, 16:20, Wanjiru: “No, that is not what I meant. I am reporting two pieces as defective; the words about delivery only confirm the count.”

27 March, 11:10, Copperleaf quality note: “We checked the two identified pieces against C-7. Burr exceeds the specified limit on both. Replace two pieces.”

The quality note is a separate finding, not a change to the delivery count. There are 118 acceptable pieces and two confirmed nonconforming pieces. Customer’s message arrived two calendar days after receipt, and the contract allows five business days. For the acceptance clause, notice must identify both quantity and requirement; Wanjiru’s email identifies two and the C-7 edge condition. A draft email from the receiving clerk says “No defects, all good,” but the clerk later explained it was a prefilled template and was never sent to Copperleaf.

28 March, 08:40, Beatriz: “We can replace two, and I have not failed to keep the gauges. Please arrange collection.”
28 March, 09:05, Wanjiru: “We have not arranged collection yet, but we are arranging a van. Please do not throw the gauges away.”

29 March — Shop reminder 1: “Your two gauges remain here. Please arrange collection.”
1 April — Shop reminder 2: “Second reminder; please confirm collection.”
2 April — Wanjiru replies: “I am not ignoring these notices. We are arranging collection for Friday 5 April.”

A clerk’s worksheet says “unresponsive after two notices,” despite the written reply. Section 6 defines a response broadly and requires no response to either reminder before disposal. Another note says, “They did not fail to reply,” which is a double-negative phrasing of the same fact, not evidence that the reply was absent. The gauges remained on the shelf on 3 April. The collection van arrived 5 April, and the signed gauge receipt records both gauges returned to Wanjiru.

DOCUMENT E — CREDIT REQUEST, 27 MARCH

Wanjiru’s email, sent 27 March at 13:12: “I am not waiving the delay credit. Under Amendment 1, the pickup receipt is dated 22 March. Please apply any credit due. This is not a claim that the carrier caused the delay after handoff; I am asking about when Copperleaf tendered it.”

Beatriz’s reply, 28 March: “Our old dispatch summary says 21 March, so I thought there was no late tender. We also had a machine outage, and we are not saying it lasted three business days. I’ll recalculate using the amendment.”

The request was delivered to Copperleaf’s accounts inbox on 27 March. The signed pickup receipt is 22 March. Count the claim deadline as five calendar days after tender, with the day after tender as day 1. The claim email therefore falls within the specified period. An accounts spreadsheet mistakenly uses 21 March from the portal label scan and labels the message “day six”; its author states below that the spreadsheet copied the label-created date rather than the signed handoff. Another internal comment says, “If the outage were three days, maybe no credit,” but it was not three business days and no such finding appears in the maintenance log.

DOCUMENT F — LATER CHAT, NOT AN AMENDMENT

Beatriz: “We should just call it 21 March; all those scans are basically the same.”
Wanjiru: “I am not agreeing to replace the signed receipt date with a portal scan. The amendment says receipt controls.”
Beatriz: “Fair, I was venting about paperwork. This chat changes no contract term.”

A copied top-line summary says “no credit, no defect, gauges abandoned.” It is labeled “quick shorthand,” not an approved determination, and each phrase is contradicted by the documents above: Wanjiru sent a timely credit request, quality confirmed two defects, and Wanjiru replied to the gauge reminders and collected the gauges. These disputes are precisely why the file was put together instead of relying on the shorthand.

APPENDIX — SHOP CALENDAR AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHATTER

The shop calendar for March and April shows weekdays as business days, with weekends shaded gray. There is no listed closure or holiday between 18 and 22 March. The production board has a handwritten arrow from “belt alarm” to “machine back 19th,” and an old sticky note says “two days?” The formal maintenance record gives the machine unavailable on 18 March and restored at 14:00 on 19 March. Because the amendment says count business days after the revised ship date and excludes the ship date itself, the eligible business-day allowance begins on the next business day. The date calculation must use the written amendment and the actual tender proof, not the sticky note or a portal status.

The customer’s order is not the only order in the binder. Nearby tabs refer to CL-477, whose ship date was 19 March and whose cartons were collected on 21 March, and CL-489, which used a different carrier. Neither order is part of CL-481. A note on the shared production board says “all Copperleaf jobs moved one day,” but it is a general estimate and was not approved as a change to Wanjiru’s date. For this contract, only the bilateral 11 March date change is effective.

At the March stand-up, Tomas in maintenance said, “Nobody should have to guess from a scan,” and asked accounting to attach signed receipts. The minute-taker mistakenly wrote, “The team agreed no signed receipt was needed.” Beatriz corrected that minute in the same document: “Correction: we agreed the opposite; keep the signed receipt.” The correction is initialed. This resembles the conflicting dispatch summary but does not alter the contract; it confirms that the summary’s shorthand is unreliable.

The accounting system uses a box marked “late shipment credit,” but that box was checked automatically when the original 18 March date passed. An adjacent field says “do not send credit unless eligibility confirmed.” The system did not issue a credit. A later operator note says “not ineligible,” but that statement is not itself an approval. The eligibility question depends on the amended date, the business-day allowance, downtime documented for the relevant period, the tender date, and the timely written claim. The amount, if earned, uses calendar days past the adjusted deadline and the stated cap; it is not calculated by counting hub scans or delivery days.

A separate replacement-parts label was generated 2 April for the two burr-affected pieces. The label date is not the original order’s tender date and does not reopen the credit deadline. Customer accepted replacement pieces on 8 April, after checking the edge condition. An internal note says “replacement resolves all claims,” but the contract says replacement does not automatically waive a separately earned late credit. Wanjiru did not sign a release. The two replacement pieces are not part of a new 120-piece quantity obligation; they remedy the two confirmed nonconforming items.

On 10 April, Beatriz circulated a reconciliation with four lines: “Base invoice $4,560”; “deposit received $1,200”; “packing $90”; “freight pass-through pending carrier statement.” The remaining base amount is computed from the base price less the deposit; packing and freight are separate. The reconciliation’s margin says “Maybe customer owes $3,450 before freight and any credit.” That figure is a handwritten arithmetic error: $4,560 minus $1,200 plus $90 is $3,450, before freight and any credit. It has no bearing on whether the late credit condition was met. No payment question is being asked here.

The packet ends with Beatriz’s note: “I know this is too much paper for 120 little brackets, but the point is not that every summary is malicious. Some are rushed, some are guesses, and some copy yesterday’s guess into today’s column. Use the signed amendment, the actual records, and the definitions. Do not transform ‘not disagreeing’ into disagreement, or ‘not no defect’ into a clean inspection, without reading the rest of the sentence.”

state:
Saltmarsh Freight / Bluefin Labs shop packet — service terms, FAQ, and production correspondence

Prepared by Dalia Alvarez for the Bluefin Labs small-shop desk. Bluefin makes short-run control-panel housings and miniature pump mounts in a rented back room with three benches, a noisy compressor, and a noticeboard that people keep covering with jokes. The packet concerns Nadia Haddad’s order BL-206 and the shop’s optional “Bench-to-Door” service. This is a long bundle because the terms were edited by several people and the FAQ kept the old wording for a while. The names and events here belong to this order only.

SECTION 1 — BLUEFIN LABS BENCH-TO-DOOR TERMS, VERSION 2.1, POSTED 2 MAY

These terms govern a shop customer’s optional delivery service when the customer checks the service box and Bluefin confirms it. Bluefin is the fabricator; Saltmarsh Freight is the contracted carrier. A customer’s own email asking whether delivery is possible is not, by itself, a service selection. A confirmed order receipt will state whether the service is active. “Dispatch” means the carrier’s signed collection at Bluefin’s loading door, not a label print, booking request, or warehouse scan.

A. Customer selection. The customer may elect delivery by selecting “Bench-to-Door” on the signed order form. If the customer leaves the box blank, Bluefin will hold completed goods for collection at the shop unless the customer and Bluefin later approve a written service change. The order confirmation repeats the selected service. A staff member must not infer selection from a question such as “Can you send it?” or from a quote that lists an optional charge.

B. Risk and handling. For an active Bench-to-Door order, the carrier takes custody at signed dispatch. Bluefin is responsible for packing damage caused by its own packing before dispatch. Saltmarsh Freight is responsible for loss or visible transit damage after signed dispatch, subject to the claims procedure. The customer must report visible damage within three calendar days after delivery, including a photo and the carton count. Hidden machining or material defects are handled under the fabrication warranty, not the freight claim procedure.

C. Service window. A confirmed service order includes dispatch by the date stated on the order receipt. If Bluefin misses that date by more than one business day, the customer may request a $40 service credit per additional business day, capped at $160. The first business day after the stated date is the one-day grace period. A customer must send the request within seven calendar days after actual dispatch. A delay caused solely by a customer-approved drawing revision moves the stated date by the number of shop days shown on the signed revision. A provisional sketch or an unsigned chat does not move the date.

D. Shop closure. A declared shop closure counts as a non-business day only if it is listed on the dated shop calendar and communicated to the customer before the due date. An unlisted closure does not extend the service date. If the compressor or laser cutter fails, that is not automatically a closure; a service manager must write a downtime record. The record may explain a delay but does not itself change a date unless a signed amendment says it does.

E. Warranty and return. Bluefin warrants that the fabricated parts meet the drawing revision identified on the order receipt. The customer must give written notice within ten calendar days after receipt, identifying the part and the relevant drawing tolerance. No response does not mean the customer agrees that the part is defective. Conversely, a statement that “I do not disagree that this is within tolerance” is not a warranty claim unless the customer also identifies an out-of-tolerance feature. The clause is meant to avoid treating a cautious acknowledgment as a defect report.

F. Contradictory records. The signed order receipt controls over a draft quote. A signed revision approved by both parties controls only the terms it changes. The dispatch definition above controls over automated portal events. A FAQ or staff note is explanatory and does not amend these terms. When an order receipt and an internal tracker conflict, use the signed receipt unless a later bilateral amendment expressly says otherwise.

SECTION 2 — ORDER BL-206, SIGNED 6 MAY

Customer: Nadia Haddad. Shop: Bluefin Labs. Product: 36 miniature pump mounts, drawing MH-4, revision B. Goods are to be wrapped individually and placed in six cartons. The stated dispatch date is 14 May. The signed order form’s Bench-to-Door selection box is blank. In the service selection field, the form says “customer collection.” A draft quote prepared the day before lists “delivery option, $68” in an unselected price row. The draft is not the signed order receipt.

Price is $1,980 total, excluding optional delivery. Customer pays a $600 deposit, with the remainder due after receipt. The order does not contain a delivery service charge because the selection was blank. At the bottom of the form, a printed line says, “I do not decline the option of carrier delivery,” but this is standard language and does not replace the checked selection box. Nadia initialed the blank service box and wrote beside it, “I’ll confirm transport after I check with my team; please don’t book a carrier yet.”

Bluefin’s confirmation email on 6 May says: “We have your order for 36 mounts, collection from our shop. Delivery remains optional and is not active. We have not booked Saltmarsh Freight.” Nadia replied: “That’s right for now. I am not saying I will never want delivery, but please leave this order as collection unless I send the change form.” The signed form and confirmation match.

SECTION 3 — CHANGE FORM AND AMBIGUOUS MESSAGES

9 May, 10:12, Nadia to Dalia: “Could Saltmarsh maybe collect these if we get behind? I’m not refusing delivery; I’m just checking capacity and price. No booking yet.”

9 May, 11:00, Dalia: “We can quote it. Please sign the service change if you want us to activate it.”

10 May, 15:26, Nadia: “I do not disagree that carrier delivery might be convenient. But that is not approval, and I have not selected it. We will collect on the 14th unless I send the signed form.”

A shop chat copied into the file says, “Nadia wants delivery, all set,” posted by an operator who saw only the first sentence of the 9 May message. A supervisor replies five minutes later: “Correction, that’s not what she authorized; no signed change form.” The correction is preserved in the thread. No signed service change form was received. The automated sales system, however, generated a draft delivery label on 12 May after a clerk clicked “quote delivery.” Its event says “shipment data received.” There was no carrier pickup and no signed handoff on that date.

The internal order tracker says “Bench-to-Door: yes — $68,” and a manager’s morning note says “customer did not fail to request transport.” The tracker was populated from the draft quote, not the signed form. A separate note says “not no service,” which is a confusing double-negative interpretation written by the clerk; it is not an approved service selection. Section 1 requires selection and confirmation, and the signed receipt identifies collection.

SECTION 4 — DATED SHOP CALENDAR AND PRODUCTION NOTES

The shop calendar, posted 1 May and emailed to active customers 2 May, lists 8 May as a planned inventory closure. It lists no closure on 14, 15, 16, 17, or 20 May. The compressor failed at 16:50 on 13 May. Dalia opened maintenance ticket M-19. The laser cutter continued to operate; the compressor was needed for the packing clamp but not for machining. The record says the clamp was repaired at 09:10 on 15 May. Shop work continued on 14 and 15 May, though packing for BL-206 moved to the afternoon of the 15th. The shop calendar does not mark either date closed.

The production board has two conflicting handwritten entries. One says “closed 14th — compressor”; the other says “not closed, just slow, benches running.” Dalia’s signed daily report says the shop was open and producing on 14 May. The first note was corrected with “not a declared closure; disregard.” Because the terms require a listed closure communicated in advance, neither maintenance trouble nor the mistaken board note automatically extends a date.

A separate job for Quentin Kaur had its deadline moved after a signed drawing revision on 13 May. Its note says “add 2 shop days.” That adjustment applies only to Quentin’s job. Someone copied “+2 days” into the shared BL-206 tracker, and later crossed it out. Nadia did not approve a drawing revision; MH-4 revision B remained unchanged. A note in the production channel says “Nadia did not request any revision,” and the part count and drawing remained stable.

Bluefin completed inspection of the mounts on 16 May. Internal quality sheet: 36 pieces counted, all dimensions checked against MH-4 revision B, one mount marked “recheck surface appearance,” no out-of-tolerance measurement. That note was later resolved: the mark was a lighting reflection, not a scratch. On 17 May, Nadia asked by email, “Are the housings as good as the mounts we saw last month?” This was about a different product and did not allege any defect in BL-206. The request for an inspection update is not itself a warranty notice.

SECTION 5 — FAQ EXCERPT, REVISION 1.8, OLD WEBSITE CACHE

Q: If I ask whether you can ship my parts, does that mean delivery is active?
A: No. A question or quote request does not select the service. Use the signed service change form and wait for a revised order confirmation.

Q: What if the portal says “shipment received” before the carrier has picked up?
A: Portal phrases can refer to uploaded shipment data. The signed carrier collection record is the dispatch evidence under the current terms.

Q: Does a machine hiccup automatically push a deadline?
A: No. A documented failure can help explain what happened, but it does not move the date unless a signed revision says so. The FAQ’s earlier answer, from an obsolete version, said “Any compressor trouble adds two days.” That sentence was removed because it contradicted the approved terms. A cached copy still shows it, and a staff member pasted the old wording into a chat: “No need to check calendars; all compressor issues are two extra days.” The terms control; no two-day extension was approved for Nadia’s order.

Q: When does the one-business-day grace period end?
A: The stated date itself is not the grace day. The next business day is. If dispatch happens on that day, the service is not yet more than one business day late. The credit begins for each additional business day after that. This FAQ answer is consistent with section C.

Q: What if the customer says, “I don’t disagree that the part is fine”?
A: That phrase alone is not a defect report. A warranty notice needs to identify an out-of-tolerance feature, part, and drawing requirement. Do not turn an absence of disagreement into an affirmative complaint.

Q: Does “I do not decline delivery” select delivery?
A: No. Check the signed selection and order confirmation. A double negative in a conversation is not a substitute for the required service change.

SECTION 6 — LATER CUSTOMER THREAD AND RECEIPTS

20 May, 08:34, Nadia: “The mounts are ready, and we are still planning to collect. I am not refusing the order; I am asking whether your front door is clear for our van.”

20 May, 09:02, Dalia: “Door is clear. We have no carrier collection booked. Your signed order says customer collection.”

20 May, 10:11, Nadia: “Thanks. The van will be there tomorrow.”

21 May, 13:20 — Nadia’s employee arrived in a blue van and collected six cartons. The shop handover sheet is signed by both parties. It records all 36 mounts and no carton damage. There is no Saltmarsh Freight signature, no carrier bill, and no freight charge. Portal activity still shows a label draft from 12 May and an automated “ready for pickup” notice, but those are not dispatch events under the terms.

21 May, 17:05, Nadia: “We collected all six cartons. I have not found a defect, and I am not claiming that a part is out of tolerance. I’ll write if inspection finds anything.”

22 May, 09:40, quality email from Nadia: “To be clear, I do not dispute that the mounts look good from the outside. One mounting slot on piece 14 may be 0.3 mm narrower than the B drawing minimum. We have not measured it yet, so this is not a confirmed defect report; can you tell me where the tolerance is shown?”

22 May, 10:02, Dalia: “The B drawing shows slot width at line 6. Please send a measurement if it is out.”

24 May, 14:18, Nadia: “We measured piece 14. Slot is within the B minimum. I am not saying it is out of tolerance; the caliper was mis-zeroed. No warranty claim.”

The first 22 May message is tentative and requests clarification, while the 24 May message expressly resolves the measurement as within tolerance. No later message alleges a defect. The shop’s warranty inbox nevertheless auto-created a ticket labelled “slot too narrow,” because it searched the email for those words. Dalia changed the status to “no confirmed defect; customer corrected measurement.” A spreadsheet copy still says “claim open.”

SECTION 7 — TICKET SUMMARY CONFLICTS AND ADMIN CHATTER

An end-of-month list prepared by an operator contains the following three short lines: “Carrier delivery active; dispatched 12 May; credit due”; “two-day closure exception”; “part 14 warranty claim.” Each line is contradicted or corrected elsewhere in the packet. The customer’s signed selection is collection; 12 May was only a draft-label event; the shop was not closed under the stated definition; and Nadia withdrew the suspected measurement issue after finding the caliper was mis-zeroed. The list was created by copying old FAQ phrases and tracker fields. It is not a signed revision, amended receipt, or customer statement.

Dalia adds: “The tracker is useful when it agrees with the source records. It is not an oracle, and if it looks more confident than the email that fed it, check the email.” She also notes that “not a carrier pickup” and “not no transport request” are not interchangeable. In this file Nadia asked questions, explicitly withheld approval, and chose collection. The signed form remained unchanged through handover.

There are two other customer records in the same folder, neither applicable to this ticket. A Bluefin customer named Tomasz Lindqvist elected carrier service for a different order on a signed change form. Another customer, Beatriz Rahman, reported a bent carton after delivery by a carrier. Their notes share the phrases “dispatch,” “damage,” and “not disagree,” which caused the search tool to suggest them beside Nadia’s order. They cannot establish a fact about BL-206.

APPENDIX — DATE AND SERVICE CALCULATIONS

For BL-206, the stated dispatch date is 14 May. Under the terms, the first business day after that date is the grace day. The calendar shows ordinary working days on 15 May and thereafter, with no listed closure on 15, 16, 17, or 20 May. A dispatch later than the grace day by more than one business day could potentially earn a credit, but only for an active Bench-to-Door order. A seven-calendar-day request period runs from actual dispatch, not from a label event. Since Bluefin’s own employee handed goods directly to Nadia’s van on 21 May, the signed handover is the factual collection record; no carrier dispatch took place.

If the optional service had been active, the amount would be based on each additional business day after the one-day grace period, at $40 per day, with a maximum of $160. A draft calculator gives $200 by counting five days from the original date, but that ignores the grace period and cap. The calculator is not evidence that the service was selected. The task of reviewing a credit must first establish whether the service terms apply at all; calculating an amount under a service nobody selected would be the wrong question.

On the production side, the shop did not approve an order-date extension for compressor trouble. The dated calendar communicated in advance lists only 8 May as a closure, which predates the 14 May due date. The maintenance record does show the compressor failed, and the handwritten board inaccurately calls 14 May a closure. But the signed report says benches ran, and the terms require a declared closure on the dated calendar. The FAQ’s old compressor sentence is expressly obsolete and contradicted by the active terms. No signed revision moves Nadia’s date.

The order count was 36, not 38. An early pick list had 38 boxes because it counted two empty returnable trays; the signed handover records six cartons containing all 36 mounts. The original quantity is satisfied. The mark on piece 14 was investigated but not established as an out-of-tolerance condition. Nadia’s correction matters: “not saying it is out of tolerance” is reinforced by a measured result within the minimum, rather than being a report of a hidden defect.

Finally, the shop terms do not make an inquiry into an order change, a draft label into carrier custody, a compressor failure into a declared closure, or a tentative question into a warranty claim. Several internal summaries do make those leaps. Their contradictions are documented so that a reviewer can use the signed records and the customer’s complete messages instead of merely matching phrases.
